Students should design their own summer projects because they can explore creative ideas, enjoy the process more, and experience less pressure during their break.

When pupils select their own topics, they often produce innovative work. By investigating scientific experiments or researching biographies, they can present something truly original. For example, a student might test different chemical reactions in the kitchen or tell the story of a notable figure in their community and explain its significance. This freedom allows them to propose new concepts, demonstrate their thought process to classmates, and illustrate how their creations might solve real problems.

Moreover, having the freedom to choose tasks makes the project more enjoyable. Instead of following a uniform assignment, students become motivated to develop something they genuinely care about. They can collaborate with friends, explore personal interests, and avoid the boredom that often comes with mandatory topics. This autonomy encourages a positive attitude toward learning.

Finally, self-directed projects reduce stress. When learners set their own goals and guidelines, they worry less about meeting rigid requirements. They can establish personal milestones and share their methods with peers, making the experience more relaxed and satisfying.

In summary, allowing students to plan their own summer projects encourages creativity, increases enjoyment, and lowers stress.

I believe students should not be required to take a music, a drama, or an art class. Therefore, it should be an elective. Not every student is excellent in the same things. However, taking a required class a student may not desire or need in the future can cause a student to fail. I believe students should not be required to take any of those classes because it's pointless, unfair, and not important.

To begin with, it should be an elective because not every student will need any of those classes to become a succesful person. Other students may want something dissimilar for their future that has nothing to do with singing, art or drama. It's also not helping a student to become smarter or to learn more. It's no where near educational related. It wouldn't be entertaining for students who do not want to take the class.

The second reason I certainly believe it is unfair to make it a requirement because it can cause them to fail and hold them back from graduating. It also shouldnt be a class that should hold you back from moving forward on to college. Students would feel as if it were a pathetic reason for them to repeat a grade over a class that is useless.

In conclusion, I believe that it should not be required classes to take. it's not important for students to take any of those classes. It's not a class that will help or provide a student to get a job. Majority jobs don't require for you to have any of those classes.

I believe students should not be required to take music, drama, or art classes; these subjects ought to be electives. Not every pupil excels in the same areas, and obliging someone to study a subject they neither enjoy nor plan to use can lead to poor results. For these reasons—pointlessness, unfairness, and lack of practical value—students should have the freedom to choose whether to take these courses.

First, making music, drama, or art optional respects each student’s ambitions. A future scientist or mathematician may gain little from acting exercises or painting lessons. Forcing unrelated classes does not improve core academic skills or deepen understanding of essential subjects. If pupils are uninterested, they are unlikely to engage or benefit from the material.

Second, mandatory requirements in these subjects can be unfair. A low grade in art or music might prevent a student from graduating or moving on to college. Many would feel frustrated at having to repeat a year because of a course they consider irrelevant.

In conclusion, music, drama, and art should remain optional. They do not play a significant role in most career paths and therefore should not be compulsory for all students.

Homework assignments can be difficult for many students, and having extra support might seem helpful. An after-school homework club could benefit those who rarely finish their exercises or find the work confusing. However, not everyone can stay after classes to attend such a club.

Firstly, a lot of pupils are already busy once the bell rings. They may have sports practices, music lessons, dance rehearsals or other commitments that make it impossible to stay late at school. Even at home, they barely manage to complete their tasks on time. For these students, an after-school club would only add to their scheduling conflicts. Likewise, teachers often have responsibilities after school—looking after family members, feeding pets or handling personal errands—so they cannot always remain on campus to supervise.

Transportation also poses a problem. Many students rely on parents or guardians to give them a ride, and those adults may be working, unwell or unavailable in the afternoon. Schools probably cannot provide rides for every child who stays behind. What’s more, if children get hungry during an extended club session, the school might not be prepared to offer snacks, leaving them uncomfortable while they try to study.

A more practical solution is to include a dedicated homework period within the regular timetable. Placing this special block as the last lesson of the day would allow students to complete assignments before going home. Those with busy after-school schedules would no longer worry about unfinished work, and teachers could use that time to grade papers or prepare materials. Alternatively, a morning session could serve the same purpose for anyone who did not finish homework the night before.

In my view, scheduling a homework block during school hours—ideally at the end of the day—offers the best balance. Everyone, both students and teachers, would get a short break, assignments would be completed on time, and afternoons would remain free for other activities.

In my cousin’s case, he was given the chance to take one subject online after moving to the United States, but the constant commotion at home kept him from studying in peace. Another problem is the lack of live interaction with a teacher, which makes learning feel tedious and confusing for some students. Without immediate explanations or discussions, they can become bored and give up on the material. A friend of mine often found himself dozing off during virtual lessons, even after downing strong coffee. Eventually, he would turn off his computer and sleep, and his grades suffered each semester.

Finally, distance learning can leave students exhausted because they still have daily chores or part-time jobs to handle before logging on. I walk half a mile home after school, finish my homework, take a shower, and by the time I start my online class, I am simply too worn out to absorb anything new. Fatigue slows down my progress and makes studying feel like a burden.

For these reasons, I am convinced that students do not really benefit from distance learning, as it often leads to distraction, boredom, and tiredness that hurt their academic performance.

I was moved by my uncle’s experience and now aim to provide more affordable treatments so that everyone has the opportunity to lead a healthy, full life.

My family’s financial hardship during my uncle’s illness taught me the importance of both reliable income and compassionate treatment. By earning a good salary as a cardiologist, I can cover my expenses and still offer heart surgeries and check-ups at prices that people from all backgrounds can manage. In doing so, I hope that no family will face the same distress and helplessness we experienced.

Another reason I am drawn to cardiology is the global shortage of heart specialists. Many people carry hidden cardiovascular defects and remain unaware of their condition until it is too late. Because cardiologists are in short supply, hospitals and private clinics often charge excessive fees, placing treatment out of reach for those who need it most. If this situation continues, countless individuals will lose their chance to enjoy life. By becoming a skilled heart surgeon, I will dedicate myself to performing operations and consultations at fair rates, bringing relief and hope to my patients.

In conclusion, my ambition to become a cardiologist is driven by a desire to save lives and to make heart care accessible to everyone. I refuse to let financial barriers prevent people from receiving essential medical attention, as my uncle nearly did. By offering affordable services and practicing with empathy, I aim to change the current model and improve the well-being of communities. I believe that through hard work and compassion, I can help create a world where quality health care is not a privilege, but a right.

I support the idea of creating an afterschool homework club. Many students struggle to complete assignments on their own, and having teachers available to guide them could significantly reduce the number of failing grades. Some pupils also lack access to a computer or other digital tools at home, so meeting at school would ensure everyone has the resources they need. Additionally, working alongside classmates gives students a chance to interact, compare methods, and learn new ways to approach tasks.

Of course, there are potential downsides. A few students might try to copy answers and leave without doing the work themselves. To prevent this, members could be asked to finish their own assignments before discussing solutions with others. Another concern is that some participants may treat the club like a social gathering and chat instead of focusing on homework. Yet, most children join because they genuinely care about their grades and will remain focused. Proper supervision and clear rules can help maintain a productive atmosphere.

In conclusion, the benefits of an afterschool homework club far outweigh its drawbacks. It offers struggling students extra help, ensures equal access to equipment, and encourages peer learning. Although a small number of pupils might misuse the opportunity, setting guidelines—such as requiring independent work before collaboration—can address these issues. Without such a program, students who need additional support would lose a valuable chance to improve their study habits and enter the next grade with stronger academic foundations.

One day, my English teacher divided the class into groups of four and gave each group a piece of paper. Then he wrote some questions on the board and told us we needed to answer them as a group. When we finished, he said we would discuss the answers. As each group shared its answers with the class, we all realized that every group had different opinions, ideas, and points of view. Each group learned something new from the others: "Every day we all learn new things in life."

Second, working in groups helps people improve because they understand better. For example, they can ask their partners questions when they do not understand something. My history teacher gave the class an assignment that we needed to complete by the end of the class. When the teacher gave the instructions, I did not understand her very well, so I asked one of my partners to explain them again. This helped me understand the assignment, share my opinions, and help my group: "We could do more if we all help each other."

Many people believe that it is better to work alone because they can concentrate more. For example, they will not get distracted and will finish the work faster. A friend of mine has always worked alone because she said that when people work in groups they tend to start talking, distract others, and do not do their work. By the end of the hour, they have only completed a couple of questions. However, this argument is meaningless because if they do not understand something well, they will not have a partner who can explain it to them. For example, they might not finish their work because they get stuck on a part. Not having someone to discuss the work with can be hard sometimes.

In conclusion, there are many benefits to working with a group. Some other benefits of working in groups are making new friends, having the opportunity to learn more about your partner, and learning more about yourself. Working with others is a good idea because you do not have as much pressure about finishing the work on time or not knowing what to do. Even though some people say the opposite, I believe that working in groups is better than working alone: "Sometimes you will need a little help from others in order for you to improve."

Some people wonder whether it is more effective to work alone or with others. While some prefer tackling tasks by themselves, I think collaborating in teams offers greater opportunities to learn and to deepen understanding.

To begin with, teamwork exposes individuals to fresh ideas and viewpoints. For instance, during an English lesson, our teacher divided us into groups of four and gave each team a sheet of questions to discuss. When we shared our answers with the class, it became clear that every group had unique interpretations and suggestions. Through this exchange, we all picked up new perspectives we would never have discovered on our own.

In addition, working in a group can make concepts easier to grasp. If someone is unclear about the instructions or a particular point, teammates can step in to explain it in simpler terms. I experienced this during a history class when I struggled to understand an assignment. One of my classmates kindly rephrased the requirements, which helped me see what I needed to do. As a result, I felt confident enough to share my ideas and contribute to our group’s progress.

On the other hand, many argue that solo work allows for better focus and faster completion. A friend of mine always chooses to work alone because she believes that group discussions often lead to chatting and distractions, so less gets done by the deadline. However, this view overlooks a key advantage of teamwork: support. If you encounter a problem while working by yourself, you have no one to ask for clarification or advice. This can leave you stuck and slow down your progress more than any brief conversation ever could.

In conclusion, although working alone has its merits, the benefits of group work—such as learning from others, enhancing comprehension, and receiving immediate help—make it the superior choice for most people. Collaborating not only eases the pressure of finding ideas on your own but also helps you build friendships and understand different ways of thinking. That is why I believe that, more often than not, working in a group is better than working alone.

When you meet someone new—at school, work, or elsewhere—you might immediately think they are unfriendly because of their expression or tone. Often, they notice your reaction and respond in kind, creating a cycle of coldness. To break this pattern, try talking with them more and learn about their background or interests.

Sharing activities you both enjoy, such as going for a walk, grabbing coffee, or attending an event, can help reveal a person’s true nature. Sometimes people seem distant because they lack friends or feel shy, and offering your company may encourage them to open up.

Life experiences can also change someone’s mood or behavior. By asking how they’re doing, you might discover they’re stressed or upset, and your support could lift their spirits. Instead of judging quickly, reach out and show you care. This approach can help people grow and display their better side.

What might be the benefits if older and younger students are paired together? Such partnerships can have a positive impact because young pupils can discover new learning techniques, receive guidance on what to expect in high school, and pick up strategies for handling stress.

One advantage of pairing students of different ages is that the younger ones can learn fresh ways of studying from their senior partners. When a younger student struggles with homework, the older student can explain how they approach similar problems and share useful tips. They might demonstrate shortcuts for solving math problems, organizing notes efficiently, or remembering key facts in history. By watching how older students work, younger pupils gain practical methods that help them overcome challenges in their own assignments.

Another benefit is that older students can offer advice about the transition to high school. They know firsthand how the workload increases, so they can warn their younger peers about the amount of homework and suggest which subjects can be enjoyable. For example, they might recommend joining a school play if they love drama or trying out a sports team if they enjoy physical activities. They can also point out important skills—like time management or note-taking—that will be essential later on. Hearing these insights early on helps younger students feel more confident and prepared before they enter high school.

Finally, older students can teach effective ways to manage stress at school. They can share their own approaches to studying for tests, such as breaking study sessions into small chunks or using flashcards to review terms. They may also explain how they set up a quiet workspace, plan their study schedule, and take short breaks to stay focused. Learning these habits can reduce anxiety and help younger students perform better when exams arrive.

In summary, pairing younger and older students offers a unique opportunity for both groups to grow. Younger students gain new learning strategies, helpful advice about high school life, and stress-management techniques. Overall, this kind of mentoring relationship not only improves academic skills but also builds confidence, making school a more rewarding experience for everyone involved.

Although some people think being inactive offers extra free time to relax and reflect, I strongly agree with Thomas Jefferson’s advice: “Determine never to be idle.” Staying busy helps us achieve more. Whether we join clubs, devote extra hours to studying, or explore new hobbies, keeping active allows us to use our time wisely and develop valuable skills.

When I first moved to the United States on January 8, 2017, I spent two months doing nothing. I stayed at home all day, watched TV, and felt restless without school or any hobby to fill my time. Finally, I decided to make a change and asked my mother if I could join the city’s soccer team. After signing up and starting regular training sessions, I not only used my time productively but also met many new people and made good friends.

Idle moments could also be turned into reading sessions. The more time we dedicate to books, the faster we learn and the stronger our reading skills become. A friend of mine grew up in a family where his parents encouraged him to read instead of hanging out. By spending most of his free hours with books, he became an excellent reader in English class. His confidence inspired other students to pick up books and practise more at home.

People who choose to remain idle often lack determination and fail to plan for their future. They tend to avoid social activities and new experiences out of laziness or fear of failure. However, trying something unfamiliar can bring unexpected benefits, even if we are not perfect at it right away. For instance, three friends and I felt bored one weekend until one suggested visiting the local UFC gym. We signed up for a one-day trial and trained for an hour. I realised the workouts caused me back pain, so I decided not to continue. Despite quitting, I gained valuable experience, while my friends stayed on and improved their fitness.

In conclusion, inactivity does not serve a useful purpose if we waste our potential. By getting involved in activities, spending more time reading, and experimenting with new experiences, we can enrich our lives and develop new talents. We should follow Jefferson’s words and never allow ourselves to remain idle.

Schools should be a comfortable place for learning, and these days students can choose different options, including studying from home. Home schooling brings both benefits and drawbacks. On the plus side, working at home means you are not interrupted by classmates who might not take education seriously. Without these distractions, it is easier to finish assignments on time. If you need to repeat a course, doing it at home can feel less embarrassing than staying an extra year at a traditional school, where classmates might notice your delay.

Another advantage of home schooling is the greater one-on-one attention you receive. In a regular classroom, teachers often have too many students to help everyone equally. Some young people, such as those with health issues or public figures who wish to stay out of the spotlight, cannot attend school in person. While home schoolers may sometimes wish for more face-to-face interaction and social life, many find that small online or community groups help them stay connected.

Home schooling can also allow students to move through lessons more quickly, since they work at their own pace. However, there are services you won’t find at home, such as free school meals or on-site facilities that public schools usually provide. Families must cover costs for food, internet access, textbooks and computers. Even so, many parents believe this investment pays off because their children get a high-quality education in return.

Whether you choose public school, private school or home schooling, each path offers real advantages for a student’s future. In the end, the most important thing is to find the learning environment that helps you succeed and grow.

Human life today is inseparable from technology; it guides us from the moment we wake up until we fall asleep. Over the years, our tools have evolved dramatically, from Alexander Graham Bell’s first telephone to the sleek smartphones we carry in our pockets. Although some worry about the downsides—like young children becoming overly dependent on screens—these issues are counterbalanced by countless benefits that touch almost every part of our daily routines.

The story of modern communication began with Bell’s invention. His original telephone was bulky and fixed in one place, serving mainly as a home appliance. At first, it wasn’t essential, since people were used to living and working without instant voice contact. But as others refined his design—reducing size, adding new features, and improving sound quality—phones became more practical and widespread. By the early 2000s, Apple revolutionized the market with the first iPhone, transforming a simple calling device into a multipurpose computer we could hold in our hands. Since then, the company has released a vast array of products—from tablets and smartwatches to wireless earbuds and portable chargers—that have woven themselves into our everyday existence.

Concerns over technology often focus on its impact on young users. It’s true that toddlers sometimes become upset when a favorite gadget is taken away, and without limits, they can spend too many hours in front of a screen. Yet parents play a critical role in setting boundaries, ensuring that children use devices safely and for a reasonable amount of time. When used appropriately, digital tools can be educational and engaging. For instance, interactive shows and apps introduce toddlers to shapes, colors, numbers, and social skills, giving them a head start before they even step into a classroom. Online platforms like ABCmouse combine learning with fun activities, helping youngsters build language, math, and critical-thinking skills in a playful environment.

Beyond childhood education, technology surrounds us at home and on the move. Inside our houses, we rely on security cameras, programmable thermostats, air conditioners, refrigerators, Wi-Fi routers, televisions, and even smart doorbells to keep us comfortable and secure. Outside, cars equipped with GPS navigation, traffic lights that regulate flow, and mobile internet allow us to travel and communicate efficiently. Students and professionals alike can access libraries’ resources and academic journals from anywhere with an internet connection, eliminating the need to visit a physical location. In hospitals, high-tech machines monitor vital signs, assist in complex surgeries, and welcome new babies into the world. Scientists and engineers continually harness technology to study diseases, develop new treatments, and search for ways to prevent future outbreaks.

Looking ahead, technology’s growth shows no signs of slowing down. Each day, innovators strive to create healthier, safer, and more efficient solutions to the challenges we face—whether finding cures for illnesses or improving disaster response systems. While no invention is entirely free of drawbacks, the overall impact remains overwhelmingly positive. Without modern tools, many medical breakthroughs and safety measures would simply be impossible.

In the grand scheme of human history, technology has been one of our greatest achievements. It has saved countless lives, reduced risks, and opened up opportunities that previous generations could only imagine. As we continue to develop and refine our inventions, we can be sure that technology will keep enhancing our world and helping to protect us from the threats of tomorrow.

One year ago, I believed that studying business was the perfect choice for me, but I quickly discovered how difficult it was. I struggled to understand the material and failed my business class, which left me feeling stressed and unsure about what to do next. It took me a while to admit that business was not the right path, and at first I thought I was stuck because it seemed too late to change. Eventually, I spoke with my counselor, who encouraged me to consider a different major. I followed her advice, chose a new field, and now I feel confident that I made the right decision. Still, I wonder if I might switch again in the future, since I can be quite indecisive. When I shared this with classmates, they told me they had similar experiences. Although some people argue that choosing a career early is beneficial because students can pick high school courses that prepare them for their future profession, I think it is actually a poor idea. Young students may select a career that does not suit them, and they might feel uncertain about what they really want to study.

First of all, deciding on a career too soon can lead students to pick the wrong path. Many young people want to follow in their parents’ footsteps. They assume that a profession which made their parents happy will be perfect for them, so they apply to the same university or choose the same major. Sometimes, parents unknowingly pressure their children into studying a field they do not genuinely enjoy. As a result, students end up in programs that feel like a poor fit, and they become unhappy and stressed. They may even think about quitting school because they believe the subjects are too hard, when in fact they simply picked a career that did not match their interests. If we surveyed students about how satisfied they are with their chosen course of study, I am sure many would say they regret their decision and wish they had waited longer before committing.

Secondly, young students often have trouble deciding which subject to pursue because there are so many options. It is hard to focus on just one field when each area of study offers different opportunities and appeals to different talents. A student might be good at science but find, for example, art more enjoyable, or vice versa. It is natural for someone at eighteen to be uncertain about their long-term goals. Making a final decision too early can close the door on other interests. In my own experience, trying out different courses helped me learn more about my strengths and preferences. Even if a choice turns out to be wrong, I see it as a valuable lesson rather than a failure. Exploring multiple subjects can guide students toward what they actually want to study and, over time, help them feel more certain about their career path.

In conclusion, committing to a specific career at a young age can backfire because students might choose a field that does not suit them and they may not yet know what they really want to study. It is better to allow young people time to explore different subjects, learn from their experiences, and make a more informed decision later on. This flexibility would reduce stress and increase the chances that students find a career they truly enjoy.

Haile Gebrselassie, widely recognized as one of history’s greatest long-distance runners, did not inherit his talent. Born into poverty, he walked miles to school each day and struggled when he first began training. Despite his initial poor times, he devoted himself to continuous practice, often running before dawn and after classes. In interviews about his journey, he recalls countless disappointments and near misses, yet he never abandoned his goal. Today, he stands among Ethiopia’s wealthiest individuals and holds multiple marathon records.

For many, success remains a dream rather than a reality. This raises a familiar question: How do we reach our ambitions? Some argue that the path to achievement is paved with failures that don’t dampen one’s spirit. I strongly support this view.

Consider the pioneers behind inventions and discoveries we now take for granted. The inventor of the light bulb, the founders of modern physics, the creator of the telephone—each faced repeated setbacks. Their stories prove that success rarely arrives without enduring failure first.

Of course, some might point to people who failed repeatedly yet never achieved their objectives. That observation holds truth, but the crucial factor is not failure alone; it is persistence in the face of defeat. When pursuing a goal, losing enthusiasm turns setbacks into dead ends. Instead, we should use each mistake as motivation to refine our approach and keep moving forward.

A clear illustration of this principle comes from early space exploration. When engineers first tried to launch rockets, they experienced many explosions on the test pad. Designers adjusted mechanical systems, scientists reviewed chemical mixtures, and teams analyzed their calculations. Only after numerous revisions did they achieve a successful liftoff—demonstrating that perseverance eventually yields progress.

Failure may feel discouraging, but it often serves as a stepping stone to success. The key lesson is to maintain determination and excitement for our aims. As the saying goes, “If at first you don’t succeed, try and try again.” By refusing to give up on our dreams and staying undeterred by setbacks, we increase our chances of turning aspirations into reality. Every hurdle teaches us new lessons that strengthen our skills. Embracing challenges is essential for personal growth.

At first, Alex started mocking the way the man walked and even imitated his speech. The man heard him and calmly asked if Alex would like to race him on bicycles. Alex accepted the challenge, confident of winning. To his surprise, the man with short legs pedaled faster and crossed the finish line first. From that moment on, Alex never made fun of anyone again. This incident shows how a simple difficulty can open our eyes and change our behavior.

A problem can also transform your life completely. Alex once shared how he had stolen, lied, refused to obey anyone, and avoided honest work. On a family trip, their car collided with a truck, and Alex was the only person who survived. In the weeks that followed, he lost all hope and even considered ending his life. Six months passed and he could not find a purpose. One day, he walked to the beach determined to drown his sorrows. As he approached the water, an older man sitting on the sand greeted him and asked his name. When Alex told his story, the stranger said, “You are still here for a reason. The breath you take is a gift that many people long for.” Those words struck Alex deeply. He realized his survival meant he still had work to do. He stopped dwelling on the accident and began to rebuild his life. This turning point proves that a tough experience can lead to a complete personal turnaround.

Moreover, a problem can teach you valuable lessons. Consider Peter, a generous father of eleven children who always shared what he had with neighbors in need. One day, a messenger arrived with terrible news: Peter’s house had caught fire, and his children were trapped inside. His home, all his possessions, and his beloved children were gone. Some friends said this must be punishment from God, but Peter denied any wrongdoing. His wife urged him to curse God and die, but he refused. Later, in a moment of anger, Peter shouted at God and suddenly remembered a vow he had long forgotten—to bring food to a poor family. Because he never fulfilled that promise, the family had suffered and passed away. Overwhelmed with guilt, Peter asked God’s forgiveness, and miraculously, everything he lost was restored. Through this tragedy, he learned never to break the promises he makes.

In conclusion, problems can push us to our limits and provide lessons we would not learn otherwise. If you ever face hardship like Alex or Peter, remember that your life has value and you should keep the commitments you give to others.

Education shouldn’t be all seriousness and pressure; it should also spark curiosity and passion. Have you ever dreamed of visiting the Bahamas? I would love to explore this island paradise because it offers some of the most stunning landscapes on Earth. Crystal-clear waters teeming with brightly colored fish, lush mountain trails, warm breezes and flavorful local dishes all combine to create an unforgettable experience. Few destinations can rival the Bahamas when it comes to natural beauty and diverse attractions.

One of the main reasons I want to go is the wide range of activities available. Adventurous visitors can climb rugged peaks or go for long hikes to admire the panorama from above. Food lovers can join cooking contests or sample fresh seafood at vibrant markets. If you enjoy music and movement, there are lively dance events, and of course, swimming in those turquoise waters is a must. Many places simply don’t offer this mix of outdoor thrills, tasty cuisine and perfect weather.

It’s true that a trip to the Bahamas can be costly, but I believe it’s worth every penny for the fun and relaxation you’ll find there. While some people prefer spending their budget on European cities like Paris, Berlin or Rome, I’m more interested in experiencing the Bahamas’ unique way of life. I’m eager to learn about local traditions and try authentic dishes. After immersing myself in the culture, I’d love to hike up a mountain just to take in the view of all the colorful plants and islands stretching out before me. I’m certain that such an adventure would melt away my stress and broaden my understanding of another society.

Visiting a new place can also be a chance to pick up fresh skills. In the Bahamas, I’d focus on improving my biking. The wide, traffic-free roads make it safe to pedal across towns and along the coast without worrying about busy cars. If I practiced often, I might even join a cycling team back home.

Have you wondered what it’s like to live in the Bahamas? Although living there is expensive—and beachfront properties can be risky because of storms—I’d choose a spot slightly inland for safety. Even away from the shore, you’re never far from green hills and tropical wildlife.

In summary, the Bahamas is a colorful, activity-filled paradise where I could relax, learn about a new culture and hone my biking skills. That is why I can’t wait to visit.

John Lubbock, the British naturalist and politician, once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” I fully support this idea because individuals need to learn to make their own decisions rather than depend on others to decide for them.

We encounter influences from family, friends, and society from a very young age, but despite this, we must form our own character by making decisions independently. Each person is unique, and blindly copying the actions of those around us does not help us develop our own identity. When we choose for ourselves, we become more resilient, gain confidence, and learn to trust our own judgment. This self-reliance helps us tackle challenges on our own and builds a stronger sense of who we are.

Although guidance from others can help us distinguish right from wrong, relying too heavily on external role models can be risky. Not everyone we look up to sets a good example, and if we follow questionable behaviour without thinking, we may end up repeating mistakes. For instance, the adults who raise us—whether they are parents, guardians, or mentors—might not always make ethical choices. In these situations, it falls on each of us to use common sense to decide what is morally correct. If you notice someone close to you behaving poorly, you should resist copying those actions and instead make decisions based on your own values.

Some people argue that when we feel lost or unsure, leaning on others’ advice is helpful. However, another strong reason for creating our own character is that personal efforts, including failures, teach us valuable lessons. Simply following others is like being spoon-fed information, which does not allow us to learn or grow. When we attempt tasks on our own, even if we do not succeed at first, we gain practical skills and confidence. Letting other people make all our choices robs us of the chance to develop independence. Over time, this habit can weaken our ability to handle new situations by ourselves.

Overall, while influences can offer direction, true strength comes from making our own choices. By relying on ourselves, we avoid harmful examples, learn from our own successes and mistakes, and build mental resilience. These benefits show why it is so important to shape our own character through personal decisions rather than mindlessly following the crowd. Ultimately, each person has the power to become the individual they wish to be, and recognising that power is the first step toward real self-improvement.

When students tackle projects on their own, they avoid conflicts over decisions and don’t have to coordinate with unfamiliar classmates. However, most learners choose to work in groups because it lets them split tasks, exchange ideas, and support each other. Teamwork often leads to better results and greater efficiency. For these reasons, I, too, believe that group work is more beneficial than working alone.

First, the amount of assignments students face each grading period can be overwhelming. On top of daily homework, there is usually a major project in each class worth around ten percent of the final grade. Handling all that workload by yourself can be very stressful. In a group, however, responsibilities can be shared. Each member can focus on the part they do best—whether it’s researching, writing, or creating visuals—and this division of labor makes the project easier to manage and improves its overall quality.

Second, collaborating in teams helps students develop important cooperation skills that employers look for. Many companies assign tasks to small teams because they understand that combining different strengths and perspectives leads to more creative and efficient solutions. Drivers of productivity often repeat the phrase “work as a team,” and it truly reflects the value of shared effort. By practicing collaboration in class, students gain real-world experience that will prepare them for future careers requiring teamwork.

Furthermore, group work can boost students’ confidence and keep them motivated. When teammates meet to discuss ideas, they can ask questions, explore different approaches, and find the best way forward together. Schools often allow students to stay after lessons, giving groups a convenient place to work. This arrangement is especially helpful for those who struggle to meet deadlines; peers can remind and encourage each other to stay on schedule. As a result, students produce better work and enjoy the learning process more.

In conclusion, students should always be given the choice to work in groups, especially when facing large projects with tight deadlines. Since companies recognize that teams outperform individuals, teachers should apply the same principle in their classrooms. Group assignments help students improve their grades, turn in work on time, and acquire cooperation skills. By combining their efforts and perspectives, students can achieve the best results and make their learning experience more rewarding.

In modern education, should schools form collaborations with businesses? Many argue for and against this idea. Since the goal of schooling is to prepare students for professional life, it seems logical that schools should link up with companies.

Critics ignore the fact that while some students might not need such connections, others greatly benefit. Without ties to industry, students could struggle to discover suitable career paths.

When schools team up with firms, learners gain access to internships and real workplace experience. This support makes job hunting less daunting and helps them identify roles that match their interests. By engaging in work they enjoy, students are more motivated and efficient in their tasks.

Such partnerships also pave the way for graduates to step directly into roles they are passionate about. Ultimately, by collaborating with businesses, schools ensure students find jobs suited to their talents and ambitions.

When was the last time you lifted your gaze away from your phone and admired the sky? Most of us reach for our devices the moment we wake. Technology has woven itself into every aspect of our lives, guiding our actions even as it continues to advance. Yet, have we paused to consider if we are growing alongside it? We pour our hopes and dreams into the digital world, constantly measuring ourselves by what others share online. It is no wonder that many end up feeling depressed, focusing on what they lack instead of appreciating what they already have. Although we all see the same feeds, we interpret them in vastly different ways.

One of the biggest issues is the hours we lose glued to tiny screens. Like followers in a herd, we chase the latest trends, bestselling products, and viral stories, caring more about our virtual image than real experiences. We upload glossy snapshots of our lives, hungry for likes and online fame, while genuine human interactions fade. We might send harsh words through messages or video calls, yet avoid honest, face-to-face conversation. Many feel pressured to own the newest, largest, or most costly items, believing higher price tags equal higher status. This constant distraction even affects our posture and health; slumps and rounded shoulders have become common, leading to chronic back pain. If our bodies remain bent over screens, how can we stand tall in the real world?

Still, technology is not all bad. It can help us finish schoolwork, meet new people, or even discover a new place to call home. The problem lies not in the tools themselves, but in how we choose to use them. If we learn to balance screen time with real-life moments, we can enjoy the benefits of technology without letting it control us.

Winston Churchill’s message about persistence resonates deeply in our daily lives. Many people experience setbacks but push themselves to pursue their objectives. Yet some conclude that a single failure means it is wise to stop trying. It is worthwhile to compare these views and understand why Churchill’s advice to keep going is so valuable.

Firstly, persistence teaches us important lessons. When an attempt fails, it does not spell disaster but offers an opportunity to learn. If something does not work out as expected, looking back on what went wrong helps avoid the same mistake later. Accepting failure as part of the journey encourages us to improve and strengthens our skills. In this way, striving toward our ambitions becomes more achievable each time we try again. By holding on to our beliefs and ideals, we often find the right path ultimately.

Secondly, determination drives us toward our highest aspirations. Obtaining anything worthwhile requires effort and resilience. Those who encounter challenges and then stop see only the wasted time. In reality, success often follows perseverance rather than immediate victory. Everyone faces difficulties at some stage, and it can be disheartening when our efforts do not succeed. Still, continuing despite obstacles brings a sense of accomplishment and boosts self-esteem. The pride of knowing we did not surrender can be more satisfying than quick but shallow achievements.

On the other hand, quitting guarantees failure. Individuals who expect to reach goals like landing a good job, gaining admission to a top school, or realizing their dreams without setbacks are likely to give up at the first sign of trouble. In contrast, those who achieve outstanding results accept that hard work and occasional mistakes go hand in hand. Even if situations become challenging, they press on because they understand the value of dedication. When struggling, many say they are not talented enough, yet they often underestimate their own strengths. Turning to friends and family during tough times provides another advantage: a supportive network can offer advice, encouragement, and assistance. We do not have to face problems alone, and seeking help is part of lasting perseverance.

In conclusion, whatever your aim may be, it is vital not to abandon it halfway. By setting clear targets and devoting effort, you move steadily toward success. If obstacles arise, rely on trusted people to give guidance and support. Above all, maintaining persistence not only helps you reach your objectives but also builds confidence that can carry you through every challenge in life.

When students work in teams, they can share ideas, improve their classroom experience, and learn from their classmates.

First, teamwork encourages idea exchange. For a large assignment or a simple piece of homework, group members can propose different viewpoints. By discussing various opinions, they can combine their suggestions into a stronger plan. Moreover, students can research together, pooling resources and finding reliable information to support their arguments. Cooperation also means they can review each other’s contributions, refining every part of the project. In this way, joint work often leads to higher quality results than individual effort.

Second, working in groups can boost performance during lessons. Team members have opportunities to talk through problems they do not understand and ask the teacher’s help as a unit. This approach not only gives each student clarity but also saves the teacher time because one explanation can benefit all. Additionally, observing peers’ mistakes helps individuals avoid the same errors. When students see what went wrong in another person’s answer, they are likely to correct their own understanding. Therefore, group work helps learners become more confident and accurate in class.

Third, students can learn valuable skills from each other. If one person struggles with a topic, others can explain it in a way that makes sense. These peer explanations often feel less intimidating than the formal style of a textbook. Likewise, students may have varied strengths—one may excel at research, another at presenting information, and another at organising ideas. By cooperating, they can support weaker areas and develop a well-rounded project. Learning to ask for help and offer assistance also builds communication skills that are vital beyond the classroom.

In conclusion, though studying alone has its benefits, working in groups brings greater value. Through sharing ideas, enhancing lesson engagement, and learning from peers, students gain deeper understanding and better results. For these reasons, group work should be encouraged in any learning environment.

Careers play a significant role in our lives. With so many options available, people can choose a profession that matches their interests and personality. I believe that students who explore a career path early on gain valuable benefits: they learn what the job really involves, discover activities they enjoy, and face less stress when they become adults.

First, by investigating a profession while still young, students gain a clear idea of what the work entails. For example, many pupils imagine the life of a doctor without knowing the day-to-day routines or medical challenges involved. By shadowing a physician, volunteering in a clinic, or attending a health-care workshop, they see first-hand how doctors diagnose patients and deal with emergencies. Even simple online research or conversations with professionals can offer facts about the education, skills, and responsibilities required. Early exposure helps students make informed decisions rather than relying on guesswork.

Second, starting career exploration in youth can help students find enjoyable pursuits. Many teenagers spend free time scrolling through social media or watching TV and end up feeling bored. If they join after-school programs related to different professions—such as coding clubs, art workshops, or science camps—they might uncover a passion they never expected. Trying out various fields allows young people to develop hobbies that bring satisfaction and purpose. This kind of engagement not only fills their free hours but also boosts confidence as they master new abilities.

Finally, students who commit to a career path early often face less anxiety later in life. Teenagers who are unsure about their future may struggle when applying for jobs or choosing a university major. However, those who have researched and experienced aspects of their chosen field feel more confident about their goals. They graduate high school knowing the steps they need to take, which reduces the pressure of last-minute decisions and helps them enter the workforce smoothly.

Some argue that young students lack enough knowledge to pick a career, but without any early effort, they risk wasting time and facing confusion as adults. By attending career fairs, interviewing professionals, or joining relevant programs, students can become well informed. In summary, exploring career options at a young age equips students with practical insights, helps them discover enjoyable interests, and makes their adult transition far less stressful.

In the same way, younger students can share fresh perspectives and motivate their older peers, creating a two-way exchange of support.

In conclusion, a program that pairs older and younger students would be highly beneficial. It would allow them to help each other with schoolwork, learn essential teamwork skills, and offer timely advice. By bringing students of various ages together, schools can foster an environment of cooperation and mutual respect that enhances learning for everyone.

Influence takes many forms: spoken messages, visible deeds, and inner drive. Each of these can sway others in different ways. Some believe that setting an example is the sole method to shape people’s thoughts and behaviors. However, by examining how words, actions, and motivation can each guide individuals, it becomes clear that leading by example is only one piece of a larger puzzle.

First, words alone can carry significant weight. People often value advice or insights shared by those they respect. Take Aaron Marino, known online as Alpha M, for instance. His engaging style and clear explanations help men of all ages improve their style and confidence. Without his strong verbal presence, his audience might ignore his tips altogether. When someone chooses the right words and shares them confidently, they can encourage listeners to think differently and act on new ideas.

Second, actions provide a powerful, nonverbal form of influence. Observing someone’s behavior can show others what to do, when, and how. Consider Lionel Messi, who began playing soccer as a child and grew into one of the sport’s greatest talents. His dedication and skill have inspired countless young athletes not only to improve on the field but also to pursue excellence in other areas of life. If Messi had never demonstrated his abilities so visibly, his impact would be far smaller. Through their deeds, leaders can model values and habits without saying a word.

Third, personal motivation can resonate deeply and encourage others to follow suit. Motivation reflects one’s determination and sense of responsibility, qualities that many admire. A police officer—let’s call him Generic_Name—has shown exceptional commitment in his work and earned several commendations as a result. His passion for serving the community has motivated others to respect the law and become more engaged citizens. Without his strong inner drive, fewer people might feel compelled to support public safety efforts.

Some maintain that demonstrating influence relies entirely on showing a direct example. Yet, relying only on one approach can limit the reach of one’s message. For instance, a teacher at Generic_school advises students not to use their phones in class and even puts away his own device. Despite this example, many pupils continue to glance at their screens. If he combined clear explanations, consistent behavior, and genuine encouragement, he would likely see better results.

In the end, influence stems from a combination of words, actions, and personal motivation. While setting an example plays a role, it is only one of three essential ways to guide and inspire others.

If you are familiar with Ralph Waldo Emerson, you might recall his remark, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” This idea champions the importance of individuality. Although some might doubt it, you deserve the ability to choose your own path and think independently.

Belonging to a group can shape your character and guide your moral choices. Sharing values and interests with others creates a strong feeling of unity and identity. This connection often inspires pride in your community, whether it is your hometown, country, or any circle of like-minded people. Such solidarity can boost your confidence and sense of purpose.

However, it is just as vital to maintain the freedom to question your group’s opinions when they seem flawed or illogical. When a set of beliefs becomes absolute and unquestionable, it turns into dogma, which can prevent you from discovering the truth. You should also be willing to doubt the advice of friends and family at times, since even well-meaning people can suggest mistakes. Nevertheless, you can still value their support and trust them on other matters.

In conclusion, true personal growth comes from combining the positive aspects of community life with your own independent judgment. By thinking for yourself and blending your unique traits with shared values, you can genuinely express who you are. In doing so, you achieve the greatest accomplishment of being yourself.

We achieve more when we take action, because every effort brings some kind of return. Whenever we set a goal and work toward it, we grow and learn. This growth often comes in the form of rewards—whether they are grades, praise, or simply the confidence that comes from knowing we can meet our own expectations. On the other hand, if we do nothing, we forfeit any chance of improvement or gain.

I learned this lesson in sixth grade when I really wanted to join my school’s annual math contest. Only the quickest and most accurate students could take part, and after-school review sessions were offered for practice. Unfortunately, I had swimming training at the same time and couldn’t miss it. I felt disappointed, but then I decided to change my routine. I began waking up two hours earlier to solve math problems, and I spent my lunch breaks in the library working through sample tests. That extra effort paid off: when the list of contestants was posted, I saw my name there. My mother always reminds me that failure is only permanent if we let it be. By trying again with a new strategy, I avoided my earlier mistakes and eventually succeeded.

Putting effort into something not only brings personal rewards but can also touch other people’s lives. Once, I saw a hungry child searching for scraps of food. I felt moved to help, so I offered him a sandwich I had with me. The joy on his face gave me a deep sense of satisfaction—no reward could compare to seeing him smile. In another instance, my mother and I cleaned the home of a lonely eighty-year-old woman who only had her dog for company. After that, I asked if I could visit her on weekends. She welcomed me warmly, calling me her granddaughter. It might come as a surprise, but learning from home can actually help students feel less stressed. Much of the pressure at school comes from having too many assignments due the next day. When studying at home, learners often set their own deadlines, which means they aren’t scrambling to finish piles of homework overnight. This freedom to manage tasks encourages students to stay motivated and take responsibility for their progress. As a result, many home-educated pupils find they have more time to review material, establish personal study routines, and ultimately earn higher grades.

One key benefit of distance learning is its flexibility. Students can choose when to start their lessons, allowing them to wake up after a full night’s sleep and work at times that suit their natural rhythms. Rather than parents having to adjust their schedules around fixed school hours, lessons can be planned to fit the whole family’s routine. Moreover, some children struggle to keep up with a teacher’s pace in a busy classroom. Studying at home lets them progress through subjects at a speed that feels right for them, without worrying about tardiness rules or dress codes. With fewer rigid regulations, learners can concentrate fully on the content they need to master.

Another advantage is the reduction of distractions. In a classroom, students may lose focus because peers are chatting or moving around. At home, learners usually find a quieter environment where they can concentrate on tests or note-taking without interruptions. They can take breaks, have snacks, or use the bathroom whenever they need, which keeps stress levels low. Feeling comfortable in their own space allows students to stay calm and work more efficiently, leading to better academic results.

Despite these positives, it’s true that attending public or private schools offers more social opportunities. Group work teaches students many things from teammates, provides inspiration, and can be fun; as students see others working hard, they do the same. But when these students work alone, they often act in the opposite way. Therefore, they may believe they can do as they please and not take their courses seriously.

In conclusion, attending classes online is not a favorable way for students to learn, because they will not learn in the same way as they do at school. They will miss out on developing communication and social skills, and they will not take their courses as seriously as required.

Attending classes from home via videoconference is not an ideal way to learn because it cannot match the benefits of being in a real classroom. If this method becomes widespread, students may miss out on key academic support and strong relationships with peers and teachers. They might also treat their courses less seriously without the guidance of instructors, counselors, and school administrators.

First, studying from home often leads to lower academic engagement than learning at school. In a classroom, students usually take homework, quizzes, and exams more seriously. If they have a question, they can immediately raise their hand and receive a clear explanation, complete with examples, which helps them understand the topic fully. At school, learners can also stay after class for extra help, retake a test if needed, or visit a learning center where classmates might tutor each other. These options are unlikely when attending lessons online. Consequently, home-based students may struggle to resolve doubts, causing their grades to drop over time.

Second, regular face-to-face classes help students develop important social and communication skills. Interacting with classmates in person encourages discussion, sharing ideas, and building friendships. At school, students not only learn academic content but also get inspired by friends who work hard and set high goals. They see their peers, counselors, and teachers as a supportive community—a second family—where they can seek both academic guidance and personal advice. In contrast, online learners often feel isolated and bored, with no one nearby to share concerns or brainstorm solutions. This isolation can be especially harmful today, given the rising rates of stress, anxiety, and depression among teenagers. Being physically present at school provides a healthy distraction from personal worries and gives students direct access to adults and friends ready to help.

Finally, online classes demand a high level of self-discipline, which some students lack. At home, there is no teacher physically enforcing rules, watching student behavior, or reminding learners to focus and complete their assignments on time. The absence of a structured school environment makes it easy to postpone work or skip tasks. Furthermore, group projects at school allow students to learn from one another, share ideas, and motivate each other by example. That collective effort is a powerful source of inspiration and accountability, something that is hard to replicate when studying alone behind a screen.

In conclusion, while online classes offer convenience, they do not provide the same quality of learning, social interaction, or motivation that in-person schooling does. For most students, attending classes at school remains the more effective and supportive way to study.

Are we more successful when we keep ourselves busy all the time? I believe so—provided the tasks we choose actually help us in the long run. When we stay active in meaningful ways, we’re more likely to move forward in life, build useful skills, and see tangible results. However, simply filling our schedules with random activities won’t make much difference unless those actions truly benefit our future.

Take sports as one example. Regularly taking part in athletic activities not only keeps us fit, but can open doors to exciting opportunities. Excelling on the field or court might lead to scholarships or special programs at colleges, giving us a head start on education without hefty fees. Even if a scholarship doesn’t appear, the discipline and teamwork learned through sports can prove invaluable in many areas of life.

Another way to stay productively busy is by exercising and maintaining a healthy lifestyle. Visiting the gym, going for runs, or doing home workouts all help us remain physically strong and energetic. Keeping our bodies in good shape today reduces the risk of health issues later, meaning we enjoy a higher quality of life as we grow older. Pairing exercise with nutritious meals—rich in vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains—only strengthens those benefits, setting us up for long-term well-being.

Work also represents an activity that yields clear rewards. Having a steady job or side gig ensures a regular income, which can cover daily needs like food, clothing, or transportation. Saving a portion of these earnings creates a financial cushion for emergencies or future plans, such as further education or travel. Beyond the money, being engaged in work gives us purpose, structure, and a chance to develop professional skills that boost our career prospects.

In conclusion, constantly engaging in worthwhile activities is key to achieving more in life. Idle time rarely leads to progress if it isn’t directed toward beneficial goals. By focusing our energy on sports, exercise, healthy habits, and productive work, we equip ourselves with opportunities, good health, and financial stability. In other words, yes—we do accomplish more when we are always doing something that truly matters.

School is crucial in everyone’s life, yet it already occupies most of teachers’ and students’ time. At a typical Maryland public middle school, classes begin at 8:15 am and finish at 3:00 pm. This means pupils spend over seven hours in lessons, receiving information without pause. Extending the school day would reduce time for essential activities both now and in the future. Students would have less opportunity for homework and studying, fewer chances for extracurricular pursuits like sports and clubs, and diminished ability to volunteer in their communities.

Firstly, expanding school hours would cut into students’ study time. After more than seven hours of classes, learners often face six to eight periods, at least half of which involve assignments to complete at home. If the school day stretched longer, pupils might struggle to finish tasks, leading to lower grades or missed deadlines.

Secondly, longer days would limit participation in after-school sports and clubs. Health guidelines recommend at least one hour of daily exercise, but some students do not take P.E., and a standard class lasts only 45 minutes. If an extra ninety minutes were added to the schedule, young athletes would have less time to train with their teams. Similarly, clubs offer experiences unavailable during regular lessons, and extended hours would leave club members with inadequate time for their interests.

Lastly, community service obligations would suffer. Many curricula call for volunteer work—such as helping teachers or organizing classrooms—for a set number of hours. In my experience, completing 75 hours of service required several two-hour sessions after school. Should the school day be longer, students might struggle to meet these requirements and risk failing to fulfill their service commitments.

In conclusion, it is more practical for the school board to maintain the current schedule so that students can balance academic responsibilities with homework, extracurricular activities, and community service.

Young people benefit when they begin to explore possible careers early, because it helps them discover their interests and set realistic goals for the future. By considering professions in middle school, students gain time to reflect on what truly motivates them. During these years, they shift from a playful attitude to one that includes decision-making. Programs that track pupils as they move from middle school into high school can monitor how their ideas evolve. Many students use this window to confirm their talents and preferences, making them more confident about their studies and, ultimately, their career choices.

While some pupils decide on well-suited careers immediately, others refine their options until they feel ready. This process builds maturity and resilience, since students learn to weigh alternatives and accept that their preferences might change over time.

By working together, adults can help adolescents understand different professions, strengths required, and potential challenges. With this teamwork, students gain the insight they need to choose wisely and adapt their plans as they grow.

Some people believe that technology is simply an extension of our bodies—like a mobile phone we carry everywhere—but it can also reduce face-to-face contact and create distractions. Although it brings certain benefits, its drawbacks have a strong impact on our daily lives.

On the positive side, technology is deeply woven into our routines. It supports us at work, where computers and specialized software make tasks easier and more efficient. Mobile phones let us stay in touch with friends and family, checking on their well-being or arranging meetings at any moment. In schools, devices such as laptops and tablets help students access information online for assignments, and teachers rely on them to present lessons more effectively.

Despite these advantages, technology often distracts us. In classrooms, for example, students tempted to check messages on their phones can lose focus, perform worse on tests, and even disturb their classmates. Beyond school, using a phone while driving—whether for texting, changing music, or reading GPS directions—can be life-threatening, since taking your eyes off the road greatly increases the risk of an accident. These habits show how easily technology can pull our attention away from what matters most.

Moreover, overreliance on mobile devices can weaken our social connections. It is common to see people, especially teens, walking with their heads down, absorbed in screens instead of acknowledging those around them. As a result, youngsters may miss out on developing important social skills, like making eye contact or greeting someone properly. Gradually, this lack of real-world interaction erodes our ability to communicate naturally.

In the end, while technology itself is not harmful, the way we use it often leads to distraction and a decline in personal interaction. Since it has become essential to modern life, removing it entirely is unrealistic. Yet if we limited our usage to what is truly necessary, we could enjoy its benefits without sacrificing our attention or losing touch with the world around us.

Should students be allowed to use cell phones in class for learning, or should these devices be banned entirely? I believe that permitting phones in classrooms for educational activities brings more benefits than drawbacks. Though some educators argue that phones distract learners, I am convinced that, when used properly, they can enhance the teaching and learning experience.

First of all, having access to a phone during lessons makes it easier for students to find information and record materials. With a quick internet search or a photo of the whiteboard, learners can review notes and resources at home, reinforcing what they studied in class. Without their phones, many students become restless and cannot focus on the lesson until they retrieve their device after school. I know someone whose father confiscated her phone to force her to study all year. Instead of working harder, she simply ignored his rule, spent more time out with friends, and ended up failing every subject. Clearly, forbidding phones may actually harm academic progress.

Second, cell phones offer a safety net if an emergency arises. Suppose an intruder enters the building or there is a lockdown; a student could immediately dial emergency services for help. Likewise, in case of fire, severe weather, or any other urgent situation, students can quickly update their families on their whereabouts and well-being. Banning phones could delay these crucial calls.

Finally, forbidding phones often backfires because people tend to do what is not allowed. Students might secretly use their devices when the teacher isn’t looking, which can be riskier than supervised use. Allowing phones openly under guidance reduces covert behavior and keeps learning on track.

In short, classrooms should incorporate cell phones as learning tools. Although some say these devices should be off-limits during lessons, I firmly maintain that their educational advantages and quick access to information and help make them far more valuable than any potential distractions.

Two heads are often better than one. Although some people choose to work alone, collaborating with classmates offers clear advantages. By joining forces, we can meet deadlines more easily, create a positive atmosphere in the classroom, and learn to respect everyone’s unique viewpoint.

First of all, teamwork helps tasks finish on time because we collect a wider range of ideas and information. In the United States, for instance, students come from many countries, each bringing distinct perspectives on the same subject. Rather than insisting that one person’s approach is superior, a group can combine the best suggestions to reach an effective solution. Someone working by themselves may struggle in silence instead of asking for guidance. In contrast, classmates in a group support one another, making it less likely that anyone will fall behind.

Working together also builds a friendly and open environment. When we focus on a shared project, we naturally communicate more, which strengthens our relationships. If everyone studies independently, there is little chance to exchange opinions or even get to know new friends. On the other hand, group activities allow students from different regions to share their customs and traditions. This not only creates a more relaxed and enjoyable space, but it also encourages respect and understanding among classmates.

Many learners prefer a setting where they can brainstorm, discuss, and solve problems as a team. Being part of a group makes challenging tasks feel lighter and more motivating than working alone. Therefore, teachers should organise more group assignments and foster an atmosphere where students feel at ease expressing their thoughts. In this way, the classroom becomes a place of cooperation and growth for everyone.

Almost everyone heads to the beach or a pool when they have free time, but I believe that joining a swimming club is the most enjoyable option. Swimming helps me unwind when I’m upset, allows me to have fun with friends, and makes exercising more exciting.

Firstly, swimming has a calming effect whenever I feel angry or sad. Once, after the school year ended and all my classmates had gone home, I slipped into the empty pool and just floated. As I moved through the water, the gentle splashes and the sound of droplets falling back into the pool soothed my mind. At that moment, watching ripples form and listening to the steady rush of water against the pool’s edge made me feel peaceful and refreshed. On another occasion during a two-day beach trip with my class, I felt reluctant to leave on the last day. To lift my spirits, I changed into my swimwear, grabbed my camera, and wandered along the shoreline. The rhythmic crash of waves and the distant calls of seabirds calmed me, and taking photographs of the scenery turned my mood around completely. These experiences show how swimming can ease stress and bring comfort.

Secondly, swimming is more fun when you share it with friends, and it’s a great way to make new ones. At first, I enjoyed swimming alone, but everything changed when my pals joined me. We challenged each other to races, tried out flips and dives, and laughed whenever someone’s head bumped another’s under water. Once, three of us surfaced at the same time and couldn’t stop giggling for minutes. Friends also help each other improve: if someone struggles with floating or the dog paddle, a buddy can offer tips and encouragement. Learning on your own can feel dull, but practising strokes and drills together makes progress feel rewarding and fun.

Finally, swimming offers a thrilling way to exercise. I started taking lessons every Friday after school to shed extra weight. At ten years old, I weighed 145 pounds, and by the end of my lessons, I was down to 111 pounds. At first, I barely noticed any change and felt impatient, but as I had more fun in the water, I became more committed. Soon, I saw improvements in my stamina and my swim technique. The key was enjoying each session rather than focusing only on results.

In short, swimming is an activity that calms my mind, brings joy when shared with friends, and turns workouts into adventures. That is why I find a swimming club to be the most enjoyable hobby.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea because it is often difficult to stay true to ourselves in a society full of judgement. Many people around us decide how we should look, act or think, and they rarely consider our feelings or opinions.

For example, in my own family it can be hard to express my real self. They frequently tell me what I should wear, which friends I can spend time with and how I should behave. If I make a mistake, they criticize me harshly and assume they know what is best for me. In this kind of environment, there is no chance to show who I really am or discover my own interests.

Similarly, strangers and acquaintances judge us by our appearance or choices. If someone sees me talking to a person with tattoos, they might assume he is a bad influence. If I am overweight, they call me unattractive; if I am too thin, they say the same. Even wearing a short skirt can lead others to label me as irresponsible or “crazy.” It seems impossible to satisfy everyone’s expectations.

Despite these pressures, we must find the courage to be ourselves. Constant judgment can cause sadness or make us think negatively about our own worth. We may start believing we are not good enough or that we cannot succeed. That is why self-love is so important: if we do not value ourselves, no one else will. We need to make choices that feel right for us and show our true character.

That is why I share Emerson’s view: learning to be yourself is a major accomplishment. I feel happier and more confident when I follow my own path and ignore the critics. Embracing my unique personality, even if it seems “crazy” to others, brings me freedom and joy.
