Having a homework club at school is an excellent idea, and every school ought to offer it at least three times a week. In this club, teachers are available to guide you through assignments or clarify any topics you find difficult. Attending homework club allows students to deepen their understanding, interact more with classmates, and boost their self-assurance in their schoolwork. There are many activities you can do there, such as completing a group project, reviewing material for a quiz or test, or simply getting your regular homework done ahead of time.

One of the main advantages of homework club is the chance to collaborate on projects under a teacher’s supervision. Working with peers not only strengthens friendships but also creates a small community where everyone pitches in. If you ever feel stuck on a question or unsure how to proceed, you can turn to teachers or fellow students for help. Projects that seem overwhelming when tackled alone become much more manageable when you share ideas and solutions. So, if you want reliable assistance with your assignments, attending the homework club is a smart move.

Another benefit is dedicated time for preparing for tests or quizzes. In homework club, teachers can help you make flashcards, go over study guides, or even organize quiz games like Kahoot. For those who struggle to focus at home, this environment keeps you on task and makes studying more engaging. Playing educational games not only reinforces the material but also adds a fun element to revision. By coming to homework club regularly, you’ll be well prepared for exams and less likely to feel overwhelmed when test day arrives.

Finally, homework club is the perfect place to finish your daily assignments early. With subject experts in math, science, history, and English on hand, you receive clear explanations and extra details that might not fit into the regular class period. Understanding your homework fully at school means you won’t need to worry about it at home, freeing up your evenings for other activities or rest. This early completion also gives you time to ask questions and explore topics more deeply than usual.

Overall, homework club is one of the most valuable after-school activities available. It helps students learn more thoroughly, increases their confidence, and encourages positive interaction among classmates. By offering support with projects, test preparation, and routine homework, the club benefits everyone involved. To make this initiative a success, we need enthusiastic students and dedicated teachers willing to volunteer. Together, they can build a supportive learning community that inspires academic achievement.

Allowing visitors to explore your premises reveals the nature of your business more effectively than any brochure or presentation.

For students and recent graduates, getting a glimpse of life inside your company could be especially valuable when choosing a field of study. Instead of spending months researching every college program, they could focus on the skills and subjects that are in demand at your organization. This insight would make it easier to decide which courses to take and which universities to consider.

Inviting people to see what you do and how you do it not only informs potential applicants but also strengthens your company’s reputation. Offering transparency about your work can foster interest, attract talent, and keep your brand visible in the wider community. I look forward to the chance to learn from your team and appreciate your consideration.

By the time students begin high school, many feel pressure to choose a career path and even start working part‐time to gain experience and money. However, deciding on a specific profession at such an early stage can be harmful. It can divert attention from academic responsibilities, interrupt the learning process, and leave little time for hobbies that boost well‐being.

First, taking on career commitments in high school often interferes with schoolwork. As students advance through grades, their courses become more demanding and require greater focus. Regular homework assignments, projects, and exams can consume most of their free time. If a teenager starts a job related to their intended career, they may struggle to balance work shifts with study hours. For instance, imagine a student who takes an after‐school position at a hair salon. Between completing assignments and preparing for tests, they find themselves too tired or pressed for time to review lessons. As a result, their grades drop and their confidence suffers. This kind of stress could easily be avoided if they concentrated on school first and deferred specialized work until later.

Second, high school is still a period of learning and personal growth. At this age, students are exploring various subjects and interests to discover what truly appeals to them. Committing early to one career risks narrowing their options before they have a chance to learn about other fields. A teenager might believe they want to become a graphic designer, yet later develop a passion for engineering or medicine. By focusing solely on one job, they miss out on broadening their horizons and may end up stuck in a role that no longer fits their goals. Instead, they should spend these years strengthening fundamental skills and exploring different disciplines, so they can make a better‐informed choice about their future profession.

Third, having a part‐time job tied to a future career can prevent students from enjoying activities that refresh them. Engaging in sports, arts, or social clubs offers an important outlet for stress relief and creativity. If a student takes on a career‐related position, they might give up the football games or music practice sessions that they love. In turn, they lose a healthy balance that supports both their mental health and academic performance. For example, a young athlete who joins a weekend internship might have to miss key practices, leading to frustration and increased tension. Free time for leisure activities is essential for students to stay motivated and emotionally well.

In conclusion, high schoolers should concentrate on their studies, personal development, and hobbies rather than committing to a specific career path too soon. By focusing first on education and exploration, they will be better prepared to choose a profession that truly fits their talents and interests, leading to greater success and satisfaction in the long run.

“To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I wholeheartedly agree with this idea because embracing your true identity leads to independence, fuels your success by boosting confidence, and empowers you to assist others.

First of all, staying true to yourself encourages self-reliance. When you learn to make decisions and act on your own, you don’t have to depend on someone else to reach your goals. Friends and acquaintances may come and go, but your ability to stand on your own two feet remains constant. By achieving things through your own efforts, you prove to yourself—and to others—that you can overcome challenges without needing constant support.

Furthermore, being authentic builds your self-esteem. Once you acknowledge and accept who you are, it’s easier to believe in your abilities. Just as it can be effortless to put on weight, it can also be simple to grow your confidence by repeatedly affirming, “I can do this.” With determination and a positive mindset, you might find yourself tackling tasks you never imagined possible—whether that means taking risks, improving your performance at work or school, or simply showing up on time and ready to learn.

Having that belief in yourself also equips you with the strength to support people around you. When someone is feeling low or overwhelmed, your own journey of self-discovery can inspire them to keep going. Offering encouragement and sharing how you faced difficulties reminds them that tough times don’t last forever. Even when life feels harsh—like what I experienced over the past six months—you can choose not to surrender. Remaining steadfast and confident helps you weather storms and offers hope to those who need it.

In the end, Emerson’s words ring true: resisting pressure to conform is a remarkable feat. Although society may push us toward certain roles or behaviors, maintaining a positive outlook and trusting in ourselves paves the way to achievement. By cultivating independence, nurturing confidence, and extending support to others, we not only enrich our own lives but also help others find their strength. Never give up; keep believing in who you are, and success will follow.

Some people believe that first impressions cannot be altered once they form. From our everyday interactions, others judge us by what we do, say and how we look. Since these aspects reveal our character straight away, many hold that once an initial opinion is set, it is very hard to overturn. Therefore, you must be aware of your behaviour, language and appearance from the very beginning.

Actions often speak louder than words, and they play a crucial role in how someone views you at first. When meeting a new person, if you are unfriendly or inconsiderate, they may assume you are not someone worth spending time with. On the other hand, showing kindness and respect leaves a positive mark. Because these early behaviours stick in people’s minds, it is essential to choose your actions carefully.

In addition to deeds, the words you choose can strengthen or weaken a first impression. Using polite, clear language shows you know how to communicate and respect the other person. Swearing or using disrespectful expressions can make others form a negative opinion immediately. Although occasional stumbles are forgiven by many, speaking confidently and without excessive pauses will help ensure your conversation reflects you in a good light.

Perhaps the most visible part of any first impression is your appearance. People often notice how you dress, groom yourself, and carry your posture before they hear a single word. A neat appearance suggests that you take care of yourself and value the meeting, while a careless look may give the opposite impression. Since we cannot change the first image others see, making sure you present yourself well is vital.

However, it is possible in some cases to alter someone’s initial view if circumstances allow. For example, on a bad day you might appear tense or withdrawn, but once someone understands you are usually more open or friendly, they might adjust their opinion. Even so, getting that second chance can be challenging, and not everyone will be ready to reconsider their first thought.

In conclusion, first impressions are powerful and difficult to revise because they are based on our actions, our choice of words and how we look. While a rare second opportunity may exist, it is far better to make a strong positive impression from the start. This way, you ensure that people remember you correctly and fairly.

I believe Emerson’s idea that each person should trust their own uniqueness. For me, being myself in a world that constantly influences who we become is essential. I feel that the environment around me pushes me to change my views, yet I can use my own perspective to choose my path. Exploring beautiful natural sites helps me stay true to myself: walking through forests, standing by a flowering grove, or climbing gentle hills always feels freeing.

I especially enjoy watching trees burst into blossom in spring. Those delicate petals falling to the ground are a vivid reminder that growth and renewal go hand in hand.

Venturing deeper into a woodland, I find that its simple appearance hides constant transformation. New shoots sprout from the forest floor, and fruit ripens among the branches. This cycle of life encourages me to embrace change without losing who I am inside. Alongside the fruit, colorful shrubs bloom, offering a comforting sense of belonging in the natural world.

Sometimes I imagine myself standing at the top of a big hill, gazing over a wide green plain. A hill, rather than a snowy mountain peak, gives me just the right balance of height and warmth. From there I can see rolling grasslands dotted with a few scattered trees. This view seems timeless, almost like stepping back into history and finding peace in simpler landscapes.

In my opinion, it is a gift to remain true to oneself amid external pressures. Emerson’s message resonates with me: by appreciating and learning from nature’s wonders, I can resist being molded by society and celebrate my own individuality. That is why I fully agree with his idea about being yourself in the world.

Thomas Jefferson once noted how much can be achieved if we work without pause. I believe, however, that inactivity serves an important purpose: to complete tasks well and keep our bodies and minds healthy. Although some people argue that nonstop effort leads to greater productivity, taking breaks is vital.

Inactivity always serves a purpose: to finish any task, we need moments of rest. For example, weekends exist so workers can recover after a busy week. Without a break, our bodies cannot function properly, and we would struggle to stay awake under constant pressure. Even animals stop to rest after a long day of activity in order to conserve energy and stay in good shape.

Moreover, working without pauses can be dangerous. When we grow tired, we might drift off at just the wrong moment, leading to mistakes or accidents at our jobs. If someone falls asleep while driving, it could harm both them and others on the road. Short, regular breaks help us stay alert and reduce the risk of injury.

On the other hand, some people insist that continuous work speeds up progress and improves results. They say that learning or building something without interruption can help you finish sooner and produce higher quality. For instance, a construction crew that works straight through might complete a house faster. Similarly, a journey without stops takes less time. This view values relentless forward movement to reach one’s goals.

In conclusion, inactivity is essential for rest, safety, and long-term performance, even if some believe nonstop effort is better. Ultimately, it’s up to each person to find the right balance between work and rest.

Attending classes at home offers fewer advantages than going to school in person. Traditional schools provide options that online learning cannot match, giving students a chance to join live lessons, choose from a range of courses, and benefit from extra help. Although everyone learns differently, attending school appears to be more effective for most learners. In physical classrooms, students have the opportunity to make friends, take part in clubs, and receive direct support from teachers.

Being in a regular school setting gives students the chance to build social connections. Many young people dislike feeling isolated and appreciate having someone to trust and confide in. When we attend school in person, we can meet hundreds of peers, start conversations, and form lasting friendships. For example, when Generic_Name was offered the choice between homeschooling or going to a local school, she chose to stay at home because she enjoyed sleeping later and avoiding a commute. At first, she adjusted well, but after a few weeks she felt lonely and missed having friends around. After talking with her mother, who reminded her of all the classmates and activities she would have at a nearby school, Generic_Name decided to attend regular classes instead. Soon, she found herself making friends and feeling more connected.

Another benefit of in-person schooling is access to extracurricular activities. Unlike distance learning, traditional schools usually have a variety of clubs and teams that students can join. These activities help young people develop skills and plan for their future. For instance, if someone enjoys playing football, they can try out for the school team and possibly earn a scholarship later on. Participating in clubs also helps students explore different interests, consider possible careers, and gain practical experience outside of lessons.

Some might say that online education gives students more flexibility, allowing them to work, care for siblings, or avoid bad influences. While distance learning can fit certain needs, it cannot replace the guidance that in-person teachers provide. In a classroom, instructors can stay after class to give extra explanations and answer questions. It is often hard to concentrate online when there is background noise or technical issues, and reading material alone does not always lead to full understanding. Discussing grades and homework face-to-face helps students grasp difficult ideas and improve their work.

In summary, attending regular school offers social benefits, opportunities for extracurricular involvement, and direct academic support. Although some people prefer online classes, they should remember that traditional schools offer experiences that distance learning cannot match. Going to school not only gets students out of the house for a few hours each day, but also gives them unique social moments, such as lunch breaks and after-school activities. These experiences help young people stay engaged, avoid trouble, and learn through a combination of fun and education. For most students, the advantages of in-person classes clearly outweigh those of staying at home to study.

Schools already demand a lot of our time, so I strongly oppose the school board’s plan to lengthen each school day. I’m not just speaking as a student; this decision would impact everyone involved. First, extra hours in class can lead to fatigue and misbehavior because sitting in the same room for too long makes it hard to stay focused. When pupils are exhausted, their grades often suffer since they can’t concentrate well. Added hours also cut into time needed for homework and studying for tests, making it tougher to keep up with assignments.

The effects don’t stop with students. Teachers, too, would face more stress. Many instructors have children or spouses waiting at home, and a later dismissal time would reduce their family time. Moreover, some students, like me, have morning commitments—mine is a monthly orthodontist appointment. With a longer school day, I couldn’t easily schedule appointments in the afternoon, so I’d miss even more classes and fall further behind on missed work.

If school days grew longer, any absence—whether for health reasons or appointments—would mean more catch-up work. Falling behind puts pressure on both students and teachers, and makes the school’s job harder. The cafeteria would need to serve extra meals, and supplies such as paper, bathroom items, and planners would run out faster. The budget would stretch thinner. The school would also have to handle more opportunities for conflict: tired students are more likely to argue, and staff would have to manage additional break passes and supervise longer periods of free time.

Another concern is traffic safety. Extending the day by an hour or more would put high school dismissal alongside elementary schools’ schedules. More buses and cars on the road at once could increase the chance of accidents during pick-up times. We already rise early to be on time; asking us to do more hours won’t make us more alert. In fact, extreme tiredness would mean we learn less, and teachers might struggle to teach effectively when everyone is worn out.

As I’ve shown, lengthening school hours creates problems for students, teachers, and the entire school system. This idea deserves a careful rethink. The school board should invite opinions from other students and staff before moving forward. I am sure I don’t stand alone in believing this proposal would bring more harm than good.

In conclusion, adding hours to the school day would drain students and teachers of energy, lower academic performance, raise costs, and heighten risks both in the classroom and on the road. I urge the board to reconsider this plan and listen to a variety of perspectives. Only by weighing all consequences can they make the right choice for our community.

Technology enables us to carry out many tasks while reducing the need for human interaction and lowering workloads. Yet this raises a question: why employ people at all if machines can perform most duties? Many employees may feel upset by automation because it threatens their jobs and might cut their hours. Additionally, when machines take over simpler roles, fewer positions remain for workers, leading to a tighter job market.

Firstly, less face-to-face collaboration can be discourteous to staff. Imagine trying to improve at a role only to find your competition is an advanced machine that seems to know every possible solution. This makes it almost impossible for employees to grow or prove themselves, since they cannot outmatch the efficiency and knowledge of a computer.

Secondly, reducing social contact through technology can harm our lives, even though machines are designed to help us. Many people do not welcome this assistance because they fear losing both their work and the opportunities to interact with others. While machines can offer convenience, the resulting isolation and job insecurity overshadow these benefits for many.

In conclusion, I believe technology has a mainly negative impact by replacing human roles and disrupting personal connections. Although some may deny it, automation does more than make tasks easier; it also steals jobs and reduces the joy that people find in their work. Therefore, the harmful consequences of technology on employment and social bonds cannot be ignored.

Every day we face choices on our own, although many people turn to others for advice before deciding. While it may seem safer to follow guidance, I believe that making choices independently brings greater benefits. When we decide by ourselves, we build self-confidence, learn to act responsibly, and enjoy a more satisfying life.

When individuals make their own decisions, they gain confidence and a sense of responsibility. Even if a choice is tough, dealing with its results helps a person grow. For example, a young adult who moves out of the family home must manage expenses, cook meals, and keep the place tidy. Handling these tasks alone teaches accountability because there is no one else to blame if something goes wrong. Similarly, students often choose their own subjects for the next school year. By picking classes they find interesting or useful, they learn to trust their own judgment. These experiences show that making choices independently can strengthen self-esteem and a sense of duty.

Choosing for ourselves also tends to increase happiness. When people follow goals based on their own decisions, achieving them brings deep satisfaction. Consider a teenager who decides not to attend university but instead trains to become a professional footballer. If that hard work pays off and he reaches the professional level, his joy will be greater because it fulfills his personal ambition. In my own experience, during my second year of high school I selected extra science classes I thought would help me most. When I saw how much I learned in those subjects, I felt proud of my choice. Making that decision on my own made the outcome even more rewarding.

Some argue that we should seek advice so we won’t make mistakes, preferring guidance from parents or experts. Although well-intentioned suggestions can be helpful, relying on them too much may lead to regret. For instance, if a student follows his parents’ wish to become a doctor even though he lacks genuine interest, he might end up unhappy and struggle in his career. His decision would reflect his parents’ hopes rather than his own. By contrast, when we choose for ourselves, we are more committed to our path and less likely to feel unsatisfied.

In conclusion, individuals should make their own decisions rather than depend entirely on advice. By doing so, they develop self-confidence, embrace responsibility, and find greater happiness. Although advice can sometimes guide us, the ability to decide on our own helps us pursue goals that truly matter and become more independent.

A positive mindset alone does not guarantee success; instead, a willingness to put in consistent effort is the true driving force behind achievement. Simply thinking optimistically will not help you reach your objectives, earn an advanced high school diploma or secure a job after years of studying in a field you dislike just because it promised a better future. To truly succeed, you must push yourself beyond your comfort zone through hard work, careful planning and determined action.

Take, for instance, the goal of owning a new car within a year. Maintaining an upbeat attitude might make you feel hopeful, but it won’t cover the practical details. You still need to find suitable insurance, budget for monthly payments and possibly negotiate financing terms with the dealership. After signing the contract, you may even have to accept a lower take-home pay to cover these extra expenses. Simply believing you’ll be cruising in a brand-new vehicle isn’t enough; you have to earn the money, set aside savings and follow through with each necessary step.

Similarly, graduating from high school with honors depends on years of dedication rather than just a positive outlook. High school is a twelve-year journey filled with exams, assignments and unexpected challenges—like the times you felt too sick to leave school and had no one to pick you up. In those moments, your thoughts revolved around getting through the day, not maintaining an optimistic attitude. It is your commitment to attending classes, completing coursework and overcoming setbacks that ultimately leads to graduation, not merely hoping for the best.

The path through higher education further highlights why hard work matters more than good vibes. Many students pick a major they dislike, believing it will pave the way to a stable career. Throughout college, they juggle part-time jobs, late-night study sessions, essays and group projects, all while worrying about the next semester’s fees. After graduation, they face stiff competition in job interviews and must prove they are the strongest candidate. This entire process demands perseverance, discipline and genuine effort—not simply a hopeful mindset.

In conclusion, real success comes from sustained effort rather than positive thinking alone. Achieving goals such as buying a car, completing high school or earning a university degree all require determination and practical steps. Not everyone has access to formal education, and some may spend their days wishing for a miracle or lottery win instead of taking action. A cheerful outlook might lift your spirits, but only hard work will carry you to your goals.

Self-esteem arises from authentic accomplishments rather than hollow praise. I hold this view because recognizing a student’s true achievements encourages personal growth, whereas applauding substandard work can stunt development. Teachers are meant to guide learners and help them enhance their skills. If students receive praise for a task they know they did not fully apply themselves to, they may conclude that minimal effort is acceptable, and this misunderstanding can harm their confidence in the long term.

First, when a student works hard on a challenging assignment and is confident in the quality of their work, positive feedback validates their efforts and builds self-assurance. Tackling difficult projects demands commitment and perseverance, and when teachers acknowledge these qualities, students feel proud of their abilities. This recognition not only boosts their self-esteem but also motivates them to pursue further challenges. Without such rewards for true effort, learners might not feel inspired to push beyond their comfort zones.

Second, rewarding lazy or careless work can have the opposite effect. If a student is aware that they did not invest their best effort but still receives applause, they may start believing that they do not need to try as hard. Such complacency prevents genuine improvement, keeping students stuck at a low level of performance. Instead of celebrating half-hearted attempts, teachers should offer constructive feedback. For instance, they could say, “You have some good ideas here, but I know you can refine them further,” to encourage higher-quality work.

Some might argue that by overlooking imperfect work, teachers make students feel supported and avoid discouraging them. However, ignoring insufficient effort can send the message that teachers do not care about a student’s learning. In reality, addressing errors and showing expectations demonstrates genuine concern. When a student approaches a teacher for help, the teacher’s focused attention reassures them that their progress matters. This kind of engagement strengthens the student-teacher relationship and promotes continued effort and improvement.

In conclusion, self-esteem rooted in real achievement leads to lasting confidence and a desire to grow. Empty praise for poor work only encourages complacency and stagnation. By matching praise to genuine effort and offering honest, supportive feedback, teachers can help students build true self-worth and academic success.

Who doesn't want to be left in the house all day using an electronic device with online access? Although students save money and time by taking classes from home. It is not beneficial to learn online because students lose focus of what they are learning and tend to easily get distracted when they're in their house, students can't have a one on one conversation with a teacher nor discuss with classmates, and students could also face technical difficulties when attending online classes from home.

Losing focus has a big impact in learning. For example, my friend Generic_Name sent me a text message last month, right when I started studying for my history mid-term exam. I responded back to Generic_Name's text, and without realizing we kept on messaging past midnight. This shows how easily students get distracted at home with a cellular device and how easy it is to lose focus. The next morning I decided to get to school an hour early and review one on one with my teacher.

Secondly, taking classes online doesn't just mean you don't have a physical teacher or instructor that you can question lively, but also means that it will be challenging to find answers to your questions. I remember in my sophomore year a kid in our econ class named Generic_Name was really sick for a while so he had ended up taking classes online. Generic_Name was a straight A student, always was first to answer the teachers questions and he also used to ask questions. Thankfully Generic_Name healed towards the end of the year and I asked him if he benefited and if he recommends attending classes from home. The straight A student Generic_Name said it was a real challenge to take the class online and he finished the class a month after he should have with a B- average. Generic_Name had also said that one of the most difficult parts about attending a class online was his laptop not functioning at all times, and not having a teacher you can talk and converse with one on one.

Finally, using your personal computer and internet connection can always be an issue. You can't always depend on your computer, not just the computers but even people aren't perfect. Another main problem Generic_Name had when attending classes online was his laptop and network connection. Generic_Name explained that he always faced technical difficulties. When his laptop wasn't functioning right, the only thing he could do was to stop the lesson and wait for his dad to get the laptop repaired, which took time. Each month, either his laptop or internet connection would not cooperate, so he finished the class a month later than everyone.

In conclusion, Everyone would like to save money and time by taking classes from home. But getting distracted, not asking your teacher questions when you need to, and wasting money on laptop repair is not worth it at all. Learning from a far distance could also be an option but when asking if it is beneficial, we can say that it is not by looking at the listed reasoning.

The straight-A student Generic_Name said it was a real challenge to take the class online. He finished the class a month after he should have with a B- average. Generic_Name also said that one of the most difficult parts of attending class online was his laptop not functioning at all times and not having a teacher you can talk and converse with one on one.

Finally, using your personal computer and internet connection can always be an issue. You can't always depend on your computer; people aren't perfect either. Another main problem Generic_Name had when attending classes online was his laptop and network connection. Generic_Name explained that he always faced technical difficulties. When his laptop wasn't functioning right, the only thing he could do was stop the lesson and wait for his dad to get the laptop repaired, which took time. Each month, either his laptop or internet connection would not cooperate, so he finished the class a month later than everyone.

In conclusion, everyone would like to save money and time by taking classes from home, but getting distracted, not asking your teacher questions when you need to, and wasting money on laptop repair is not worth it at all. Learning from a far distance could also be an option, but when asking if it is beneficial, we can say that it is not by looking at the listed reasoning.

Many people appreciate the convenience of attending classes from home because it saves both time and money. However, online learning has serious downsides: students often lose concentration amid home distractions, they miss out on direct interaction with teachers and classmates, and technical problems can interrupt their studies.

Staying focused at home can be a real challenge. For instance, one evening I began reviewing for my history midterm when my friend sent me a message. We exchanged texts without even noticing the time, and before I realized it, it was well past midnight. Because I had lost track of my study plan, I decided the next morning to arrive at school an hour early and review the material face to face with my teacher.

Another drawback of remote classes is the lack of immediate support from instructors and classmates. In my sophomore year, a classmate became seriously ill and had to switch to online economics lessons for a few months. This student usually earned straight A’s and was always first to answer questions in class. Yet when he worked from home, he struggled to get quick feedback or ask follow-up questions. By the end of the year, he finished the course with a B- average and was one month behind his classmates.

On top of that, relying on your own computer and internet connection can backfire. My classmate from economics often faced laptop malfunctions or slow network speeds. Whenever his computer failed, he had to pause the class until his father could fix it—a process that sometimes took days. By dealing with these interruptions almost every week, he missed lectures and fell further behind.

In conclusion, although online classes can cut down on travel costs and scheduling hassles, the risks of distraction, limited teacher interaction, and frequent technical issues make this mode of learning less effective. Despite its appeal, studying from home simply does not provide the same benefits as attending classes in person.

Seeking advice from several people can lead to wiser decisions because it offers diverse viewpoints, a greater variety of choices, and practical solutions to problems. Without more than one opinion, someone might miss important information and make poor decisions.

To begin with, hearing different perspectives is a key benefit of asking for several opinions. For instance, imagine Generic_Name goes to the mall looking for a particular shop but cannot find it. She first asks a man who tells her it’s on the second floor. When she doesn’t see it there, she asks another shopper, who says it’s next to the ice cream parlor on the first floor. She follows the second suggestion, buys an ice cream, and finally locates the store. Thanks to asking more than one person, she succeeds; otherwise she would have left empty-handed.

Another advantage is that having multiple opinions increases the chance of getting accurate directions or advice. Suppose Generic_Name is in New York on her first day of high school but has no idea where the building is. She spots a girl who looks like a student and asks for directions, but that route leads her to the wrong entrance. Realizing she’s lost, she approaches several classmates and every one points her toward the main office. Because she listened to many students instead of just one, she ends up in the right place on time.

Finally, multiple opinions can help solve unexpected problems. Let’s say Generic_Name is at a sleepover and the oven catches fire while she and her friends are cooking. One friend panics and suggests throwing water on the flames, but another advises calling emergency services. By choosing to dial 911, the fire department arrives and puts out the fire safely. If she had listened to only the first friend, the situation might have become much worse.

In conclusion, seeking various opinions brings fresh perspectives, more reliable advice, and effective problem-solving. Thanks to this approach, Generic_Name found her store, reached her school, and kept her home safe. Without different viewpoints, these successes might not have been possible.

There are two main ways our character develops. One is by consciously selecting the qualities we wish to embody, taking responsibility for our own personalities. The other way is through forces we cannot control—upbringing, social pressures, or unforeseen events that shape us without our choosing. Of these two, deliberately choosing our character traits seems the most sensible, since it gives us a chance to manage our emotions rather than be ruled by them.

Character traits come in many forms: humor, enthusiasm, kindness and more. They arise partly from our deliberate decisions and partly from how we react to life’s challenges. In daily life, we usually have the ability to steer our feelings—calming ourselves when we feel anxious or cheering ourselves up when we’re down. This self-awareness allows us to refine the traits we value most.

However, some powerful emotions resist our control. Anger, deep sadness or bouts of depression can suddenly overwhelm us. When these feelings take over, we may act impulsively, sometimes causing harm to ourselves or others. That is why character traits are not inherently good or bad; their impact depends on whether we can keep them in check.

People disagree about which influence is stronger. Some insist they deliberately choose their personality traits by practicing certain behaviors—for instance, nurturing patience through meditation or developing confidence through public speaking. They feel these efforts give them command over their emotional life. Others believe their reactions come unasked, driven by biology or past experiences; no matter what they try, emotions simply arise and take hold.

Both views recognize that emotions like anger or sadness often dominate without warning. Yet those who advocate for self-direction argue that, with simple strategies—such as pausing before reacting or talking through feelings with a friend—anyone can learn to guide their own traits. In contrast, those who feel powerless accept that their character unfolds on its own.

In the end, allowing outside forces to shape us leaves our actions open to chance, while choosing our traits places us firmly in the driver’s seat. Learning to control and cultivate our own character qualities not only helps us make better decisions but also leads to a more balanced, fulfilling life.

Most students look forward to summer break as their favorite time of the year. While some pupils appreciate an extended summer vacation, others would rather shorten it and expand breaks in spring, fall, or winter. Although there are arguments on both sides, I believe a long summer holiday and shorter breaks during other seasons are more beneficial. Two main reasons support my view: lengthy vacations allow better planning, and frequent short terms are less effective for learning.

First, a long summer break makes it easier for students to arrange detailed plans. Many young people want to travel, explore new countries, or spend quality time with relatives who live far away. If their holiday lasts only a few days, they must juggle schoolwork and trips, which turns travel into a stressful experience. For instance, if you have relatives overseas, a brief vacation often means rushing back before you have truly reconnected. With ample time off, families can enjoy each other’s company without worrying about returning to classes in just a week or two. This freedom to organise a meaningful trip is a clear advantage of a longer summer vacation.

Second, having a longer study period followed by a substantial break works better than several short terms. Athletes follow training seasons to maintain peak performance, and musicians practise their instruments day after day. The same principle applies to students. If you study intensively for two weeks and then stop for a week, you lose the learning momentum you had built. On the other hand, regular daily study, even for shorter periods, helps you remember and master subjects more effectively. In this way, a longer uninterrupted term keeps students engaged and makes the transition into a break more rewarding.

Some people learn best by working hard in a brief period and then resting, but this approach has its risks. Cramming facts from math, science, history, and language subjects in a short time might lead to decent grades on tests, yet students often forget the material soon afterward. Longer vacations, by contrast, give them time to reflect on what they have learned and apply it in real life.

In summary, summer vacation offers a unique chance for students to explore new places, spend time with loved ones, and truly rest before the next academic year. While adjusting other holiday lengths may suit some learning styles, extending summer break provides more opportunities for personal growth and effective study.

They say you should never judge a book by its cover, and this idea holds true when meeting people for the first time. In this case, the “cover” refers not only to someone’s appearance but to the initial impression they make. Just like a book whose cover might seem dull or misleading, a first impression can hide the real personality beneath. It is only after spending time with someone—asking questions, listening, and observing—that you discover who they truly are. Various factors, such as a person’s character, the situation they face, and the way they present themselves, often make these snap judgments unreliable.

One important influence on first impressions is personality. Shy or reserved people, for instance, can seem standoffish, even though deep down they are warm and friendly. When I moved to a new high school in my junior year, I noticed a classmate who never spoke. At first, I assumed she was unfriendly or uninterested in making friends. Later, I realized we shared the same shyness. We gradually began to say hello, then talk about our classes, and eventually spent time together outside school. Over time, her outgoing nature surfaced, and we became best friends. This experience taught me that a quiet demeanor often masks a lively spirit, and judging someone solely by their initial hesitation can lead to a false view of who they are.

Another reason first impressions often miss the mark is that you have no idea what someone might be going through at that moment. People carry personal concerns—stress over exams, worries about family, or grief from a recent loss—that influence their mood and behavior. Without knowing this background, you might interpret their silence or distraction as rudeness or disinterest. I experienced this myself on the first day of my senior year. Rushing to my first class and anxious about being late, I barely greeted anyone and ate lunch alone, focused entirely on finding the next classroom. My classmates likely saw me as unfriendly or aloof, when in reality I was simply overwhelmed by nerves and a tight schedule.

Appearance also affects first impressions. The way someone dresses, speaks, or carries themselves can suggest traits that may not be accurate. A person wearing plain clothes could have a creative mind, while someone who dresses sharply might be more down-to-earth than they appear. Relying only on these outward signs is like reading a book’s cover and assuming you know the plot.

Ultimately, first impressions combine many unreliable clues—personality traits we misunderstand, situations we know nothing about, and surface details that can mislead us. If all friendships were based on these quick judgments, we would miss countless opportunities for genuine connection. Only by getting to know someone beyond that first moment can we truly appreciate their character and values.

Year-round schooling may seem to offer more frequent pauses, but it actually shortens the long summer break and leads to greater stress, reduced vacation time, and fewer earnings during the summer months.

First, having shorter, more frequent breaks can increase pressure on both students and teachers. Young people often worry about what to wear each day, feeling they must buy extra outfits just to avoid repeating clothes and keep up with peers. Meanwhile, teachers face the constant challenge of planning lessons for changing schedules and grading assignments without a substantial break to catch up on their workload.

Second, the summer vacation in a year-round calendar typically lasts only three to four weeks. This shorter period makes it hard for students to take extended trips or spend quality time with family, and parents who need a longer break to travel can find it impossible to plan a proper holiday. As a result, families lose out on valuable opportunities for relaxation and bonding.

Third, the limited summer leave also means students have less time for summer jobs. Instead of having three months to earn money and gain work experience, they only get a few weeks, which significantly reduces their income. Local businesses may notice this drop too, since fewer young workers are available to help over the summer.

Some people argue that more breaks spread throughout the year prevent learning loss, but these short pauses do not offer the same rest and recovery as a longer holiday. Others claim that frequent breaks improve focus, yet the constant change in routine can actually cause more stress than a traditional school calendar with a longer summer break.

For these reasons, high school should require four years, giving learners a better understanding of what lies ahead.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I agree, since standing firm in your identity can feel overwhelming when others expect you to conform. In eighth grade, a classmate I trusted insisted I abandon my true self to seem cooler. At first, I blamed myself, but I eventually learned that real friends never demand you change. Owning who you are is difficult—shyness, lack of confidence and fear of judgement can all hold you back. I used to believe I was worthless and kept my struggles hidden, even contemplating ending my life, though I was too frightened to act. I then put on a smile and pretended to be happy, but that façade quickly collapsed. Now, in eleventh grade, I’ve met someone special—my girlfriend—whose presence fills me with genuine happiness every day. Emerson’s words ring true: staying authentic in a world full of pressures is a rare feat, and I wholeheartedly share his belief.

Should schools limit the number of extracurricular activities students join? I believe that decisions about how many clubs or teams a student takes on should primarily rest with the student and their family. Schools should only step in when academic performance or attendance in those activities is suffering. In those cases, parents and school staff can work together to find a better balance.

First, families know their children best and can judge whether there is enough time for homework, test preparation, and other commitments. If parents notice their child is overwhelmed, they should discuss the issue with them and decide if some activities should be dropped. Once that choice is made, parents must inform the student’s guidance counselor and the leader of each activity so everyone understands the new arrangement.

Second, if a student’s grades begin to fall, school counselors should meet with the student to explore possible causes. If overcommitment to extracurriculars appears to be the problem, the counselor and student can review which activities might be paused or ended until academic performance improves. This meeting reminds students that they must keep up their schoolwork in order to enjoy their extracurricular interests.

Finally, consistent attendance is essential. If a student misses more than five meetings or practices in a month without a valid reason, they should temporarily lose the privilege to participate. Parents would be notified of this decision, and the student could face a short suspension from all meetings until attendance is reliable again.

In conclusion, schools should have only a limited role in controlling extracurricular participation. Families should lead these decisions unless a student’s grades slip or attendance becomes a serious issue.

Students can gain many advantages by studying from home rather than commuting to a school building, mainly because they have the freedom to work at their own speed. Without the pressure of early wake-ups, they arrive at lessons feeling rested and are less likely to lose focus during class. Studying online also means they are not bound by a fixed schedule; if they need more time on an assignment, they can pause and return later, avoiding the stress of unfinished work.

When illness forces a student to miss several days, remote classes make it easy to keep up with lessons without falling behind. Likewise, schools that offer online instruction don’t have to worry about canceling lessons for snow or other weather delays. Being at home reduces the need to move between classrooms and allows teenagers to concentrate more fully, since they are not distracted by hallway conversations or crowded desks.

Students who often skip school can catch up on missed lessons online, which usually results in better grades because they complete the coursework. If they hit a difficult topic, they can search the internet for explanations or ask a parent or sibling for help. Short breaks can be scheduled to prevent mental exhaustion, and over time learners strengthen their computer and research skills—abilities that will benefit them in further study and future jobs.

Parents also have a clearer view of their child’s progress when schoolwork happens at home, making it easier to discuss grades or reward effort. For students who dislike early mornings or prefer a quieter setting, online schooling offers a comfortable alternative. It saves travel time for both teachers and pupils, yet still meets daily deadlines. Overall, virtual classes provide a flexible, accessible way to learn and help make education more enjoyable.

Today’s digital advances let us accomplish a wide range of tasks without meeting others in person, and that is a positive change. Technology is constantly simplifying our routines and offering a glimpse of what lies ahead. Rather than seeing this as a drawback, it makes sense to appreciate how it improves our daily lives. For instance, if you need a quick ride but don’t own a car or can’t find a taxi, ride-hailing apps allow you to share your location and destination with a driver. In just a few taps on your smartphone, you can be on your way. This kind of innovation shows how much better our tools become over time.

Smartphone applications cover almost every need you might think of. Imagine you’re home and starving but don’t feel like going out—apps such as Grubhub solve that problem. With a delivery service, you choose your meal, supply the restaurant’s address, and enter where you want it dropped off. In minutes, your food arrives at your door. Installing these apps doesn’t cost anything, though you still pay for the dishes you order. The fact that a device as small as a phone can organize this process with minimal typing is remarkable. It reminds us that convenience often comes with a small price.

Computers remain a vital element of modern technology, too. Whether for academic research, office work, or personal projects, desktops and laptops help us find information and complete tasks efficiently. Laptops add extra flexibility since they fold up and are easy to carry on the move—perfect for travelers or people who work remotely. Today’s models have features like touchscreens, 360-degree hinges, and powerful processors, and each year they grow more advanced. Thinking about how far computers have come makes me excited to see what the next generation will offer.

Overall, technology makes life easier every day. Without it, I couldn’t access emergency services if I were in danger or quickly reach friends and family. I view these developments as entirely beneficial. We rely on technology to stay informed and safe, and I believe it will continue to serve us well in the future.

While some believe that attending lessons from home is the future of education, others maintain that on-site schooling offers unique benefits. Without pupils attending school, these professionals would lose their roles and the school community would suffer.

In a school setting, pupils benefit from a structured routine and consistent supervision, which helps them stay focused on coursework. At home, distractions such as smartphones, television, or household chores can easily pull students away from their assignments. Conversely, teachers in classrooms provide explanations, set clear expectations, and offer encouragement to help students understand complex topics.

One topic often discussed is whether technology has a positive or negative impact on our lives. I believe that technology brings many benefits because almost everything is available online. For example, books can be read electronically, we can communicate with others through laptops or smartphones, and we can write and store documents digitally. Although some people focus on negative news about technology, its advantages outweigh the drawbacks.

First, having books in digital form makes reading easier and more convenient. You no longer need to visit a bookstore or carry heavy paperbacks. Online libraries and e-readers allow you to download any book within seconds. This is especially useful during travel; you can read on your smartphone or tablet while sitting in a car or plane. Digital books are also user-friendly: you can set bookmarks to save your page, look up definitions instantly, and even translate words or phrases into other languages. If you lose your device, you still have your entire library backed up in the cloud, so you never have to worry about losing your place.

Second, technology revolutionizes how we stay in touch with people far away. Traditional letters take days or weeks to arrive, but emails arrive in seconds and can be edited by multiple recipients. Video calls on tablets or computers with cameras let friends and family see each other in real time, no matter where they live. You can talk face-to-face with several people at once, schedule calls at any convenient time, and avoid the waiting time of a postal service. This constant connection helps us maintain relationships despite busy schedules and long distances.

In addition, technology in education and writing has greatly improved learning and productivity. Many schools now provide students with laptops or tablets so they can research information for projects and do homework online. Children can use educational apps to practice their ABCs and basic maths in a fun way. Digital word processors offer spell check and formatting tools that make writing essays or reports easier. Teachers can share resources instantly, and students can collaborate on documents in real time, receiving immediate feedback on their work.

Looking ahead, technology will continue to evolve and replace many traditional tools like paper and pencils. Devices may become even more advanced and integrated into our daily routines. While new gadgets can be expensive and need proper care, their long-term benefits—reduced use of paper, instant access to information, and improved communication—make them a worthwhile investment.

Overall, technology offers efficient and flexible ways to read, write, and communicate. I believe it will play an even greater role in our lives in the future. Embracing current innovations will help us adapt as they grow, making life easier and faster for everyone.

The benefits of working in as a group or working alone.

I believe working as a group is more beneficial for the students.

My friend Generic_Name is very capable of doing school work by himself.

However, even he needed others help to understand somethings.

I am very capable of doing a school project by myself.

However, even I could use some one else's input in the matter.

I believe working together as a group is beneficial .

For example, my friend Generic_Name he is a very smart person.

He was on the top of the class with grades but, even he could not do it by himself.

One day the teacher assigned us projects.

Generic_Name decided to do it alone.

On the due date, which was later that week Generic_Name turned in the project.

The teacher told him he failed he did not understand why.

The teacher later on the day took him aside and explained that he was not understanding the question.

He asked her how he could make up the points for the failed project.

Two weeks after that she assigned another project.

She took Generic_Name aside and said ' this time work with somebody".

Generic_Name listed so he asked somebody to work with him.

The day the project was due, he was nervous because he does not work with people often.

The teacher told him they got a perfect score.

The teacher took him aside and told him why he passed.

She told him he passed because when you have more than just one persons input.

Things become clear so when you do not understand something that other person's input can help.

Another reason I believe working as a group helps is when I was in high school we were assigned a two part project.

The first part I had to do by self.

I got it done when the due date came the teacher told us to pick a partner.

I picked a friend of mine, Generic_Name.

The teacher told us to compare our papers.

However, our paper even though they were on the same subject, they were very different.

She later told us to now write a paper on the same subject but working together.

When we were all done with the two parts she told everyone to rotate their papers to the right once.

Everyone passed them on the teacher then told the whole class to read all three papers and to pick which one made more sense.

When every one was done they all picked the one that made the most sense and gave it to her.

Every single one of those papers she got were all the one people worked on together.

She then asked the class why they did not pick the other one.

They all said because the other papers were one sided as in only one perspective.

Some students may say working alone is better.

However, Generic_Name and I both learned that in some places you need two sides to a story, argument and debate.

If I would have gone on with my life thinking the way I thought before I worked with some one, it would be very different in some perspective.

My friend Generic_Name's life would have been very different too.

Thanks to the team work skill and the skill to listen to other peoples side, Generic_Name and I can make decision with some one instead of just making it alone.

I recommend you talk to your teacher about this and get more group projects going.

Talk to your parents about how you could use those skills in the outside world, become surprised by how much you use them, and by how easier your life become.

When you do not have to make decision alone, decision making becomes much easier.

What subject would you choose for elementary school students? Would you pick math because they enjoy numbers, or science because they love hands-on experiments? I would lean toward science, since we experience it every day when we flip a light switch or toss a ball into the air. Moreover, science appeals to many children because it’s both interactive and entertaining. For these reasons, I believe a science lesson is ideal: it’s fun, relatively easy to teach, and directly relevant to students’ everyday lives.

Firstly, science lessons are engaging and enjoyable for both kids and adults. Experiments bring concepts to life, so learners can see ideas in action rather than just reading about them. If you want to teach the difference between kinetic and potential energy, for example, you can have students throw a ball and observe how it speeds up and slows down. Because everyone in the class witnesses each experiment together, the entire group can share excitement and insights. Finally, discussing results helps students compare their observations and learn from one another. For instance, after an egg-drop challenge, pupils might talk about which designs protected the egg best and why, turning a simple drop test into a rich learning experience.

Secondly, science is one of the easiest subjects to teach effectively at the elementary level. Unlike language classes, which often rely on memorizing roots and vocabulary, or math, which requires mastering numerous formulas, science mostly asks students to remember clear terms and ideas. Experiments do the rest, allowing learners to witness principles firsthand. If they pay close attention during a demonstration, they grasp the concept without endless repetition. Drawing diagrams also simplifies complex notions: a quick sketch of the water cycle or the parts of a plant often makes more sense than pages of text. This visual approach means teachers can spend less time lecturing and more time guiding students through hands-on activities.

Thirdly, science connects directly to daily life, making lessons meaningful outside the classroom. Everything from how our homes stay cool to why magnets stick to the refrigerator involves scientific ideas. A lesson on air flow can explain how an air conditioner works, while a simple compass activity shows how Earth’s magnetic field guides explorers. When students learn how electric circuits function, they gain insight into why lights turn on instantly and grasp the basics of fixing a broken appliance. By illuminating the science behind everyday objects, lessons help students understand the world they live in.

In conclusion, teaching science to elementary students makes perfect sense because it combines entertainment with easy teaching methods and real-world relevance. Conducting experiments keeps young learners excited, while clear terminology and visual aids make concepts easy to master. Finally, the connections between science and daily routines give lessons a lasting impact beyond the classroom. With a science lesson prepared, elementary students will not only have fun but also build knowledge they can use every day. Would you teach science? Why or why not?

Technology brings both benefits and drawbacks. On one hand, it has simplified our daily routines and opened new horizons. On the other, it can reduce real human contact and cause serious problems. I believe that overreliance on devices and screens can lead to depression or isolation, a distorted sense of reality, and negative impacts on physical and mental health.

First, technology often contributes to feelings of loneliness and sadness. Social media platforms can be a breeding ground for bullying, and many young people suffer emotionally when they face criticism or exclusion online. As a result, they may withdraw from friends and avoid school or social activities. Video games can be equally isolating when players spend hours alone immersed in virtual worlds, forgetting to interact with family or participate in face-to-face conversations. Even our smartphones can become a barrier: people glued to their screens may stay indoors all day, neglecting personal relationships and deeper connections.

Second, heavy use of technology can make it harder to distinguish fiction from reality. Children, in particular, can be easily influenced by online content. Many videos on YouTube present misleading information or sensational stories that young viewers accept as truth. Adults, too, can fall prey to online manipulation, believing conspiracy theories or accepting false claims without question. In some cases, gamers who spend countless hours in virtual environments start to treat those experiences as if they were real life, blurring the line between game actions and real-world behavior.

Third, continued exposure to screens and digital gadgets affects both body and mind. Ophthalmologists warn that staring at devices all day strains the eyes and may lead to long-term vision problems. Mentally, people may adopt the attitudes, appearances, or lifestyles of their favorite internet personalities, changing how they dress or behave to match an online ideal. Even more dangerously, some individuals attempt risky stunts seen in viral videos, ending up injured after trying to replicate dangerous feats.

Despite these concerns, technology does offer clear advantages. In emergency situations, advanced medical equipment can save lives. Modern communication tools help coordinate disaster relief, and innovations in transportation and industry have made work more efficient than ever. In warfare, technological progress can give nations a strategic edge. Overall, many everyday tasks have become quicker and less stressful thanks to digital tools.

Yet the very features that make technology appealing can also turn against us. Devices can fail without warning, and overdependence on machines means people often skip the exercise they need to stay healthy. If we let gadgets handle every task, our physical fitness can decline rapidly. Moreover, factories, power plants, and electronic waste all contribute to pollution, threatening the natural world we depend on.

In conclusion, although technology has changed our lives in remarkable ways, its overuse can limit genuine human interaction, distort our grasp of reality, and damage our health. We cannot simply ignore technological advances—they are here to stay—but we must use them wisely and preserve the human connections and well-being that truly matter.

We all live in a society where relying on other people is essential. Nobody enters this world fully equipped to face every challenge alone. It’s important to stay true to yourself, yet it’s also natural to adapt when you feel a need for growth. Still, if someone else forces you to alter who you are, that can be harmful—perhaps because their views are distorted or overly negative. In my view, being yourself means deciding for yourself how much you want to change, rather than allowing others to dictate your identity.

I disagree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s claim that pure individuality is always best. In reality, forming bonds with others—like family members or close friends—can make life smoother and more fulfilling. For example, I count on my parents, my sister, and friends who feel like family. Without these connections, we risk drifting into a lonely existence. Mutual trust is crucial; we need people we can lean on during tough times.

When I was around twelve to fourteen years old, I struggled academically at the start of each school year. I felt anxious every morning, convinced I lacked the motivation to improve my grades or to reach out to classmates. After school, I often went home feeling dejected and unhappy. Eventually, I realized I couldn’t handle everything on my own. With encouragement from my teachers and friends, I began to work harder and opened up to others. Over time, I noticed I was changing for the better—and I hardly recognized the person I’d become. This experience taught me that growth often happens naturally when you interact with others; you don’t even need to force the change yourself.

Another drawback of complete isolation is boredom. If you spend all your time alone, there’s no one to share experiences with or to keep you company. By contrast, having friends lets you enjoy activities together—playing games, talking about life, or traveling. Each shared adventure brings new lessons and lasting memories. Some people believe our society is indifferent, that nobody really cares. In truth, it’s not society itself but the attitudes of certain individuals. Negative people may push others away, and as a result they end up isolated. However, by reaching out or asking for help, anyone can break free from that cycle.

In the end, excessive focus on individuality can lead to an empty path. We need others to lift us up and remind us that no one is alone or worthless. Offering support makes both you and the person you help stronger. Yet even while we grow with others, it’s important not to lose sight of our authentic selves. You are the main character in your own life story, and the choices you make—about both change and self‐acceptance—belong to you.

Throughout history, humans have survived and thrived because we learned to unite and share tasks. This idea, that two heads are better than one, has guided us from simple hunting groups to modern societies. Today, we design complex buildings, launch rockets into space, and travel between continents in a few hours. It is hard to imagine one person managing all the skills and labour these achievements require. Teamwork makes such progress possible.

When you join a team, you bring a special skill that benefits the whole group. For instance, a firm that creates websites for government agencies might have a coder, a graphic designer, and a content writer. Each member focuses on their strength. You, as the writer, produce engaging text, while your colleagues handle layout and programming. In this way, everyone acts like a gear in a machine, fitting perfectly into the system to keep it moving at a steady pace.

Another advantage of teamwork is that tasks can be divided according to each person’s abilities, ensuring no one is overloaded and resources aren’t wasted. In a construction team, workers measure and mix concrete in precise portions to avoid leftovers. In a restaurant kitchen, one chef slices vegetables, another prepares sauces, and someone else arranges the final dish. By sharing these responsibilities, the group works more efficiently and prevents bottlenecks at any stage.

In conclusion, teamwork offers countless benefits for all kinds of projects. Like a well-oiled machine, effective collaboration depends on clear communication, trust, and coordination. When each person knows their role, errors become rare and the team moves forward as a unified force. Keep in mind that some challenges are too large for one individual to handle alone. Mastering the art of working together is one of the most important lessons we can learn in life.

The statement is "the first impression is almost impossible to change" which is a different feeling for everybody, but for me, I disagree. In fact, the first impression is really important and sometimes true, but I think the first impression does not define a person, an object or a situation. Having a first impression is a human reflex, like having an opinion or a judgment. We are doing it unconsciously.

The first impression is most of the time not real, you need to search deeper to make an opinion and when you really have an opinion, then, the first impression is not important anymore. For example, when you meet someone, your first impression might be that you think she is supercilious and even a little bit mean. Therefore when you really get to know her deeper then you will find that she just had a bad day and that she is nice and sociable. Sometimes it's the contrary, a person seems really nice but in reality she is not, so your first impression was wrong. It is not good to stay on a first impression because most of the time it's wrong.

Moreover, the physic, behaviors or attitude can change an impression. If the person do not smile and seems to be rude but in reality is the nicest person, then it will be awkward for you because you thought she was bad. Sometimes a person can have a bad reputation because of the first impression he shows and it is not his fault, some persons just don't smile every time. Sometimes you can be disappointed because you didn't get to know the person because of your first impression.

The first impressions is not only for people but also for a situation or an object. For example if you are in a library and you want to buy a book, the first thing you are going to do is looking at the cover of the book. If it's pretty you will more easily choose this one instead of a book with a black cover and only the title, because it is your first impression. But your first impression is wrong because you didn't take time to read the resume and you will find soon that the pretty book is actually boring instead of the black book which is really interesting. An object can look nice but have a bad quality. The first impression is the color and the shape of the object, like the physic and the attitude of a person.

In conclusion I would say that the first impression is sometimes right but most of the time it's not. In my opinion, you must not keep in mind your first impression of a person, it's most of the time wrong. You have to get to know the person to build your own opinion. It is normal to have a first impression, like judging, but you must not take the habit to stick with your first impression.

Most students look forward to a lengthy summer holiday, while others think it should be much shorter. At present, schools usually give about three months off, but some people suggest cutting it to just four weeks, lengthening the winter break, and adding brief pauses in spring and autumn. I disagree with this plan. Even though students might forget some of what they learned, a long summer break offers valuable time for travel, chances to work full-time, and a much-needed reduction in stress.

First, an extended summer vacation makes it possible for families to take longer trips or visit relatives who live far away. If your cousin lives in another state or your grandparents live across the country, you need enough days to make the journey, settle in, and really enjoy your time together. You cannot pack up the car, drive across several states, explore, and return home within just a few weeks. Having two or three months off gives everyone the freedom to plan properly and make the most of their holidays.

Second, older students often rely on summer to earn their own money, and a longer break lets them work full-time. Parents want their teenagers to experience the realities of adult life—paying bills or saving for a car, for example. If a student only has part-time hours, it may take the entire break just to cover small expenses. With more weeks available, teenagers can pick up full-time shifts, improve their financial independence, and learn important skills like time management and responsibility.

Finally, a long summer holiday provides a vital chance to relieve school-related stress. Academic pressures, family worries, or personal problems can build up over the school year. Struggling with grades, coping with parents’ expectations, or juggling extracurricular activities can all feel overwhelming. A two- or three-month break lets students decompress, focus on hobbies, spend time with friends, and return to class feeling refreshed.

In conclusion, although some argue for a shorter summer and more breaks elsewhere, the traditional three-month vacation best serves students’ needs. It supports meaningful travel, allows for full-time work experiences, and helps reduce stress. For these reasons, we should keep our long summer break just as it is.

Many people today like to give advice to others. Sometimes it is about life, work, or personal relationships. But the question now is: “Example is not the main thing in influencing others; is it the only thing?” I think it is, for two main reasons.

Firstly, when you talk to others, you sometimes give an example from other people’s experiences. For example, you might mention someone who was a bad person in the past and who has now changed. You can change bad relations or yourself. By using reasons, examples, and actions, you influence that person, and he can change himself if he wants.

Second, we are always influencing people with reasons—maybe bad ones or good ones—but it is the only way to influence others. Influencing people is not easy; you need to be prepared with the examples they need to hear.

In conclusion, the only way to influence people is with examples, actions, reasons, and your personal advice.

Many people today enjoy offering advice on life, work, or personal relationships. However, I believe that example is not just important—it is the only true way to influence others. First, when you speak to someone, you often share stories from real life. For instance, you might describe a person who behaved poorly at one time but later improved. By combining this story with clear reasons and helpful actions, you demonstrate how change can happen if someone is willing. Second, influencing people always depends on reasons—positive or negative—supported by concrete illustrations. Persuading someone is not easy; you must provide the right example for them to follow. In conclusion, the sole effective method to impact others is through examples, actions, logical reasons, and personal guidance.
