Being yourself allows you to become the best version of who you are. When you stay true to your own values and habits, you won’t lose sight of your identity. Of course, it’s natural to grow and adapt over time, but you should avoid changing so much that you end up regretting who you’ve become. Your attitude and character define you, so any transformation should make you stronger, not less genuine. Many people alter their behavior because they want to seem more outgoing or improve themselves, yet going back to your original self once you’ve changed can feel almost impossible.

Each person is unique, and embracing that uniqueness is important. You don’t need to modify your personality to prove anything to others. Even if you think you’re too quiet or too opinionated, that’s simply part of what makes you, you. Life events—such as losing someone you love, experiencing stress, or facing health challenges—can influence your behavior and push you away from your true self. Still, choosing to act and speak in ways that reflect your real feelings can bring positive changes, not only for you but also for those around you. If you do decide to improve, make sure it’s to become better than your current self, not someone entirely different.

Changing yourself too much can lead you to lose your inner core. If you begin to act like someone you admire or fit in with a certain group, you may no longer recognize who you were before. Any change should come from your own wishes, not from pressure by friends or strangers. At the end of the day, only you live with your decisions—others will move on. As my grandmother always said: “Don’t change who you are for anyone; your family loves the real you.” Even if some traits seem annoying or odd, they are part of your uniqueness. Let your true qualities shine instead of hiding them.

Your personality also shapes your relationships. People generally respect honesty and confidence, especially when you show your background without shame. Pretending to be richer, louder, or more popular than you really are won’t win genuine friends. If someone cares about you, they will value your true self. And if a family member or friend steps away because you stay honest and kind, they probably weren’t right for you in the first place.

After you change into someone you’re not, it is very hard to revert back. Some who drift away from you might never return, and the chances to rebuild those connections can slip away forever. If you’ve chosen to grow, accept and cherish that new version of yourself. Who you become now will shape the person you continue to grow into.

Ultimately, remain true to yourself. Being genuine sets the foundation for your future and helps you build honest relationships. Even as you mature and face new challenges, don’t let others decide who you should be. Trust your own values, let your individuality guide you, and live confidently as the person you truly are.

Students work hard there is no arguing that. They have schoolwork, homework, extracurricular and maybe work, all these things make a students life stressful so it is important that they get a break every once in a while. I believe that students should get a long summer break, instead of a year-round school year, because, firstly, there are other activities that can be done during the summer that keep students minds active, secondly their health is at risk and lastly, summer break is beneficial to school staff as well.

From time to time, people need to get a break from their day-today life they need to take a moment to relax and enjoy their life and maybe discover an interest that they may have. Although school is important and necessary for success later on in life, so are outside experiences that can contribute to the development of a student's 'real life skills'. During summer break there are multiple activities that can be done in order to keep a student's mind active, whether it may be sports, summer camps, summer jobs etc. All these activities allow for their minds and bodies to stay active. Eventhough, they are not keeping their brains engaged in terms of school work and studying they are exposing themselves to new activities that might require them to think critically, open-mindedly and collaboratively; which I feel is essential for real life. For example, a student might be at summer camp and they are put in a group with four strangers and are given a challenging task that requires them to collaborate with the other member of the group, critically analyzing the situation and coming up with solutions and be open-minded to listening and trying to understand the perspectives of their peers. This also reflects their environment in school therefore, it can be said that they are keeping their minds active while outside of school.

Although, not all students might be involved in activities outside of school, some are taking a break from the stress of life itself. Due to all the demands in their life during the school year summer break is a good way to take a breather and take care of themselves mentally. Depression has been very common in teenagers in recent years, and although it may not be entirely due to the stress of school, school does contribute to the detirriation of their mental health. In addition, over-working ones self has negative impacts overall whether they are depressed or not. Too much stress in ones life can have negative effects on their health overall. High blood pressure, hypertension, severe weight loss are a few examples of the effects stress. Furthermore, when stressed our body releases a neurotransmitter called Cortisol, this neurotransmitter in excess can impair a persons thinking and reaction time; which is very important for students as they are required to think in order to complete school work and homework, therefore, if they dont take breaks their grades are probably going to drop due to their inability to think effectively, further contributing to their detirriating mental health.

Lastly, summer break is and essential time for everyone that is involved in schools, such as teachers, administrators, councilors etc. Although schools are intended to educate students, its the school staff that make this possible. This is why we need to give our school staff a break because all the points I stated above also applies to them. In addition, with a long summer break teachers are able to have more time to thoroughly think about their lesson plans for their students as well as have an extended amount of time to live their lives and enjoy time with their family and friends, after all, teachers are humans too and they need to be able to life their lives and forget that they are required to do so much for such little pay.

To emphasize further, I believe that schools should give students a long summer break instead of a year-round school year because a students mind will stay active during the summer through various activities that require students to think open-mindedly, critically and collaboratively. Also, students need a break in order to de-stress for the sake of their health mentally and physically. Lastly, a long summer break is needed for school staff as well because they also need to take a break, as well as the students.

I hold the view that a traditional long summer vacation is preferable to a year-round schedule because it offers opportunities for leisure and growth, protects students’ health, and also benefits teachers and other school staff.

First, summer provides a chance for young people to stay mentally engaged outside the classroom. While academic study is essential, real-life experiences can foster critical, creative and cooperative thinking. Activities such as sports teams, summer camps or paid jobs require participants to solve problems, work with strangers and adapt to new situations. For example, campers might be divided into groups and given a challenge that demands teamwork, open-minded discussion and quick decision-making. Though these tasks are not formal lessons, they mirror the collaborative environment of school and keep students’ minds active in a different context.

Second, a long break is important for students’ overall well-being. The school year’s demands can lead to chronic stress, which in turn may harm both physical and mental health. Teen depression has risen in recent years, and although not solely caused by academics, school-related pressure contributes significantly. Prolonged stress can result in symptoms such as high blood pressure, weight loss and fatigue. Moreover, excess cortisol—the hormone released when we are stressed—impairs clear thinking and slows our reactions. If students never really rest, their academic performance may suffer as their ability to concentrate and solve problems declines. A proper summer break allows them to relax, recharge and return to school more focused.

Lastly, long holidays benefit the adults who work in schools. Teachers, administrators and counselors work hard throughout the year to support learners, yet they too can feel overwhelmed. A summer recess gives them time to review and refine lesson plans, explore new teaching methods and spend quality moments with family and friends. After all, educators need a chance to step away from the demands of their jobs and enjoy life outside school. In turn, this break helps them return refreshed and better prepared for the next academic term.

In conclusion, a lengthy summer vacation is crucial not only for students’ intellectual engagement through diverse activities but also for preserving their mental and physical health. It also offers essential rest for the school staff who dedicate themselves to educating young people. For these reasons, maintaining a traditional long summer break is a more balanced and humane choice than a year-round schedule.

Many people believe that aiming for ambitious goals is the best strategy, while others feel it is safer to set modest targets. Although some argue that high ambitions can end in disappointment and lead to giving up, this view ignores the fact that goals come in various forms and difficulty levels. Pursuing lofty aims often means people can achieve more, stay motivated, and develop a stronger sense of success.

Opponents of high goals warn that missing a challenging target can sap motivation and create a fear of failure. They say that when someone falls short of a big aim, it can leave them feeling empty and unwilling to try again. In their eyes, avoiding lofty objectives protects self-esteem by preventing painful setbacks. However, this approach overlooks how aiming high can actually inspire growth and resilience.

First, setting ambitious goals can help people accomplish more overall. When someone chooses a high standard, they often break it down into several smaller milestones. Reaching each milestone boosts confidence and offers a sense of progress. Even if one sub-goal is missed, this does not stop a person from meeting other targets. In fact, working toward multiple achievements teaches valuable skills—persistence, planning, and adaptability—that make future goals more attainable.

Second, ambitious aims enhance feelings of success and self-worth. Completing a difficult project shows a person what they are capable of and helps reduce anxiety about future challenges. This success builds inner confidence that carries over into other areas of life. As people tick off major objectives, they feel proud of their efforts, believing they have meaningful accomplishments rather than settling for easy wins.

Third, high targets fuel motivation by giving clear direction and purpose. When a meaningful goal is set, it becomes the main focus of one’s energy and thoughts. This mental concentration creates excitement—an inner drive that encourages regular effort and keeps people committed, even when obstacles appear. The more demanding the aim, the stronger this motivational push often becomes.

In conclusion, aiming high brings the opportunity to achieve more, feel genuinely successful, and maintain strong motivation. Although failure can be discouraging, it is also a natural part of learning and growth. By setting ambitious goals and embracing the challenges they bring, individuals can overcome self-doubt and make real progress toward their dreams.

Many people insist that first impressions cannot be altered, but I believe this is not true. In fact, initial opinions often shift as we mature, because of the influence of those around us, and through the unexpected challenges life brings.

As we grow older, our character and behavior naturally change, causing others to see us in a new light. When I was a child, I was quiet and timid. My mother often reminds me that she hardly recognized the shy little boy she once knew. Now, I am more self-assured and polite when I meet new people. Had I stayed the same as a seven- or eight-year-old, I would still avoid conversation and worry about making mistakes. Growing up usually brings better manners, different interests, and sometimes healthier habits—so our first impression can disappear as we develop.

The people around us also have a strong impact on changing how we are perceived. My younger brother used to be too shy to say more than a few words to anyone. He watched me interacting with classmates and relatives: speaking clearly, standing up straight, and remaining calm. Gradually, he felt encouraged to open up too. Today he chats easily with friends and enjoys social gatherings. In this way, someone you respect can model new behavior, helping others rewrite their initial judgments of you.

Finally, life’s ups and downs can alter how people view us in surprising ways. Just before I turned fourteen, my father was arrested. I felt numb and refused to celebrate my birthday. At school the next day, classmates noticed I no longer laughed or joked as before. They assumed I was deeply upset and gave me space instead of their usual morning greetings. It surprised me how quickly their impression shifted from “happy-go-lucky kid” to someone in real distress. That change showed me how a single event can completely transform people’s original opinions.

In conclusion, I disagree with the idea that first impressions never change. As we grow up, as others influence our behavior, and as life challenges us, people naturally adjust their views of us. First impressions may set a starting point, but they do not have to stay fixed forever.

For example, in a show called Masterchef, chefs must impress the judges with their cooking skills, but one chef is eliminated every episode. When a chef gets eliminated, their dreams may get crushed. However, they have the courage to go on, do their best, and learn what they did wrong. Another example is taking the permit test as a teenager. The permit test is something big for teens since it relates to their future. When I took the test, I was nervous and failed by one question. I checked the answers I got wrong, studied them a bit more, and passed the next time I took it. These examples prove that you have the ability to learn from past mistakes, grow as a person, and take the risks needed to do so.

Taking risks is mostly involved in big decisions that affect jobs, education, and so on. I believe that taking risks is better than making small decisions, even if those risks don’t turn out the way you wanted them to. In a show called Shark Tank, people come in to persuade investors to invest in their products, but they do not always succeed. The people who do not get investments keep moving forward and take their own risks to find an investor. If you learn to take risks, you later get used to it and can speak more confidently in front of people and state your opinion. Another example is having a meeting for a job. It is better to have a meeting in person than online because it is more challenging. The interviewer can get to know you better, and you are more likely to get the position. Taking risks can make you a better person as a whole, and those mistakes can help you improve.

Michelangelo and I agree that having a bigger goal and failing is better than having a small goal and achieving it. Having a bigger goal can increase your confidence and help you focus on the task you want to overcome. People view their mistakes and overcome them so they can do better next time. Small goals do not involve as much effort and work as bigger achievements. By choosing to accomplish a simple task, you may get used to the easy way out and become lazy over time. Setting a higher aim for yourself is better because you can improve your skills and knowledge. Bigger goals are better because of how much they help you improve.

A great artist once said that it is a great danger to set a small aim for yourself. Setting a bigger aim and failing is best because you learn from your mistakes, you learn to take risks, and bigger goals help improve oneself. Smaller aims are a scapegoat compared to bigger aims because they are much easier. It is best to challenge yourself so that you are ready for anything that comes your way. Even if you take the high route and fail, you can try again. In conclusion, setting a bigger aim and failing is alright and better than setting a small aim because small aims are too easy.

Many people believe it is wiser to set modest objectives that we can definitely achieve rather than reach for something grand and risk failure. However, I disagree with this view and support the opinion of Michelangelo, who warned that aiming too low and succeeding can be dangerous. He came to this conclusion after experiencing failures and setbacks before earning his reputation. Michelangelo preferred to attempt great works and possibly fail rather than complete only small tasks. I side with him because striving for larger goals teaches us from our errors, encourages us to take risks, and ultimately fosters personal growth.

First, tackling big ambitions gives us the chance to learn from mistakes. When we fall short, we can examine what went wrong and improve our approach. Take the cooking competition show MasterChef, for instance. Contestants often leave the contest because their dishes do not meet the judges’ standards. Although elimination can feel crushing, participants gain insight into their weaknesses and return stronger in future challenges. Similarly, I remember taking my driving permit exam as a teenager. I missed passing by just one question, which felt disappointing. Yet by reviewing the incorrect answers and studying harder, I succeeded on my next attempt. These experiences show that failure can be an important teacher, helping us identify gaps in our skills and knowledge.

Second, setting ambitious goals pushes us to take risks that build confidence and resilience. In the television series Shark Tank, entrepreneurs pitch their ideas to potential investors, knowing they might not secure funding. Those who are turned down often persist, finding other backers or refining their proposals. Learning to face such high-pressure situations makes it easier to share ideas and express opinions in public. Another example is attending an in-person job interview instead of an online meeting. While face-to-face interviews can seem more intimidating, they offer a better chance to connect with the interviewer and demonstrate enthusiasm, which can increase the likelihood of landing the position. By daring to accept these challenges, we become more adaptable and confident.

Finally, larger objectives drive us to develop our talents more than simple tasks do. Small aims can be accomplished with little effort, which can lead to complacency or laziness over time. In contrast, a significant project demands sustained focus, careful planning, and perseverance. Setting the bar higher encourages continuous learning, whether that means mastering a new technique, building stronger teamwork skills, or deepening our understanding of a subject. This commitment to improvement not only yields better results but also strengthens our self-belief.

Michelangelo’s warning about the danger of low expectations remains relevant today. Choosing to aim high—even if success is not guaranteed—offers valuable lessons, builds courage, and promotes self-development in ways that achieving minor goals cannot. In the end, it is better to challenge yourself with an ambitious target and risk failure than to settle for something easily attained.

People often claim that a positive attitude is the secret to achieving success in life, and I agree. Keeping an optimistic outlook can help you overcome difficulties, improve yourself, and even boost your career prospects.

First, a positive mindset changes the way you react to setbacks. Instead of dwelling on what went wrong, you look for lessons and opportunities. For instance, if you fail a test in your government class, you view it as a signal to study harder and prepare better for the next attempt. This hopeful perspective stops you from getting stuck in self-doubt and motivates you to keep moving forward.

Second, maintaining optimism can also make you a kinder, more helpful person. Many people around us face serious issues like money troubles or family conflicts. When you carry a positive spirit, you are more likely to reach out and support others. Offering encouragement or simply listening can lift someone’s mood—and you’ll feel proud knowing you made a difference.

Third, employers today value staff members who bring a cheerful attitude to work. Whether you’re already employed or looking for a job, showing enthusiasm and willingness to help customers or colleagues can set you apart. Companies believe that positive employees improve the workplace atmosphere and customer satisfaction, so they often seek people with that mindset.

In conclusion, adopting a positive attitude truly paves the way to success. It guides you through tough choices, helps you grow personally, and enables you to assist friends and strangers alike. With an upbeat outlook, life becomes more enjoyable and rewarding, steering you toward your goals.

First impressions vary from person to person, and our initial thoughts can shift once we learn more about someone’s life. These first reactions are important because they mark our immediate judgment, yet they may change after an hour or even a day.

For example, if you find a class dull on the first day, you may form a negative impression. However, if you discover the next day that the class is actually engaging, your opinion can turn positive. Often our attitude shapes those first impressions: a negative mindset tends to produce negative judgments. If someone responds poorly at first sight, it can reveal aspects of their character.

In some cases, impressions remain unchanged because people cling to their initial reactions. On the other hand, a positive first impression can be spoiled if someone acts badly later on.

Another situation involves a job: you might feel excited and comfortable on your first day, believing the work is easy and enjoying friendly colleagues. But if you then meet a boss with a bad attitude, your view of the job can sour, and you may no longer like it. This shows how quickly first opinions can shift once new information surfaces.

In conclusion, first impressions are significant as they represent our earliest thoughts about people or situations. While they often evolve based on attitude and additional experiences, they sometimes stay fixed. If first impressions never changed, we would miss the chance to understand others more fully.

Imagine a school where older and younger students join together in one program to complete activities, work on projects, and learn from each other. Such a group could improve learning by combining different perspectives and skills.

Think about including in your school a program designed to help students grasp subjects more quickly and deeply. You could receive peer support in topics you find challenging, and since your classmates are closer in age, their explanations might feel more relatable and easier to understand. Often, students hesitate to ask adults for assistance because of pressure or fear of judgment, but talking with peers can feel more relaxed and encouraging.

Now consider how valuable it would be to have a regular gathering where anyone can seek help, exchange ideas, and socialize. While you usually spend time with your usual friends at school, a program open to everyone would introduce you to new classmates you might not otherwise meet. Building connections across different grades can make the school environment friendlier and more inclusive.

With this setup, you would not only bond with peers but also learn something new each day from students who offer their own strengths and experiences. Whether you struggle with math, writing, or science, someone in the group can help and, in turn, benefit from your knowledge. This exchange fosters a sense of community where everyone contributes and receives support.

If you believe such a program could enhance learning and social life at your school, talk to a teacher or the principal. Share your ideas, gather interested students, and work together to launch a new initiative. By taking this step, you can help create a more collaborative and welcoming school for all.

Having a good attitude is not just helpful; it can be essential for achieving success in your career, relationships, and personal life. A friendly and positive demeanor often opens doors to new chances and helps you advance more easily. For instance, someone who supports coworkers and completes tasks carefully is more likely to earn praise or promotion. In a romantic context, a warm and attentive partner usually attracts affection in return, creating a loving bond.

First of all, a constructive attitude at work can make you stand out. Employers and colleagues prefer people who are cooperative and approachable, since such individuals contribute to a pleasant environment and boost team performance. I remember when my uncle was considered for a promotion last year; out of three candidates, most coworkers voted for him because they found him kind and reliable. His positive attitude convinced everyone that he was the right choice, and this trust won him the new role.

Furthermore, a healthy attitude combined with open communication is key in romantic relationships. Respecting each other's views and discussing problems calmly can prevent bigger conflicts later on. For example, my parents taught me how they solve disagreements through conversation instead of arguments. Their peaceful approach has helped them stay together without unnecessary tension and has shown me that a loving relationship grows stronger when both partners stay positive.

Some argue that success does not always depend on having a good attitude. There are those who believe a tough or even rude manner does not block professional or political achievement. A case in point is the president of El Salvador, whose unfavorable personality has not prevented him from rising to power. However, many people admit that although they accept his leadership, they do not truly admire him for his style. This example suggests that you may reach a high position despite an unpleasant attitude, but you will gain little genuine support or respect.

Overall, people with positive personalities find it easier to build friendships and maintain helpful connections. Those who remain unkind or aloof risk being avoided, no matter what they accomplish. In conclusion, cultivating a friendly and engaging attitude helps you achieve your goals and enjoy stronger relationships throughout life.

At Generic School, 89% of students are opposed to the idea of adding an extra hour and a half to each school day. They feel that this change would interfere with their important after-school responsibilities, such as part-time work, homework, and caring for younger family members.

A large number of students hold jobs once classes end. They need this income to help cover living costs and to support their parents. Because many parents work long shifts, students often look after their siblings at home. This duty involves more than just watching them play—it means making sure they eat well, stay safe, and have clean clothes. When younger children nap, older students can tackle household chores like cleaning or doing laundry. In doing so, they ease the burden on parents, who don’t have to worry about chores after coming home from work.

High school brings its own challenges. Regular homework must be finished to maintain good grades, and bigger projects can demand hours of planning and research. If students fall behind, their overall performance can suffer. To avoid this, many form study groups with friends. Not only does this help them learn, but it also makes studying more enjoyable. Celebrating graduation and making their families proud motivates them to keep up academically.

Having a job also teaches valuable skills. Earning their own money means students don’t always have to ask for an allowance. They learn about responsibility, time management, and teamwork. Working after school, though, can be exhausting—especially when they have early classes the next morning. Some students are fortunate to work with friends, which makes the experience more pleasant, but it still takes away hours that could be spent resting or studying.

Because most students juggle jobs, family care, and academic work, they believe an extended school day would be impractical. For these reasons, the vast majority at Generic School disagree with lengthening the school hours.

Some people argue that students need cell phones in class to access the internet for assignments, but I believe these devices do more harm than good. They distract classmates, encourage chatting during lessons, enable cheating on tests, and even harm students’ health.

First, cell phones often create disruptions. Instead of paying attention, some students play music or watch videos while the teacher is speaking. This noise and movement make it hard for others to concentrate. If a student insists on using their phone against the teacher’s wishes, an argument can erupt, upsetting the whole class. When one pupil constantly disturbs the lesson, schools may eventually decide to exclude them to keep order.

Second, having a cell phone in class tempts students to chat with friends instead of listening. While the teacher explains a topic, some students send messages or share jokes online. Their focus shifts from learning to socializing, which damages their image among peers. In extreme cases, rude or embarrassing images might be circulated, causing the victim to feel ashamed or anxious about returning to school.

Third, cell phones make it easier to cheat during tests. If a student brings a phone into an exam room, they can quickly look up answers instead of relying on their own knowledge. This not only gives dishonest students an unfair advantage, but also discourages honest students who study hard. Over time, students may lose confidence in their own abilities and depend on cheating rather than learning.

Finally, constant use of phones in class reduces participation in activities and discussion. Students spend more time staring at screens than engaging with classmates or the teacher’s questions. This habit also harms their health: too much screen time can strain the eyes and limit brain development. When students are glued to their phones, they miss valuable social interaction and critical thinking exercises.

In conclusion, cell phones in the classroom create disruptions, lead to chatting and cheating, and prevent active participation, all while posing health risks. For these reasons, students should not use their phones during lessons.

Thomas Jefferson once asked whether constant activity leads to greater achievements or if taking time to pause also has value. While some people find comfort in inactivity, others believe that hard work opens doors to new possibilities. I support the idea that staying active, embracing challenges, and seeking connections are essential for creating opportunities.

Not everyone agrees, though. Many feel they lack the resources or support to expand their options. For example, someone with limited money or a difficult background might think they cannot improve their situation. Yet life rarely offers easy solutions. My grandfather shared how tough his childhood was: his family was poor, and there were days when his five siblings could only eat once. Despite these hardships, he never lost hope. He often said, “One day, everything will change.” By holding onto this belief, he found chances to build a better life for his family. His story reminds me that if we want something, we must be prepared to struggle for it.

Moreover, making the most of our time can help us reach our dreams more quickly. When we dedicate ourselves fully, we can achieve goals we once thought impossible, whether it’s owning a nice car, buying a big house, or finding ways to support others. People who never give up often see results faster and inspire those around them. Through hard work, they discover new paths and help their communities grow.

Finally, staying connected and curious every day is vital. If we limit ourselves to one path, we might miss other rewarding directions. I remember thinking about my own dreams and realizing that exploring different options would bring me closer to them. By asking questions, building relationships, and refusing to stay stagnant, we create a world of possibilities. Nothing happens by itself; we must step out of our comfort zones.

In short, moving forward, working hard, and forming connections are key to unlocking opportunities. Those who stay idle may never experience the remarkable achievements that await those willing to explore, persevere, and reach for more.

Many schools decide against offering distance learning because they believe it is not the most effective way for students to study. First, when students attend classes from home, they often miss the immediate support that teachers and classmates provide in person. If a learner does not understand a concept, it is much easier to ask a question right away in a traditional classroom than to wait for an online response or struggle with technical issues during a video call.

Second, the school environment itself plays a key role in education. Being on campus gives students a routine and a focused atmosphere that encourages concentration. Classrooms are designed for learning, with fewer home-related distractions such as household chores, siblings, or personal devices. This structured setting helps students stay on task and develop good study habits, which they might find hard to maintain when learning from home.

Third, home-based classes often come with too many temptations. Phones, social media, and television can easily interrupt an online lesson. Without the physical separation between “home” and “school,” students may find it difficult to stay motivated or organized. This distraction can lead to lower quality of work and missed learning opportunities.

Despite these drawbacks, distance learning can be helpful for certain groups. Students who must work after school or those who have family responsibilities—like young parents caring for a baby—can benefit from the flexibility of online courses. Immigrant learners, who need extra time to practice a new language, may also find video lessons more convenient than juggling travel and class schedules. For these individuals, being able to study from home allows them to balance education with other essential commitments.

However, these positive cases are exceptions rather than the rule. Most learners gain more from face-to-face interaction, immediate feedback, and a disciplined environment provided by schools. When education becomes too flexible, it can lose the structure that helps students progress steadily and confidently.

In conclusion, distance learning does offer advantages for specific situations, but for the majority of students, attending classes in person remains the best choice. The support of teachers, the dedicated learning space, and fewer distractions all contribute to a stronger educational experience. For most learners, going to school and engaging directly with teachers and peers leads to deeper understanding and better results.

A positive attitude plays a crucial role in achieving success throughout life. When people approach situations with optimism, they are more motivated to improve their work, focus on studies, and get better results overall. By staying positive at school, in the workplace, and in everyday interactions, individuals can overcome obstacles and make significant progress toward their ambitions.

The first benefit of a positive mindset is that it strengthens relationships with others. When we treat friends and colleagues with kindness and understanding, we create a supportive environment. For instance, if someone is frustrated or upset, offering encouraging words and a cheerful outlook can help them feel valued and calmer. This approach builds trust, improves communication, and leads to deeper connections in both social and professional settings.

Another advantage of maintaining an optimistic attitude is that it encourages perseverance in reaching personal goals. Difficult challenges often require persistent effort, and a hopeful outlook prevents us from giving up too soon. I have experienced times when a task seemed too complex, yet by reminding myself of past successes and keeping a positive spirit, I continued practicing until I succeeded. This persistence and belief in oneself are essential for accomplishing even the most demanding objectives.

In addition, a positive attitude can enhance job performance and career development. Employees who greet new assignments with enthusiasm tend to learn quickly, adapt well to changes, and demonstrate leadership qualities. These traits draw the attention of managers and can lead to promotions or salary increases over time. Furthermore, a positive approach helps in managing stress and staying organized during busy periods at work.

In conclusion, a positive attitude is an invaluable asset for success in every aspect of life. Without optimism, people may struggle to take action or lose motivation when challenges appear. By cultivating a positive outlook, we improve our relationships, persist until we achieve our goals, and excel in our careers, ultimately leading to a more fulfilling and successful life.

I believe strongly in the power of individuality. It’s inspiring when people make their own decisions and follow their own paths. Many of my friends simply imitate what others do, but I prefer to choose for myself. I like doing things because I want to, not because someone else tells me to.

At home, my family often reacts negatively whenever I speak up. They rarely listen to my ideas, and that frustrates me. This lack of support only makes me more determined to assert my own views and act on my own wishes. I want my voice to count in my life, rather than always bending to someone else’s opinion.

I’ve noticed that too many people depend on others for guidance, and that dependence can limit personal growth. Even in history class we learned that in the past individuals had little freedom and were pressured to conform. Today, many still feel they need approval from friends or family before they dare to be themselves.

Two years ago, I moved from Puerto Rico, and that change showed me how much I value independence. Arriving here completely transformed my life. I began to appreciate every opportunity because I understood the sacrifice behind it. Learning a new language and adjusting to unfamiliar customs was hard, but it taught me the true meaning of perseverance.

School became one of my biggest challenges. I often felt alone in class, unable to ask questions or join discussions. It was painful to sit silently while everyone else participated. After a while, I even started skipping classes because I felt I had no support—neither at school nor at home.

Sometimes I questioned whether I belonged here. I faced prejudice simply for speaking Spanish, even though Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens. That unfair treatment hurt, yet it also motivated me to keep going. I remind myself each day that I have a purpose and that my background is part of my strength.

The main reason I stay committed is my mother. She did everything she could for us back in Puerto Rico, always giving us her best despite hardships. Now I want to succeed for her, to repay her sacrifices and show that her efforts were not in vain.

Because I believe in myself and value my own opinions, I choose to live according to my own principles. I know that by trusting my judgments and working hard each day, I will overcome obstacles and continue to grow as an individual.

When you need guidance, it’s rare that you rely on just one person’s view. Talking to several people can help you make a wiser decision and lower the cost of missed opportunities. Most of us seek more than one opinion so we can weigh different perspectives, rather than depending entirely on a single viewpoint.

One advantage of consulting multiple people is the variety of choices you gain. Each person offers distinct ideas, and you might adopt one of their suggestions. That choice can turn out well or poorly, but by hearing many options, you understand the potential consequences of each. Every decision involves opportunity costs—you might gain something valuable or face drawbacks that affect your mood, your progress, or even shape your future. By considering various ideas, you’re better prepared to choose the path that aligns with your goals.

Another benefit is learning from others’ experiences. When you listen to different voices, you can cross out the options that have already led to success or failure in someone else’s life. This way, you pick the advice that seems most reliable, whether it promises a positive outcome or warns of pitfalls. Later on, you can share what you’ve learned with friends facing similar issues. In this way, gathering opinions not only helps you handle your own situation but also enables you to support others, turning that knowledge into a helpful resource.

However, asking for many viewpoints isn’t without its downsides. Too many opinions can leave you feeling confused or pressured. You might start doubting the idea you first liked or feel overwhelmed by the differences among suggestions. This stress can make the decision feel even harder, and the outcome—whether great or terrible—can depend on which advice you finally choose. Sorting through conflicting recommendations takes time and energy, and it’s stressful to know that one wrong choice could lead to disappointing results.

Overall, talking to several people for advice gives you a wider range of options and valuable lessons from others’ experiences. Yet it also brings the challenge of deciding among conflicting viewpoints. Balancing these pros and cons is key to making an informed choice that feels right for you.

Thomas Jefferson famously observed that taking action, no matter how small, is better than remaining idle. When we devote ourselves to tasks, we move forward and achieve more. Some achievements are remarkable, like designing a new invention. Others are simple, such as learning to play an instrument by practising every day. Even if we dream of exploring other dimensions or travelling back in time, we might begin designing a machine that could one day make it possible. Everyday chores also count: tidying up the home, preparing a meal, or completing school assignments contribute to our sense of accomplishment. Without consistent effort, we would lack many of the comforts and technologies we enjoy today.

Our successes can be individual or collective. In sports, teammates combine their talents to win matches. In music, an orchestra’s performance relies on each musician’s dedication. In a video game company, designers, artists, and programmers join forces to create a game that players later enjoy, whether they compete alone or in teams. Collaborating not only produces results but also teaches us communication and cooperation. Moreover, personal hobbies—gardening, painting, or simply playing outside—help us stay active and productive.

While action is important, rest also has its place. Taking occasional breaks, getting enough sleep, and relaxing for a while help us reduce stress and recover our energy. After hours of hard work or study, we might have a short nap, cook a favourite meal, watch some television, or chat with friends. These moments of pause prepare us to return to our duties with renewed focus. However, spending all day doing nothing—sleeping without any activity—deprives us of progress. Chronic laziness can become a habit, tempting us to choose the easiest path in every situation. It is far better to adopt a balanced approach: stay active, take only necessary rests, and keep our motivation high so we can continue achieving meaningful goals.

To conserve energy and resources, some businesses have adopted a four-day work week, with each day consisting of ten hours. Should your school follow this model by extending the school day two hours? I do not agree with adding those two hours, because it would be very stressful for students and leave them with insufficient time to do their homework after school. On the other hand, it would also pose significant problems for schools.

In the first place, I think this plan would disadvantage students who have other responsibilities after school. For example, I have a job after school and need to be there at four o’clock, but if my school followed this model, I would lose my job because school would end two hours later and it would be too late for me to go to work. This shows that if the school adopted this model, not only I but also other students who work after school would be affected.

Second, two more hours of school would be very stressful for students, because classes would be longer than usual, so students would get tired and would not concentrate on what the teacher is saying. Also, students would not have enough time to do their homework after school, because they would arrive home late and tired and would not feel like doing their homework, knowing that they need to rest for the next day of school. With this in mind, students’ grades would suffer, since they would not turn in their homework.

Some say that extending the school day by two hours would be a big problem for student attendance, because students would not show up every single day, being tired from the day before. Therefore, following this model would not be a good idea, because attendance is very important for schools and necessary for students to pass their school year.

In the final analysis, this routine would not be easy for students to face, even knowing that there would still be only four days of school. As a student, I would be affected in my daily routine. Students would be very stressed and tired during class, and this would affect their attendance and, as a result, their grades.

Some companies have switched to a four-day workweek with ten-hour shifts to save energy and resources. Could our school adopt a similar plan by adding two hours to each day? I do not believe this change would be beneficial. Extending the school day would place undue strain on students, leave them with little time for homework, and could even undermine school attendance.

First of all, many students juggle responsibilities outside the classroom. For instance, I work part-time and must arrive at my job by four o’clock. If classes ended later, I would no longer be able to keep that position and would lose important income. I am not alone in this situation—numerous classmates rely on afternoon jobs or have family duties. A longer school day would force them to choose between work or household obligations and their education, creating serious conflicts.

Moreover, adding two extra hours of lessons would make the school day feel excessively long. Sitting in class from early morning until late afternoon can lead to fatigue and a drop in concentration. When students finally return home, they are often too tired to tackle assignments or study effectively. As a result, homework may be rushed or skipped entirely, which can lower grades and increase stress. In the long run, falling behind on coursework undermines learning and damages students’ confidence.

Another major issue is attendance. If the day drags on well past its usual finish time, some pupils might start missing days more frequently simply because they feel exhausted. Regular attendance is crucial for absorbing material and meeting the requirements to pass each grade. Lower attendance rates would counteract any benefits the new schedule was meant to provide.

In conclusion, although a four-day week with longer school days might seem economical, it would place too heavy a burden on students’ schedules and well-being. It would interfere with jobs, limit time for rest and homework, and could even discourage students from attending regularly. As someone who would be directly affected, I feel strongly that our school should maintain its current hours rather than add two more each day.

In today’s world, there are so many tasks waiting for our attention. If each of us looked out for our neighbourhood, we could create a cleaner, healthier environment. For example, rather than dropping litter whenever we walk, we could pick up trash and show that even small efforts bring noticeable improvements.

I have seen groups around the world making a real impact by cleaning rivers, parks and streets. Their determination proves that waiting for someone else is not an option. We can follow their example by doing our part every day. When we keep helping and stay committed, our surroundings become better and our quality of life improves.

Taking action should be a shared goal in every community. Being determined and productive means making things happen instead of hoping they will. Doing something—no matter how small—is always more effective than doing nothing. By giving our time and energy, we keep our neighbourhoods vibrant, possible and full of promise.

One reason you do not have to say that first impressions are almost impossible to change is that if the person you are meeting is not having a good day, that can affect the first impression. He or she is not going to be comfortable talking or having a conversation in that moment.

If i would have to give an example, it would be the history of me and my best friend. The first time when i met him was in my math class; he did not even want to talk to me or be my partner. When i asked him about problems that i did not understand, he ignored me and did not answer.

To conclude, if i would have to take a position on this issue i would disagree. In my circle of friends there are two of them that did not give me a good impression, and if you look at us today we are good friends. That is why you do not have to say that the first impression is literally impossible to change.

Based on my own experiences, I do not believe it is true that first impressions cannot be changed. People have the ability to grow and reveal different sides of themselves over time. Often, a first meeting fails to capture someone’s true character, especially if they are distracted or just not interested in that moment.

One reason a first impression may be misleading is that someone might simply be having a bad day. If a person is tired, stressed, or preoccupied, they can come across as unfriendly or uninterested when actually they are quite the opposite. Judging someone solely on that brief encounter is unfair because it ignores the possibility of future interaction.

For example, I met my best friend in a math class. At first, he refused to partner with me and ignored my questions about the homework. I assumed he was rude and unfriendly. However, as we spent more time together on group work and projects, he realized I was a helpful and dependable classmate. Our relationship gradually grew into a strong friendship.

In my wider circle, I can think of two other friends who also gave poor first impressions. Yet, once we got to know each other better, those impressions completely changed. Today, we are very close.

In conclusion, I disagree with the idea that first impressions are impossible to alter. Given more time, patience, and understanding, initial judgments can be overturned and genuine relationships can form.

Students gain self-confidence through both positive feedback and tangible successes. While they often dedicate themselves fully to their tasks, recognition can push them to reach higher. Even when their work is not flawless, a few words of encouragement can inspire them to improve. In this way, praise and achievement both contribute to developing a respectable level of self-esteem.

First, when teachers or peers acknowledge a student’s effort, it boosts the student’s belief in their own abilities. Compliments for hard work, regardless of the final result, reassure students that their efforts matter. This sense of appreciation not only motivates individual learners to perform better but also sets an example for classmates. Observing someone receive praise can encourage others to work harder, raising the overall standard in the class.

Second, real achievements are powerful sources of self-esteem. When students succeed in a project or overcome a difficult challenge, they experience genuine pride. Such accomplishments show them what they are capable of, reinforcing their confidence for future tasks. Moreover, successful students serve as role models, inspiring their peers to aim for similar achievements. In this way, one student’s success can have a positive impact on the whole group.

In conclusion, both constructive praise and real successes are essential for nurturing healthy self-esteem in learners. Praise encourages students to continue striving, while achievements provide concrete evidence of their capabilities. Together, these elements help students develop motivation, resilience, and confidence in their own skills, creating a positive cycle of effort and accomplishment.

I believe that having a 10-hour day is far more effective than an 8-hour schedule, because it helps us save energy, water, and time. Working four days of 10 hours equals the same 40 hours as the traditional five-day week, yet it leaves an extra day for rest or overtime if needed.

At school, shifting from 8 am–4 pm to a 10-hour day could bring similar benefits. If classes ran two additional hours, students would finish after ten hours and attend only four days of school per week. That extra day off would give them more sleep, extra time for chores or part-time jobs, and weekends free for assignments. Likewise, teachers would also enjoy a longer weekend.

Teenagers who struggle with early mornings would benefit from better rest, which improves concentration and energy in class. Many high school students juggle schoolwork with up to 32–38 hours of paid work each week, leaving little time for homework. Adopting a four-day schedule would give them much-needed flexibility and help them meet their goals without sacrificing rest.

It’s surprising how people’s behavior changes once they really get to know you. I’ve always tried hard to get along with others, but not everyone is kind. Some hurt or exclude people without even trying to understand them. Because of this, I often find myself alone. Too many people gossip about others, and those who are targets of bullying usually stay silent out of fear.

I’ve learned not to let hurtful words affect me too much. People are free to say whatever they want, but their opinions are their problem, not mine. Still, when someone who has ignored you in better times needs help, they suddenly come back looking for support. Whenever I feel upset or stressed, I turn to soccer. Playing helps me forget my worries and clears my mind.

If I could, I would organize regular soccer games so everyone who wishes could join. This way, they could forget their problems for a while, just as I do. Sports exist because they let people enjoy themselves without fighting. Another idea is to go to the movies or to watch live sports—basketball, volleyball, whatever—to meet new people. In my view, there’s always a solution to problems if we all treat each other with respect.

One thing we all want is to feel safe in our communities, far from gangs that only make things worse. Parents and neighbors should work together to protect those who are vulnerable. Education is also important: many young people study hard so they can lift their families out of poverty. Even a high school diploma can open the door to a decent job, which is a big step toward a better future.

If someone steals from you or you feel threatened, going to the police can help recover what was lost and stop bullies from acting again. No one should be too afraid to ask for help, because showing fear often encourages bullies to push harder. Being clever in one area doesn’t mean people will treat you kindly, especially if you react angrily.

When friends get upset, they can change and scare you. To prevent conflicts, it’s better to invite potential bullies—or anyone you want to get to know—to join a sports game or a day at the beach. Shared fun can turn strangers into friends. Still, it’s wise not to reveal your greatest weakness, because if you do, others might use it to hurt you. That’s why I guard my private struggles closely.

Failure is often seen as an obstacle, but it actually helps us learn and grow so we can reach our goals. When we make mistakes, we discover what doesn’t work and avoid repeating those errors. Imagine I dreamed of becoming a professional soccer player. I had played for top youth teams, earned the title of best player, and never been dropped from a squad. One day my coach told me about an upcoming trial for a professional club and asked me to prepare. He handed me a training plan that included a strict diet and daily workouts. Even on days when I felt worn out or tempted to eat junk food, I pushed myself to stick to the program.

When trial day arrived, I was as ready as I could be. We warmed up, ran drills, and I felt I performed better than anyone else on the field. Yet at the end of the day, when they announced those who had succeeded, my name wasn’t called. I had failed to make the team. In that moment, I faced a choice: give up on soccer or pick myself up and try once more. This kind of failure shows how dedicated you truly are. It tests your patience, your passion, and your commitment to push forward even after being knocked down.

A real-life example of this spirit appears in the book Pursuit of Happyness. The main character invents a portable device and tries to sell it, but no one shows interest. He’s also a single father who loses his home and spends weeks living on the streets. Despite homelessness and constant rejection, he continues knocking on doors to find buyers. Finally, someone gives his device a chance, and after they spread the word about how useful it is, others begin purchasing it too. His success comes not from avoiding failure but from refusing to quit when everything seemed hopeless.

These stories illustrate that setbacks are not the end but a vital part of any journey toward achievement. Each failure teaches us valuable lessons, builds resilience, and prepares us for future challenges. In the end, it is our ability to learn from mistakes and keep going that leads us to success. Failure, in fact, is the key to unlocking our greatest potential.

John Lubbock, a British naturalist and politician, once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make.” At first glance, our upbringing and past experiences may seem to shape who we become, but in reality, we hold the power through the choices we make each day. Even if someone grows up with abusive parents, they do not have to repeat that cycle. Instead, they can use those difficult moments to grow stronger and develop a character built on resilience and compassion. While people often mistake personality—how someone acts in a given situation—for character, which is the deeper set of moral qualities we cultivate, it’s important to remember that only we decide what kind of person we want to be. At the end of the day, we answer to ourselves, not to the opinions of others, and our character is ours to create.

Outward appearances can lead to hasty judgments. Someone might hear a rumor and label a person as unfriendly or selfish without ever learning their story. Yet when you share the struggles you’ve overcome, like standing up to adversity, people stop judging and start admiring. They ask, “How did you become so persistent?” or “What gave you the courage to stay independent?” Because you chose to face challenges and learn from them, you leave a legacy that others respect. Only you control the steps that reveal your true character.

Character is not defined by a single action or statement. Consider the impact of losing a family member to illness. At first, you might be overwhelmed by grief and disbelief. However, in time you can decide to honor their memory by persevering and making each day count. Although you may still feel sadness, you push forward, showing that your character grows stronger through hardship. This steady determination proves that you shape who you are, rather than being shaped solely by loss.

Everyone encounters moments of self-doubt when the mind whispers, “You can’t do this,” or “You’ll never succeed.” These negative thoughts can hold you back if you let them. But your character exists to help you break down the walls life puts in your path. By trusting your instincts and following what you believe is right, you turn impossibilities into achievements. In doing so, you stand out not just for what you do but for who you are at your core.

Life isn’t a menu of choices offered by others; it’s a journey where you decide what fits you best. As Lubbock reminds us, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make.” So embrace every moment, enjoy the process, and build your character with every decision you take.

Many people believe that being inactive has its own place, but in reality everyone needs to stay busy and pursue goals throughout their lives. When a person remains active, they are more likely to achieve success and create positive change not only for themselves but also for future generations in their families. In contrast, inactivity often shows a lack of motivation, which can lead someone to neglect their own life and the well-being of others around them.

A clear example of this problem is unemployment combined with laziness. Some people have no job but do not make any effort to find one. Instead of using their time to apply for positions or learn new skills, they waste hours doing nothing. As a result, they remain poor and struggle to secure a better future. In many countries, you can see people begging on the streets instead of seeking honest work. Although opportunities may exist, an inactive person simply ignores them. This reluctance to work also affects their children, who often have to accompany their parents in asking strangers for money. Clearly, inactivity in adults can harm the prospects of the next generation.

Students, too, can develop habits of laziness. In group projects, some pupils choose only the easiest tasks and leave the harder work to others. This attitude may seem harmless at school, but it carries on into adult life, where most challenges are not simple. Many young people expect their future careers to be effortless, so they avoid taking on responsibilities or learning the necessary skills. If students do not adopt an active approach while they are still young, they may struggle to find purpose and direction later on.

Some argue that unemployment allows people more time with family, but free time should not mean doing nothing. Even when they are unoccupied by a regular job, individuals can volunteer, study, or contribute to their community in other ways. Reducing inactivity could also benefit national economies. When fewer people are idle, productivity increases and poverty levels drop, leading to a stronger society overall.

In conclusion, living without purpose is often a result of prolonged inactivity. To build a successful future, people must always be engaged in meaningful activities. Active individuals work with clear objectives and are more likely to reach their goals. On the other hand, those who choose to remain lazy miss out on opportunities and fail to grow. Therefore, everyone should strive to be active rather than idle, because only then can they achieve real success in life.

I believe Ralph Waldo Emerson overstates the value of complete independence. While being self-reliant has its benefits, there are many moments in life when we must rely on others. True personal growth comes from balancing independence with collaboration. In the following paragraphs, I will discuss how teamwork can improve our work life, our social interactions, and the choices we make.

At work, you may find yourself paired with someone whose attitude you dislike. Instead of insisting on going it alone, you could try to cooperate and learn from each other. That openness can forge stronger relationships and make tasks easier. Also, if your current job doesn’t align with your dream career, you shouldn’t simply resign yourself to unhappiness. You can pursue your goal with help from colleagues, mentors, or networks, rather than isolating yourself. Many businesses succeed because employees unite in pursuit of common objectives. In the same way, an individual worker can benefit by joining forces with others instead of sticking strictly to their own methods.

In social settings, some people prefer to keep to themselves, either out of comfort or a desire for attention. Their background or past experiences might have shaped this tendency. Living in society is often more complicated than it seems, especially if you know someone who avoids contact. Still, with patience and kindness, you can encourage them to connect with others—or they might seek help on their own. Over time, individuals who once avoided social situations can grow more open, showing that support and companionship play a key role in personal change.

Every day we face decisions that shape who we become. You can let outside forces dictate your life or choose your own path. For instance, even a president cannot act entirely alone; they need cooperation from Congress to pass laws. Similarly, we can decide whether to pursue our goals with the aid of others or to let circumstances push us in a different direction.

In conclusion, we each decide how much we rely on ourselves versus others. As I have shown through workplace examples, social relationships, and decision-making, embracing collaboration does not diminish our individuality. In fact, it enriches our ability to become the person we truly wish to be.

Partnerships between schools and companies give students a firsthand view of different careers before they head to college. By working closely with businesses, students can see what daily tasks look like and decide which fields truly appeal to them. If my school teams up with various firms, I would gain insight into the kinds of roles I might enjoy. I believe I am a good candidate for this opportunity because I thrive around people, I want to discover what job suits me best, and I hope to get real experience in a professional setting.

I enjoy being around others and find that it lifts my spirits. Whether I am among friends or newcomers, starting a conversation quickly makes me feel at ease. For instance, during a recent class project, I was placed with classmates I had never met. At first, I hesitated, but once I spoke up, we connected and later became friends. This shows that I can adapt easily to new teams, which is essential when working in a company.

Many students already have a clear idea of their future careers, but I’m still exploring my strengths. I often wonder what skills I excel at and have yet to find a definite answer. If I’m chosen for this partnership, it will open doors for me to test different roles and learn where my interests lie. Knowing my preferred type of work early on would help me avoid spending years in a job that doesn’t fit my talents or passions.

Gaining hands-on experience is crucial before committing to a career. When I considered working in a restaurant, I spoke with a friend who worked there to understand the tasks involved. Likewise, some jobs require practical experience to qualify. I dream of becoming a nurse and have always wanted to explore what nursing entails day to day. Being part of this program would allow me to step into a healthcare setting and learn directly from professionals.

In short, selecting me would benefit both the company and myself: I bring enthusiasm for teamwork, a genuine desire to find my ideal job, and a readiness to gain workplace experience. This partnership represents a smart way for students like me to learn about careers before making long-term decisions.

Michelangelo’s statement suggests the real danger is not aiming too high and missing our target, but setting our sights too low and reaching it easily. I agree that achieving success depends more on the effort we invest than on being the best, so we can accomplish anything if we work hard. However, I disagree with the idea that we must lower our expectations; I believe we can and should set our goals high, since a challenging aim pushes us to develop. At the same time, even a modest objective can be met with enough determination. For instance, I am preparing for my SOL exams to enter 12th grade and earn my diploma. If I strive for top marks, I might not get a perfect score but will learn a great deal; if I only aim to pass, I will succeed but miss the chance to grow. Everyone faces this choice in work, school, or personal life—whether to choose low standards that ensure easy wins or higher ones that drive us forward. In the end, it is our commitment, rather than the level of our goal, that determines how far we go.

No one is born successful; everyone must work hard and overcome obstacles.

In conclusion, experiencing failure can be an important step on the path to success.

An enjoyable way to spend time outdoors is to ride your bike, especially in summer. You can see places such as stores, the river, birds, and cars, and you can bring food and have a picnic. You will also see other people riding their bikes, and you can stop at a store to buy food while you ride. As you cycle, you can visit famous places like a museum or a restaurant and watch people there. Riding your bike lets you go wherever you want, so you can discover truly beautiful spots. Along the river, you might see people taking pictures, and you can visit the zoo to see beautiful flowers. You will notice other cyclists who enjoy biking, too. It is an enjoyable activity because you see many beautiful places and feel excited while riding.

It is also enjoyable because you get to see places, and if you would like, you can bring your own food. You can ride with your kids and see different places together or take your friends for even more fun. You can have a picnic with them or with your family, whoever you would like to bring while riding. You may see beautiful art and designs as you explore these locations. This activity is fun because you discover new places and learn more about them.

Riding a bicycle outdoors is a great way to enjoy summer days. As you pedal through the streets, you can pass by stores, rivers, parks and even historic buildings. You might spot birds flying overhead, cars passing by, and other cyclists enjoying the weather. If you bring a packed lunch, you can stop by the riverside for a small picnic and relax under a tree.

Cycling also lets you discover popular spots like museums, restaurants or parks. You can easily pause at a café to buy a snack or cold drink before heading to the next place. Riding freely means you choose your own route, so you might turn down a quiet lane to find a hidden garden, or head towards a zoo where you can admire the animals from afar. Some people pause to take photos of colorful flower beds, sculptures or street art they find along the way.

This activity is family-friendly and suitable for all ages. You could take your children to explore new neighbourhoods, or invite friends to join you for a group ride. Bringing everyone along makes it even more fun, and you can finish the trip with a picnic in a park. Sharing this experience creates happy memories and lets you learn more about your city’s culture and design.

Overall, cycling is a fun and exciting outdoor hobby. It combines exercise with the chance to see many beautiful places, try local foods and enjoy nature. Whether you ride alone or with others, every journey offers something new to explore.

People have the freedom to choose their own paths in life, and they decide what they want to become or do. However, not every choice is simple. Some options require a lot of effort, like studying hard to get good grades and then working long hours. Others may seem quicker, such as using savings or family money to start a career, but that route can be difficult too and is not available to everyone.

Where someone stands financially also affects how they make decisions. For instance, a person with plenty of funds can focus on their future more directly because they do not worry about daily expenses or debt. In contrast, someone with limited resources must consider bills, loans, and other costs, so reaching their goals takes longer and demands extra effort.

I once knew a friend who was balancing high school and a part-time job. He decided to quit school, believing that working would bring in more money than further study. Now he does customers’ nails, which sometimes pays well but is unstable. He passed up the chance to go to college and later get a higher-paying job, and he regrets it. My brother faced a similar situation. After two years of college, he chose to stop and start working. If he had stayed in school, he might have secured a better position today.

People must think about their future carefully and make plans based on what they have and what they want to achieve. Although everyone can make their own decisions, they often need help and encouragement from family or friends. With support and hard work, they can shape their lives in a way that not only benefits them but also gives their children an easier start in making their own choices.

In my view, the greatest achievement someone can offer you is encouragement to be yourself. There’s no need to pretend or adopt a different personality; it feels far more rewarding to live honestly in this world.  

When people pretend to be someone they’re not, they mislead others about their true character. Choosing a false identity is one of the worst decisions anyone can make. I know some believe that adopting a different persona is somehow beneficial, but I firmly disagree.  

We should stop worrying about other people’s opinions and concentrate on our own happiness and the approval of those who accept us as we are. The friends who let us be genuine without passing judgment are priceless. Their acceptance is a gift, reminding us that we don’t have to change ourselves to fit in. That, to me, is the most meaningful encouragement we can receive.  

I can’t agree with Emerson’s idea that we need to conform to external expectations. We shouldn’t allow society to reshape who we are. The real triumph isn’t adjusting ourselves to meet others’ standards; it’s proudly revealing our unique qualities. Everyone has something special inside, and only by embracing our individuality can we contribute positively to the world.  

These days, many people still struggle to be authentic around others. Some mock anyone who behaves naturally, while others simply mind their own business. In modern society, we see a wide range of identities—whether someone is gay, transgender, bisexual, or heterosexual—and though this diversity can feel confusing to some, it’s perfectly normal. Acting in line with one’s true self should not be a source of judgement.

Because of her stories, she made many new acquaintances, and even some of my friends began to favor her and exclude me, since I refused to join their parties and didn’t share her fake lifestyle. Why should anyone decide what really matters in life or dictate the choices we make? Each person should be free to shape their own path. By trusting ourselves, we do not need someone else to direct every step we take.

Individuals ought to believe in their ability to choose, even when they feel uncertain. Errors often come from wrong decisions, but these mistakes teach us valuable lessons. Learning from them builds confidence, which is essential for making better choices later. In addition, understanding what truly matters comes from personal experience and self-reflection rather than outside advice.

It is common to consult experts when facing important decisions because we fear making the wrong choice. While professional guidance can be useful, it is more important to trust our own judgment first. Relying on others to solve our problems may give quick answers, but it also prevents us from developing crucial decision-making skills.

When we decide for ourselves, even if some choices prove to be errors, we learn how to improve. This process reinforces our self-reliance and equips us to handle future challenges without needing expert help.

People have different values and priorities. What is vital to one person may be unimportant to another. Therefore, everyone should take time to reflect and determine what truly matters to them personally, rather than follow a universal rule.

In conclusion, making our own choices creates a sense of security, fosters confidence for future decisions, and helps us discover what really matters in life.
