Dear Principal,

I believe updating our cafeteria menu to include healthier options is a wonderful idea. Introducing fresh, nutritious dishes and a variety of foods that many students have never tried before will benefit everyone. As a student, I am excited about the chance to enjoy more balanced meals each day.

Offering a new lunch menu will please many students who are tired of eating the same dishes almost every day. Of course, there are some students who are happy with the current offerings and might be concerned about changes. To find a solution that works for everyone, you could ask the cafeteria manager to share a list of the most and least popular meals. Based on that information, you and the cafeteria team can decide which items to replace with healthier alternatives while keeping the favorites on the menu.

Making this change will have several positive results. First, students will appreciate having their preferred meals still available, along with new choices to enjoy. This variety could set our school apart and inspire others to follow our example. Schools in other districts might see our success and update their own menus. Additionally, offering appealing healthy options can help families save money. When students dislike the cafeteria food, they often ask parents to buy takeout, which can be expensive. A more attractive school menu could prevent this extra cost and reduce the number of students leaving campus during lunch.

Trying different types of meals is exciting for many of us. Some students love experimenting with new flavors, and a more balanced menu would include both tasty and nutritious dishes. It’s also important to consider those with food allergies who sometimes cannot eat anything at school and end up skipping lunch. By adding a range of healthy options, we ensure every student can find something safe and satisfying. Moreover, if students no longer need to go off campus for food, they are less likely to miss classes or face safety risks outside school grounds.

In conclusion, asking the cafeteria manager for a survey of students’ favorite and least favorite foods will guide the menu update in a way that pleases almost everyone. This approach can help us keep top choices while replacing unpopular items with healthier options. Students will be happier, parents will spend less on outside meals, and the school’s reputation will improve. Healthy lunches can support better nutrition, lower fat intake, and increased protein in our diets. I hope you will consider these suggestions and make changes that benefit the entire school community. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Many people believe that summer vacation is too short and should be adjusted. They suggest removing spring break and extending the summer holiday to run from June through August instead of ending school in May. According to this view, May is often too cool for a true summer feel, and shifting the final day of school to June would allow students to enjoy warmer weather and take family trips.

Eliminating spring break could also bring academic benefits. That week could be used for reviewing and taking important exams like the SOL tests. Schools would have extra time for students to practice key skills, and teachers could use the period for small-group lessons or fun in-school activities. Rather than pausing learning, students would receive targeted support, making them better prepared for end-of-year assessments.

Starting summer in June offers practical advantages outside academics, too. May weather can sometimes be chilly or unpredictable, but June usually brings reliable warmth. With a longer break that truly matches the season, families could plan vacations more easily, and students would have more time for outdoor recreation, sports, or simply relaxing under the sun.

In addition, replacing spring break with a week of school-based events would help students discover new talents and hobbies. Schools might organize art museum visits, music performances, or college tours, giving young people fresh experiences without losing a week of learning. This approach combines education with enjoyment, keeping students engaged right up to the end of the year.

Overall, adjusting the calendar by ending school in June, extending summer through August, and removing spring break would give students both a longer, warmer holiday and important extra time in school for tests and enrichment. This change would balance fun and learning more effectively.

By admitting you were wrong right away, you show responsibility, and things can often be resolved more smoothly. Although telling someone what they do wrong can hurt their feelings at first, it prevents false expectations. In the end, they usually appreciate your honesty because it saves them from further disappointment.

Still, I prefer honesty in my life because finding out harsh truths later from others can be much more painful. Honest feedback helps me grow and prepares me for real-life challenges, like work or family responsibilities. Life is not always fair or simple, so being ready to face reality with honesty sets us up for success.

In my view, students do not gain any real benefit from attending lessons at home via online platforms or video calls. I believe that learning in a traditional classroom is more beneficial, and here are my reasons.

Firstly, home environments are filled with distractions. Video games, social media, household chores and family members can all divert attention from studies. For example, if a student has three brothers and one sister at home, it becomes almost impossible to concentrate fully. In school, on the other hand, the atmosphere is more orderly and students can focus entirely on the lesson.

Secondly, face-to-face teaching allows for more precise guidance. When a teacher is physically present, they can immediately notice if a student is struggling and offer personalized support. This direct interaction makes it easier to grasp challenging topics than simply watching a screen.

Thirdly, the routine of going to school in the morning helps students retain information better. Being in a dedicated learning space and following a clear timetable keeps them attentive and motivated throughout the day. Video conferencing cannot match the structure and energy of a real classroom.

In conclusion, distance learning from home presents more disadvantages than advantages. Both students and their parents agree that attending school in person leads to better learning outcomes and overall engagement.

Are we more productive if we constantly engage in tasks? Historically, those who dedicate themselves to work have produced new inventions like cars, radios and televisions. Without effort and research, technological progress slows. Developing and refining devices not only provides jobs but also shapes our lifestyles. As more individuals invest time and creativity in innovations, our daily routines transform worldwide. Radio, television and computers exemplify these changes, becoming essential parts of everyday life.

The invention of the radio marked a major breakthrough. Early engineers struggled to find the correct frequencies and circuits, but their persistence paid off when radio broadcasts became clear and widespread. This success inspired them to tackle the next challenge: television. Engineers who had mastered radio technology applied their knowledge to transmit both images and sound. When TV sets finally appeared in homes, they offered viewers a new way to experience news and entertainment. This demand for televisions created many opportunities, from manufacturing sets to producing shows and broadcasting services.

Building on the momentum from radio and television, inventors turned to computers. Initial models were large and silent machines used for simple calculations. However, designers were determined to make computers more accessible. They added user-friendly interfaces, storage capabilities and eventually sound systems, which allowed people to interact with software, run tests and explore new fields of research. Thanks to continuous effort and innovation, computers have become vital tools in education, business and science. In conclusion, ongoing work and improvement drive technological achievements and benefit society by creating jobs and improving our quality of life.

I disagree with the proposal to shorten high school from four years to three. Although graduating earlier might seem attractive, squeezing all required courses into a shorter period would place undue pressure on students. They would need to study through summers and evenings, leaving little time to rest. As a result, their minds would grow tired, and they might struggle to master important subjects, especially elective classes that broaden their education.

In a three-year plan, schools might rush lessons and reduce the variety of courses available. Students would lose the chance to explore different interests or take part in electives that could guide their future choices. Without this freedom, they risk entering university or the workforce less prepared, missing out on experiences that help shape career goals.

Another major issue is student well-being. Trying to complete all credits quickly would increase stress and raise the likelihood of burnout. Balancing intense study, summer work, and evening assignments could overwhelm many teens. By contrast, a four-year curriculum offers a more balanced pace, giving students time for extracurricular activities, hobbies, and personal growth—elements that boost motivation and focus when they move on to higher education.

Moreover, four years in high school allow students to make informed decisions about their futures. They can consult teachers and counselors, improve skills in subjects they enjoy, and gain confidence in their choices. By graduation, they often have a clearer idea of the path they want to follow in college or in their careers.

In conclusion, while completing high school in three years might seem efficient, it leaves too little time for thorough learning, exploration of electives, and healthy rest. Maintaining the traditional four-year program ensures that students are better prepared, both academically and personally, for the challenges ahead.

I firmly believe that it is better to remain true to ourselves wherever we go rather than bend to the expectations of others. Being genuine means having confidence in our own abilities and decisions, rather than simply accepting whatever anyone tells us. When we trust ourselves, we stay on the path that leads to our personal goals. For instance, by showing others that we value our own opinions, we demonstrate strength and commitment to our self-improvement.

In a world where many people change to fit in or to chase success, holding fast to our own identity helps us resist negative influences. Society often tries to shape us into its idea of “successful,” but that model may not fit who we really are. By trusting our own judgment and focusing on our personal growth, we inspire others to do the same. Remaining true to ourselves not only preserves our sense of self-respect but also encourages those around us to believe in their own paths.

Sometimes we notice groups or individuals adopting new behaviors that promise improvement, yet these methods might not suit everyone. They may urge us to follow their rules, even if we do not feel comfortable. If we simply copy their approach, we risk losing sight of our own values. Instead, we should choose a route that aligns with our own principles, because we see where it leads and whether it truly benefits us in the long run.

There will always be people who try to discourage us or divert us from our dreams. They might point out potential failures or argue that our goals are unrealistic. However, if we maintain faith in our own vision and work hard toward it, no one can derail our progress. Trusting ourselves and aiming high helps us overcome those doubts and succeed on our own terms.

In summary, embracing who we are and pursuing what genuinely makes us happy is the best strategy. Even when society shifts and pressures us to change, we should listen to our own voice. By doing so, we achieve our dreams in an authentic way and earn the respect of others. Staying true to ourselves ultimately leads to personal satisfaction and shows others that they too can follow their own path.

Modern technology lets us do many everyday tasks without meeting anyone in person. We can borrow books online, shop through apps, and play games with a few taps on a screen. Although these options are handy, they also cut down on our face-to-face interactions.

Human contact has been the foundation of communities for centuries, and we still need it for our emotional and social health. Ordering things online or spending hours gaming may feel easy, but it stops us from speaking to new people and making unexpected friends. To keep our social skills sharp, we should set aside time to talk with others and step away from our devices.

Today’s children often have tablets before they can even walk, and it is normal to see both students and workers glued to their phones. If we don’t put down our screens now and then, we’ll lose the chance to connect with those around us and miss out on real, lasting relationships.

I agree with Winston Churchill’s view that success is about moving from one setback to another while keeping your spirit high. We all make mistakes or face disappointments, and it is unrealistic to expect perfection every time. Instead, our ability to bounce back and remain positive defines genuine triumph.

One clear example comes from my own experience in an English class last year. I prepared diligently for a test, hoping for an A+ or at least a B+, but I failed. I felt discouraged and disappointed. Then my teacher kindly offered me a second chance. I studied again, worked on my weak points, and retook the exam. This time I earned an A-. That experience taught me that a single failure does not determine our worth. What really matters is how we respond to challenges and learn from our mistakes.

A second example involves my aunt’s attempts to visit our family in El Salvador. First, she called the airline to buy a ticket but found the prices too high, so she postponed her trip for a few months. When she checked again after seven months, ticket costs had risen even more, but she decided not to wait any longer and tried to purchase a ticket. Unfortunately, the staff informed her that her ID card had expired, and she could not complete the purchase. Although she felt upset and guilty for forgetting to renew her documents, she applied for a new ID soon afterwards. After waiting three months for the updated card, she still hadn’t received it and was unable to book her flight. Despite these setbacks, my aunt remains hopeful and determined to visit this year. Her unwavering enthusiasm shows how failures need not break our resolve.

Some people argue that Churchill’s quote is not valid because they believe constant failures prove someone is a loser or incapable. They criticize those who don’t succeed at first as “stupid” or “weak.” However, I think their harsh judgment comes from a lack of perseverance and a tendency to give up too soon. True success requires patience, resilience, and optimism.

In conclusion, failures are an essential part of any journey toward achievement. Both my own test experience and my aunt’s travel attempts illustrate that the path to success often includes mistakes and obstacles. By maintaining our enthusiasm and pressing forward, we can overcome difficulties and grow stronger, ultimately reaching our goals.

Some people propose a four-day school week to reduce energy use, believing that fewer days on campus will save resources. However, I disagree with this idea because it actually means longer days. Students would spend around ten hours at school every day, which would increase their energy consumption during those extended hours.

Longer days also demand more materials and utilities. Schools would need extra supplies like paper and water to support classes running later into the afternoon. In addition, the greater reliance on electronic devices—such as computers, tablets, and monitors—would drive up electricity usage.

For these reasons, a four-day schedule may worsen resource waste rather than conserve energy in schools.

I firmly believe, as Emerson suggested, that being in situations where we must constantly give our best pushes us toward success. Embracing our individuality and relying on our own efforts helps us meet goals that might otherwise seem out of reach.

This responsibility encourages me to work harder, because I want my work to stand out. For instance, when I tackle an assignment without support from others, I focus on producing excellent results so that my effort is noticed. The possibility of earning recognition or a bonus motivates me even more. In this way, working on my own builds my confidence and sharpens my skills, which is essential if I want to become one of the top performers.

Competition also plays a key role in boosting productivity. When everyone at work knows there is a reward for the person who achieves the most or produces the best outcome, they naturally strive to surpass one another. Other employees may feel challenged and decide to improve their own performance so they can win similar benefits. This friendly rivalry raises overall output, since each person searches for new methods to increase efficiency. Similarly, in a business, someone aiming to become a leader has to outperform colleagues who share the same goal. Overcoming these personal hurdles strengthens our resolve and helps us keep moving forward, no matter how tough the circumstances.

Ultimately, being placed in demanding environments where we rely on our own strengths and face competition brings out our best qualities. It forces us to be creative, hardworking, and determined. By believing in our individuality and welcoming challenges, we learn to set high standards for ourselves and to keep improving. That is why I agree with Emerson: when we are frequently asked to give our all, we grow into more capable and accomplished individuals.

In today’s world, individuals enjoy greater freedom to form their own opinions and make decisions. Over the years, human society has changed dramatically, and now people often feel confident handling important choices by themselves. However, this confidence can sometimes lead to risky decisions made without any advice from specialists or experienced authorities.

Whenever someone faces a major decision—whether in business, health, or personal matters—it is wiser to consult an expert first. An adviser who has dealt with similar issues can point out options and warn against pitfalls. Without this help, even intelligent people can choose the wrong path. For instance, many celebrities rely on managers or agents to guide their careers. These professionals plan schedules, negotiate contracts, and steer stars away from damaging moves. If famous figures tried to handle every detail alone, many of them might find their careers in ruin.

A clear example of the danger of going it alone comes from the story of Christopher McCandless in the book Into the Wild. Believing he could survive the Alaskan wilderness by himself, he ventured out without proper gear or guidance. Because he refused to seek advice or bring adequate supplies, he was unprepared for the harsh conditions and ultimately lost his life. Had he listened to experienced outdoorsmen or planned his trip more carefully, his journey might have ended differently.

Most people seek success, but few achieve it without making careful, informed choices. Even those who initially thrive by acting independently often find they need mentors or advisors later to maintain their progress. In business and in life, obtaining expert guidance increases the chances of making the right decision. Relying solely on one’s own judgment raises the risk of serious mistakes.

In conclusion, consulting experts and authorities when faced with significant decisions is always more beneficial than acting alone. Seeking advice not only helps avoid dangerous errors but also supports a smoother path to success.

Using clear examples is one of the most effective ways to help others learn. When a teacher takes the time to show how something is done, it feels like genuine support rather than just a list of rules. Demonstrations guide students step by step and make new ideas easier to grasp.

I remember how my grandmother taught me early on. She showed me how to organize my school supplies, offered advice on solving simple problems, and encouraged me to pass that knowledge along to friends. I wanted to explain things I knew well—how to kick a soccer ball properly or how to locate information online. By showing rather than simply telling, I saw my friends understand more quickly.

Over the years, I surprised myself by mastering skills I never imagined—repairing my old toys, fixing computer issues, and tackling other small projects around the house. Each time I followed a clear example, I felt more confident to try it on my own.

I’ve had teachers who used examples in every lesson, and I learned much faster in their classes. In contrast, some instructors seemed irritated or impatient, which made students avoid asking questions. When a teacher gets angry or just lectures without illustrations, many learners lose interest and say they dislike school.

Showing an example doesn’t just explain the task—it also models good behavior. How we act in class or at home matters, because others notice our attitude and may ask us for tips. If they see someone calmly solving a problem, they feel more comfortable seeking advice from that person.

Of course, examples aren’t the only influence. We also learn by simply observing people around us. Just by watching, I’ve picked up new tools and techniques that will help me in the future.

I don’t have a definite plan for after high school yet. Right now, I’m drawn to technology and electricity—two fields I find fascinating. Life can change in a moment, so I want to make the most of every opportunity.

Everyone makes mistakes. The important part is to learn from what went wrong or ask someone for guidance on improving our behavior, whether at school or in other settings. That way, each error becomes a lesson and a chance to grow.

Besides examples, we can learn from newspapers, TV news, or simply by asking thoughtful questions. There are many paths to knowledge, and each person finds the approach that suits them best.

A good example also shows us our own abilities. It doesn’t matter how old we are or where we come from—we all have special skills to share. Even a small piece of advice can make a difference in someone’s day.

People often come to me for a listening ear or some guidance because they trust that I will be patient and helpful. I try to empathize with their situation and offer support without judgment.

We live in a world full of family, friends, and neighbors who care. Each of us has a purpose, even if it isn’t clear right now. We can rely on others and, in turn, be there for them.

Finally, I set personal goals like arriving on time to every class and passing my SOL exams. Punctuality and commitment matter to me, and I find inspiration in teachers who demonstrate responsibility and kindness. School is a place where examples truly shape our future.

I am convinced that everyone should be in charge of their own choices rather than depending entirely on experts or friends. First, no one is infallible—people can offer advice, but they might be mistaken or overlook important details. Second, only you really understand your own tastes, goals, and limits, so it makes sense for you to decide what is best. Finally, following the crowd blindly can lead you into trouble, since you might end up repeating someone else’s bad decisions instead of making a well-considered choice.

Relying too much on others’ opinions can backfire. Consider asking your best friend what career path to follow or how to handle a personal problem. Even though they mean well, they don’t know your situation as deeply as you do, and their suggestions could steer you in the wrong direction. If you act on bad advice, you might waste time or find yourself in a difficult position that could have been avoided if you had trusted your own judgment from the start.

Another reason to make your own decisions is that only you know what truly suits your dreams and values. Friends, family, or experts may have their own priorities, and their recommendations often reflect those rather than your personal needs. If you let others decide for you, you risk living according to someone else’s plan. Worse, if things go wrong, you might blame them instead of accepting responsibility for your life. In school, for example, many students get in trouble because they copy their friends’ poor choices—like skipping class or cheating on assignments—instead of focusing on what they really want to achieve.

It is important to pause and think before taking action. Whenever you face a choice, ask yourself whether it is a good one. This habit can guide you toward better outcomes and help you learn from your mistakes. When I was new at high school, I was careful about who I befriended. I watched how different groups behaved and chose friends who encouraged me to study and act respectfully. By doing this, I avoided negative influences and stayed on track with my own goals.

In the end, making your own decisions empowers you to control your life and learn from the results—whether they turn out to be successes or failures. It may feel safer to follow someone else’s lead, but that path often means surrendering your independence and risking confusion later on. Always give yourself time to think through your options, weigh the possible outcomes, and then commit to the direction that feels right for you. Even if you make a mistake, you will gain valuable experience, and you won’t have to wonder, “What if I had chosen for myself?”

In everyday life, when we need guidance, is it wiser to consult just one person or seek opinions from several individuals? I believe gathering advice from multiple sources is more beneficial.

First, hearing from different people offers varied perspectives on the same issue. Each person may notice different details or suggest unique solutions, which helps form a complete understanding.

Second, comparing opinions makes it easier to judge potential risks. For example, a parent may discourage you from taking a chance to protect you, while a friend who enjoys challenges might encourage you to go ahead. Hearing both views helps you find a balance.

Finally, relying on a single opinion can lead to mistakes and difficulty. In contrast, advice from several people increases the chance of making the right choice and avoiding trouble. In conclusion, asking more than one person for advice can help you see both the pros and cons before deciding.

Some schools should offer distance learning through online platforms or video conferencing so that students can join classes from home. Many people support this idea because virtual lessons provide clear advantages: learners often absorb more information, produce higher-quality work, and enjoy extra time with their families. By choosing online education, students gain the flexibility they need to balance studies, personal responsibilities, and future ambitions.

Firstly, attending classes at home gives students a flexible schedule that suits their lives. Without the need to travel to campus, learners save valuable hours each day. For example, someone who works part-time to pay rent or cover travel expenses can use the same time slot for studying, completing assignments, or reviewing course materials. This approach helps busy individuals manage both their jobs and their education effectively, making it possible to graduate without sacrificing one goal for another.

Secondly, remote learning often leads to better academic performance. At home, students can create a comfortable study environment free from the distractions of a crowded classroom. With fewer interruptions, they can dedicate more time to researching projects, preparing detailed homework, and revising for exams. The wealth of resources available online—digital libraries, videos, and interactive tools—enables students to deepen their understanding and turn in assignments that reflect thorough effort and critical thinking.

Some critics argue that online classes might encourage students to waste time on their phones or social media instead of studying. While it is true that self-discipline is essential, virtual learning also offers the chance to enjoy family life and to recharge mentally between sessions. After finishing coursework, students can join relatives for activities such as playing sports in the yard, watching a movie together, or going out for a walk. This balance of study and leisure can improve motivation and overall well-being.

In conclusion, distance learning presents significant benefits by allowing students to attend lessons from home. It enables them to learn more effectively, submit better-quality work, and spend valuable moments with their families. By embracing online education, learners gain flexibility to juggle work and study, stay on track toward their goals, and ultimately build a path to a successful future.

The comfort of studying at home also reduces stress and makes concentrating easier. Given all these benefits, I believe that enrolling in online courses is one of the best choices today’s students and adult learners can make. Personally, I would choose virtual classes over attending a campus every day.

In many cultures, teenagers are often expected to choose a career path by the time they start high school. While some students feel ready to decide early, others prefer to delay thinking about their professional futures until later.

One reason young people believe it is important to pick a career early is that it gives them direction. At this stage, they can focus on relevant subjects and develop the skills they need. Planning ahead also helps students set clear goals, making it easier to work hard in their studies. Moreover, knowing their intended field allows them to take advantage of internships or extracurricular activities that strengthen their resumes.

Another strong argument for early career decisions involves family support. Many students hope to ease financial pressures on their parents by preparing for well-paid jobs. When a young person has a clear career plan, families can guide them with practical advice and even help them find mentors in that industry. This cooperation not only benefits the student but also gives parents confidence that their child is on the right track.

On the other hand, some teenagers resist choosing a career too soon. They feel they are still young and want to explore different interests, spend time with friends, or simply enjoy school life without the pressure of future responsibilities. While it is natural to value social experiences, delaying all career planning can leave students unprepared for college or job applications and limit their chances of success later on.

In conclusion, I agree that deciding on a career before high school graduation is a positive step. Early decisions can sharpen focus, help students build relevant skills, and enable families to support their plans. By choosing a path in advance, young people can work more confidently toward their goals and, ultimately, improve their own lives and those of their loved ones.

I believe that an afterschool homework club would be very helpful because it lets students get the extra support they need and improve their grades. Just like anyone who asks for help when they’re stuck, students often need guidance on assignments that can be tough to finish alone.

Without some kind of support, many students give up on hard homework and turn their attention elsewhere. But if there were a homework club after school, they could stay behind, work on their tasks, and receive guidance from teachers. For instance, I sometimes hire a tutor at home to help me, but my parents have to pay for each session. Not every family can afford that expense. A school-based club would provide that same assistance without the high cost.

Another benefit is having enough time to get things done. Right now, students might only have about forty-five minutes to meet with a teacher after class, which isn’t always enough. A longer club period would allow more work to be completed and questions to be answered.

In the end, an afterschool homework club would save families money, help students pass more tests, and make challenging work feel manageable. If teachers need a break, they can encourage students to support each other, too. Overall, this idea would greatly benefit both students and their parents.

Music, Drama, and Art courses are offered as electives rather than compulsory subjects in most schools. Students choose these classes according to their interests, often seeking extra credit or the chance to explore a creative field. For instance, someone might enroll in an Art course simply because they enjoy painting, not because it counts toward the core credits needed for graduation. If a student replaces one of their required classes with an Art course by mistake—thinking it fulfills a graduation requirement—they could find themselves short of the credits they actually need.

Core classes typically include subjects like English 11, Geometry, Mathematics, Computer Information Systems, World History, and others. These mandatory courses form the backbone of the high school curriculum and each one has an associated Standards of Learning (SOL) test. Students must pass these exams to earn credits toward graduation. The SOL tests are administered twice a year, and learners must score at least 300 points to pass. Only after achieving this minimum score do they receive the credit; otherwise, they must retake the exam until they succeed.

While seniors sometimes use elective slots to take Music or Drama—perhaps because their schedules are lighter—underclassmen can also pick these options to boost their transcripts. However, no matter how appealing these artistic subjects may be, they do not replace the essential courses and tests required for graduation. In short, Music, Drama, and Art remain valuable electives, but students must still complete and pass all core classes and their corresponding SOL exams.

This process proves that no matter how many times we fail, there is always something to learn and explore.

Only topic that is frequently debated today is whether or not to conserve energy and resources, since some businesses have adopted a four-day work week with ten-hour days. Should your school follow this model by extending the school day by two hours? Some people think that extending the school day will conserve energy and resources. They feel that longer hours mean more energy use—for electricity, lights, charging computers, electric blackboards—and that water use will also increase because some students forget to turn off the taps in the bathroom. I believe we should follow this model by extending the school day by two hours because it will teach us to conserve energy and resources and, last but not least, give us more time to make the world better and develop awareness.

One reason I believe this model works is that we can conserve more energy for the future. The school should also instruct each student to be careful about how to use energy; for example, to teach which appliances to focus on at home and give tips for paying the lowest possible electricity bill.

Another reason is that we can save water at school. Students use the bathroom almost twice and often forget to flush properly. I think they can make posters showing the importance of saving water. Other resources the school can save include plastic and paper, since it spends money to purchase them. With the money saved, the school could become better, and students would learn to be more careful with these resources.

The final reason is that if the school adds two hours to the day, students and teachers will have more time to do things. One activity could be a campaign to show society how to prevent global climate change and instruct people on caring for the world. Another idea is for students to create an online page to teach other students and people outside the school how to be careful with resources.

As you have read, I think the school should add two hours per day because everyone in the school will develop more awareness to save energy and resources—and, last but not least, that awareness can help the world. Only when we become conscious of changing the world will we have a better world one day.

As businesses experiment with four-day weeks of ten-hour days to save energy and resources, some wonder if schools should follow suit by lengthening each day by two hours. Although critics worry that adding time at school will raise costs for electricity, lighting, computers, and water, I believe this extension would actually help everyone learn to conserve resources and give us extra time to work toward a better world.

First, a longer school day offers more opportunities to teach students practical ways to reduce energy use both at school and at home. Teachers could give lessons on setting heating and cooling systems efficiently, turning off unused lights and devices, and choosing energy-saving appliances. By giving clear advice and real-life examples, students will know how to cut their own utility bills and protect resources in the future.

Second, extending the day creates space for campaigns about saving water, paper, and plastic around the school. For instance, students could design posters reminding classmates to turn off taps, flush toilets responsibly, and reuse scrap paper. Money saved on these materials could then be invested in school improvements, benefiting everyone. Developing these habits early will encourage lifelong respect for limited resources.

Finally, with two extra hours each day, teachers and students could lead awareness projects on climate change and environmental protection. They might create online guides or host presentations for the local community, showing simple steps to reduce carbon footprints. This hands-on work not only spreads important messages but also strengthens teamwork and leadership skills.

In conclusion, adding two hours to the school day is more than just extra class time. It provides a platform for teaching conservation, launching resource-saving initiatives, and engaging in environmental advocacy. Only by raising awareness and taking action at school can we hope to build a greener future.

Attending classes online is an excellent choice because it helps students use their time more efficiently. First, many learners must juggle jobs that don’t fit a fixed schedule. Since most employers cannot adjust working hours for study, being able to log in from home after a shift means students arrive at lessons feeling more rested and ready to learn. They also save the time they would spend commuting, leaving room to relax, eat properly, or even join a sports club or meet friends.

Second, online lessons solve problems caused by illness or unreliable transport. When students feel unwell, they can still follow lectures without risking the health of classmates. Those who live far from campus avoid long drives, bad weather delays, and parking fees. This not only makes attendance more dependable but also reduces stress about getting to school on time.

Third, distance learning greatly benefits anyone with family duties or physical challenges. Parents can look after young children while attending classes, and students with disabilities don’t have to worry about arranging special transport or assistance. Being at home means they can pause the lesson if they need a break and return without missing important material. This flexibility offers peace of mind, knowing that neither childcare nor personal care will force them to skip courses.

In the end, modern technology has transformed education by saving time and making study more accessible. Online classes give busy or bound students a real opportunity to balance their responsibilities while still achieving their academic goals.

When we’re born we come out of our mother’s womb. First, the thing we naturally do is screech and cry, and if we don’t cry the doctor hits us on our backs and tries to make us cry. From that cry on, we develop our own kind of sound and our own screech with its own pitch. They also take our fingerprints—there will never be two the same; even when we’re born with our twin, it will never be the same no matter how much alike we are. From there on, we start to learn and develop our own persona.

After we’re born, our brain starts to function even with little stuff. For example, babies learn to cry when they’re hungry, want to be changed, are in pain, or simply want attention. Then, when children get older into the toddler stage, they begin to learn how to walk by observing everyone else; likewise, they learn to talk by listening to everyone around them. We learn how to grab our bottle, pick up a fork or spoon, and handle our daily doings. In each case, we learn by observing and listening to everyone else.

Moreover, when we hit the 6–12 years of age, we tend to want to fit in—be in the cool kids group. We watch TV and see celebrities: musicians, actors, painters, policemen, firemen, dentists, doctors, mayors, chefs, soccer players, basketball players, football players, baseball players, hockey players, tennis players, volleyball players, etc. The list could go on, but the point is that we are influenced.

However, as we get older in our teen years (13–19), we begin to have our own voice—at least until we’re old enough to make our own decisions. We all take our own paths and choose the decisions we make; our parents don’t go with us throughout the day telling us what to do or not do. They give us plenty of advice because they already went through that stage and don’t want to see us fail or get hurt. Yet sometimes it’s good that we fail and make mistakes, because then we learn what we can and cannot do.

Now, as you turn into an adult, the net we used to have under Mom and Dad’s roof is gone. We no longer have that privilege, and therefore we need to grow up and officially create and develop our own persona. When you get a job, it comes with responsibilities; from there we learn if we’re responsible or irresponsible, social or non-social, lenient or non-lenient, patient or impatient, forgiving or unforgiving.

I’d like to think that we’re all born to grow and learn about our rugged society—and moreover, based on what we’ve lived through is how we’re going to act. We can literally live in a shit hole of a place and still have the happiest attitude ever—better than a boy or girl complaining that she didn’t get the car she wanted—versus the kid who saw his mother get beat by his deadbeat dad, the kid up all night wondering if his mom was going to come home, or the kid who went to sleep hungry. So honestly, I don’t think we’re born with labels; I feel we all can decide what we’re going to make of life. If you’re going to sit there and make everyone see you as a pity case, then a huge part of your character—your mentality—will be broken and weak, giving off negative vibes and a deadbeat character. But if you have a strong mindset and the will to get stuff done, then you’ll build a broad and respected character.

In conclusion, I’d like to think that we create and build our own character and that we’re not given a label by any higher power dictating what our character must be in life.

From the moment we enter the world, each of us displays our own distinct traits. A newborn’s first wail arrives before anything else, shaping the sound that will become uniquely theirs. Doctors even record our fingerprints at birth, ensuring that no two people are ever exactly the same. These early signs hint at the individuality we carry from the start.

As babies grow, they quickly learn to use crying as a way to communicate. Hunger, discomfort, pain or simply a desire for attention become clear signals. Without any instruction, infants master this language of need, showing how naturally we adapt to express ourselves.

When children reach the toddler years, observation becomes their main teacher. By watching family members and friends, they figure out how to take their first steps, form words and handle objects like spoons or toys. Daily routines—dressing, eating, playing—are all learned in this way, proving that we absorb much of our early knowledge through imitation.

Between ages six and twelve, social circles and popular culture start to shape us more visibly. Kids want to belong, so they look up to celebrities, athletes and various community figures. Whether it’s a musician, a firefighter, a doctor or an artist, the number of potential role models grows, offering different paths to follow. Yet these influences don’t determine who we must become; they simply show what’s possible.

Teenage years bring a new level of choice. As we move toward adulthood, our own voice gains strength. Parents still offer advice based on their experiences, but they cannot make every decision for us. Mistakes during this phase are important lessons, teaching us limits and possibilities in a way that advice alone never could.

Adulthood removes the safety net that family often provides. Entering the workforce brings fresh responsibilities and shows whether we handle them responsibly or not. We find out if we are patient, forgiving, strict or easygoing—and how social or reserved our personalities turn out to be.

Our environment can be challenging, but it does not have to define us. A person who grows up with few resources can still hold a positive outlook, while someone who has everything might remain unhappy. Attitude and mindset shape our behavior far more than external circumstances.

Ultimately, we are not born with fixed labels. Our character is built by the choices we make and the attitude we adopt. A strong mindset leads to respect and achievement, while a defeated one invites negativity. In the end, each of us creates our own identity through daily decisions and personal growth.

Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” Though some may disagree, I believe Emerson is right. Society often pressures us to adjust our views, traditions, and beliefs. To resist this influence, we must do three things: never give up on who we are, embrace and value ourselves, and stay true to our roots.

First, perseverance is key. The world around us pushes us to conform, but we should not quit. Even when others criticize or reject us for being different, it is important to remain authentic. Ultimately, we are the ones who have to live with ourselves, so our comfort and self-esteem matter most.

Second, self-love and pride in our identity keep us strong. Everyone makes mistakes, yet errors do not define us. Instead, they offer opportunities to grow. Admitting flaws and learning from them takes courage, but it strengthens our character. Celebrating our unique qualities—our personality, values, and talents—reminds us why we are special and why fitting in at any cost is unnecessary.

Third, we must not forget where we come from. For those who migrate or live far from home, it can be tempting to hide one’s background to feel accepted. However, our origins shape our perspective and enrich our identity. By honouring our heritage—including language, customs, and memories—we show that we value who we are rather than trying to be what others expect.

In conclusion, standing firm against society’s demands is essential. Never give up on showing your true self, always love and be proud of who you are, and remember the experiences that have made you you. Doing these things is the best way to achieve Emerson’s greatest accomplishment: being yourself.

First, people no longer go out to shop. In my home country, I used to walk or cycle to the nearby market. Ever since we moved to the United States, my mother simply phones the store, and they deliver groceries to our door. This convenience removes chances to chat with vendors and neighbors.

Second, playing games with friends has shifted indoors. Last week, I spoke to a friend back home about whether they still gather to play soccer on the field or other street games. He told me they now spend most of their free time on popular mobile apps and rarely leave the house to play outside.

Third, children lose interest in other activities and spend all their time staring at screens. For example, my two-year-old brother cries when my mother takes away the phone because he only wants to watch videos or play games. He refuses to join his older siblings in other games or even to play with toys.

Fourth, visits to relatives or new places become boring without a device. Whenever I go to see family members, I feel restless if I don’t have my phone. During trips to unfamiliar sites, I focus solely on taking pictures instead of enjoying the experience.

Finally, excessive use of phones or computers can lead to addiction. A school friend of mine often uses his phone in class to play games or watch videos. Even when the teacher reminds him to put it away, he hides it in his backpack so she won’t see.

In conclusion, while modern technology has its advantages, overusing devices can harm our communication skills and social life.

One of the most pleasurable ways to enjoy the outdoors is to gather your family and friends for a backyard or park cookout. Begin by grilling burgers, hot dogs, tender carne asada, tacos, and even barbacoa over an open flame. While the food sizzles, you can play sports like soccer, football, baseball or organize a fun bike ride or sprint race with everyone. Just remember to keep the music at a reasonable volume to avoid disturbing others. You might also invite your children’s boyfriends or girlfriends—and even their parents—for an afternoon of snacks and games.

If you choose a camping-style outing near a river where fishing is permitted, you can try your luck catching your own dinner. Nothing beats the satisfaction of cooking fresh fish you just pulled from the water. More important than the menu is enjoying quality time together: admiring the scenery, listening to birdsong and leaving daily worries behind. These moments help you strengthen family bonds and remind you how fortunate you are to have loved ones around, especially since not everyone is so lucky.

As evening falls, build a small campfire and roast marshmallows to sandwich between two cookies. Gather in a circle to share spooky tales or swap jokes under the starlit sky. The crisp air and crackling fire make even simple treats taste wonderful, and the laughter brings everyone closer.

Parks—whether community, state or national—play a vital role in our well-being. They offer space for parties, dog walks, jogging or peaceful strolls that clear the mind. We should all do our part to protect these green areas because they are home to many plants and animals, and they give us a chance to recharge. Spending time outside with friends and family is not only fun; it also nurtures our connection to nature and to each other.

What does it mean to be self-reliant? In my view, self-reliance is the ability to make thoughtful choices—whether as a student, a worker, or a citizen—while also knowing when to seek advice. Today, our nation faces challenges that show how important these skills are. For example, a government shutdown does more than halt services; it hits businesses, farms, and communities across America. If we rely only on one person’s opinion, we miss out on fresh ideas. By bringing more voices into the conversation, we can find better solutions.

Teaching self-reliance doesn’t turn children into followers; it helps them grow into leaders. True leaders are comfortable asking questions and gathering information. At first, their knowledge may be limited, but over time they learn more and become confident decision-makers. Yet even the most experienced leaders continue to seek feedback and new perspectives.

These abilities are valuable not only in school but also at home, in our careers, and in everyday life. By learning to research, ask for help, and listen carefully, we become more effective at work and more fulfilled in our personal lives. Then, as we grow, we pass these habits on to others. In that way, self-reliance and collaboration go hand in hand, and neither skill is ever wasted.

Consider the military as an example. Soldiers and officers must be ready to act on their own judgment, sometimes in life-or-death situations. Before they ever enter the field, they train in boot camp to sharpen both their minds and their skills. There, they learn to ask questions, share information, and think through hard problems. That preparation not only keeps them safe; it shows how crucial these habits are for all of us whenever we face big decisions—about careers, family matters, or even our finances.

No matter who you are—regardless of your age, background, or job—cultivating self-reliance and a willingness to learn from others will benefit you now and in the future. Imagine teaching your own children about managing money or starting a project. If you encourage them to speak up and do research, they’ll grow into active participants in our society. Our government, our economy, and our communities depend on citizens who can think clearly and offer new solutions.

When the government stops working and paychecks are delayed, all of us feel the effects. Business owners worry about losing their shops, and families struggle to pay their bills. That’s why it matters more to ask, “How can we work together to prevent another shutdown?” than to think, “Should I buy a new car this year?” By seeking advice, sharing ideas, and asking questions, we gain new perspectives that guide us toward better choices.

None of us has all the answers—and that’s okay. We learn every day, and we teach what we learn to others. So let us keep asking questions, listening to different viewpoints, and offering our own suggestions. In this way, we build a stronger community, a healthier economy, and a government we can trust. Always remember: stay curious, stay informed, and never stop seeking guidance.

I believe summer exists so we can enjoy warm days, spend quality time with family and friends—and if you have a pet, include them too—without worrying about schoolwork. No one really wants to spend their vacation trying to solve homework problems or stressing over unfinished projects. After a long academic year, students deserve a real rest to recharge their minds and bodies.

It’s not just young people who need a break. Adults, too, often feel drained and under pressure after months of work. While their responsibilities—bills, families, careers—may be heavier than a student’s, everyone benefits from time off to recover from stress. Many jobs only offer a single week of vacation, which is rarely enough to fully unwind. Students, on the other hand, enjoy a much longer summer holiday, giving them the chance to relax, catch up on sleep, and gather energy for the year ahead.

Another reason to appreciate the summer holiday is the freedom it brings. The warm breeze, open skies, and no tests to study for create an entirely different atmosphere compared with a short spring or fall break. Teachers, too, need a reprieve; the prospect of reteaching material and reminding students of last year’s lessons can be just as exhausting for them. So a generous summer holiday benefits both learners and educators.

Many students use these months to set goals or find part-time work. Having a summer job helps them save money for daily expenses or even college fees—an opportunity not every family can fully support. This financial independence is a major incentive for young people to value their summer break. In fact, even some teachers take on summer positions to boost their income or pursue personal projects.

Although educators aim to keep students motivated and prepare them for future success, a long break followed by shorter winter, spring, and fall holidays seems like a well-balanced schedule. It maintains continuity in learning while still offering regular rests throughout the year.

In the end, the summer vacation we already have is ideal for most students. The weather is perfect for beach trips, family visits, and outdoor adventures. It’s also enough time for those who want to work a few hours a day, earn extra cash, and feel productive. All in all, a lengthy summer break strikes the right balance between relaxation, family time, and personal growth.

In my view, the way technology limits face-to-face contact can bring both benefits and drawbacks, depending on the person. For some, digital tools offer a helpful escape from loneliness. If someone feels isolated, they can turn to reading e-books, browsing online stores, playing video games or listening to music on apps like Pandora. They might also watch their favorite series on YouTube or Netflix. These activities can lift spirits and prevent people from feeling alone, which is important for mental health.

On the other hand, technology can weaken our interest in real-life interactions. I’ve noticed that some people no longer value family gatherings or casual conversations. Even when we meet friends or relatives, it’s common to see them staring at their phones instead of listening. To me, this behaviour can seem rude, as if the person doesn’t care about what you’re saying. Over time, these habits may push others away and even damage relationships.

Moreover, the convenience of modern devices can lead to laziness. Why go shopping in person when you can order everything online? Why meet someone for a chat when you can text or video-call? As technology handles more tasks, we might stop making the effort to do things ourselves or to connect with others in person. In the long run, this could leave people feeling lonely even though they have all these digital options.

In conclusion, technology is one of the greatest inventions of our time and can make life easier and more entertaining. However, it works best when we use it in moderation and do not let it replace real human contact.

Technology has become an indispensable part of our daily lives, offering help in many different areas such as work, communication, and leisure. Today, advancements in devices like smartphones, tablets, and computers happen at a rapid pace. With just a few taps, we can read about events happening around the globe, chat with family and friends, or complete various tasks more efficiently than ever before.

One of the greatest benefits of modern technology is its ability to guide us when we are in unfamiliar places. Using a smartphone’s GPS and map applications, we can easily find our way to a destination, whether it’s a friend’s house or a new shop in town. This practical feature saves time, reduces stress, and makes travelling in unknown areas much safer.

When it comes to relaxation, technology offers countless options. Music lovers can stream songs from any artist or genre at any time. Gamers have instant access to a wide variety of online games, from sports and adventure titles to puzzles and strategy challenges. Readers can download e-books in seconds, without needing to go to a bookstore. All these forms of entertainment are available on a single device, making it simple to stay amused wherever we are.

Communication has also been transformed by technology. Social media platforms and messaging apps such as Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger allow us to stay closely connected with people, regardless of distance. We can share photos, videos, and updates in real time, keeping our relationships strong even if loved ones live far away. This ease of contact brings families and friends closer together and helps us feel supported.

Technology is equally valuable when we face practical problems at home or work. If we need to cook a new recipe, repair a car engine, or fix something around the house, we can search for instructional videos or step-by-step guides online. Websites like YouTube and other tutorial platforms provide clear demonstrations that help us learn new skills quickly. In many cases, we can find professional advice from specialists who explain complex tasks in simple terms.

Another important role of technology is in finding employment. Most companies now post job openings online and allow candidates to complete applications via websites or mobile apps. This process is convenient and saves resources for both employers and job seekers. Moreover, the internet enables businesses to reach a global audience, promoting their products and services worldwide. As a result, small firms can expand into international markets, increasing their profitability and offering more job opportunities.

In conclusion, technology is a powerful tool that enhances various aspects of our lives. It helps us navigate unknown places, enjoy games, music, and books, stay in touch with loved ones, solve everyday problems, and pursue career opportunities. By bringing together an endless array of applications and services, modern devices make our world more connected and efficient. As long as we use technology wisely and responsibly, its positive impact will continue to improve our daily routines and support our personal growth.

Technology has changed the way we live by letting us do many things without meeting others face to face. We can borrow books online, shop from home, and enjoy games alone. Although some worry about losing human contact, I believe technology has improved our lives in several ways. It lets us keep in touch with family far away, work from home without commuting, and connect with new people and cultures.

First, technology makes it easy to communicate with relatives who live in another city or country. Through video calls or instant messages, we can share daily events, celebrate special occasions together, or simply catch up whenever we feel lonely. Without these tools, it would be hard to know how our loved ones are doing, and distances would feel much greater. In emergencies, a quick call can help doctors or rescue teams find us if we are hurt far from home. Also, if you wake up unwell, you can inform your workplace right away and avoid misunderstandings. All these features prove how valuable technology is in keeping families connected and safe.

Second, working online has become a huge advantage for many people. Employees no longer have to spend hours commuting to an office or pay for fuel and parking. Instead, they can set up a workspace at home, which is especially helpful for parents who want to stay close to their children. For those who cannot drive or live in remote places, internet access makes it possible to earn a living without traveling long distances. Even when you’re on vacation, you can still check emails and finish tasks, increasing your productivity and income. Technology truly offers flexibility that was impossible just a few decades ago.

Third, technology opens doors to new friendships, languages, and traditions. Social media and online forums bring together people from all over the world, encouraging us to learn about different customs and beliefs. If you visit a foreign country and don’t speak the language, translation apps can help you ask for directions or order a meal. You can also join international chat groups to practice a language or discuss your hobbies with strangers who share your interests. This global exchange helps us understand each other better and builds a more connected community.

In conclusion, despite concerns that technology isolates us, it has had overwhelmingly positive effects. It allows us to maintain relationships at a distance, work efficiently from home, and discover new cultures and friends. As long as we use it wisely, technology remains one of the most useful tools in our daily lives.

Another time, a friend of mine had some money in his pocket and said, “Let’s go to the cinema to watch a film.” We all said no, explaining that the movie was already available on DVD, which cost much less than a cinema ticket. When he listened to our different viewpoints, he saw the situation from another angle. Although he really wanted the cinema atmosphere, he realized buying the DVD would still let him enjoy the movie without wasting money.

Similarly, people often ask more than one person for advice. One day my father gave me money to buy whatever I wished. I knew I would need a white shirt for an appointment the next day, but I chose to spend the cash on a video game instead. The next morning I asked him for more money to buy the shirt. He reminded me, “I told you yesterday to buy the shirt, but you didn’t listen.” That moment taught me to consider advice carefully and to save for things I really need.

These stories show how important it is to listen to different voices before deciding. By doing so, we can avoid mistakes and make better use of our resources. And you? Do you sometimes ask more than one person before making a choice?

Online courses and video conferencing offer an excellent opportunity for students who cannot afford traditional campus education, as well as for older adults who missed earlier chances to pursue further studies because of financial limitations. Today, many learners face rising tuition and accommodation fees, whether they live in on-campus dormitories or off-campus housing. These costs force some students out of their dorms, and others must take on part-time jobs just to cover basic expenses. Balancing paid work with in-person classes can be exhausting and stressful, making it difficult to focus fully on learning.

Another challenge that online classes solve is transportation and parking. Students who live far from campus or lack a car may struggle with delays or high parking fees. By attending lessons from home, they avoid the stress of rush-hour traffic and crowded parking lots. They can start their day’s study whenever it suits them best, especially after a tiring commute or a long work shift.

Studying online also helps many learners stay on task and complete their work more efficiently. With fewer interruptions at home, students often understand the material more deeply and can concentrate on assignments. They have the advantage of replaying recorded lectures, asking questions through chat or email, and going back over difficult ideas until they are clear. Instructors often adjust the volume of assignments for virtual classes, ensuring that students can manage their workload without feeling overwhelmed.

Overall, taking classes online or via video conferencing gives people the flexibility to handle other responsibilities, arrive on time for lessons, and even support fellow students who might not otherwise afford college. It saves money on transport, helps learners stay organized, and develops valuable time-management skills that benefit them throughout life.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” I fully support this idea for several reasons. First, without preparing ourselves in more than one area, we limit our future options. Second, having a variety of skills and knowledge gives us an advantage over others. Finally, if we never challenge ourselves with difficult tasks, we miss the chance to develop.

To begin with, people who focus on just a single skill often find their lives lacking direction and opportunity. In today’s job market, most employers look for candidates who can handle several responsibilities. Someone who only knows one narrow field may struggle to find work or advance in their career. For instance, a person seeking a promotion or a position in a new industry will be at a disadvantage if they lack the required background. They cannot contribute as much to their company or community without a broader set of abilities.

My second point is that knowledge is a powerful tool. When we learn about different subjects, we open more doors for ourselves and enrich our lives. Many believe you cannot simply buy true knowledge—you earn it through study and experience. For example, a student who devotes time to mastering both language and technical skills will have a better chance of landing a high-paying job because they can adapt to various tasks. In this way, every new topic we explore makes us stronger and more competitive.

Lastly, personal growth often comes from tackling tasks that feel too difficult at first. If people stay within their comfort zone, they will never realize their full potential. Consider a teacher who is content with classroom work but never seeks leadership roles; without striving for a school principal position or similar challenge, they miss out on growing professionally and personally.

In conclusion, I agree with Emerson’s message. Trying activities that stretch beyond what we already know is essential for growth. By preparing in multiple areas, gaining diverse knowledge, and facing hard challenges, we ensure that we continue to develop throughout our lives.

In many places, young people are encouraged to pick a career path even before they reach high school. While some claim that deciding early helps students get advice from counselors, prepare for college, and secure a job sooner, rushing into a choice can backfire. In fact, choosing a profession too soon often leads to dropping classes, excessive worry, and simply wasting precious time.

First, when students lock in a career plan at a very young age, they may lose interest after only a few weeks of study. For example, a teenager who enrolls in a specialized course might attend for two or three weeks but then feel it does not suit them and quit. This early frustration makes it harder to return to studies later and can damage their confidence.

Second, selecting a career path involves a lot of thought that most young teens are not ready for. Adults often take years to settle on a field because they balance job goals, financial needs, and personal interests. In contrast, children and early teens may feel pressured to decide quickly without understanding the practical side of work life, which leads to stress and indecision.

Finally, committing to a career too early can waste time that could be spent exploring different subjects or hobbies. Many students who face a forced choice simply default to “undecided” or return to leisure activities like video games. Without a clear plan, the effort they put into career assignments ends up unused.

Overall, choosing a profession before truly knowing one’s strengths and interests is unwise. It causes some pupils to abandon courses, places too much pressure on young minds, and uses up valuable years better spent on broad education and self-discovery.

First impressions can be misleading, because the way things appear at first glance is often different from reality. Many people judge situations or individuals too quickly, assuming something is negative simply because that’s their initial reaction. In truth, we might overlook important details and form opinions that turn out to be incorrect.

Jumping to conclusions about someone without giving them a fair chance can lead us to misunderstand who they really are. We might believe we “know” a person based on a brief encounter or a single comment, yet we miss the chance to discover their true character. For example, when I was in tenth grade, I avoided speaking to a classmate whom I thought was disrespectful to both students and teachers. Because of my early impression, I kept my distance and refused to interact with him.

Later on, I realized how wrong I had been. That same classmate turned out to be one of my closest friends—kind, trustworthy, and supportive. If I had stopped judging him after our first meeting, I would have missed out on a friendship that has meant a great deal to me. This experience taught me that giving people and situations more time often changes how we see them.

Some people might argue that aiming low shows a lack of ambition, but I believe beginning with realistic goals helps you spot and fix small mistakes right away. When you set modest objectives, you give yourself a clear chance to identify what needs improvement. Those early corrections become the building blocks of greater success, making you more confident and capable over time.

By choosing a lower starting point, you can focus on gradual progress instead of overwhelming yourself with huge challenges. This approach lets you concentrate on developing essential skills and habits step by step. Each small achievement brings a sense of accomplishment and strengthens your motivation to move forward. As you grow more skilled, you will feel encouraged to raise your targets without fearing a sudden failure.

In contrast, people who aim too high at the beginning often overlook warning signs and underestimate the effort required. They expect everything to fall into place without careful planning or practice, so a single misstep can lead to disappointment. When someone dives into a difficult task without breaking it into manageable parts, they risk losing their confidence and giving up altogether.

Setting lower-risk goals also helps you protect what you have already gained. By advancing in small stages, you can maintain control and avoid unnecessary risks. This cautious yet steady approach allows you to review each step, learn from experience, and refine your strategy before moving on. I agree that to build a successful life, you need to develop habits that simplify your path and show others you are someone special—polite, calm, and resilient, no matter what they say. Handling difficulties with a positive mindset helps you solve problems more effectively than if you react with anger. That’s why treating everyone kindly, keeping peace in your heart, and nurturing strong relationships with those around you are essential. Approaching life with a cheerful attitude makes each challenge feel less daunting.

When you treat people with respect and kindness, you not only boost their spirits but also feel a sense of satisfaction yourself. Being a genuinely good person sets you apart in a world where many act selfishly or harshly. However, encountering negative people doesn’t justify losing your own optimism; instead, it’s wiser to distance yourself from harmful influences and look for those who share your values. These like-minded friends can feel almost like family and improve your well-being. For instance, I always try to be friendly with my family and friends. I took the time to learn what makes each of them happy, and in return, they see me as a reliable, positive person. This mutual understanding has enriched my life and convinced me they will succeed in the future because they, too, maintain a good attitude and support one another.

Finding inner peace is another key element of a successful life. When your soul is calm, you experience comfort and clarity. On the other hand, unrest can make you uneasy and distract you for days or weeks over a single issue. To preserve peace, I focus on activities I truly enjoy, so boredom and frustration don’t have room to grow. I also work on controlling my anger: I know that losing my temper rarely fixes anything. I still remember an argument I had with my younger brother when I was twelve—it stayed on my mind for years. Now that I’m twenty, I make an effort to let go of any lingering resentment and remind myself how much I love him. Sharing my thoughts with him always brings me back to a peaceful state of mind.

Finally, surrounding yourself with positive, goal-oriented people can greatly influence your future. When friends are driven and supportive, you learn from their habits and passion. On the contrary, those who avoid responsibilities or ignore their studies can drag you down. I once had a classmate who excelled in seventh grade, but in ninth grade he fell in with a crowd that skipped homework and showed little ambition. His grades plummeted, and he lost interest in college. This example taught me that good connections are vital if you want to stay on a path to success.

In conclusion, adopting a kind and calm approach to life, nurturing inner peace, and choosing uplifting friends are the three pillars of a positive attitude. By practicing these habits every day, you make it easier to overcome challenges and build a more successful, rewarding future.
