I firmly believe that being honest at all times is the best policy. When I tell the truth, I avoid lying and allow others to trust me. This trust means people feel comfortable asking me questions or seeking my help, knowing I won’t deceive them.

Honesty has always been a key part of my personality. As I grow older, I understand more clearly how truthfulness guides my choices and shapes my relationships. For example, by admitting honestly that I expect to do well on a test, I avoid unnecessary worry over failure. Yet, speaking the truth isn’t always easy. Sometimes friends or family become upset when they hear something they don’t want to believe. They may feel hurt and decide never to trust me again. It hurts deeply when someone I care about rejects me simply because I was honest instead of telling them what they wanted to hear.

Still, I believe honesty can lead to reconciliation. Once emotions settle, those who once doubted me often apologize, and we rebuild our relationship on a stronger foundation. If, however, they choose to trust other people more than me, that could spark a conflict that seems endless. To avoid that, I find direct, face-to-face conversations help clear misunderstandings without causing long-term damage.

I also see honesty as a way to encourage positive thinking. By being truthful, I help friends and family focus on solutions instead of dwelling on negative thoughts that can lead to stress or even harmful ideas like self-harm or risky behaviors. Even when someone doubts my sincerity, I stand firm in my honest intentions. Mistakes do not make honesty fail; they simply show me where I need to improve. If I perform poorly on a test because I didn’t study, that’s not honesty’s fault—it’s mine.

Being committed to truth helps me achieve my goals. When I trust my own honesty, I work harder on exams and personal tasks. If I ever lose sight of honesty, I risk losing direction and becoming a failure. I wish everyone valued honesty as much as I do, because it resolves conflicts that are otherwise difficult to solve. Though some say honesty must be learned, I believe anyone—smart or not—can practice and improve their honesty through life’s experiences.

Many think that only very intelligent people can be honest, but I know honesty and intelligence are not linked. Someone who isn’t “book smart” can prove themselves honest and win respect, while a once-brilliant person may start lying if they forget the importance of truth. To keep honesty strong, guidance from family members or teachers is essential. While friends might tempt us away from truth, our loved ones can help us remember why honesty matters.

In the end, I am convinced that honesty should be everyone’s top quality. By being truthful, we build trust, solve problems, and grow as individuals. Honesty truly is the best policy.

Technology is everywhere today. Without it, we would miss many chances to learn and grow. Thanks to advanced devices, we can talk to someone on the other side of the world in seconds, either by calling or messaging. In my opinion, technology often brings positive changes, but it also has drawbacks. Below are some examples.

First, technology has improved our work and education. Many people earn their living through jobs that rely on computers and the internet. They can find answers to questions online instead of asking others. In schools, teachers and students use digital tools for lessons and assignments. For instance, students often submit their tasks online and search for resources on the web, reducing the need for printed books. In hospitals, modern medical equipment helps doctors perform surgeries more safely and save lives. Even factories depend on machines to carry out tasks that used to require tiring manual labour.

Second, while most people use technology for good, some misuse it. Parents sometimes rely on mobile phones or tablets as babysitters, giving them to children to keep them busy when they need time to work. On the other hand, criminals learn to trick or steal from others online. They defraud bank accounts, kidnap vulnerable victims through social media, or hack private information. Such cases show that if technology is widely available, not everyone will use it responsibly.

Third, technology has changed how we live and think. Advanced security systems make us feel safer at home. Social media platforms let people express themselves and even earn income, like YouTubers sharing their hobbies without knowing their audience personally. Older generations also benefit; instead of writing letters, they now send texts or video calls to stay in touch. Online games can bring friends together from different continents, allowing them to chat in real time despite the distance.

To sum up, relying on technology has both advantages and disadvantages. In workplaces and personal relationships, face-to-face conversations help build trust and understanding. Text messages alone are not enough for strong bonds. Yet technology also offers a quick way to find information and connect with others when meeting in person is not possible. In the end, I believe that while we should embrace the benefits of technology, we must not forget the importance of direct human contact. Let's balance both to enjoy the best of each world.

Dear City Council,

I am writing to express my support for a 10 p.m. curfew for teenagers in our city. This rule would help keep young people safe and prevent them from getting into trouble late at night. At the moment, some teens stay out past dark and can annoy or even threaten others. By asking them to be home by 10 p.m., we encourage responsible habits and reduce the chance of mischief.

A clear law should state that any teenager found outdoors without a valid reason after 10 p.m. would be breaking the rule and face a consequence. Many young people already end up in police stations for small offences like loitering, underage drinking, or carrying items they shouldn’t have. By limiting their time on the streets, we can lower these incidents and make it harder for gangs or harmful influences to recruit them.

Some people argue that a curfew unfairly restricts teenagers’ freedom. It’s true that it places limits on their movements, but its purpose is to protect them rather than punish them. Late at night, when there are fewer adults around, young individuals may feel pressured into risky actions or become victims themselves. A curfew provides a simple guideline that keeps them off the streets during those vulnerable hours.

In conclusion, I believe implementing a 10 p.m. curfew for teenagers will benefit both the youth and our community by reducing disturbances and ensuring teens return home safely. I urge the council to adopt this measure to safeguard our city’s young residents.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” He has a point. To fully grasp Emerson’s message, recall that mastering something means performing it without mistakes. Personal development starts when we set goals that push our abilities. Even small steps forward add up, guiding us toward greater accomplishments. Learning new skills or refining old ones often takes time and effort, but with confidence and perseverance, mastery is within reach.

For instance, if you can ride a bicycle, challenge yourself to learn to ride a motorcycle. If you can bake cupcakes, take the next step and make a full cake. Or if you know how to float in water, practice swimming strokes. These modest goals build on what you already know and help develop stronger abilities. By pushing yourself in this way, you open doors to more advanced tasks. Remember, if you avoid challenges, your progress will stall. It may take many attempts to succeed, but every try moves you closer to mastery and personal growth. Ultimately, it is your choice: embrace growth by stepping outside your comfort zone or remain at the level you’re familiar with.

Thomas Jefferson, one of America’s presidents, encouraged everyone to keep working consistently because regular effort brings lasting benefits. When we stick to our tasks every day, we build skills more quickly and tasks become easier over time. Although repeating the same work can sometimes feel tedious, this steady practice deepens our understanding and makes us more proficient.

I apply this principle in my own life. By practising my job responsibilities, studying for exams and training in sports without skipping sessions, I reinforce my knowledge and improve my performance. For instance, reading books on a daily basis broadens my horizons and teaches me about subjects I might otherwise never explore. In contrast, people who neglect regular work often lack progress and fall behind, simply because they do not give themselves the chance to learn from repetition.

If we observe closely, we can spot the difference between those who follow routines and those who do not. Students who complete homework every day, athletes who train on schedule, and employees who show up punctually tend to achieve better results than those who skip these habits. We should encourage others to adopt regular routines, offering support and reminders when they struggle.

I experienced this myself at the start of high school. I rarely did my homework or reviewed my notes until friends persuaded me to work consistently. Once I established that habit, my grades improved significantly and studying became less stressful. I hope everyone forms similar positive routines—whether it’s doing schoolwork, exercising or eating healthy meals daily—because good habits help us grow and stay well without frequent visits to the doctor. Keep practising regularly.

When people form a first impression, their reaction can vary greatly. Some individuals remain unchanged because they simply do not care about others’ opinions, while others allow that initial judgment to shape their behavior. No two people respond in exactly the same way, since each person’s outlook is influenced by their unique past experiences.

Often, a negative first impression is the catalyst for real change. At first, someone might ignore comments or continue the same habits without concern. But if they later realize that their actions upset others, they may pause and reflect on what went wrong. Genuine transformation usually requires time and deliberate effort; it does not happen overnight. People who repeat their mistakes often do so because they fail to consider the consequences before acting.

This process is especially clear in romantic relationships. Feelings of betrayal, jealousy, or toxic behavior can strike deeply, and partners may act on these strong impressions. For some young people, discovering infidelity or dishonesty leads to intense emotional turmoil, and in extreme cases they suffer serious harm. Healthy relationships are not built on impressing others or stirring jealousy. Instead, recognizing one’s faults and working on them—even when it is difficult—can strengthen the bond and prevent recurring problems.

However, requiring every student risks ignoring personal commitments. Instead, community service days on weekends could suit those who are willing but occupied on school days. In this way, students who struggle with rules gain practical lessons and the chance to change, while others are not burdened by mandatory service during their busy schedules.

Many people argue that high school students should decide on their future career when they begin high school and pick courses that lead to that profession. I disagree with this idea because teenagers lack the maturity and real-world understanding to make such an important choice so early.

Firstly, high schoolers often have little insight into different jobs. Without firsthand experience in the workplace, it’s hard for them to know what a career truly involves. They need time to explore various fields before committing to one path.

Secondly, teenagers’ interests and priorities can change rapidly. A student might choose subjects in freshman year, only to realize later that their passion lies elsewhere. For example, a friend of mine enrolled in a technology class during his freshman year but discovered later that the salary expectations didn’t match what he hoped for, so he switched to construction courses to learn about building and designing homes.

Finally, selecting a career too soon can lead to regrets and wasted effort. It is better to concentrate on academic performance and personal growth throughout high school. By the time students reach their junior and senior years, they have gained more life experience and are in a stronger position to pick classes that align with their interests and future goals.

In conclusion, high school is a period for learning and self-discovery. Students should focus on studying hard and wait until they are older to decide on a career path, choosing suitable courses when they have a clearer vision of their goals.

I firmly believe in Ralph Waldo Emerson’s words that we cannot grow unless we attempt challenges beyond our current abilities. In my seventeen years, I have seen that remaining in a safe zone only breeds stagnation. If we always choose the easy path, we rob ourselves of opportunities to develop and become stronger versions of who we are.

Comfort can feel appealing, but it deprives us of meaningful progress. When we settle for what we already know, we waste precious time that could be spent learning new skills or broadening our understanding. Embracing challenges not only boosts our own potential but also equips us to share wisdom and experiences with others.

It seems clear to me that everyone should accept this idea. Refusing to work on our own flaws or expand our talents does little good. By pushing ourselves—studying more, facing difficult tasks, and even enduring failures—we gain knowledge that might help people who are struggling. It’s our responsibility to offer support when others are in need, and the insights we gather can be the very thing that makes a difference.

Some might disagree, arguing they have reached a level of mastery or that they are content. Yet no matter how much we learn, there is always room to grow. We can improve as friends, parents, children, or colleagues. Settling for mediocrity prevents us from making the most of our lives and the lives of those around us.

To really progress, we need to challenge ourselves daily—learning something small each day and lending a hand when it’s needed. As Emerson’s quote reminds us, without stepping outside our comfort, we remain unchanged. By striving to overcome new obstacles, we become individuals others admire and trust.

Working with others can bring clear benefits, such as combining different skills and sharing tasks with people you get along with. If everyone knows what they are doing, the project often moves faster and more smoothly. Yet working alone also has its own advantages. When you tackle a task by yourself, there is no chance that someone will borrow your ideas without credit or repeat exactly what you have written.

In group projects it sometimes feels like not everyone contributes equally. Some members end up doing less, relying on others to finish the work. This can make you doubt your own abilities and depend too much on the group rather than trusting yourself. Instead of growing more confident, you may start to feel insecure and believe you cannot succeed without constant help.

From my experience as a student, I have often enjoyed studying with friends, but I have also felt frustrated when they copied my work. It makes me uncomfortable to think they might not do well on their own. They seem to need a team just to appear capable, and it is unfair when those who did little still receive the same praise as those who worked hard.

I prefer working by myself because it suits my style. When I work on my own, I can focus better and avoid problems like cheating or uneven effort. Being alone lets me express my own voice and keeps me motivated without having to manage others. I know that I can achieve more when I do not rely on anyone else.

Through my experiences, I have learned the importance of putting yourself first and standing up for your own work. In my view, group work often leads to feelings of uselessness, so I choose to work alone. It allows me to value my own strengths and to feel confident in what I can accomplish.

I believe it is essential to support others in achieving something meaningful, and I back this idea with three main points: doing good deeds for people, guiding them toward suitable jobs, and using personal skills to assist them. I will explain each reason in detail and share my view on why helping others leads to greater accomplishments.

First, offering kindness and support to others can inspire them to reach their goals and find purpose. When you help someone overcome obstacles or encourage them in their efforts, you give them confidence to pursue their dreams. For instance, by volunteering your time to tutor students or by listening to a friend’s struggles, you can boost their motivation and make a real difference in their lives. Seeing families proud of a loved one’s success or watching someone grow stronger because of your support shows how powerful simple acts of generosity can be.

Second, helping people discover a suitable career path is another way to create positive change. By gathering information about different professions, advising on necessary qualifications, and sharing job opportunities, you can guide others toward work that fits their interests and strengths. For example, if someone dreams of becoming a graphic designer, you can research relevant courses, internships, and portfolio-building tips, so they have clear steps to follow. In this way, by focusing on a specific job, you help individuals find roles where they can thrive and feel fulfilled.

Third, applying your own skills to assist others is one of the most rewarding contributions you can make. Whether you have talents in writing, programming, or leadership, using those abilities to mentor and teach can open doors for people eager to grow. If you excel at public speaking, you might offer workshops that build others’ confidence in presentations. By sharing what you know, you empower others to use their hidden talents and reach levels they never thought possible.

In conclusion, helping people discover purpose and achieve great things—through supportive actions, career guidance, and the sharing of personal skills—not only brings joy to others but also enriches your own life. By continuing to encourage and guide those around you, you ensure that dreams stay alive and that everyone has the chance to succeed.

I believe students can really benefit from attending classes at home because it allows them to arrive mentally prepared and stay more focused.

First, many pupils feel embarrassed showing their strengths in front of classmates. At school, some might fear being judged for speaking up or answering questions in English. Learning online removes that pressure. For instance, if a student studies alone at home and encounters a confusing topic, they often look for solutions independently—searching online guides or asking a teacher by message. This self-directed approach builds confidence and problem-solving skills.

Being at home also makes daily routines easier. If I’m studying and suddenly feel hungry or tired, I can pause my lesson, quickly prepare a snack in the kitchen, and return without losing time. When I have a question, I simply send a quick text to my instructor instead of raising my hand in front of everyone. This flexibility can be a huge relief for students who are shy or who need more one-on-one time with a teacher to grasp a difficult concept.

I’ve seen how online classes help others in special situations, too. A friend of mine continued her lessons online throughout her pregnancy and after her baby was born. She told me how exhausting it was to commute to school with a large belly, and then to worry about leaving her newborn at home. Studying from home meant she could pause whenever her baby cried or needed feeding, and then jump right back into the lesson. It allowed her to finish her studies without feeling guilty or overwhelmed.

Online education also offers more options for those who must balance work and study. If a student needs to earn money, they can work a few hours, then return home to attend classes online. They might choose to work one day and study the next, or arrange shorter shifts so they can keep up with coursework. This kind of arrangement prevents students from skipping school just because they need extra income, and helps them stay on track with exams like the SOL tests.

Of course, there are challenges. Online classes usually require a reliable internet connection and sometimes tuition fees that not every family can afford. Yet I think schools and communities can offer subsidies or loan programs so that no student misses out simply because of cost. If we solve these financial and resource issues, then remote learning becomes a powerful tool for many learners.

We must also remember that success depends on effort. When we face difficult subjects, it’s important to “never give up.” Seeking help when confused, researching good information online, and practising regularly are key steps. Even if someone doubts our abilities, our dedication can prove them wrong and help us reach our goals.

During the school year, video lessons and interactive platforms can clearly demonstrate how to solve math exercises or study other subjects. Some of the main advantages of home-based learning include:
- Fewer distractions, so you can finish tasks faster  
- Freedom to use your phone or computer for quick research  
- The ability to study at any time of day  
- No need to worry about cold mornings or picking the right outfit  
- Less social pressure and fewer opportunities for conflict with peers  

All these benefits show that attending classes from home can improve students’ focus, wellbeing, and academic success. By providing the necessary support and encouraging self-discipline, schools can offer a flexible alternative that meets the needs of shy learners, working students, young parents, and anyone else who struggles with the traditional classroom. This, in my opinion, is a great step forward for education.

I believe that by always being authentic you open the door to remarkable accomplishments. When you maintain confidence in your abilities and hold onto faith, no goal seems out of reach. In fact, the notion that “the sky is the limit” applies only when you trust your own potential. Faith in yourself gives you strength, and that self-assurance clears away barriers.

Consider Martin Luther King Jr., who famously declared, “I have a dream.” He imagined a world where people would not be judged by their skin color. His unwavering belief in equality fueled his determination, and he remained positive even when progress was slow. Years of peaceful protests and inspiring speeches finally led him to deliver his vision in Washington D.C., creating lasting change. If you carry a dream and persist with confidence, there is no reason you cannot bring it to life.

Cristiano Ronaldo’s journey also shows the power of self-belief. Growing up in Portugal, he faced financial hardship and missed his father’s support. Yet he never gave up. By the age of thirteen, he balanced school, early-morning training sessions, and extra work to help his family. His passion and faith in his skills pushed him forward. Before long, he joined his national youth team and later became one of the world’s best footballers. Obstacles may stand in your way, but believing in yourself makes every challenge surmountable.

Even when doubts creep in, remember that persistence and faith can turn possibilities into realities. Start each day with confidence. Whenever you face setbacks, remind yourself of your strengths and keep going. Your aspirations can become achievements if you stay true to who you are and refuse to give up.

Modifying the school lunch menu would likely cause more harm than good. Many students are very selective about what they eat, and a new menu might not suit their tastes. Another concern is food allergies. Not every student feels comfortable telling others about their dietary restrictions, fearing teasing or misunderstanding. If the cafeteria introduces different ingredients without knowing exactly who is allergic to what, a harmless change could become dangerous. It’s better to stick with familiar recipes that staff already know are safe for everyone.

Even schools with generous budgets would lose money if students discard the new meals. When kids refuse the dishes, uneaten food must be thrown away, and the school’s investment goes down the drain. If the goal is to keep students happy, it makes little sense to spend funds on a menu that most pupils won’t enjoy.

In the end, keeping the current lunch options unchanged prevents waste, protects students’ health, and ensures the school uses its resources wisely.

In idleness, we miss out on growth and health.

In contrast, staying active offers many rewards. Pursuing a career or education gives structure to our days and boosts self-confidence. Holding a job helps us learn new skills, earn a living, and feel valued. Enrolling in classes or practising hobbies keeps our minds sharp and expands our horizons. Volunteering or helping others brings satisfaction and strengthens our community ties.

Even small steps—going for a walk, joining a workshop, or setting a simple daily goal—can build self-esteem and spark fresh opportunities. As Jefferson observed, “It is wonderful how much can be done if we are always doing.” Regular effort lays the groundwork for success, health, and a richer life experience.

People will always debate the right balance between rest and activity, but it’s clear that engagement outweighs idleness. By choosing action over passivity, we set ourselves on a path to well-being and accomplishment.

Taking something that isn’t yours is simply stealing.  

Many parents and schools teach children to leave found objects where they lay or, better yet, return them to their owner. I remember posters in my elementary school corridors reminding us to “Respect others’ property” and “If it’s not yours, don’t take it.” Most kids listened, but some didn’t care. They saw an opportunity and seized it, even if they didn’t need the item. That’s the difference between needing and wanting. If you really need something—a pair of glasses, for example—you might go to a store and buy it. But wanting something just for fun, or to show off, is different. If you don’t genuinely require it, but you take it anyway, you’re not fulfilling a need; you’re acting on impulse.  

If you happen upon a lost object, don’t pocket it. If you see someone drop something, hand it back or at least tell them. Be aware of your own behavior, resist peer pressure, and offer help when you can. Kindness is a choice, and returning what doesn’t belong to you shows respect and honesty.  

Imagine you lose your favorite toy. Maybe it’s the one you saved up all your allowance to buy. You search everywhere, but it’s nowhere to be found. You’d feel upset, angry, or even heartbroken. Now picture someone finds that toy and picks it up. If they kept it, you would never get it back. You would be left with the memory of the toy and perhaps some bitter feelings toward strangers. But if a good person saw you drop it and ran to hand it back, you’d feel happy, relieved, and grateful. That simple act makes a big difference.  

I learned this lesson the hard way when I lost my iPad years ago. I had left it on a bench and walked off without noticing. Later, I discovered it was gone and thought I’d never see it again. Until that moment, I’d never considered that someone might simply keep it. I ended up borrowing my mother’s phone and waiting until my father could replace my device. I was upset for days. That experience taught me how painful it is to lose something valuable and how unfair it feels when someone takes advantage of your carelessness.  

Today’s smartphones can cost over a thousand dollars—sometimes as much as a small used car. Losing a phone means losing access to calls, messages, and important apps. If someone steals your phone, you’d likely search everywhere for it and feel desperate to get it back. You’d understand just how personal and vital your possessions can be.  

This is why the lesson of returning found items matters so much. Taking what isn’t yours is never necessary and can leave someone else in distress. Let’s all choose honesty over temptation, kindness over convenience, and respect other people’s belongings as if they were our own.

I believe genuine self-esteem grows from real accomplishments. When students devote time and effort to their studies, they earn awards, grades, or praise that make them feel proud. This pride builds true confidence in their own abilities.

Yet many students fall into two common traps. First, some work very hard, finish assignments on time, even hold part-time jobs, but they still lack self-confidence. Without believing in themselves, they cannot turn their successes into lasting self-esteem. Second, other students feel confident in general but never push themselves to achieve anything noteworthy at school or during their free time. Without tangible achievements, their confidence never develops into genuine self-esteem.

To avoid these pitfalls, students should aim both to strengthen their self-belief and to pursue clear goals. Keeping a planner or checklist helps them stay punctual and organized. By setting deadlines and ticking off tasks each day, they create a path toward real accomplishments. When they see their efforts recognized—in a report card, competition, or teacher’s praise—they begin to feel proud of what they have achieved, and their self-esteem naturally follows.

I worry today’s students often fail to work hard. Perhaps technology makes them lazy, or they simply lack motivation to set academic goals. I get frustrated watching young people ignore their textbooks and then wonder why they fall behind. If they opened their backpacks and studied diligently for just two hours each evening, they would start earning more success at school—and this success would give them something to be proud of.

Teachers also play a vital role. Since students spend more time each week with their teachers than with anyone else, educators should guide them toward achievable goals. They do not need to deliver formal lessons on self-esteem or confidence. Instead, teachers can model good study habits, suggest productive activities, and show students how to break big tasks into smaller steps. As students experience these small victories, they will be inspired to build their own confidence and sense of worth.

I saw this process in my own life. When I arrived in the United States in 2017, I knew no English and had no friends. I was so shy that my face turned bright red whenever someone spoke to me. But I kept working—studying vocabulary, joining clubs, and talking to classmates. Over time, I learned to read, write, and speak fluently. Today, I have many friends and feel proud to be in school.

In the end, true self-esteem comes from a combination of self-confidence and real achievements. Students should focus on setting and reaching goals in school or wherever they learn. Parents and teachers can encourage them, but ultimately each student must believe in themselves and strive for success.

Thomas Jefferson once observed, “It is wonderful how much may be done if we are doing.” This idea suggests that constant effort leads to achievement, but it also raises the question: does inactivity ever have value? Some people believe rest is essential to regain strength, while others argue that staying busy helps us reach our ambitions and benefit society.

Every morning, millions wake up ready to work hard and give their best. But even those without a paid job can contribute—to their community or personal development—through volunteering, learning new skills, or helping neighbors. Of course, everyone needs occasional breaks to recharge. Yet, too much idleness can keep us from fulfilling our dreams and goals.

Actively pursuing worthwhile tasks is rewarding. When we work passionately, whether to pay bills, support family, or simply follow our interests, we feel motivated. My mother often tells me, “If you want something, go after it.” Her advice reminds me that building a better future requires effort. That belief explains why so many people choose to stay productive rather than remain idle.

From a societal perspective, being active is almost a necessity. We need a job to afford food, housing, and other expenses. But work does not have to mean only paid labor. While pauses for rest and reflection are important, they should not become excuses for endless inactivity. Some people argue that every student should be required to take art classes, while others think learners ought to choose their own electives. I believe it is best to let students pick the courses they find interesting. This freedom helps them discover what they enjoy, build useful skills, and prepare for life after high school.

First, being forced into a class you dislike can kill your motivation. If a student ends up in an unwanted elective, they may feel bored or frustrated and begin skipping lessons. Missing too many classes often leads to poor grades and a lack of credits, which can block graduation. Without a high school diploma, students have fewer options for college or meaningful jobs, and they may struggle to make a living or even risk homelessness. By choosing electives they care about, students are more likely to show up, stay focused, and earn the credits they need.

Second, everyone has unique talents, and picking the right elective can help students strengthen their abilities. When learners select a subject they are good at—whether it’s music, drama, coding, or design—they approach it with enthusiasm. This positive attitude usually results in better grades, deeper understanding, and the development of real skills. Those skills can open doors: a student who excels in drama might join a theatre company or appear in productions, turning a passion into a career. Likewise, someone skilled in graphic design might find freelance work or internships that lead to a rewarding profession.

Finally, having a clear idea of personal strengths and interests makes the future less daunting. Students who enjoy their electives gain confidence and set goals for life after graduation. They can choose college majors or vocational paths that suit their talents, rather than feeling lost or stuck. Although some might worry that giving students too much choice will lead to distraction or jokes, guided counselling and supportive teachers can help maintain seriousness and keep learners on track.

In summary, allowing students to choose electives they truly care about encourages attendance, uncovers talents, and lays a solid foundation for future success. This approach ensures young people graduate with confidence, useful skills, and a clear direction for their adult lives.

Four-day School

This essay debates the benefits and disadvantages of replacing the regular five-day school week with only four days.

Choosing a four-day school week is an option that should be adopted not only by some businesses but also by every high school and institution of higher education once they consider the following reasons.

It would mean losing ten hours of class time per week, but those missing hours can be recouped by extending the school day by two hours and increasing class time each day. This option can boost attention, allow students to complete any project or assignment assigned by their teacher, and give us more time with friends and teachers for support in any class where someone is failing.

We could also use the extra two hours on the fourth day for library time, which would be amazing for students who love reading or who want extra time for sports or any after-school activity.

The fifth day of the week could be reserved for doctor appointments or any health-related matters. Normally, the best excuse for missing class is a note from parents explaining that the student will be absent for some periods. Scheduling these appointments outside regular school time will decrease the number of missed classes.

We must not forget teachers who are also parents; they need an extra day for family time and regular activities with their children.

Seniors face the most difficult decisions of their lives—choosing a future path—and they need time to consider all university and college options, as well as part-time weekend jobs. Freshmen, coming from middle school, also need understanding and time to adjust to extra activities in high school that differ from their previous routine.

Another option for the free Friday or Monday is community service. With parental permission and adult supervision, any student who wishes can help clean up streets and rivers or engage in other community service projects. Schools can also create programs that partner with large companies that want to help students find jobs on this new free day and possibly part-time positions on weekends.

Considering only a four-day school week means forgetting the fifth day of school. Rather than coming for a little time on five days, we use the full time on four days. This gives us three free days per week to spend with family or friends or do anything we and our parents want. We would not have to wake up on Friday mornings—or possibly Monday mornings—depending on the school’s decision about which day is the third free day. Students could use that time to rest and complete responsibilities.

This idea might not be convenient for students with part-time jobs, because extending the school day by two hours reduces their available work time. Even so, anyone in this situation could use the free fifth school day for full-time work and earn a full workweek.

Being involved in two different activities per day can be hard and exhausting. Going to school and then work leaves no time to rest. But if school is only four days—even with two extra hours each day—students will have time after school to rest, work on any project or homework, and use the other three days for any job they choose.

When we acknowledge disadvantages, we also find solutions and benefits for each objection to this project, since more than 90 percent of students would benefit.

After considering all the benefits, disadvantages, and proposed solutions, I conclude: “Everyone needs three days free from school and just four days of school.” Even though every student’s situation is different—some may stay home, follow family routines, help with house chores, work, or study—if we all agree with this proposal, together we will have the power to fight for this new right for high school and college students. With the same power, together for a new right.

Having a four-day school week is an idea that should be considered by both businesses and educational institutions. By adjusting the usual five-day schedule, students would gain an extra day off while still completing the same amount of instruction.

Currently, a typical week provides about fifty hours of teaching over five days. If each day were extended by two hours, schools could cover the same content in four days. This change would allow longer lessons, giving teachers and students more time to work on projects, clarify difficult topics, and deepen their understanding.

An extended school day also creates extra opportunities for support. Struggling pupils could spend longer in class working with teachers or peers to catch up. Small group workshops or one-on-one tutoring could be built into the new schedule, helping more students stay on track.

Moreover, the additional hours in each of the four days could be used for after-school activities such as library research, sports training, or arts workshops. A student who loves reading could use the library more fully, while others interested in clubs or teams could participate without sacrificing academic hours.

One major benefit of cutting out the fifth day is that it becomes available for doctor’s appointments or personal errands. Currently, parents often send notes to excuse absences during class. Reserving a specific day off would reduce unexcused absences and interruptions in learning.

Teachers, many of whom are parents themselves, would also gain from a four-day week. An extra day off each week could be spent with their families, planning lessons, or engaging in professional development, leading to lower stress and higher job satisfaction.

High school seniors face pressure over college applications and part-time work. A three-day weekend would give them time to visit campuses, prepare for exams, and earn money. Younger students moving up from middle school would have a gentler transition, with extra time to adjust to new subjects and routines.

Schools could also offer community service options on the free day. With parental permission and adult supervision, students could volunteer in parks, libraries, or local charities. Partnerships with businesses might even lead to part-time job opportunities, giving teens valuable work experience.

Admittedly, balancing longer school days and fewer days in class could be tough for students with evening jobs. However, the dedicated free day could be used for full work shifts, allowing more consistent hours and better rest.

Considering all these benefits—from improved learning and support to a healthier work-life balance—a four-day school week appears to be a promising solution. While some challenges remain, the advantages for most students are clear. Everyone deserves a longer weekend and a four-day school week. By coming together in support of this change, high school and college students can secure the right to a more balanced education and personal life.

Many schools ask students to complete summer assignments so they keep learning during the break. I believe these projects should be chosen and planned by the students themselves rather than assigned by teachers. When learners pick their own topics, they focus on areas where they need improvement or find the subject most exciting. This personal investment makes it easier for them to stay motivated and develop new abilities.

First, creating their own project lets students explore a subject they care about. Because they decide the theme and scope, they fully understand the goals and methods. This familiarity makes the work more enjoyable and less intimidating than a task set by a teacher. For example, a student who struggles with writing in English can design a project that targets that skill, such as keeping a daily journal or writing short stories.

Second, working on a self-chosen project during the summer helps prevent gaps in knowledge. When students stop practicing altogether, they risk forgetting what they learned during the school year and losing confidence. By continuing to work on their own ideas, they stay engaged and build good study habits. An English learner, for instance, can keep improving vocabulary and grammar simply by reading articles or watching videos related to a hobby.

In conclusion, allowing students to design their summer assignments encourages responsibility and creativity. They remain active learners and return to school better prepared and more confident. I am convinced that student-created projects are not only more enjoyable but also more effective at keeping skills sharp over the break.

Some argue that our school shouldn’t switch to a four-day week or lengthen each day by two hours because they believe we aren’t wasting energy or materials. They point out that electricity, paper, and other supplies are essential for learning, helping us benefit from computers, smart boards, and science labs. In their view, changing the schedule would not bring any real savings and might even disrupt students’ routines without cutting resource use.

Despite these concerns, I believe a four-day week with longer days would help protect the environment. A recent county report revealed that our school’s resource consumption has jumped by 70% over the past few years. This overuse has led to more trees being felled nearby, harming local wildlife and tarnishing our school’s reputation. If we had one fewer day of classes each week, classrooms, cafeterias, and offices would all use less power, water, and paper. That would send a clear message that we care about conserving natural resources.

In addition, extending daily hours by two would let us fit in the same amount of teaching while reducing the number of times we switch on computers, projectors, and other devices. According to an energy-saving website, technology accounts for 80% of a typical school’s electricity use. Fewer mornings and afternoons of running equipment would lower our bills and give us more time to plan lessons or clean up materials between the four days.

Many still worry that this plan wouldn’t work, but cutting one day a week and lengthening the others offers real benefits for both nature and our budget. Imagine doing the same at home—turning off gadgets one day a week cuts your bills and helps the planet. Isn’t it worth trying at school, too?

“To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment,” wrote Ralph Waldo Emerson. I agree with this idea because when you stay true to your own values and talents, people notice something genuine and remarkable in you. Even if your first attempts aren’t perfect, you keep trying, and in doing so, you stand out among others. There are three main reasons why being yourself matters: others will want to follow your example, you will inspire those around you, and your achievements can shift people’s attitudes.

First, when you act with authenticity, others are likely to imitate you. Think of a student who goes out of their way to help classmates understand a math problem, even though it’s not part of their responsibility. Because they take that extra step, their peers admire them and begin to do the same. In this way, your honest efforts set a standard that others are eager to reach.

Second, being true to yourself makes you a source of inspiration. Whether it’s in your neighborhood, at home, or at church, people notice when you consistently act kindly and responsibly. For instance, if you regularly tidy your yard or lend a hand to a neighbor in need, your caring behavior motivates others to follow suit. Your example becomes a spark that encourages people to improve their own actions.

Finally, your personal accomplishments can influence how others think about what is possible. When people see your progress—perhaps starting a small business despite challenges—they often wonder how you did it. By sharing your methods and experiences, you give them hope and practical advice. They realize that if you could achieve your goals, they might succeed too.

In conclusion, staying true to yourself not only highlights your unique strengths but also benefits the wider community. As Emerson suggested, refusing to conform leads to personal victories that encourage others to do more and become better. Your genuine achievements can become a powerful example that inspires positive change in many lives.

In addition, a homework club encourages students to stay motivated and try new problem-solving methods. Rather than feeling isolated when facing hard tasks alone, pupils gain confidence from working alongside others. This supportive atmosphere reminds them that everyone has the ability to learn and succeed.

In conclusion, establishing a homework club offers multiple benefits: it helps students improve their grades, frees up time for personal activities, reduces fatigue, and builds a supportive community. Participants would also appreciate having a reliable space to ask for assistance and share experiences with peers. Such an initiative would be a positive step toward helping learners thrive both academically and personally.

People need to trust their instincts and follow their ideas because believing in ourselves is the foundation for success. Without confidence in our own judgment, it is hard for others to have faith in us. When we decide for ourselves, we rely on what our mind creates, rather than borrowing thoughts or copying from others. This approach sharpens our thinking and encourages genuine originality.

When people trust their ideas, they reduce the need to seek suggestions from friends or the internet. For instance, writing an essay using one’s own imagination not only builds skills but also brings satisfaction. By crafting something unique, we avoid plagiarism and develop a personal style that reflects our character.

Moreover, following our instincts enables us to address challenges immediately instead of waiting for external guidance. If a problem occurs, trusting your intuition allows you to act quickly and find a solution. This self-reliance fosters confidence, which is essential in both personal and professional life.

Self-belief also influences how others perceive us. For example, if you must give a class presentation but doubt your abilities, your teacher may notice your uncertainty and lose trust in your work. Nervousness about making mistakes can hurt your performance and even affect your grades. However, when you believe you can succeed, you speak more clearly and impress your audience.

In conclusion, people should always follow their instincts and develop their own ideas because self-confidence is the key to independence. Believing in yourself first makes it easier to seek help when needed, and it shows others that you are capable and valuable. By putting faith in your own thoughts, you build a strong sense of worth and open the door to genuine achievements.

I have always enjoyed drawing, especially when I sketch things like the moon, stars, forests, and the sea. For me, drawing is a powerful way to show my thoughts and emotions. There are many forms of art, but my favorites are drawing and painting. When I draw, I can create whatever comes to mind, and if I make a mistake, I can erase or adjust it. Painting is similar, but it also lets me express how I feel—whether I am happy, sad, or angry—through colors and brushstrokes.

Art is one of my greatest talents because I can turn an idea into something visible. Many people are willing to pay large sums for beautiful artwork, even if the price seems very high. Yet some artists doubt their skills and discard pieces they think are imperfect. They do not realize someone else might love those works and offer to buy them. Others choose to keep their art rather than sell it, either for personal memories or to share with family. In some cases, they sell only to relatives, not aiming for huge profits.

I believe artists should consider selling their work because it can bring in real income. Creating art is not an easy job—it demands patience and practice. Mistakes happen, but instead of starting over, we can turn them into something unique. Art often involves seeing something imperfect and transforming it into beauty.

Some people say art is boring, but that only shows they have not discovered its appeal. When you are passionate about art, you lose track of time and simply let your body guide the process. The result might not be perfect, yet the experience is joyful and exciting.

Of course, stress can arise when a piece does not turn out as planned. I feel this too, but I remind myself that patience and regular practice will help me improve. Even though art remains challenging, with persistence it becomes more manageable. I enjoy learning and will continue to develop my skills one drawing at a time.

Do students really gain anything by taking their lessons from home? I believe they do not, because many simply exploit the situation and fail to complete their work or absorb the material. I saw this firsthand with a friend who joined classes online. Instead of focusing on her studies, she used that freedom to delay tasks, find excuses, and spend time on anything but school. In the end, she learned very little.

To begin with, some students use home-based lessons as a chance to put off assignments and do personal errands. For instance, they might turn in projects days or even weeks late, claiming that they forgot or faced technical problems. While not everyone behaves this way, those who do see online classes as an open door to have fun. They might go shopping, hang out with friends, or spend hours scrolling on social media instead of logging in on time and finishing their schoolwork.

Even when confronted with a clear deadline, many avoid doing what they are supposed to. They know that teachers are not right there to watch them, so they postpone or ignore tasks until the last moment. Rather than using their time effectively to study or research, they choose to relax, play games, or chat with their partner. This lazy approach prevents them from practicing important skills and mastering new topics, which could help them in future classes or careers.

Perhaps worst of all, students often end up learning almost nothing in a home-based setup. Without the structure of a classroom, they skip lessons and rely on cheating to get through. Some simply copy answers from classmates or search for solutions online, never taking the chance to think through problems themselves. Others view remote schooling as an extended break, spending their days partying or browsing the internet. When lessons are supposed to be happening, they treat them as optional entertainment rather than serious education.

In conclusion, allowing students to attend classes from home does more harm than good. Many take advantage of the lack of supervision to delay work, ignore their responsibilities, and focus on leisure instead of learning. As a result, they miss out on valuable knowledge and skills. Rather than benefiting, these students fall behind and lose motivation, proving that for them, remote classes offer little real advantage.

Moreover, taking classes at home enhances student safety. With over a hundred school shootings reported in recent years, attending classes on campus can sometimes feel risky. In my view, letting students learn from home also reassures parents, who no longer have to fret over their child’s well-being during the school day. 

In summary, although group work is more challenging remotely, the comfort and security provided by home learning outweigh this drawback, making online classes a valuable option.

Some schools create mentoring programs that pair older students with younger ones. These initiatives aim to show older pupils how to handle responsibility while giving younger learners an idea of what they will face as they grow. At the same time, juniors benefit from the guidance and experience of their senior partners, and older students gain insight from teaching and supporting others.

Through these programs, older students can share the lessons they’ve learned from their own mistakes. Since everyone makes errors, seniors can point out better ways to study, solve problems, or behave in school. By explaining what worked for them and what did not, they help younger students avoid common pitfalls and make wiser choices in their academic and personal lives.

Younger students, in turn, feel more confident asking questions and admitting when they are struggling. When they face difficulties—such as confusing homework, language barriers, or social challenges—they know they have someone closer to their age to turn to rather than going straight to teachers. This trust makes it easier for juniors to express their concerns and learn from older students’ advice.

The relationship is not one-sided. Older students also learn valuable skills by working with juniors. They practice patience, improve their communication, and develop leadership qualities. Sometimes a younger student’s fresh perspective can even help a senior see a problem in a new light. In this way, both groups support each other’s growth.

Of course, these programs face challenges. Not every older student is eager to help, and some younger students may hesitate to listen. When either side refuses to cooperate, the benefits are lost. It takes commitment from both mentors and mentees, along with guidance from teachers, to keep the partnership strong.

Overall, pairing older and younger students promotes mutual respect and teamwork. Seniors learn to guide and protect, while juniors gain knowledge and confidence. By encouraging cooperation instead of competition, such programs help all participants understand right from wrong, share responsibilities, and grow together.

I believe many students do not give their studies their full attention because they confuse feeling good about themselves with genuine success. They think that self-esteem alone proves they have achieved something, but real accomplishments take effort and planning. In my view, young people often live only in the present, without understanding that life is more than simply getting by today. If we want success, we must look ahead and prepare for the future.

It is not easy to reach our goals, yet the sense of achievement that comes from hard work makes all the difference. True confidence grows when we trust our skills and ideas—being “confident” means believing in what you can do, while “confidence” refers to having faith in something or someone else. A student might say, “I have every confidence in my ability to pass this exam,” which shows they trust their own talent. To strengthen such trust, we must learn continually and respond to guidance, even when it feels like an order we cannot refuse.

Achievement is the feeling of satisfaction after completing a difficult task. If we lower our standards or avoid challenges, we miss out on growth. Life should offer us opportunities to improve, but we cannot enjoy each moment fully if we work without pause. It is important to balance effort with family time and simple pleasure, taking moments to appreciate our surroundings and to imagine where we want to be in years to come.

What exactly is the future? It is the time that lies beyond today, and planning for it requires both patience and thought. Whether thinking of where to live, what career to choose, or how to develop as a person, we need to look further ahead than the next few weeks. A profession—such as medicine or teaching—demands special training and often many years of study. A career, however, can span several jobs in the same field, each one building on the last and adding responsibility. In contrast, a trade usually involves manual skills taught through practice. Students often avoid part-time work because they feel inexperienced, but even an entry-level job can teach valuable lessons.

Experience means encountering new situations and learning from them. When a student first fails at something, they gain insight to do better next time. Alongside experience, honesty and sincerity matter greatly; being genuine in what you say and do builds trust. When we praise others sincerely, we show respect and encouragement, which helps everyone work together more effectively.

At the same time, we should take precautions to avoid mistakes—simple steps like organising our study schedule or saving money for emergencies can prevent bigger problems later. Tolerance is another vital quality: it means accepting opinions or behaviours that differ from our own, even when we disagree. By contrast, intolerance breeds conflict. Compassion also makes a difference; understanding others’ difficulties and offering help strengthens community.

Finally, before making any major decision—about a job, a move, or a relationship—we must weigh the risks. Careful consideration ensures we choose wisely. With respect for ourselves and others, and with both experience and patience, students can overcome insecurity and build real security for their future. By combining hard work, honest relationships, and thoughtful planning, they will turn self-esteem into true achievement.

In conclusion, I do not agree with Churchill’s statement. Success does not have to consists of going from failure to failure. You do fail a lot of times, but if you don’t give up and work really hard you can success in your goal or your big dream. Just never lose the enthusiasm that you have for something. That keeps you up for it. The warm feeling you have—the inspired interest for it—is strong, so don’t give up. Always work hard for what you want and you will success. Life isn’t easy, not even for rich people.

I believe that achieving success isn’t just about moving from one failure to the next, as Winston Churchill suggested when he said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” While setbacks are a part of any journey, I disagree that failure alone shapes success. Instead, hard work, determination, and a constant sense of enthusiasm are the real keys to reaching your goals.

First of all, everyone experiences failure at some point. No one goes through life without making mistakes or facing disappointments—whether it is missing out on a job opportunity, getting lower marks than expected in school, or letting others down. Even close friends or family can feel the impact when we fail to keep a promise or simply fall short of expectations. Perhaps a small number of people seem never to fail, but they are rare exceptions. For example, my cousin has always excelled in her studies, earning top grades and a scholarship to Virginia Tech University. Still, she too must have encountered challenges that required effort and resilience to overcome.

To turn dreams into reality, you need to work tirelessly and maintain a positive mindset. If you fail, don’t let sadness or frustration stop you. Instead, remind yourself that every setback offers a chance to learn and improve. Life is hard, and nothing worthwhile comes easily. If one plan doesn’t work out, brainstorm new ways to move forward or explore different paths. By remaining persistent and flexible, you can discover fresh opportunities and ultimately reach your goals.

Enthusiasm plays a crucial role in this process. When you are genuinely excited about something, you give it more energy and care. People who lack enthusiasm often treat life as a series of obligations, accepting whatever comes without passion or vision. In contrast, those who feel inspired pour their hearts into their efforts, whether it’s a personal project, a career goal, or learning a new skill. I experienced this firsthand when I moved to the United States and had to start learning English from scratch. My initial struggle turned into a source of motivation, and my enthusiasm helped me make rapid progress.

In conclusion, I do not agree that success is merely a sequence of failures. While setbacks may arise, triumph depends on hard work, creative problem-solving, and maintaining enthusiasm. By staying determined and passionate about what you pursue, you can move beyond each disappointment and ultimately achieve your dreams. Remember, life may be tough, but with effort and excitement, success is within reach.

All students, whether they have finished school or university, deserve the chance to work in places where they can learn and develop. Taking a job lets them put their classroom knowledge into practice and show what they can do. This hands-on experience helps them gain confidence and useful skills.

Even younger pupils—such as fourteen or fifteen-year-olds—should not be prevented from having part-time positions if they are willing and able. Refusing these opportunities would only hold back their personal growth and delay their understanding of the working world.

I believe every student has the right to demonstrate their abilities, gather new ideas, and gain experience that will support their future careers. Part-time work encourages them to give their best effort, improving their time-management and problem-solving skills. It also promotes independence and helps them value the support their families provide. Furthermore, early work experience allows students to explore different industries, helping them decide which career path matches their interests and strengths. In conclusion, giving students the freedom to work and apply their talents is essential for preparing them to succeed in adult life.

Attending courses online offers significant benefits for students with hectic schedules, and it can also support anyone keen to continue their education. Online classes provide a practical solution for those who struggle to find time to prepare meals, complete assignments, and travel to campus. Many people also balance work and study, and traditional class times can seem like a barrier to their academic goals.

By studying from home, learners can arrange a daily routine that fits their needs. They can cook or order food without rushing, finish their homework at their own pace, and handle household chores when it suits them. These flexible study hours ensure that important tasks at home do not conflict with class obligations.

Parents, in particular, gain from remote learning. If you have a small child, you can look after them and still attend lectures via the internet. Similarly, those who must work can join lessons during their breaks or after a shift, making it easier to keep both job and education on track.

Another advantage is for students who live far from an institution or lack reliable transport. They can log in from their own home and avoid a long commute. Even during the summer, learners who wish to stay academically active can take extra courses online or through video conferencing.

In my view, online education is a great opportunity for many people. Busy individuals or anyone interested in learning can benefit by choosing virtual classes that fit their life.

Making thoughtful decisions can make life more enjoyable and less stressful. When we plan carefully before acting, our experiences tend to be smoother and more fulfilling.

Too often, people waste time on choices that harm their future. For instance, if I skip classes at school, my teacher will inevitably contact my parents, and I end up in trouble. Missing lessons can also hurt my academic record and make it harder to reach my goals. Later on, when I look for good jobs, employers might offer me lower salaries or fewer advantages because I didn’t complete my education properly.

In my home country, I once made a serious mistake by playing soccer instead of attending a class. My friend and I thought it would be fun, but we didn’t pause to consider the consequences. As a result, I failed that course, my grades suffered, and my parents were disappointed. This situation taught me how important it is to think before making decisions.

My brother experienced something similar. In ninth grade, he spent most of his time hanging out with friends and told me he didn’t care about the SOL exams. However, by twelfth grade, he realized that passing those tests was crucial for graduation. He regretted not preparing earlier and often reminded me, “Don’t make the same mistake I did.”

I believe that weighing our options before deciding is essential for achieving our ambitions and protecting our future. When we act thoughtfully, we increase our chances of success and can even inspire positive changes around us. Thinking before acting does not only benefit us as individuals but also those around us. If everyone practiced this habit, communities would grow stronger and more harmonious. Ultimately, careful decision-making paves the way for a brighter future.

How technology affects people’s lives and human relationships is a topic many discuss today. I agree that technology is not the greatest invention, since it can weaken family ties and reduce face-to-face contact. When people say technology is harmful, they usually mean it changes the way we live and interact. Here are three main reasons why it can have a negative impact: addiction to phones, excessive online shopping, and a lack of personal communication.

First, many become so absorbed in their smartphone or video games that they forget about others. If someone nearby needs help, a person glued to their screen may ignore them, believing the device is more important. This happens to both adults and children, and it shows why kindness and attention to others matter more than any gadget.

Second, online shopping offers freedom and convenience, especially for independent women choosing clothes or gifts. Yet some people develop a real shopping addiction, buying things they don’t need and harming their budget and well-being.

Finally, when individuals stop talking to friends or family in person, they lose motivation and inspiration for the future. Without real conversations, life can feel dull and uninspiring.

In conclusion, we should support those who are hooked on technology and help them find a healthier balance. Overusing phones and apps can damage relationships and limit future opportunities. For these reasons, I agree that technology is not the best creation humans have made.

Albert Einstein once said, “Imagination is more important than knowledge,” and I completely agree with him. Imagination can bring us joy, help others feel better, and even lead to the ideal career. In the following paragraphs, I will explain how it achieves these benefits.

First, imagining pleasant scenarios can boost our happiness. If you long to fly like a bird, picture yourself soaring above the clouds, feeling the wind against your face. You might imagine the freedom, the lightness, or even the challenge of flapping your wings. You could also fantasize about what you will look like at one hundred years old, or recall a favorite childhood memory in vivid detail. In each case, using your imagination makes you feel lighter and more joyful.

Second, imagination is a powerful tool for helping other people. Imagine a young child crying in a busy shopping mall because she feels different from the crowd. You could kneel beside her and say, “Don’t be upset—everyone is staring because they think you’re a princess visiting her kingdom. You must be polite and graceful.” By encouraging her to view the situation through a playful story, you might turn her tears into laughter.

Finally, imagination can guide us to our dream jobs, even if some parents believe otherwise. A home designer without creative ideas will struggle to create appealing spaces and might lose clients. In contrast, a writer with a rich imagination can invent dozens of captivating books and earn as much as—or more than—many professionals. Clearly, imagination can open doors to fulfilling and successful careers.

In conclusion, I strongly believe, just as Einstein did, that imagination matters more than knowledge. It can make us happier, comfort others, and help us find the perfect job. Imagination truly is one of our greatest assets.

One valuable skill I’ve developed is reading aloud. When I speak the words instead of just moving my eyes over them, I understand the ideas more clearly. Hearing my own voice makes the information stick in my mind, and I find it much easier to explain key points afterward. This habit also proves useful whenever I need to write an essay about what I have read.

Reading aloud benefits me in several ways. First, it helps me notice the flow of each sentence and whether I’m pronouncing terms correctly. If I stumble over a phrase or a word, I can pause and figure out its meaning before moving on. That extra moment of reflection deepens my understanding and makes the text feel more familiar.

Another advantage is that reading aloud keeps the details of a story alive in my head. Once I finish a chapter, I can still recall characters, events, and important facts without struggling to piece them together. In contrast, when I read silently, I often find that I’ve missed or forgotten significant parts. I’ve also seen classmates remember plots more easily when they read aloud, since speaking reinforces their memory.

When it’s time to write an essay, reading the source material out loud gives me a clear outline of what I want to say. I can collect plenty of examples and ideas just by vocalizing the text. That way, when I start writing, I’m not at all nervous about what to include—I’ve already internalized the main points. Reading aloud also helps me stay focused on the topic, ensuring that my essay reflects the author’s intent.

In summary, reading aloud is a technique I rely on because it improves my comprehension, strengthens my recall, and simplifies essay writing. By speaking the words, I make the information my own and feel more confident when I write about it.

Working with others brings many advantages. First, group members can generate ideas, share examples, and supply useful information. When you work on your own, there is no one to back up your suggestions or to offer feedback.

One major advantage of teamwork is the chance to discuss the task with others. You can ask questions, compare examples, and get advice on how to approach your assignment. This support makes it easier to refine ideas and find solutions.

On the other hand, working alone has some positive points. You can rely entirely on your own ideas without interruptions, and you have full control over your examples. However, finding all the information yourself can be more difficult, and you miss out on encouragement from peers.

Imagine a high school English class where students form groups of four for a project. One person researches information, another writes it down, a third adds examples, and the fourth prepares to present the work. In this way, each student has a clear role, and the group effort reduces stress and leads to a more polished final product.

If a student chooses to work alone, they may enjoy the quiet and independence, but they lack the chance to discuss ideas. This can lead to nervousness and boredom in class.

Some people avoid group work because they feel uncomfortable or prefer to concentrate in silence. Most, however, enjoy collaborating with friends, exchanging questions, and benefiting from mutual support.

Every student faces challenges at school and learns to persevere even without constant congratulations. Although a kind word now and then can uplift spirits, celebrating every small success can weaken genuine self-confidence. I believe that real self-esteem grows out of personal effort: it keeps students humble, prevents them from becoming self-centered, and helps them cope when praise is no longer guaranteed.

When someone truly applies themselves, their hard work becomes clear in both their results and their attitude. Plenty of young people have given their best without ever hearing “well done.” If students must rely on applause for every achievement, they miss the lesson of genuine effort. They might start believing that every good deed deserves a reward, rather than valuing the satisfaction of overcoming a challenge.

Constant praise can also encourage arrogance. A student who is always told they are excellent may lose empathy for classmates who struggle. Instead of offering help, they might boast about their grades and hurt others’ feelings. On the other hand, pupils who quietly work toward their goals often develop a stronger inner drive and respect for their peers’ efforts.

Moreover, if praise becomes the main motivator, students learn to chase rewards instead of embracing hard work. They may ask, “What’s my prize?” instead of thinking, “I want to learn.” When they finally see that genuine achievement needs persistence rather than applause, they feel a deeper sense of pride. Knowing you’ve earned success on your own terms is far more empowering than any external compliment.

In conclusion, true confidence comes from disciplined effort, not from constant praise. Students who find satisfaction in their own progress remain grounded and keep striving, even without applause. Those are the individuals who deserve recognition.

Working with a team offers many advantages over completing assignments on your own. When people join forces, tasks become more manageable and can be finished more quickly. In a group, each member contributes their own perspectives and suggestions, making it easier to tackle challenges and find efficient solutions. By sharing the workload, no one person has to shoulder every responsibility, so the overall effort feels lighter and more enjoyable.

Collaborating with others also means that everyone’s strengths come into play. Some members might excel at research, while others are good at organizing information or presenting ideas. This division of labor ensures that each part of the project is handled by someone well-suited to the task, which not only speeds up progress but also improves the quality of the final result. Instead of spending hours alone trying to figure out every detail, group members can exchange feedback and support one another, leading to a deeper understanding of the assignment.

A clear leader within the team can further streamline the process. This person assigns specific tasks, tracks everyone’s progress, and steps in when someone encounters an unexpected problem. For example, if a member has to deal with a family emergency and cannot complete their section on time, the leader can rearrange responsibilities so that the work continues smoothly. Such coordination would be impossible when working solo, leaving you with no one to rely on for help.

In summary, collaborating in a group not only reduces the time and effort required but also enhances the final product through shared ideas and mutual support. By distributing tasks and relying on each other’s skills, you can achieve better results more efficiently than if you tackled the assignment alone.
