Working in a group offers many advantages for students and can benefit them now and in the future. First of all, when people join forces, they bring together more ideas than a single person could. If someone is unsure about what to do, their classmates can explain and guide them. This kind of support makes it easier to understand difficult tasks and often leads to better results. Moreover, collaborating helps students pass their classes more easily, since they can check each other’s work and fill in any gaps. In addition, working with classmates you might not have spoken to before gives a chance to make new friends and learn about different perspectives.

Another important benefit of group work is the development of communication skills. By discussing projects, each member practices expressing thoughts clearly and listening carefully. Students who feel confident in writing or speaking can show others how to improve these skills. At the same time, learners who struggle—perhaps because of language barriers—receive extra help. Regular teamwork also teaches negotiation and problem-solving. These abilities are not only valuable in school but will continue to be useful in everyday life, like talking to family members or cooperating with coworkers in a job.

Group work can also build strong relationships and lead to personal growth. When classmates share responsibilities, they learn how to trust one another and be generous with their time. This trust often turns into lasting friendships and a positive classroom atmosphere. Teachers benefit too, since classes with good teamwork often see higher grades and fewer conflicts. Beyond school, people who are used to working well in a team tend to succeed in workplaces, sports teams, or community projects. Cooperation becomes a habit that can open doors in many areas of life.

Of course, sometimes working alone is necessary for focus or to prevent copying. It is true that some students may get distracted by chatting in a group. Yet when guided by a teacher who sets clear goals and roles, a team can stay on track and overcome obstacles together. If one person feels stuck, others can step in right away. This immediate support is something that working alone cannot provide.

In my opinion, teachers should encourage more group assignments because the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks. Through teamwork, students gain fresh ideas, learn vital skills, and form better relationships. They also prepare themselves for future challenges at work and in their personal lives, where cooperation is often essential. I enjoy working in groups myself because I can ask for help when I’m unsure and contribute in areas where I feel strong. Overall, learning to work well with others is a valuable experience that helps us all achieve more than we could on our own.

Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” Failures play a crucial part in reaching our goals because they push us to grow, teach us valuable lessons, and make us tougher.

First of all, mistakes help us get better in many areas—at school, at work, and in everyday life. We cannot expect to succeed in everything on the first try. When we do fail, it’s important to pause and examine what went wrong. By identifying our weak points and experimenting with different methods, we gradually improve our performance.

Secondly, failures teach us about our own errors. If something isn’t working, it usually means we need to adjust our approach—whether that involves reorganizing our study habits, refining our professional skills, or improving how we communicate with others. Learning from each misstep encourages us to discover new strategies that lead to better results.

Finally, encountering setbacks makes us stronger. Instead of staying down after a failure, we should stand up, keep moving forward, and maintain confidence in ourselves. Almost everyone hopes for success and stability, but only those who persist through difficulties can truly achieve their dreams.

In conclusion, setbacks do not hold us back; they propel us forward. By using failures to refine our actions, learn from mistakes, and build resilience, we become better students, employees, and individuals.

Science experiments are among my favorite school activities. They stand apart from other assignments such as math or language arts tasks, which often involve solving problems or writing essays. In contrast, science projects let us explore real phenomena up close. For example, during one dissection, I examined a frog’s inside. Although it smelled unpleasant and some might find it gross, I was fascinated by how few organs the frog had compared to humans. Perhaps some organs were not visible, but overall the frog’s anatomy seemed simpler.

I also noticed the vivid colors inside the frog. While human tissues are mostly shades of red, I saw patches of blue and pink. The specimens had been frozen, so their tissues were a bit dry, making it easier to cut. My group members and I carefully sliced open each part, eager to learn more. The most revolting discovery was a cluster of flies in the frog’s stomach, which made me shiver, but did not spoil my curiosity.

After we explored, our teacher identified each organ and explained its function. One of my classmates thought it would be funny to poke the frog’s eye before it thawed completely. Unexpectedly, a stream of fluid spurted out, drenching him. He hurried off to the bathroom while the rest of us watched, stunned but amused. Following that incident, our teacher decided to end the dissection early, but everyone agreed it had been exciting.

More recently, we did another activity related to our light unit, this time in a darkened room. We sprayed a fine mist in front of a flashlight to see light waves. At first I saw nothing and felt disappointed, but after a few seconds I noticed faint streaks of light particles. Although the experiment was brief and the explanation took some time, I still found it interesting.

These experiences show that science experiments can be thrilling and memorable. Even if you think they might be unpleasant, you should try them. In my opinion, hands-on activities are the best way to learn, making classes far more engaging than traditional assignments.

Thus, although phones can be useful educational tools, they also lead to misconduct and distraction in the classroom.

A simple act of kindness may seem minor, but it can brighten someone’s day and even improve their well-being. A genuine smile, a helping hand, or a few encouraging words cost little but can leave a lasting impression. No matter how small the gesture is, it can lift a person out of a difficult moment and remind them that they are not alone. By offering these small tokens of care, we carry forward the message that every life matters.

When someone receives a kind act, they often feel valued and supported. That warm feeling inside—knowing another person took a moment to think of you—can boost your mood and your health. Kindness can make you feel uplifted both inside and out, creating one of the most positive emotions you can experience. There is no need for expensive gifts or grand displays; sometimes a simple compliment or genuine attention is enough to make someone feel special.

Once you have experienced this kindness yourself, you usually feel inspired to share it with others. You might help a neighbour with their groceries, offer to tidy up around the house, or simply give a friendly wave to a passer-by. These small repayments of goodwill spread positivity and help build stronger communities. In this way, each act of kindness fuels another.

Have you felt the impact of a small, caring gesture? What moments have made you feel truly seen and appreciated? And how do you choose to pass on that feeling to others?

Many schools now offer distance learning, letting students join lessons from home through the internet or video calls. I believe this approach helps learners in three main ways: it creates a quieter study environment, supports those with health issues, and gives busy people flexibility to balance work and education.

First, studying at home often means fewer distractions. Classrooms can be crowded and noisy, which makes it hard for some students to focus. In contrast, when attending classes online, students can choose a quiet corner at home and concentrate on the lesson. This calm setting helps them complete tasks faster and take more interest in what they are learning.

Second, distance learning benefits students who cannot attend school because of sickness or health problems. Instead of falling behind, they can log into a virtual classroom and participate just like their classmates. This prevents gaps in their education and allows them to keep up with coursework even when they are at home recovering.

American jazz icon Duke Ellington once said, “A problem is a chance for you to do your best.” He meant that facing a difficulty gives you the opportunity to improve the situation. I disagree with this idea because sometimes attempts to solve a problem can actually make matters worse.

For example, suppose your kitchen sink starts leaking and you have no idea how to repair it. You call a plumber, but he must leave for another job before finishing. Later, you try to imitate what you saw him do, hoping to save time. Instead, you tighten the wrong pipe and water sprays everywhere, flooding the floor. Now you have to hire the plumber again, pay extra fees, and clean up a bigger mess. In this case, trying to do your best without full knowledge only worsened the situation.

Another case involves children and their pets. When a beloved dog or cat dies, some parents think they can help by getting a replacement right away. However, that new pet cannot fill the same role in the child’s heart. When my dog Lucky passed away, my brother and I barely ate or spoke for days. Our father brought home another puppy, but neither of us could forget Lucky, and the new dog never felt like the same friend.

Finally, imagine you see a classmate looking upset at school. You ask what’s wrong, and when he stays silent, you offer to come over after class to help with homework—telling him to check with his dad first. At that moment, he starts crying. You learn his father died in a car accident just the night before. Your well-meaning suggestion only made him feel deeper sorrow.

Because these attempts to “do your best” can backfire, I believe that problems do not always present a helpful chance to improve things.

I believe that first impressions are very hard to change for three main reasons. To begin with, when you meet someone for the first time, you form immediate feelings about them—whether you feel drawn to them or put off by their behavior. These instant reactions often stick with you long after the initial meeting. Second, sometimes you never cross paths with that person again. In such cases, the one encounter you had becomes the only basis for your opinion of them, and since there is no chance to see a different side, your judgment remains unchanged. Third, even if you do see the person regularly, your initial perception tends to influence every future encounter. You keep interpreting their actions through the lens of that first impression, making it difficult to adjust your view.

For example, I once met someone new at a gathering and found his manner of speaking and attitude off-putting. Since I never saw him again, my negative opinion of him stayed the same. This shows how hard it can be to alter our first impressions of people.

Jefferson’s message warns us against laziness: while we all need downtime, excessive inactivity prevents us from reaching our ambitions. His statement reminds us that consistent effort can yield impressive results. Many memorable quotes come from people who made a lasting impact, and Jefferson’s words continue to inspire readers to take action rather than remain idle.

I strongly agree with Winston Churchill’s view that persistence in the face of difficulty is essential to success. At first glance, many people assume that achieving their dreams will be smooth and effortless. However, as we move through life, we often face obstacles that test our strength. Enduring repeated setbacks can feel discouraging, but these experiences also teach us resilience. By maintaining hope and focusing on our goals, we can keep pursuing our ambitions even when nothing seems to go right.

Furthermore, failure is inevitable at various stages of life. For instance, a student may receive poor grades, a young professional might fail to secure a desired job, and later in life one can run into money troubles or difficulty finding a home. Instead of viewing these moments as permanent defeats, we should treat them as signals to develop practical plans. This means setting realistic steps, exploring possible solutions and, if needed, asking for advice from friends, family or mentors. In this way, we learn how to navigate challenges rather than avoid them.

Another important point is that overcoming failure often leads to self-discovery. When we find a way to solve a problem, we uncover more about our strengths and weaknesses. This insight helps us prevent the same mistake in the future and gives us confidence to try again. By continuously practising improved strategies, we build a stronger mindset. In the end, each failure becomes a stepping-stone, guiding us toward better approaches and eventual achievements.

To conclude, difficult times affect everyone and can leave us feeling lost. It is helpful to share our struggles with someone we trust, as discussing setbacks often leads to fresh ideas and encouragement. Whether we tackle obstacles on our own or with support, it is our courage to continue—sparked by others and fueled by our own hope—that transforms failure into success.

The city council is considering a 10 pm curfew on weekdays and a midnight curfew on weekends for all teenagers. I firmly support this plan because it will protect young people from danger and help them avoid trouble. By requiring them to return home at a set time, we can reduce the risks they face on the streets late at night.

First, when teens are not allowed to roam around after curfew, they are far less likely to encounter people who use drugs or behave aggressively. The nighttime environment can be unpredictable and unsafe, so restricting their time outside decreases the chance of harm. Second, an earlier bedtime means teenagers can spend more quality time with their families. They can work on homework, share conversations about positive events, and enjoy a calming evening routine. This kind of family interaction strengthens bonds and supports young people’s emotional well-being.

Finally, obeying a curfew teaches teenagers the importance of following rules and respecting laws. Failing to comply could result in legal or school-related consequences that affect their future. In short, implementing a curfew keeps teenagers safer, encourages family engagement, and promotes responsibility—making it a beneficial policy for our community.

Although it may seem that “unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow,” it is actually right. But mastering something does not mean that trying something new would make you fail. Giving up is what would cost you growth. For example, changing your lifestyle by eating right and going to the gym is not going to be easy, but you are still going to give it a try. That is why we try new things: we want to challenge ourselves in a situation we never knew we could solve or might give up on. Another reason is that we love trying new things because we are curious if we can master them. Another example would be raising a kid, wondering if we have everything and teaching them what is right and what is wrong. That is why we love trying new things: to see if we can do it or not. That is what is more important—trying new things and seeing if we can master them—because we are capable of doing things a computer can’t do and that is trying to learn new things.

We can master anything in our way because we are willing to find out if we can do this; if we cannot, we do not fear it; if we got this, we give ourselves ideas that anything we do is possible. When we put our mind to it, nothing can stop us. For example, we got our freedom from England a long time ago, we ended slavery, and we ended racism, which was big in the United States. Those are the reasons why we can master things even if they are hard to master. We do it for a reason, and the reason is that we love to try new things even if they are bad. When our mind and our body just don’t want it and we don’t keep trying, at some point we start calling ourselves losers, quitters.

But people who have mastered it—because they did give it a try and successfully mastered those emotions that give us a hard time in life—are therapists who want to understand those types of emotion because they want to help people who don’t understand why they react like that.

That is what makes us try new things in life: we are curious about what interests us as human beings and want to see if we can master it. So, “unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, keep trying new thing that you would be able to do and get your attention to it.”

People often claim that “unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow,” and I believe this is true. Learning new skills or facing unfamiliar challenges may lead to mistakes, but giving up is what really prevents us from improving. For example, adopting a healthier lifestyle by changing eating habits and starting a workout routine can be tough, yet many of us attempt it because we want to push our limits. We take on these new experiences not only to see if we can succeed but also to discover activities we might enjoy.

Consider learning to cook. Even if you have never prepared a meal before, the desire to challenge yourself drives you to try. You might burn a dish or follow a recipe wrong the first time, but each attempt teaches you something valuable. This curiosity extends to other parts of life—like raising a child. New parents often wonder if they can guide their children correctly, teaching them right from wrong. By stepping into such a demanding role, they test their abilities and learn from every success and mistake.

Human history also shows how attempting extraordinary goals leads to major achievements. Our nation’s quest for independence from England, the abolition of slavery, and the fight against racial segregation in the United States all required people to go far beyond what they had previously experienced. These milestones were not easy to reach, yet the willingness to face daunting challenges led to lasting progress.

One of the toughest areas to master is our own emotional world. When we struggle with feelings like sadness, anger, or fear, it can be tempting to give up and label ourselves as losers. This emotional pain often hurts more than any physical injury. However, those who work through these feelings—sometimes with the help of professionals—learn to understand and manage their emotions. Therapists study human reactions precisely because they have faced these issues themselves and found ways to overcome them. Their success shows that even our inner challenges can be tackled if we are brave enough to try.

In every aspect of life, from personal goals to historical achievements and emotional growth, attempting new things is essential. Even when failure is a possibility, pushing our boundaries opens the door to real development. As the saying goes, keep trying activities beyond your current expertise—only then can you truly discover what you are capable of achieving.

We may fail more than once, but each mistake brings us closer to our aim.

Second, overcoming failures can motivate and support others. Attitude is crucial: positive energy can lift those who feel discouraged. For example, my cousin repeated 12th grade three times. After failing the first year, she lost confidence and almost abandoned her goals. This year, however, she studied hard and is finally on track to graduate. Her journey shows how persistence after failure can lead to success.

Some argue that failure has no place in society. I disagree. Learning always starts with mistakes. My third reason is that repeated failures teach us what not to do, guiding us toward future success. As the saying goes, “You may lose the battle but not the war.” We might lose moments but never our drive.

In conclusion, failure plays a vital role in achievement. It allows us to develop personal strengths, encourage others, and build experience. Everyone faces setbacks, but we must keep going, stay positive, and never give up on our dreams.

Ralph Waldo Emerson declared, “Unless you try something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” I consider this statement extremely wise. Although people frequently share thoughtful advice, its true value vanishes if we do not put it into practice. Beyond our physical maturation, I believe personal and intellectual development depends on embracing challenges outside our comfort zones.

If someone simply repeats the same routine each day without exploring anything new, they will find it hard to make meaningful progress. To me, this idea seems almost self-evident—there really is no strong argument against it. During my seventeen years, I have experimented with a variety of hobbies and skills, from learning to play instruments to trying different sports. Even when these ventures didn’t go as planned, they all contributed to my growth by teaching me resilience and expanding my outlook.

Too often, people reject new experiences because they judge them merely by first impressions or fear that they lack the necessary ability. For example, someone might dismiss a unique art workshop because its style seems strange, or avoid meeting people from different backgrounds because they appear unfamiliar. Yet, if individuals would grant these opportunities a chance, they might uncover hidden talents or gain insights that shape their future in unexpected ways.

Reflecting on Emerson’s insight, the decision to step beyond what we already know rests with each person. If I choose to leave my comfort zone and explore something entirely different, I am likely to learn and feel more fulfilled. Conversely, if I stick to a dull routine, I will eventually become bored and stagnant. Some may argue that success often comes through repetition—like athletes drilling the same plays or dancers rehearsing identical steps until they perform flawlessly. Undeniably, mastery in those fields requires practice. Still, others achieve success by trying fresh approaches and facing new challenges that lead them to surprising achievements.

In the end, attempting new things can transform us, either by strengthening our abilities or teaching us valuable lessons through failure. While some people age gracefully, growing wiser with each experience, others remain stuck in youthful habits, missing opportunities for real growth. Emerson was right: without testing ourselves beyond our present limits, we hold back our own development.

Without experiencing failure, achieving success in life is almost impossible. Although failure means not yet reaching your objectives, it can be a catalyst that drives you toward your future goals and personal growth.

I support Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea because recognizing our errors is vital. If we only ever succeed, we lack the chance to learn how to respond when things go wrong. By facing failure early, we uncover our weaknesses and develop strategies to improve. This process makes our future successes more meaningful. Additionally, experiencing setbacks enables us to understand the effort and challenges involved in reaching ambitions, so we know what is required to triumph.

On the other hand, one could argue that too much failure limits our achievements. Repeated setbacks might discourage us from pursuing new goals. Excessive failure can also damage our confidence if we don’t reflect constructively. While success feels good at the moment, it can create a false sense of security that leaves us unprepared when unexpected problems arise.

In my opinion, failure and success complement each other. I choose Emerson’s viewpoint because life often takes surprising turns. Embracing failure helps us build the resilience and skills needed for lasting success when unforeseen events occur.

I believe every student should join an activity or sport at their own school because it offers a chance to enjoy something meaningful. First of all, choosing a hobby you love helps you stay motivated. If you find an activity that excites you, you’re more likely to stick with it and improve. Many students doubt themselves and never realize their potential. But if you trust your abilities and spend time on what you enjoy, you can develop real skills and even reach high levels of success.

The second reason is that participating in school activities keeps you active and healthy. Instead of spending hours doing nothing, being involved in a sport or club encourages movement and exercise. Regular physical activity strengthens your body, boosts your energy, and can even lead to future opportunities, such as scholarships or a professional career. Staying busy with something you care about also prevents boredom and teaches you discipline.

My third point is about reducing screen time. Spending all day on phones, tablets, or video games can be distracting and tiring. If you replace some of that time with outdoor fun or a team sport, you’ll feel more awake and focused both at school and at practice. Playing with friends outside, going for a hike, or working on a project together not only is more exciting but also helps you sleep better and be more productive.

In summary, you only get one life, so it’s important to make the most of it by joining activities you love. Trying new things builds confidence and shows others that you can lead, not just follow. When you commit to a sport or club, you grow as a person, inspire those around you, and make your school years much more rewarding.

Some schools now allow students to join classes online or through video conferencing. However, this option raises issues if families lack a computer. In addition, parents who work may worry about leaving their children unsupervised during lessons. Purely online courses without a live instructor can leave learners confused when they face problems alone. Despite these challenges, video conferencing can be more effective than self-guided online lessons. A live teacher can explain tasks in detail and answer questions immediately. Many learners prefer having someone present to support them while they complete their work. Studying from home also brings benefits for students who feel overwhelmed by crowded classrooms. They often find it easier to concentrate alone in a quiet space, especially when guided by a patient instructor moving at their pace. Moreover, home-based classes allow learners to decide when and which days they want to study. This flexibility helps them balance education with other commitments. Although technology access and childcare are valid concerns, the advantages of personalized instruction, a calm environment, and scheduling freedom show how video conferencing can improve the learning experience.

Imagine there is an event but afterwards someone must tidy up as community service. Doing this work is the right thing to do. Community service plays a key role in improving neighborhoods, so residents enjoy a better environment in the future. Although some people refuse to help or have other plans, taking part in these activities is similar to how students help in school.

Have you ever needed examples to learn something, or do you learn better with different ways instead of receiving examples? Well, as Albert Schweitzer said, "Example is not the main thing to influence others." Therefore, this means that there are other ways to influence others without using or giving examples.

For instance, one way that people may get influenced is if they receive help from others instead of examples; in fact, this can be better than giving examples. Specifically, in the ceramics class, the teacher mostly gives us examples of how to make clay stuff. Moreover, she almost never helps me, and as a result it is difficult for me and for others to make things because she only explains one time how to do it, and some of the students forget about it. However, when she helps someone, their project results always turn out to be the best in the class because of her help.

On the other hand, other people say that when they receive examples, sometimes they get confused. This happens when the examples they get make them change their perspective over what they are doing. For example, when doing a drawing, sometimes the teacher tells you to make a drawing of your imagination—this means of your thinking and whatever is on your brain. What could happen when the teacher tells you what to draw after she said that the drawing is about your imagination, and then she gives examples on what to draw? This makes you think that she wants you to draw other things that are not in your thinking. Consequently, this shows that sometimes examples do not work on specific subjects because they tend to confuse you.

Although others may say that when they use examples they are more able to influence others—because they show the experience that they have on it and also teach how to do something—and there are many people that learn better and get more influenced when they use examples, I think that there are a few ways that are stronger, which make the examples less useful or powerless to influence others. For these reasons, I think that there are better ways to influence others without using examples.

Have you ever needed examples to learn, or do you prefer other methods besides demonstrations? As Albert Schweitzer once noted, examples aren’t the primary means of influencing people. In fact, various approaches can sway others without relying on sample models.

One effective method of influence is providing direct assistance. In my ceramics class, our teacher often showed us how to shape clay but rarely offered individual guidance. As a result, many students, including myself, struggled to remember the single demonstration she gave. Conversely, when she took the time to help someone personally, that student’s work usually stood out as the best. This shows that hands-on support can be more impactful than merely illustrating a process.

Some learners even find examples misleading. For instance, during a drawing assignment intended to spark our imagination, our teacher first encouraged us to create freely. Later, she shared sample sketches, which led some classmates to doubt their own ideas, wondering if they needed to copy her illustrations. Clearly, in certain creative tasks, examples can restrict originality and cause confusion.

Admittedly, examples do benefit learners by showcasing experience and offering clear steps. Yet I believe stronger methods—such as personalized coaching and encouragement—often make examples unnecessary. Thus, focusing on tailored feedback and ongoing support can shape understanding more effectively than giving examples alone.

Many people believe that maintaining a positive attitude is vital for success in life. I fully agree, because an optimistic mindset can create opportunities and help us reach our goals.

First, having a positive outlook improves our relationships. When you greet colleagues with enthusiasm and offer encouraging words, you build a friendly atmosphere and become more approachable. For example, arriving at work with a smile can lift your own spirits and boost the mood of everyone around you, making teamwork more enjoyable. This positive energy often spreads, inspiring others to adopt a similar approach.

Furthermore, optimism gives us the drive to face challenges. My grandparents are a perfect example of this. Despite facing financial hardships and personal struggles, they never lost faith in their abilities. My grandfather often said, “A confident mindset leads to real progress.” Their hopeful attitude helped them discover new paths and achieve stability in life. Their cheerful spirit also attracted clients and friends, helping them expand their small business.

Often we feel uncertain when trying something new, fearing failure. At those times, focusing on the possibility of success rather than on potential mistakes encourages us to take action. Even a small shift in attitude can lead to remarkable outcomes, whether we are tackling a difficult assignment or learning a fresh skill. It reminds us that our mindset can be the difference between giving up and persevering until we succeed.

In contrast, people who lack optimism may miss out on chances. They might see every setback as definitive failure rather than as a chance to learn. Without a hopeful perspective, it is harder to take risks or keep going when things become difficult.

Looking ahead, positivity will continue to be essential in a rapidly changing world. As industries evolve and new challenges arise, those who stay optimistic will adapt more easily and seize fresh opportunities. By staying hopeful, we can navigate the future with confidence.

In conclusion, choosing to maintain a positive attitude brings many advantages. It strengthens our relationships, fuels our motivation, and helps us overcome obstacles. Ultimately, a positive attitude is not just a mindset, but a powerful tool for shaping our future, and it greatly increases our chances of enjoying a successful and fulfilling life.

Over the past several years, mobile phones have become more common among students than they were over the previous decade and a half, when these devices first began to play an important role in our daily routines. Back then, using phones in classrooms was usually forbidden, but attitudes have shifted and many schools now permit students to bring and operate their phones during lessons. This essay will explore the positive and negative consequences of allowing mobile phones in the classroom.

On the positive side, having phones at hand can improve the learning experience for both teachers and pupils. Students can quickly look up facts or access educational resources online without waiting for a shared computer. This instant access helps them research topics more efficiently. Teachers, in turn, can introduce interactive apps or digital tools that might not run on school computers, making lessons more engaging and diverse. Such flexibility can stimulate students’ interest and support different learning styles.

However, there are clear drawbacks when phones are allowed without strict rules. Some students may check social media or play games instead of paying attention to the teacher’s explanation. Others might use their phones to chat or show videos, distracting classmates and interrupting the flow of the lesson. These irresponsible behaviors can harm concentration and reduce the overall quality of instruction.

In conclusion, permitting mobile phones in class brings both advantages, like easier access to information, and disadvantages, such as increased distractions. Effective guidelines and supervision are essential to maximize the benefits and minimize the downsides of cellphone use in schools.

The idea of shortening summer vacation to prevent students from forgetting what they have learned sounds practical at first. However, cutting down this long break would cause more harm than good. I believe that summer holidays are essential for students’ well-being, personal growth, and overall success in school.

After months of classes and exams, young people need time to recharge. During a two-month break, they can leave routine school tasks behind and explore other interests. Traveling with family or friends lets them discover new cultures or simply spend quality time with loved ones they rarely see during the busy school year. These experiences boost happiness and create lasting memories.

Summer also gives students a chance to catch up or improve grades if they struggled during the year. By retaking a failed course over the break, they can regain credits without adding pressure to the regular term. This flexibility can help some learners feel less anxious about falling behind.

For those who enjoy sports, the long vacation means more hours on the field or court. Without homework deadlines, student-athletes can focus on training, build stamina, and develop teamwork skills. Similarly, book lovers benefit from the extra free time to read widely, visit libraries, and expand their imagination far beyond assigned textbooks.

Another advantage is the freedom to pursue hobbies and document adventures. Whether they write in a journal, take photographs, or share stories with classmates afterward, students can practice creative skills that benefit them in and out of school. These personal projects often boost confidence and motivate young people to learn more.

If the summer break were shortened, students would face more days in classrooms and fewer chances to relax. With less time for leisure, many would feel overwhelmed by continuous studying. Stress levels could rise, making it harder for them to concentrate when classes resume. Moreover, family trips and social gatherings would have to be rearranged or canceled, limiting valuable bonding opportunities.

In conclusion, reducing summer vacation would strip students of vital rest, exploration, and self-development. Two months away from school provide a well-deserved pause that helps learners return refreshed and eager to tackle new challenges. For these reasons, I strongly argue that summer break should remain unchanged.

Churchill’s remark that failure is essential to success holds true for people who really want to change their lives. I believe that setbacks contribute greatly to achievement, provided individuals are willing to learn and adapt from them. There are three reasons why failure matters: it teaches us valuable lessons, it reveals who truly supports us, and it encourages us not to repeat the same mistakes.

First, every failure offers a chance to gain new insights. Since humans naturally err, those who reflect on what went wrong can use that knowledge to improve. Rather than fearing errors, we should see them as a path to growth, because mistakes are inevitable in any life.

Second, failures show us who our genuine friends are. While some people may distance themselves when things go badly, true companions stand by our side. For instance, a caring partner will stay close even after our first setback, whereas someone less reliable may disappear.

Third, it is crucial to avoid making the same errors repeatedly. Constantly facing the same problem can drain our enthusiasm, making it harder to stay motivated. Learning from each failure helps maintain our drive and prepares us for future challenges.

To sum up, everyone experiences failure, but the most successful individuals are those who move forward having learned something valuable. Ultimately, change depends on one’s willingness to grow and accept the lessons failure brings.

Many students look forward to an extended summer break because it lets them relax and catch up with family and friends. Beyond a simple rest, a longer vacation can serve as a well-earned reward for those who have worked hard throughout the school year. Stepping away from homework and exams helps reduce stress and gives young people a chance to recharge, preparing them for future challenges with renewed energy and confidence.

Critics sometimes argue that students forget much of what they learned during extended holidays, but this doesn’t have to be the case. While it’s true that people are more likely to set aside academic topics when they’re enjoying their free time, simple habits like reading short articles, magazines, or the news can keep minds active. Younger learners, in particular, can quickly pick up where they left off, especially if they stay curious about the world around them. A longer break doesn’t necessarily lead to gaps in knowledge if students maintain even a light study routine.

For many, summer is a perfect opportunity to travel, whether to another state or abroad. Spending extra weeks away from school gives students enough time to explore new places, learn about different cultures, and gain first-hand experiences in history and geography. These adventures not only broaden their horizons but also become stories they can share with classmates and teachers, enriching classroom discussions when they return.

Not every student spends the break relaxing or vacationing. Some choose to work part-time jobs to earn money for their personal needs, while others take on family responsibilities or volunteer in their communities. These activities teach valuable life skills such as time management, empathy, and work ethic. Altogether, an extended summer holiday offers diverse benefits: academic rest, cultural enrichment, family bonding, and personal growth, making it a worthwhile period for students and their loved ones.

I believe that the most effective way to inspire others is by the way we act ourselves. When you behave with honesty and kindness, you build trust, demonstrate your willingness to help, and leave a strong, positive mark on the people around you.

First of all, trustworthy behavior earns respect and confidence from others. For instance, if I sprain my ankle badly and cannot walk, my friends will realize I really need help. Because they trust me, they will come to my aid without hesitation. Teachers also rely on trustworthy behavior to guide students: when educators are consistent, fair, and genuinely concerned about our progress, we feel safe asking questions and relying on their support. Even within families, trust grows when relatives show they care about one another day after day. In all these relationships, behaving honestly and thoughtfully creates a solid foundation of mutual respect.

Showing that you are willing to help is another powerful way to influence others. My family once traveled to a town in need and spent a weekend building homes and delivering food to struggling families. That kind of hands-on assistance not only improved life for those people but also inspired me to volunteer more. Friends too play a key role: whenever I feel stressed or upset, they lend an ear and offer encouragement until I feel better. Teachers help in a similar way by spending extra time explaining difficult topics so students can pass their exams. By offering our time and energy to support others, we encourage them to act generously as well.

Finally, our behavior can create a big, positive impact on a wider scale. When you treat friends with warmth and understanding, they often mirror that affection back. A caring attitude in a family can lift everyone’s spirits, making home life happier. Even heroes like firefighters exemplify this idea: by risking their lives to save others, they inspire gratitude and generosity. In one story, a rescued woman’s husband was so thankful that he donated money every month to help firefighters buy better equipment. That single act of courage had a ripple effect of kindness.

In conclusion, our actions speak louder than words. By building trust, offering help, and making a positive impact, we can truly influence the people around us and encourage a more caring community.

Do curfews really protect teenagers, or do they simply restrict their freedom at night? I believe that setting a curfew for young people is important because it helps keep them safe. By requiring teens to be home by a certain hour, we reduce the chance that they will face dangerous situations when they are unsupervised.

At night, when the streets are mostly empty, unsupervised teenagers might get involved in risky behavior or end up in trouble, since there is no one around to guide or help them. A curfew makes it clear that they must follow rules designed for their own good. Just as most adults stay home in the evening to rest or spend time with family, teenagers should also be encouraged to do the same.

Moreover, nighttime can bring higher risks of theft or violence. Someone walking alone might become a victim or try to intervene in a crime and get hurt. Some people argue that teens should be free to enjoy nightlife, such as going to clubs. However, since they often don’t know other patrons, they could unintentionally put themselves in harm’s way. Incidents like the Las Vegas club shooting a few years ago show how quickly a fun evening can turn dangerous. In conclusion, curfews serve as a protective measure that benefits teenagers by keeping them out of harm’s way.

A positive outlook plays a crucial role in achieving success and making each day more enjoyable. When you approach life with optimism, you treat both yourself and others kindly, and you notice better outcomes in everything you do. By choosing to see situations in a hopeful light, you build a mindset that supports continuous growth and happiness.

For instance, imagine you work in customer service and receive harsh criticism from a client who says you are not doing your job well. Instead of letting their words discourage you, you remind yourself that people often speak from their own frustrations. By keeping a constructive attitude, you can stay calm and professional, learning from the feedback without allowing it to affect your confidence or work ethic.

Maintaining this kind of positive mindset brings many advantages. When you meet someone who looks tired or upset, you can tell they lack enthusiasm. In contrast, presenting yourself with a friendly smile and energetic posture signals that you are ready to engage and collaborate. This welcoming presence not only lifts your own mood but also encourages others to respond in a positive way, making daily tasks smoother and more pleasant.

Furthermore, following your dreams and reaching your goals depends a lot on how well you understand and respect yourself and others. Your attitude reflects your character, so if you aim for a new job or want to start a project, a confident and upbeat approach will show potential employers or partners that you are reliable and motivated. A positive mindset can open doors and help you manage large tasks in the future.

Finally, during a job interview, it is essential to display honesty, clarity, and enthusiasm. By clearly explaining your strengths and maintaining a polite demeanor, you prove to the interviewer that you have the right attitude for the role. In the end, a positive outlook not only helps you earn money, secure good housing, and build a better future, but it also spreads good energy to those around you, encouraging everyone you care about to feel happier and more hopeful.

I firmly believe that first impressions are almost impossible to change completely. The initial snapshot people form of us often sticks in their minds, influencing how they think of us later. Even if we try to modify our behaviour, that first image tends to remain firmly in place.

First impressions include more than just our appearance—they cover the way we speak, walk, and even gesture. For example, a person’s confident posture or calm tone of voice can leave a lasting mark that is hard to erase. When we attempt to act differently afterward, listeners and observers often still recall that very first moment we presented ourselves.

Trying to reproduce an earlier impression by copying someone else’s style usually falls short. Imagine tasting a friend’s homemade dish and then following the same recipe at home. Even with identical ingredients and steps, the meal rarely turns out exactly the same, because the friend’s unique touch cannot be duplicated. In much the same way, a first impression cannot be perfectly reconstructed by imitation.

There are times when our initial impression is based on misunderstanding or even deliberate falsehood. A student might exaggerate details about her life to impress classmates, and at first, her peers believe the story. Even after the truth emerges, many still cling to that original, incorrect perception. This shows how powerful and enduring our first judgments can be, right or wrong.

In the end, we must accept that first impressions hold strong sway over others’ opinions. Rather than trying to erase or copy them, we should focus on presenting our true selves from the start. Recognising the lasting impact of that first encounter reminds us why authenticity matters so much.

In conclusion, making a career decision early gives students the advantage of time and direction, helping them approach their future with confidence.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to suggest that our school lunch menu strikes a balance between healthy options and students’ favorite treats. While offering nutritious meals is important, completely removing popular dishes can have unintended consequences. First, many students already eat fast food or snacks outside of school, so when familiar foods like pizza remain on the menu, they often choose these items. Although pizza can upset their stomachs and lacks vegetables or lean protein, students feel more comfortable picking foods they know.

Second, including healthier meals during the week helps students feel more energetic and focused in class. Foods rich in protein and vitamins support growth and can reduce the likelihood of getting sick. By eating a balanced diet at school, students will not only perform better academically but also build good habits that benefit them as they grow older.

My third point is that if the lunch menu only offered healthy dishes, many students might refuse to eat at all. For example, when “Fried Chicken Friday” was canceled, a lot of students skipped lunch entirely. To avoid this, it makes sense to combine both nutritious and popular choices.

In conclusion, I believe our school should mix healthier meals with occasional favorite foods. This compromise would keep students happy while also supporting their well-being. Thank you for considering this proposal.

It is often said that first impressions are almost impossible to alter. Some believe they can manage these judgments whenever they wish, but that is not true. First impressions occur so quickly—often in less than a second—that they leave little room for thought or deliberate response. While certain impressions may change depending on the context, others remain fixed no matter what we do. I agree with this idea, since an impression is essentially an emotion, feeling, or mental image that lingers after an experience.

Sometimes these initial feelings have a strong negative impact on our lives. Imagine a student who isn’t feeling well in class and accidentally emits a loud fart that everyone hears. His first reaction would be to pretend nothing happened, but this is nearly impossible. He would feel embarrassed, his cheeks might flush, and his heart would race—all involuntary responses that he cannot control.

The emotions triggered by awkward first impressions—shame, confusion, discomfort, and even pain—are almost always intense when the situation is unusual. However, if these moments occur regularly, they can start to feel normal, even amusing. For instance, when my family teases me with personal questions, their jokes no longer embarrass me; they make me smile and laugh because I am used to that playful atmosphere.

Having repeated experiences like this helps people respond calmly in many situations. In my own life, I used to feel terribly self-conscious when asked about my romantic life. Now, whether my mother asks if I have a girlfriend or my friends quiz me about someone I like, I answer simply and confidently. What once caused me shame now just makes me happy.

I hope that in the future, whenever I face an embarrassing question or situation, my past experiences will kick in. Instead of letting my initial embarrassment take over, I want to stay composed so the moment won’t become more awkward or stressful than it needs to be.

I believe that although learning from home through online classes can help some students, attending school in person offers greater advantages. Face-to-face lessons give pupils a chance to play sports they enjoy, keep boredom at bay, and explore a wide range of elective subjects or vocational programs. While distance learning may be the only option for those who cannot travel to campus, most students gain more from being in a school environment.

First, schools provide excellent facilities and organized times for sports, which many young people love. Taking part in a team or individual sport helps students stay active and improves their mood. For instance, when I feel upset, playing soccer with friends can lift my spirits by giving me something fun to focus on. Regular exercise also discourages unhealthy habits, such as drug use, and offers a positive community where students share goals and support one another.

Second, being in a classroom keeps students engaged and prevents the monotony of staring at a computer screen all day. In person, children can interact with classmates, ask immediate questions, and receive quick feedback from teachers. If I find a math problem confusing, I can raise my hand and get help right away. Beyond academics, going to school gives us the chance to visit libraries, museums, and university open days, which enrich our understanding of history and culture in ways that an online lesson cannot match.

Finally, schools often offer a variety of elective courses and specialized academies that help students discover their talents and future career paths. From cooking and piano to cosmetology, fitness training, and emergency medical assistance, these practical classes allow pupils to earn credits and build skills. My own school guided me through applying for university scholarships and choosing the right subjects for my intended career. Such resources are hard to find when studying solely from home.

In conclusion, while distance education serves an important role for students who cannot attend school due to family responsibilities, work commitments, or lack of transport, most learners benefit more from being in a school setting. On campus, they can enjoy sports, stay motivated, and access a wide choice of elective classes that prepare them for life after graduation.

Some people believe that attending classes online from home is a great idea. They say it saves time on commuting and makes studying easier. However, I disagree. In my view, learning in a real classroom is more effective because teachers are there to guide you, classmates keep you motivated, and schools offer helpful distractions that support your education.

First of all, while some students can study independently, many need a teacher’s explanation to understand difficult topics. For example, my sister often stays after school for extra help. Thanks to this one-on-one support, she learns much more than she would alone. Teachers usually have busy schedules, but they choose to spend extra time helping students succeed.

Secondly, going to school allows students to build friendships and enjoy activities that enrich their lives. My brother, for instance, loves playing basketball at school. He finds it fun to compete with friends and meet new classmates. Being at school also helps him stay informed about events, clubs, and sports teams. This social interaction not only makes learning more enjoyable but also teaches important skills like teamwork and communication.

Some might argue that online classes let people work quietly on their own without the distractions of a school environment. Yet I believe that school distractions—like chatting with friends during breaks, joining a club meeting, or browsing interesting books in the library—actually help students stay engaged. Talking to teachers and older students also offers valuable perspectives on life and future careers.

In conclusion, attending school in person is better than taking classes online because teachers can explain concepts in real time, and the school community provides both support and enjoyable breaks. By being at school, students gain academic guidance, develop friendships, and discover interests that shape their futures. For these reasons, I think students should go to school rather than learn entirely from home.

I support the school board’s plan to lengthen the school day by an extra ninety minutes because it would allow more in-depth learning and benefit both students and teachers.

Firstly, having additional class time means we no longer rush through worksheets or lecture notes. At present, lessons sometimes end before we finish the planned material. With the extra hour and a half, we could complete assignments in class instead of taking them home, reducing stress and improving our retention of the content.

Secondly, teachers would also gain from the longer schedule. They would have enough room to cover all the topics they have prepared without feeling pressured by the clock. This could help them deliver more thorough explanations and avoid skimming over important details.

Moreover, an extended day provides more chances for revision. If a topic is unclear, students can ask questions, and teachers can revisit difficult sections step by step. This support would help us grasp complex ideas and build confidence in our abilities.

In addition, the extra time is especially valuable for subjects we find challenging. One-on-one support during class could boost our grades because teachers could guide us through problems before a test, ensuring we are well-prepared.

Furthermore, the additional hour would give educators more opportunity for lesson planning and grading, ensuring all unfinished classroom activities are addressed. This would make the learning environment more organized and effective.

Without this extension, lessons may be cut short, leaving students confused and falling behind. Those who struggle would have to catch up later, while others move ahead, widening the gap.

For these reasons, I firmly agree that adding ninety minutes to the school day would be advantageous for everyone involved.

The British author John Lubbock once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” This idea raises questions about how young people often change who they are simply because they feel insecure or carry heavy thoughts. While our personal traits have a strong influence on our behavior, it’s worth asking whether we really stay in control of ourselves when outside pressures push us to act differently.

People’s opinions of us can make us doubt our own qualities. From the moment we are born, we receive influences from our parents, our community, and now more than ever, from the internet. These influences can be powerful and even overwhelming because they are not regulated by any single authority. There are countless voices online, each offering its own set of values, and it can be hard to decide which ones to accept. Society is always evolving, and different viewpoints challenge us to adapt, but we must choose carefully which influences will guide us.

In my own life, I have seen how environment shapes character. When I moved from California to Virginia, I had to get used to new customs and ways of thinking. Back in California, I was surrounded by artists and musicians whose lifestyles seemed exciting and glamorous. Rappers often speak about relationships and material success, and many young people listen closely to these messages. Virginia felt more traditional at first, so I had to find a balance between being true to myself and fitting in with my new friends.

Even though we are constantly exposed to ideas that we cannot always control, we still have the power to decide which ones matter to us. We choose our own path by accepting certain influences and rejecting others. In that sense, I agree with Lubbock: we shape our character. 

Of course, not all influences are positive. Every year brings new challenges like conflicts, environmental pollution, or harmful viruses. Media coverage can make these issues seem even scarier, but it also reminds us to stay informed and take action. In the end, each day offers a chance to learn, to choose wisely, and to move forward. Have a nice day—sometimes that simple wish is what keeps us going.

People should seek advice from experts and authorities on important life matters because relying only on one’s instincts often means acting without enough knowledge. People who make decisions without guidance may believe they are right, even when they break rules or put themselves and others at risk.

First, laws control activities such as using drugs and alcohol, carrying guns, and driving. In many places, certain drugs are illegal and require a prescription to obtain. Alcohol is legal but limited to those who are at least 21 years old. Buying a firearm also demands permission and a minimum age. To drive, you must get a license, typically at age 16, and new drivers often have to travel with an experienced adult in the passenger seat until they gain enough practice. These regulations exist to keep people safe and prevent harm.

In the workplace, employees must follow set schedules and duties. If everyone decided their own working hours, businesses would become chaotic. For example, if an accountant chose to arrive in the afternoon instead of the morning, critical financial tasks might be delayed, harming the company’s operations. Each job role is assigned based on specific skills, and ignoring these assignments can lead to serious mistakes or even job loss.

In society, individuals cannot act solely on personal impulses. Burning down a library because it seems like a “fun idea” is unacceptable. Likewise, assaulting people for amusement or trespassing on private property to pick flowers violates others’ rights. Rules help protect people’s safety and property, ensuring everyone can live together peacefully.

In conclusion, although everyone has rights, we cannot make every decision on our own. Guidance from experts and authorities is essential, particularly when we lack the experience to determine what is right. Their direction helps maintain order and safeguards both individuals and the wider community.

Many high schools now offer distance learning so that students can join lessons online or by video conference from home. I believe this option would benefit certain pupils who face special challenges, such as those who work at night and young mothers-to-be. Allowing these students to study remotely would give them the flexibility they need to succeed in both school and life.

First, consider teenagers who hold evening jobs. My friend works from 5 p.m. until midnight several nights each week. Yet he must be up by 5 a.m. to catch the bus for his 7:30 a.m. classes. As a result, he is often exhausted and struggles to concentrate during the first lesson of the day. However, he still needs a high school diploma to improve his chances of finding better opportunities in the future. If he could attend classes online, he could finish work, get enough rest and then log in later without missing important material. Many students in his situation miss or rush their homework because they simply lack time and energy. Distance learning would help them manage their schedules, rest adequately and complete assignments on time, which could lead to higher grades and less stress.

Second, pregnant girls in high school often feel isolated and unwelcome. Some choose to quit school because they worry about judgment from classmates or because they must care for their baby during the day. An online program would allow these young mothers to continue their education at home, where they can study between prenatal appointments or while their infant naps. This approach not only helps them earn their diploma but also supports them in building a more secure future for themselves and their children. By keeping up with lessons from home, they do not have to choose between being a parent and being a student.

In conclusion, providing a distance learning option is an excellent idea because it offers a flexible solution for students who cannot follow the usual school routine. Those who work late or who are caring for a newborn would gain the chance to complete their high school education without sacrificing rest or family responsibilities. Ultimately, this program would help many young people overcome real obstacles and achieve academic success.

Having a positive mindset plays a crucial role in achieving success. People who think optimistically not only improve their own lives but also benefit those around them. I fully agree that a good attitude brings advantages at home, in the workplace, and throughout society. Unfortunately, many individuals struggle with negative thinking and miss these opportunities for growth.

First, a cheerful outlook strengthens family bonds and contributes to a healthier community. When parents and siblings approach each other with patience and understanding, conflicts become easier to resolve. For instance, many families face stress when children act out or chores go unfinished. By responding calmly and encouraging cooperation, family members can work together to find solutions. Over time, this positive behavior spreads beyond the home, inspiring neighbors and friends to treat each other more kindly. Thus, improving one’s outlook at home can spark broader social change.

Second, a good attitude is essential for success on the job. In any profession, employees who remain friendly and attentive create a pleasant environment for colleagues and customers alike. Consider a retail worker who greets each shopper with a warm smile and listens carefully to their questions. Even if a client arrives frustrated, a calm and courteous response can turn the situation around. On the other hand, an impatient reply often makes both parties feel tense. By practicing patience, workers not only build customer loyalty but also enjoy smoother interactions with coworkers. Ultimately, this positive conduct enhances job performance and opportunities for advancement.

Third, teachers and mentors can use their enthusiasm to guide others toward a more optimistic perspective. In a classroom, an instructor who praises students for their efforts rather than only focusing on mistakes encourages confidence and better behavior. As these pupils grow into adults, they carry this supportive approach into their own careers and communities. Graduates with a positive attitude tend to make thoughtful decisions, treat others respectfully, and give back when families or neighbors need assistance. In this way, one person’s optimism can influence many others over time.

In conclusion, maintaining a positive attitude is vital for personal achievement and collective well-being. Whether at home, in the workplace, or through the influence of educators, optimism lays the foundation for stronger relationships, improved performance, and a more caring society.

I agree with Thomas Jefferson that we can achieve far more when we work together. Too often, people remain inactive and miss out on valuable chances. By becoming involved in our communities and taking the initiative, we not only improve our own lives but also contribute positively to society as a whole.

First, staying engaged helps us avoid procrastination. When we consistently participate in tasks or events that benefit ourselves and others, we develop a sense of responsibility and set higher standards for our community. This active attitude shapes our character and encourages those around us to follow suit.

Moreover, success is not limited to reaching major goals. It also includes completing everyday duties with care and making small improvements whenever possible. By treating routine tasks as opportunities to grow, we build momentum and strengthen our confidence.

Personally, I used to be inactive and let many chances slip away. Looking back, I realize that by hesitating or waiting for the perfect moment, I lost experiences that could have helped me learn and connect with others. Recognizing this has motivated me to adopt a more proactive outlook.

Being an active person means more than just pursuing personal goals. It involves offering help, sharing time, and supporting friends and neighbors. Small actions—like volunteering or simply taking part in local projects—can spark meaningful change in our communities. Since time is limited each day, using it wisely to take positive steps brings us closer to our ambitions.

In conclusion, it does not matter who we are or where we come from; what counts is our willingness to engage and seize every opportunity. By working together, fighting for what we believe in, and lending a hand to those who need it, we can create a better future for ourselves and for society.

Author Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I disagree with Emerson’s view. Instead of thinking the world limits our freedom, I believe we must seize control of our own lives. To succeed, we should make our own choices, follow our passions, and trust ourselves rather than let outside forces decide our path.

First, you must take responsibility for your decisions. If you allow society, friends, or trends to dictate your actions, you risk feeling lost and exhausted. Choosing for yourself gives your life purpose, because you understand why you took each step. On the other hand, people who passively follow others often find themselves unhappy, since they never made a genuine choice.

Second, doing what you enjoy is crucial for real achievement. When you pursue activities you love, whether it’s art, sports, or a particular subject, you won’t grow weary of them. Work done with enthusiasm never feels like a burden. If you simply follow the world’s expectations, you may end up stuck in a role you dislike. But by focusing on your true interests, you stay motivated and satisfied.

Third, only you truly know your strengths, weaknesses, and dreams. This self‐knowledge helps you choose the right career, set meaningful goals, and recognise good or bad opportunities. Far too many people regret their paths because they let others decide for them. They spend years wondering how life would have turned out if they had trusted their own judgment.

In conclusion, never surrender your power to the world. Always be true to yourself by making your own decisions and following what you love. If you let others shape your life, you will likely feel disappointed and bored. To achieve your greatest success, stand firm in who you are and control your own future.

I agree with Albert Einstein’s idea that imagination is more important than knowledge. Imagination lets us picture things we have never seen before and leads us to discover new facts. When we dream up ideas, we often find ways to learn more that we might not have considered otherwise. Of course, imagination can sometimes get ahead of itself. If we imagine too much or go far beyond what we know, our ideas can become confusing and harder to manage.

On the other hand, knowledge can be more practical when you face a real challenge. For example, during a difficult math test, you rely on the formulas and techniques you have studied. Without that foundation, it would be nearly impossible to solve complex problems under time pressure. Similarly, when you read books, you not only gain information but also improve your vocabulary, which helps you understand and express ideas more clearly.

In many cases, imagination and knowledge work together in a creative process. Suppose you want to design a new piece of furniture but do not know exactly what it should look like. Your imagination will suggest different shapes, styles, or functions. Once you decide on a concept, your knowledge of tools, materials, and construction methods lets you turn that vision into reality. In this way, your mind uses both fresh ideas and existing skills to build something useful.

Yet there are times when both imagination and knowledge can cause problems. If you feel sad, your imagination might tell you that nothing ever goes right, making it harder to find solutions or to seek help. Playing games with friends can also go wrong if your imagination convinces you to change the rules unfairly—you might lose trust or even end a friendship. Knowledge can be harmful as well. Imagine you achieve the highest mark on a test and boast about it in front of a friend who scores poorly. Such behavior can damage your relationship and make you seem insensitive.

A more serious example involves a sixteen-year-old who struggles with poor grades. Without enough knowledge or good study habits, he may be unable to get a job after school. Other students with better records find work, while he ends up borrowing money from friends just to buy food. Over time, his debts grow, and without a steady income, he risks becoming homeless because he cannot pay back what he owes.

Young children show the power of imagination every night. They might hear a creaking floorboard and become convinced there is a monster hiding in the closet. They call out to their parents, who reassure them nothing is there. Yet the child’s fear remains until, finally, they discover that the strange sounds were just their parents making a playful noise. This example proves how the mind can create a reality more vivid than what we actually experience.

We achieve our goals best when we take action on the tasks we are given and plan them in advance. From factory workers to students and company leaders, finishing assignments depends on breaking them down into clear steps and then following through. Without a plan and the effort to carry it out, deadlines can slip by and important work may remain undone.

People in various jobs rely on planning to complete their daily duties. For example, a factory employee might write out each stage of the assembly line, collect all the necessary tools, and then work through the steps in order. By organising their tasks ahead of time, they avoid wasting minutes searching for parts or assembling components incorrectly. This keeps the production process smooth and prevents delays that affect the entire team.

Students use the same method when tackling their schoolwork. By splitting a project into smaller parts—such as reading chapters, researching information, and drafting answers—they can check their progress and correct mistakes early. Completing class assignments on schedule also frees up free time later, whether for hobbies or relaxation. Turning in homework promptly not only helps maintain good grades but also prevents a heavy workload from accumulating.

Company leaders follow this principle on a larger scale. A CEO might decide on a new product, figure out what resources are needed, and outline a marketing plan. Each phase—from testing samples to arranging shipments—must be planned carefully. By doing so, the business can introduce its product efficiently, attracting customers without wasting time or money.

Working step by step ensures that each task is finished before moving on to the next. When one assignment is completed properly, it does not get carried over, so nothing interferes with future work. This habit builds confidence as well: each success shows us that we can meet deadlines and handle responsibilities.

Ultimately, taking the time to plan and then acting on that plan leads to real progress. Simply talking about what we want to do is not enough—projects stall without action. But when we organise our ideas and start working immediately, we make steady strides toward our goals, whether they are daily chores, school projects, or long-term career ambitions.

In conclusion, no matter what role we have—factory worker, student, or executive—we accomplish our tasks most effectively by planning carefully and then putting in the effort to follow through. This approach not only completes the work at hand but also prepares us for new opportunities in the future.

Some schools now let students join classes from home through online lessons or video calls. I believe this kind of distance learning does more harm than good. Without a teacher’s direct supervision, many students struggle to stay focused. They might browse social media, look up answers without understanding, or simply ignore assignments because nobody is watching. As a result, they learn far less than they would in a classroom setting.

Another problem is that students at home miss valuable personal support. At school, if a pupil feels upset or faces a family issue, they can speak with teachers, coaches, or counselors who notice changes in their mood. But when learning remotely, young people often feel isolated and have no one to turn to. This lack of emotional help can make them unhappy and less motivated to study.

Online lessons also make it harder for learners to get quick assistance. If a student finds a video lecture confusing, they cannot immediately raise their hand or ask for a different explanation. Rewinding or replaying a long video can be time-consuming and frustrating, and many students simply give up. Consequently, when it comes time to take a test, they may not understand the material and end up failing.

Moreover, remote learning cuts students off from important social experiences. Plenty of teenagers discover new interests by joining school clubs or sports teams. A talented soccer player at home misses the chance to train with peers, compete for a school team, and perhaps earn a scholarship. Without these opportunities, students lose out on teamwork skills, friendships, and the fun memories that make high school special.

Overall, distance learning and video conferencing deny students the attention, support, and social life they need. They are more likely to cheat, feel lonely, and fall behind academically. In my opinion, schools should continue to offer in-person classes rather than replace them with virtual sessions. By attending school every day, students gain knowledge, receive help when they need it, and enjoy a fuller, more balanced high school experience.
