Enthusiasm is what keeps us moving forward, even when we face setbacks. Life can be challenging, and it’s easy to feel discouraged after a failure. Yet, by holding onto energy and hope, we can turn those stumbles into stepping stones. I agree with Winston Churchill’s idea that true success lies in going from one failure to another without losing enthusiasm. With a positive mindset, we become more patient, experience less stress, and discover new opportunities to achieve our goals.

When we give in to negative feelings, everything seems harder. Imagine you dream of going to college. Without motivation, you might skip studying, ignore assignments, or delay saving money for tuition. In that case, your goal becomes out of reach. Or picture wanting a car, a house, and the chance to travel. If you avoid working hard and lose interest in your job, you risk being fired and missing out on the income you need. Negative thoughts can trap you in a cycle of disappointment, preventing you from chasing what you truly want.

On the other hand, enthusiasm brings clarity and energy. It helps us handle pressure more easily and stay patient when progress is slow. For example, if you aim to pass a demanding school exam, a positive attitude will motivate you to attend all classes, complete homework on time, and ask questions when you’re confused. Rather than worrying nonstop, you focus on preparing step by step. Even if you fail that test, you don’t have to give up. You can seek extra help after school or spend more time reviewing the material, turning that failure into a lesson for next time.

Failing without losing enthusiasm paves the way for future success. Suppose you miss graduation because you failed one required class. Instead of feeling defeated, you could look for night courses, ask for tutoring, or even enroll in a refresher program. Each option offers a chance to improve and eventually complete your diploma. Similarly, if you lose a beloved job for accidentally breaking an important item, you might feel upset at first. Yet, by staying proactive—updating your résumé, reaching out to contacts, or applying to other companies—you use your experience as proof of your work ethic. Employers will appreciate your willingness to learn and your positive outlook.

Falling down doesn’t have to lead to more setbacks. Negative thoughts can block our path, but a determined spirit can open doors we never imagined. Working hard with a joyful attitude not only brings better results but also inspires others around us. Life is full of obstacles, but some people show us that giving up is never the only option. By embracing Churchill’s wisdom, we learn to face each defeat with enthusiasm. In doing so, we turn failures into lessons and pave the way for true success.

Although technology makes it possible to study online, shop from home, and keep in touch with others, I believe it also brings many drawbacks. First, people now have less real-life interaction. Not long ago, friends and families would meet in parks to talk, share meals, or simply enjoy each other’s company. Today, students often can’t pay attention in class because they are busy with their phones, and children prefer screens over books or outdoor play. In this way, technology has reshaped how we live and weakened our personal connections.

One clear example is the decline of local stores. Many shops have closed because customers choose to buy clothes, electronics, and everyday items online. Giant websites like Amazon record far higher sales than any physical retailer. I recently learned about two small businesses—let’s call them Shop A and Shop B—that are on the brink of shutting down. With fewer visitors in their aisles, their profits have fallen dramatically. As a result, owners worry about reducing staff and laying off employees since online platforms attract almost all the buyers.

Public spaces are also feeling the impact. Parks, lakesides, and shopping malls that once bustled with people now seem unusually quiet. Instead of walking outside or meeting friends, many prefer to stay indoors playing video games or clicking through shopping sites. This shift not only affects businesses but also makes our neighborhoods less lively and welcoming.

Some argue that technology offers new ways to express creativity, such as digital art or social media posts. Yet, we still have traditional activities like painting, writing, dancing, and playing music. For instance, I attend a dance class where my teacher once pointed out how dependent we’ve become on our devices. When I arrived in the United States in 2016, I relied on Google Translate to understand challenging words. That tool was helpful at times, but I’ve also seen classmates who spend lessons on their phones and then struggle to answer simple questions when the teacher calls on them.

Others say technology improves our lives by helping us communicate with friends and relatives. While it is true that we can share messages instantly, it also reduces our need to express thoughts directly without a screen. Modern devices can even harm our culture and slow down children’s development. My cousin, for example, is in middle school and plays Fortnite for hours each day. He goes to bed very late, his grades have dropped, and he rarely reads a book or goes outside. He misses many experiences that would otherwise help him grow.

In conclusion, I think technology will continue to undermine our traditions and social bonds. People may stop visiting stores, parks, or gathering with family entirely. Although digital tools can sometimes assist us, overall they limit our communication, stunt our curiosity, and reduce our happiness. We should remember the value of face-to-face contact, outdoor activities, and personal expression to keep our lives rich and balanced.

Many people, including both pupils and educators, believe that virtual lessons do more harm than good for learners and schools. They argue that when classes are held online, students often fail to jot down important points and become easily sidetracked. As a result, these learners miss key information and cannot make the most of their education. In this essay, I will explain why lack of note-taking and poor focus prevent students from gaining real benefits through online instruction.

First, pupils commonly do not record notes during digital lessons. In a traditional classroom, most students take notes because they know the teacher is observing them and may even check their work. When the same lesson happens on a screen, however, that supervision disappears. Without someone looking over their shoulder, many learners simply skip writing down definitions, examples, or explanations. Yet taking notes is essential: writing information in your own words helps you understand ideas better and remember them for tests or homework. If no one can see your notebook, you might not feel motivated to fill it with useful details, and your grasp of the subject will weaken.

Second, maintaining attention in an online environment is a big challenge. In a physical classroom, if a student’s eyes wander away from the board or the teacher, they miss vital instructions. It is even easier to get distracted at home—whether by a phone notification, a pet, or a sibling calling for help. When crucial facts slip by unnoticed, students might not understand what they are supposed to do for an assignment or how to solve a problem. This lapse can lead to confusion, stress, and lower grades. Paying attention is the only way to pick up every step of a lesson and apply it correctly.

In conclusion, virtual classes fail to offer real advantages because students often do not make notes and struggle to concentrate. Without the teacher’s physical presence, learners may neglect to record important material and allow their minds to drift. These habits cause them to miss key explanations and instructions, undermining the entire purpose of education. For these reasons, online learning is not as effective as traditional classroom teaching.

Online schooling can be an appealing choice, yet it does not fit everyone’s learning style. While some students excel in a home-based curriculum, others find it too challenging. Virtual classes require discipline and motivation, and they can be tough to pass without the structure of a traditional classroom.

One advantage of learning at home is freedom from early alarms and rigid schedules. You decide when to study and can work at your own pace. However, that flexibility also brings pressure; assignments must be completed independently, and without face-to-face interaction, it can be hard to get help when you are stuck. Questions linger longer when a teacher is not immediately available.

A further issue is the lack of a safety net: in a regular school, if you struggle with a subject, teachers or classmates often step in to clarify concepts and guide you. In an online program, falling behind may mean missing important explanations entirely. Recovering from a poor grade is more complicated when you cannot speak directly to an instructor about makeup work.

Students who learn from home also miss out on many social experiences. There are no fire drills, lunchroom chatter, or school dances. Without classmates nearby, it is harder to build friendships and share moments that make school memorable. Research even suggests that a significant percentage of those who start homeschooling eventually return to brick-and-mortar schools or drop out altogether.

For most learners, attending traditional school offers a better chance of success. Working alongside peers encourages cooperation and gives opportunities both to receive and to offer support. Ultimately, putting in consistent effort and seeking help when needed are what lead students forward, and regular schools provide the environment where that is most achievable.

“Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it,” wrote the British naturalist and politician John Lubbock. I fully agree with this idea. Each person has the power to decide who they want to be, regardless of the situation they face. We can choose how to react to good or bad events and select the kind of people and places we surround ourselves with. In the end, our character is shaped by our own decisions and efforts.

My grandmother is a perfect example of this. At seventy-eight, she had spent her life working hard and always maintained a positive outlook. She used to say, “If I don’t do it myself, no one will do it as well.” Her energy and optimism were constant. Then one day she suffered a severe stroke that left her unable to move half of her body and robbed her of her voice. The doctors told us she would need a wheelchair forever. It was heartbreaking to see her so full of life suddenly confined to a chair. Many of us felt despair, but my grandmother refused to give in. Even with her limitations, she chose to stay upbeat. She kept smiling and found new ways to stay active. Her determination showed me that, no matter how difficult life becomes, we have control over our own attitude and character.

Another way we shape ourselves is by selecting our environment. We decide who we spend time with and where we live or work. If surrounding people are negative or toxic, we can step away or try to turn the atmosphere positive. A supportive community will encourage us, while a harmful one can drag us down. Yet ultimately, it is up to us to recognise these influences and make choices that reflect the person we want to be.

How we react to others also reveals our true character. Our responses—whether calm or harsh—show which qualities we value. It might be tempting to imitate someone we admire, but copying another person’s behaviour is not the same as building our own character. Each of us has the freedom to decide how to respond in every moment.

In conclusion, no matter the challenges we face or the people around us, our character belongs to us. We always have the choice to develop our own traits and decide the person we want to become.

Pushing students to finish high school in three years by taking summer classes is not a good idea. I believe this plan would place too much academic pressure on young people, interfere with their summer jobs, and eliminate the chance to take a break before college.

The first problem is that many students simply do not have enough credits to graduate early, so they would have to overload their schedules. Trying to fit extra courses into each semester, plus summer sessions, can lead to high stress and exhaustion. In a traditional four-year program, pupils have time to participate in clubs, sports and other activities without feeling overwhelmed. These experiences also look attractive on college applications. However, if a student attempts to cram all those activities alongside a much heavier course load, they will likely feel burned out and may not perform well in any area.

Another issue is that many high schoolers count on summer jobs to earn spending money or save for college and other expenses. If they must attend classes during the summer, they lose their main opportunity to work full time. For many teens, those summer earnings go toward buying a car, paying for application fees or simply gaining financial independence. Replacing summer income with extra coursework could create financial strain and reduce the sense of freedom that comes from having a job.

Finally, after four years of continuous schooling, students often want some time off to rest, reflect on their goals and prepare for adulthood. A break between high school and college can offer a chance to travel, volunteer, or work full time and build savings. This “gap” period can help young people decide on a career path or simply recharge before tackling more intensive studies. Forcing them to rush straight into their final year removes that valuable breathing space.

In summary, encouraging students to graduate in three years by attending summer classes has too many downsides. It risks overloading their schedules, conflicts with summer employment, and eliminates a well-deserved break. Keeping high school at four years allows students to balance academics, work and personal growth in a healthier way.

There is an ongoing debate about whether a positive attitude serves as the foundation for success. Although some argue that optimism alone cannot guarantee achievement, I feel that adopting a hopeful outlook can transform many areas of our lives. Maintaining positivity not only helps us connect with others but also leaves a memorable mark on people and brings us more joy.

A cheerful disposition makes us more approachable and invites conversations. When others respond kindly, you are likely to build lasting friendships. A wider circle of friends means less time spent alone and fewer chances for worry, since social interaction keeps us busy and uplifted.

Furthermore, optimism plays a key role in making a strong first impression. Presenting yourself with energy and kindness, whether in academic or professional settings, makes you stand out. People tend to remember those who greet them with warmth, opening doors to new opportunities and collaborations.

Research shows that chronic stress poses risks to both physical and mental health. By focusing on the positive side, we can reduce stress levels and improve our well-being. Optimistic individuals also tend to form deeper bonds with neighbors and co-workers, ensuring they have a support network when challenges arise. This combination of lower stress and reliable friendships fosters a healthy and content life.

In conclusion, a positive attitude truly acts as a key to success. It encourages stronger relationships, helps us make favorable impressions, and promotes happiness and good health—essential elements of a fulfilling life.

Dear Mr. Principal, today I would like to discuss how employers often seek specific qualities in job candidates even when they lack prior experience. I believe this is valid because people can learn new tasks when given the right attitude and support.

When someone starts a new position, it is common not to know all the details. Companies know that proper training from an experienced colleague or manager can fill that gap. For example, when I first moved here, I worked with my stepfather putting up roofing. At the start, I had no idea how to handle the tools or mix the materials. However, as I spent more days on the roof, my stepfather guided me patiently and I picked up each skill. Later, I got a job as a restaurant cashier. Counting coins was another challenge for me because the currency looked different from my home country. Thankfully, my manager showed me the distinctions between each coin and note, and I practiced diligently until I became confident. By being eager to learn, I managed to improve quickly and help the restaurant run smoothly.

Hardworking employees also play a key role in a company’s success. Once someone learns the basics, they usually push themselves to discover more about their responsibilities. Many people I know work long hours not just for a paycheck but to build a better future for their families. They hope to set an example for their children, showing them that dedication and effort can lead to success. Parents often strive to demonstrate that hard work matters, hoping their children will follow this path. Others aim to grow in their careers or reach personal goals, and this motivation drives them to continue learning and improving each day.

Being responsible is another fundamental quality employers look for. Punctuality, attention to detail, and reliable performance make a worker stand out. In my home country, I saw small shops fail because the owners hired staff who were often late or skipped tasks. As a result, customers lost trust and the business could not survive. In contrast, companies that hire reliable people tend to grow. When an employee shows they can complete assignments on time and handle duties without constant supervision, managers feel confident giving them more important roles. This trust helps the company expand.

Patience is equally important, especially for managers training new staff. A good manager understands that teaching someone unfamiliar with the work takes time and practice. If a supervisor rushes through instructions or grows frustrated, the new hire may never grasp the necessary skills. In many successful restaurants and stores I have visited, the managers always took time to answer questions and demonstrate proper techniques. Their calm and supportive attitude made trainees feel comfortable and motivated to learn. This patience ultimately benefits the entire team because it produces capable employees.

In conclusion, I believe that candidates do not need to arrive with every skill mastered if they demonstrate responsibility, enthusiasm, and a willingness to learn. No one is born with experience—instead, we acquire it through the challenges life offers us. Employers value qualities like hard work, reliability, and patience because they lead to long-term success for both the worker and the company.

I strongly oppose the idea of extending the school day because it would quickly become dull, stressful, and exhausting for students. Young learners need a balanced schedule that allows them to study effectively but also to rest and enjoy other activities. Forcing them to stay longer in class would harm their motivation and well-being.

First of all, spending more hours at school would feel monotonous. Children look forward to their free time after lessons, when they can pursue hobbies, play with friends, or simply relax. If the day were stretched out, they would no longer have the chance to unwind. For example, after regular classes, Sara always goes to the playground to kick a ball around with her classmates. Failure is something most of us dread and try to avoid at all costs. Many people steer clear of any situation where they might stumble, while a smaller group welcomes these challenges. Those who embrace failure see it as a chance to learn and often achieve remarkable results in their lives.

Fear influences almost everything we do. We worry about how others perceive us and whether our decisions will turn out well. Because we cannot be certain of success, the fear of negative consequences divides people into two groups: the cautious and the daring. Each approach has its own benefits and drawbacks.

Cautious individuals rely on their existing knowledge, which they have built up over years, to ensure they do not make mistakes. Labeling them as shy is not entirely fair—they simply hesitate to try something unfamiliar. By avoiding risks, they virtually guarantee they won’t fail, but they also miss out on potential successes. Whether it’s speaking up in class, trying a new sport, or dressing in a different style, fear stops them from discovering what might happen. Their past experiences—like saying something awkward in front of peers or feeling out of place at the gym—reinforce their reluctance. While they lose nothing by not trying, they gain far less, keeping their achievements modest but their comfort intact.

On the other hand, those who step into the unknown and collect experiences tend to leave a lasting impact. A prime example is Winston Churchill, the former British prime minister. His journey shows how important it is to keep trying. He faced many setbacks before rising to his famous wartime leadership. Instead of being discouraged by failures, Churchill treated each defeat as a lesson, refining his ideas and decisions until they succeeded. He understood that making mistakes is part of improving, and he even took pride in learning from them. His perseverance and willingness to learn from failure fueled his eventual success.

Enthusiasm for a goal keeps people moving forward despite setbacks. It doesn’t matter if the aim is as grand as leading a country or as simple as mastering a musical instrument—what counts is the determination behind it. In my own life, I learned this lesson through martial arts, especially when I decided to learn nunchaku with my non-dominant hand. Spinning the weapon left me bruised and sore as I struck my forearm countless times. Many asked why I persisted, but my passion for mastering that skill drove me on. After months of practice, I managed to control the nunchaku smoothly, and though I’m not an expert yet, I no longer injure myself. My commitment turned pain into progress.

Sometimes failure involves real danger or even life-changing consequences. For example, a boy who loved riding his bicycle lost his leg in a car accident. He spent months in a wheelchair before receiving a prosthetic limb. Determined to return to his hobby, he struggled again and again, facing anger and disappointment each time he fell. Yet he refused to give up. Eventually, he rode confidently as before the crash. His story shows that resilience can be stronger than tragedy and that the will to overcome can restore hope.

I agree with Churchill’s view that we must fail in order to learn and truly appreciate our achievements. We should practice not until we get things right, but until we cannot go wrong. Having a clear goal inspires us to keep our enthusiasm alive, even when we face setbacks. We can stay in our comfort zone and dodge failure or embrace risks and gain valuable experience. The choice is ours, and though failure may be uncomfortable, it is also the path to growth.

Listening to music on headphones should also be allowed, provided it’s done quietly and doesn’t disturb others, whether during tests or classwork. Students can benefit from taking classes online at home for several reasons. First, some pupils simply feel more comfortable away from their peers. They might believe that others in their school are unkind or disrespectful. In these cases, parents may prefer their children to study at home because they worry about them facing bad influences or even being laughed at if they have health issues. Allowing students to learn online can protect them from these fears.

Second, certain students dislike the routine of going to a physical classroom every day. They often feel judged or embarrassed by classmates, especially if they have had negative experiences in the past. Studying from home gives them a chance to focus without worrying about being stared at or bullied. This flexibility can help students with medical conditions or anxiety feel safer and more confident in their learning environment.

However, if I had to choose between learning online or attending school in person, I would choose to go to school. I enjoy meeting new people and believe it is important to support classmates who might be struggling. By being there face to face, I can encourage others, share advice, and help them realize they do not need to feel ashamed or alone. In my view, school offers valuable opportunities for social interaction and personal growth.

In conclusion, students should be free to decide whether they want to study online or in person, since both options allow them to learn. Ultimately, what matters most is that they focus on their own needs and do not worry about what others think.

Dear members of the city council, I appreciate your concern for teen safety and the plan to set a 10 PM weekday curfew along with a 12 AM limit. While I understand the purpose of these rules, I believe a 10 PM cutoff is too early for many of us who have part-time jobs or after-school activities, and sometimes get held up by traffic. We often drive later because we volunteer, play sports, or work evening shifts. Although tiredness can affect our driving, many teenagers can still focus and stay alert because we stay up for important reasons and want to show we can manage our own responsibilities.

On the other hand, I agree that drivers under 18 should be off the road by midnight. Late-night hours bring greater risks from drunk drivers, animals crossing the road, or people with harmful intentions. After a long day, anyone can become drowsy behind the wheel, increasing the chance of an accident. Ending our driving privileges at 12 AM would help lower these dangers while still allowing time to finish essential tasks.

In conclusion, I ask you to rethink the 10 PM rule but keep the midnight curfew. This solution respects teenagers’ busy schedules and promotes road safety.

We shape our character through the decisions we make and the actions we take. Whether it is how we talk to someone or how we act in a given situation, every moment teaches us something important. These discoveries can lead to real change in our behavior and attitudes. However, beginning this journey often means facing unexpected challenges. It is only by struggling at first that we realise where improvement is needed.

These initial difficulties push us to grow. At times we feel thrown into situations that test our strengths more than we anticipated. It is then we learn to choose wisely, thinking ahead about how our current decisions might affect our future self. By planning carefully, we develop traits that will serve us better over time, even though the process can be tough.

Going after the qualities we want can also bring conflicts with loved ones. Friends or family may not understand why we act differently, causing arguments or distancing. We might start to doubt ourselves when support seems to vanish. Yet, we choose this path to refresh our outlook and begin anew, hoping for positive change and fewer regrets. A new start helps us let go of past negativity and focus on a happier future.

Admitting that we need to change often comes when things start to fall apart. Like missing pieces in a puzzle, certain elements of our life may feel incomplete. We might also be influenced by environments or people beyond our control, which can make progress seem impossible. Changing a deeply rooted habit takes more than a single moment—it requires patience, time, and consistent effort. It also helps to ask for support when challenges feel overwhelming, though many avoid speaking out if others are still unaware of their own struggles.

Still, many decide to take control of their character because it offers a second chance to correct earlier mistakes. Identifying what is missing, like finding that last jigsaw piece, lets us rebuild ourselves more positively. In the end, the effort we invest in changing shapes our true personality and improves how we connect with others, leaving us with a sense of fulfilment and without regret.

I believe technology should be restricted in many places because it can lead to addiction, mental strain, broken family ties, and even serve as a means for bullying.

At home, excessive screen time can harm family relationships. Children often become so absorbed in devices that they ignore responsibilities and real-life interactions. Over time, staring at screens may contribute to eye strain and vision problems, while constant notifications disrupt mental focus. As a result, families drift apart and household peace suffers.

In schools, banning digital gadgets would help maintain academic honesty and improve learning. With easy access to phones or tablets, students might cheat on tests or assignments rather than practice handwriting and develop critical thinking. Technology also opens the door to cyberbullying or sharing inappropriate images, creating an unsafe environment. Frequent pings and apps distract learners from lessons, harming overall performance.

On the road, phone use is one of the main causes of accidents. Drivers who text or browse while behind the wheel endanger themselves and others. Beyond driving, technology can be misused for fraud, hacking bank accounts, or stealing personal information, which causes financial and emotional harm.

In conclusion, overdependence on technology can cause addiction, vision damage, family separation, academic dishonesty, and serious safety risks. Limiting its use at home, in schools, and in vehicles will help safeguard our health, relationships, and well-being.

Some companies have already switched to a four-day workweek with ten-hour days, and now schools plan to hold only two hours of classes each week. However, this idea brings several problems: it shortens learning time, leaves teachers earning only hourly wages, and weakens the economy.

I believe that school hours should not be cut simply to save energy. Pupils need around eight hours of instruction each day to fully understand their subjects. With just two hours per week, teachers would struggle to cover the curriculum and students’ education would suffer from constant interruptions.

Another drawback is that educators would lose their regular salaries and be paid only for the hours they teach. This change would greatly reduce their income, forcing many teachers to take on second jobs just to pay their bills and support their families.

Finally, reducing work and study hours would hurt the broader economy. People have ongoing expenses such as loan repayments, health and car insurance, and rising food costs. With fewer paid hours, many households would find it hard to meet these obligations, which could slow economic growth.

That experience showed me that one setback does not mean you should give up. Instead, you should return stronger and prove to yourself what you can achieve.

As a child, I dreamed of becoming a lawyer. When classmates doubted me and asked how I could ever complete such a demanding career, I told them that no matter how many times I stumbled, I would keep working toward my goal. Giving up would have meant accepting defeat, but I wanted to show everyone—and especially myself—that perseverance pays off.

Now, at eighteen years old, I have faced many failures, but each mistake has been a lesson that prepares me for the real world. Learning from errors has built my resilience and taught me to handle future challenges with confidence.

To succeed in life, we must move forward one step at a time and never allow any failure—no matter how big—to stop us. Rather than listening to those who say “You can’t do it,” we should stay focused on our dreams, learn from our mistakes, and prove that determination wins in the end.

As a student, I believe that working in a group is much more effective than working alone. Being part of a team motivates me and keeps me engaged throughout the project. There are several reasons why I prefer group work over individual effort.

First, we can finish assignments more quickly when we share the workload. While one person researches, another writes and someone else edits, the task moves ahead on several fronts at once. Second, dividing roles among group members ensures that everyone has a clear responsibility. This structure helps us stay organized and prevents us from duplicating work. Third, when one of us struggles with a concept, the others can step in to explain and support. Having immediate help from classmates makes the learning process smoother.

However, working in a team does have some drawbacks. We sometimes get distracted by off-topic conversations or social interactions. Also, each person brings different ideas, and reaching a consensus can take extra time. When opinions clash, we must negotiate and compromise, which can slow us down.

On the other hand, working alone has its own benefits. There are no distractions, so I can focus entirely on the assignment. I also have complete control over the structure and style, shaping the work exactly as I imagine it. In addition, I can consult the teacher directly about any questions, which ensures that I meet all the requirements.

But doing everything by myself can be time-consuming. I must handle every detail on my own and rely solely on my own skills. If I get stuck on a difficult point, there’s no peer to turn to for quick assistance.

In the end, whether I choose to work in a group or by myself, I will face similar challenges, such as deciding on ideas and completing all the tasks. Personally, I know that I am more likely to finish my work when I share responsibilities with others. In a team, I can focus on one part of the project and trust that the rest will be completed too. Some might say I choose group work to do less effort, and they would be right—at least the assignment actually gets done. For me, “teamwork makes the dream work,” so I prefer working in a group rather than alone.

However, if teens are not inclined to behave responsibly, no law will change how they act. Regarding the curfew time, this law does not imply that young people cannot hang out with friends; it simply helps more people stay safe from the trouble on the streets. I see two viewpoints: reasons to worry and reasons not to worry. For example, teens like to have sleepovers—would these be included? Must they stay in their own home, or can they stay elsewhere? On another note, right now there is no general curfew for when teenagers should be home, but there is a curfew for those who have a driving permit. This restriction means no young teenager is driving late; the only time you see them in a car is when they are leaving school. There are pros and cons to this law, but I think the pros outweigh the cons because everything is reasonable and understandable. The only con I can think of is getting caught and having that on one’s record, which does not sound good. Overall, there are many advantages to this law, and it should be seriously applied across the United States, not just in one city. This will keep more people safe. Of course there will always be someone who wants to break the law as a joke, but this curfew is not something to play around with—young people should take it seriously.

In conclusion, this curfew will help prevent thieves from targeting young girls and boys and reduce cases of rape, which often occur in darkness when perpetrators are harder to detect. It will likely lower the chance of these negative events happening so frequently. It will also keep young people out of trouble by reducing the dangers of being out late at night.

I believe setting a curfew for teenagers under eighteen is a positive step for several reasons. First, during weekdays most young people spend the day at school, so requiring them to be home by 10 p.m. encourages them to avoid unnecessary late-night outings. This simple rule would reduce the number of youths wandering the streets after dark, when criminal activity is highest. If fewer teenagers are out at night, there is less chance they might become victims of violence or fall into dangerous situations with other offenders.

Second, limiting weekend hours until midnight still allows some freedom but keeps teens from staying out until the early hours. Late-night gatherings often lead to poor decisions, including experimenting with drugs. Many dealers operate under cover of darkness, so an earlier curfew would make it harder for teens to encounter or buy illegal substances. By returning home at a reasonable hour, adolescents are less likely to be influenced by those wishing to sell them harmful products.

It makes sense to apply this curfew only to people under eighteen. Once a person is legally an adult, they generally understand societal expectations and face adult responsibilities. Teenagers, on the other hand, need clearer boundaries while they are still developing judgment and self-control. Establishing a nightly deadline gives parents and communities a shared standard to keep young people safe without overly restricting those who are already mature enough to make responsible decisions.

Of course, any law needs fair enforcement. A first violation might earn a warning, followed by more serious consequences for repeated breaches. One concern is that a formal record could harm a student’s future college applications. To avoid this, authorities could handle minor curfew violations through parent notifications or community service rather than criminal charges, so that a single mistake doesn’t stay on an academic or criminal record forever.

Currently, many regions already limit how late teenagers can drive under their learner’s permits, precisely because driving at night carries extra risks. Extending similar rules to all teens on foot or in public spaces simply recognizes that night hours are dangerous no matter how people travel. Though some might argue that a curfew is too restrictive, the benefits—fewer accidents, reduced chances of assault or abduction, and lower drug exposure—far outweigh the inconvenience of returning home a little earlier.

In the end, this curfew is not meant to punish young people but to protect them. By keeping teenagers off the streets after dark, communities can greatly reduce incidents of theft, assault, and other crimes. It also reassures parents, who know their children must be home by a set time. Overall, the proposal strikes a fair balance between safety and personal freedom, making neighborhoods safer and giving teenagers a clearer structure until they reach adulthood.

Working on my own is more challenging than being part of a group, yet it teaches you more in the long run. Whether you work alone or with others, you will complete the task and learn along the way. However, group projects often expose you to diverse viewpoints and information, which can be helpful. Unfortunately, some people use teamwork as a shortcut, simply copying answers to finish quickly. That approach never truly deepens your understanding.

Personally, I prefer working independently because I want to truly grasp the material. It might take me longer to complete tasks, as I carefully explore every detail, but the sense of achievement in the end is rewarding. When you finish an assignment by yourself—without relying on classmates—you can feel proud of your effort and the knowledge you gained through your own hard work.

I’m not against group work; it has its advantages. Sharing ideas and resources can speed up progress, and some students genuinely collaborate and learn from each other. Still, too many people use teamwork to cheat or copy answers, missing the chance to develop their skills. Even though group projects may feel easier, working alone offers greater benefits for your education.

For those who are used to depending on peers, independent tasks can be both exciting and intimidating. They push you to search for facts, gather evidence, and think critically on your own. Of course, if you run into difficulties, you can always ask a teacher or mentor for guidance. Plus, working independently helps you avoid distractions. In a group setting, conversations and differing opinions can pull your focus away from the work you need to do.

Relying on other people’s ideas also carries a risk: if their information is incorrect, your work will suffer too. Miscommunication is common in teams, which can lead to mistakes and confusion. By working alone, you can organize your own thoughts and approach the task in the way that makes the most sense to you. These reasons show why, despite its challenges, independent work is ultimately more beneficial than relying on a group.

Attending school in person is far more effective than taking classes at home. From my own experience, studying online comes with several drawbacks that make learning harder and less enjoyable. Without a teacher standing next to you, it can be difficult to get immediate explanations when something is unclear. Students often drift off task, wandering around the internet instead of focusing on their lessons. For these reasons, I firmly believe that learning remotely does not benefit students as much as traditional classroom instruction.

One of the biggest advantages of being in a classroom is having a teacher available to answer your questions on the spot. During a lesson at school, you might think of a question right away and simply raise your hand. The teacher can provide examples, clarify difficult points, and adjust explanations to suit the entire class. In contrast, online courses force you to work alone. You might send a message to the instructor, but you won’t receive an instant response. You also lose the chance to turn to a friend for a quick explanation or discussion. Because of this, you end up taking extensive notes, replaying videos, and re-reading materials multiple times. In my own online classes, I often had to watch three to five lessons each day, write down detailed notes, and complete several quizzes just to grasp the main ideas. Although this process taught me discipline and independence, it also felt overwhelming compared to learning in a live classroom.

Another problem with home-based classes is the number of distractions you face. In a school setting, teachers enforce rules: phones are put away during lessons, and students are expected to concentrate on the task at hand. At home, however, it’s tempting to check your messages, scroll through social media, or switch to unrelated websites. Since there is no teacher monitoring you in person, it’s all too easy to lose focus. If you spend more time on your phone than on your coursework, you risk not understanding the material and potentially failing. Having someone in the room who can remind you to pay attention makes a significant difference in how much you learn.

That said, I understand why some students prefer online classes. It is nice to wake up a little later, enjoy a leisurely breakfast, and avoid rushing for the school bus. For someone like me, who values sleep, this flexibility is appealing. Nevertheless, taking classes from home demands strong time-management skills. You must schedule study sessions, meet deadlines, and balance schoolwork with personal life. If you fail to organize your day properly, you can quickly fall behind. Ultimately, remote learning places the responsibility squarely on each student to stay motivated and disciplined.

In conclusion, while virtual classes offer convenience, they lack the immediate support and structure of a traditional classroom. Without a teacher by your side and classmates nearby, it is easier to get distracted and harder to fully understand lessons. Although online learning helps you become more independent, it also requires a level of self-discipline that many students find challenging. For these reasons, I believe attending school in person remains the best option for most learners.

Do we gain confidence from our successes, or must we first believe in ourselves to achieve anything? Some people argue that students need self-confidence before they can learn, while others claim that confidence only follows accomplishment. In my view, believing in yourself comes first. Confidence drives us to work hard, stay positive, and tackle tasks with determination.

Success certainly feels rewarding, but without confidence, how would anyone even begin? First, self-confidence motivates us to keep learning every day. Take doctors as an example: they must trust their own abilities to study new diseases and treatments continually. Similarly, someone learning a new language—let’s say a Spanish speaker picking up English—needs confidence to face confusing grammar and expand their vocabulary. They may never fully master every nuance, but by trusting their capacity to improve, they will keep adding new words and phrases to their knowledge.

Second, a positive, confident attitude helps us complete important tasks. Imagine the final weeks of school, when major exams and state tests are approaching. If you’re convinced you can prepare well, you’ll attend classes, review notes, and study even on days when you feel stressed. That belief in your own potential makes it easier to focus and remember what you learn, so when the big test day arrives, you feel ready rather than overwhelmed.

Third, confidence means being sure of yourself when facing unknown situations. Suppose you have a job interview at a new company. You can’t predict exactly what questions they will ask or how they will react, but if you trust your own skills, your calm and self-assured manner will impress the interviewers. Employers are more likely to hire someone who seems poised and ready rather than someone who appears anxious or doubtful.

On the other hand, some people think that self-esteem comes only after you achieve something. They say that reaching a goal builds the confidence that you lacked before. For instance, students who pass difficult state tests after months of preparation feel a great sense of pride. They believe that once they see a passing score, their confidence naturally grows stronger for future challenges.

Another example is the driving test. If you study hard and succeed on the first try, you feel relieved and happy. That success can boost your self-confidence, making you more willing to take on other new experiences. However, if you fail, you may doubt yourself until you pass—showing clearly how confidence can depend on achievement.

Positive people often say that optimism itself leads to both success and confidence. They compare learning a new skill to a toddler learning to walk: a child falls repeatedly, but each small step forward builds courage. After those first independent steps, the child no longer depends on others to move around. This achievement brings genuine self-belief.

Despite these points, I remain convinced that confidence must precede achievement. It acts like a spark, giving us the courage to start and the resilience to continue when things get tough. Without that inner belief, many challenges would remain out of reach. Therefore, my advice is simple: nurture your confidence first. Let it cover your fears, guide your efforts, and you will find that achievement follows naturally, while your self-esteem endures long after the goal is met.

Former British prime minister Winston Churchill famously remarked that success is the ability to move from one failure to the next without losing enthusiasm. Every time we stumble, we gain valuable insight into what went wrong, which brings us closer to our goals. Failing doesn’t have to mean defeat; it can be the first step toward learning and improvement. In fact, nobody reaches true success without experiencing setbacks along the way. Embracing failure is crucial because it teaches us resilience and motivates us to keep trying until we achieve what we set out to do.

At first, failure can feel discouraging. I remember how upset I was when I didn’t pass my world history exam last year. I thought I would never succeed, but my teacher encouraged me to review my mistakes. When I looked over the test, I realized I had rushed through questions without fully understanding them. From that moment on, I made it a habit to read each question carefully before answering. The next time I took the exam, I applied this new approach and earned the highest grade in the class. This experience showed me that paying attention to details can transform failure into success.

Another lesson I learned was the value of consistent effort. After my first disappointing result, my mother insisted I study a little every day. She even arranged for me to stay after school for extra help sessions. By focusing on class lessons and asking questions whenever I felt unsure, I gradually improved my understanding of the material. When I finally retook the final exam, I not only passed but also maintained a strong average in the class. This taught me that hard work and persistence are essential, especially when a subject seems difficult at first.

Sometimes the hardest part of failing is believing you can do better. One afternoon, I came home in tears because I had once again fallen short on that world history test. My mother sat me down and shared that she, too, had struggled with her classes as a young student. She explained that failure doesn’t define intelligence but highlights areas where we need more effort. She encouraged me to keep trying and reminded me that she was proud of my determination, no matter the outcome. Inspired by her words, I devoted extra time to studying and finally passed the exam. That victory felt even more rewarding because I had learned to persevere.

Some people claim that you don’t need to fail to succeed—that hard work alone is enough and that mistakes aren’t necessary. However, they overlook the fact that failure often provides the best lessons. When we fail, we see our weaknesses clearly and find ways to improve. Rather than avoiding errors, we should accept them as part of the learning process. In the end, failure is not a setback but a stepping stone, guiding us toward the success we truly want.

It is widely acknowledged that keeping adolescents away from risky situations is essential. Introducing a rule that requires teenagers to be home by 10 pm can benefit them in four key areas: academics, social life, health, and finances.

First of all, a curfew helps students get enough sleep, which boosts their learning ability. When teens aren’t out late, they can follow a regular bedtime and wake up rested. As a result, they are more attentive in class and retain information better. Moreover, spending evenings at home gives them extra time to complete assignments and study. With more focused revision and fewer late-night distractions, their grades are likely to improve.

Secondly, staying off the streets at night can improve how young people interact with others. Wandering around after dark might make residents feel uneasy or suspect teens of mischief, so they may avoid them. By remaining at home in the evening, teenagers can participate in family conversations, phone calls, or supervised group activities that foster trust and friendships. In this safer, more positive environment, they can practice communication skills and build stronger bonds without worrying that others will be suspicious of their intentions.

The third advantage of a curfew is enhanced physical safety. Late-night gatherings on the street can sometimes lead to confrontations or accidents. If teens follow a 10 pm rule, they are less likely to encounter situations that could end in fights, injuries, or hospital visits. Instead, they can spend their nights in a secure setting—whether that means relaxing at home, reading, or pursuing hobbies—reducing the chance of harm.

Finally, a curfew can encourage responsible earning habits. Teenagers who wish to be active in the evening might look for part-time night shifts, such as at retail stores or movie theaters. Working these hours not only keeps them off the streets but also helps them earn money, learn work ethics, and save for future needs. Managing a small income teaches budgeting skills and provides financial security in case of emergencies.

In summary, enforcing a 10 pm curfew for teenagers offers clear advantages. It allows for better sleep and study habits, promotes healthier social interaction, prevents injuries, and motivates young people to seek productive employment. Altogether, these measures can guide adolescents toward safer, more successful lives.

It feels wonderful when someone offers a simple “thank you” or “you’re welcome.” Polite words and good manners show that you appreciate what others do for you. Whenever someone lends a hand, gives you a gift, or just does something kind, responding with gratitude encourages them to reply in kind. By speaking kindly and showing respect, you create a positive cycle of politeness. Being grateful and courteous makes daily life smoother and happier for everyone.

When you treat others with kindness and use polite expressions like “please,” “thank you,” or even “yes, sir,” they often mirror your behavior. If you smile, speak respectfully, and listen carefully, people tend to do the same with you. Politeness is like a boomerang: when you send it out, it comes back. So if you want to be treated well, start by treating others well. Simple phrases can build mutual respect and trust in any relationship.

Keeping a cheerful attitude and offering friendly remarks can help you make new friends and lift people’s spirits. A genuine compliment or a warm greeting can turn someone’s bad day into a better one. Saying “Thank you for helping me” or “You did a great job” might only take a moment, but it can mean a lot to someone else. Being positive and encouraging shows you care and helps others feel valued, too.

Of course, everyone makes mistakes or forgets to use polite words sometimes. If you ever hurt someone’s feelings, don’t hesitate to apologize. A sincere “I’m sorry” can heal many misunderstandings. Remember, kindness and good manners go both ways: you must give them before you expect to receive them. If you want people to say “thank you” or “you’re welcome,” be the first to say these words yourself.

You can practice good manners in many everyday situations. For instance, when you pay at a store, thank the cashier and ask how their day is going. Even if you don’t know them, a friendly question shows you care about their well-being. If someone wishes you a “good day,” reply with “Thank you, you too.” These small gestures can brighten a stranger’s day and encourage them to pass on the kindness.

At restaurants or cafés, showing appreciation for the staff is important. Saying “thank you” to your server, leaving a tip if you can, or offering a kind word when you see someone working hard all help build goodwill. If a worker seems tired or stressed, you might invite them to join you for a meal or offer to buy them a drink. A little generosity can make a big difference in someone’s mood and makes the world a kinder place.

Using good manners and showing kindness reflect who you are as a person. The more you practice polite language and considerate actions, the more you will experience them in return. Kindness spreads, and good manners help to create a friendly community. By choosing to be polite, you help everyone feel respected and happy.

Who wants to tackle a task on their own when teaming up is an option? Working in a group offers clear advantages, such as faster completion and greater efficiency. Besides, collaborating with classmates or colleagues lets you share feedback and improve your work together.

Of course, some people prefer to work solo because there are no group interruptions. They avoid moments when one member slacks off or distracts everyone else. Even so, the benefits of cooperation usually outweigh these occasional setbacks.

First, group projects often move more quickly than individual efforts. Imagine you have a short essay due in one week plus a presentation to prepare. If you split the work among three or four people, each person handles a portion, and you finish much sooner than if you did everything alone.

Second, being part of a team means you can discuss ideas and receive immediate reactions. When you explain your plan to others, they point out strengths and weaknesses you might have missed. This kind of interaction helps everyone learn and refine their work.

Third, having several minds on the same topic brings a wealth of perspectives. Each member contributes unique thoughts, whether they match or contrast with yours. By combining these different ideas, the group can create something more impressive than any individual could produce.

Whether you’re collaborating on a school assignment or joining a professional committee, teamwork usually leads to better results. The speed, feedback, and creative variety you gain from working with others make group projects far more rewarding than going it alone.

One topic often discussed is whether schools should manage students’ extracurricular time. Some people argue that schools must organize all student activities to add educational value. I disagree. I think students should choose how to use their after-school hours because many students need to work for their families, others care for younger siblings, and many simply wish to spend their free time on sports, art, or extra study.

Firstly, a number of students hold part-time jobs to support their parents and siblings. Balancing work and study can be very tiring, leaving little energy for quizzes or homework. While study halls at school might help them complete assignments, these students still miss out on extracurricular clubs because of their tight schedules. On the positive side, earning money for college is a smart investment in their future. Therefore, it makes sense that these students have to give up some voluntary activities to meet their financial goals.

Secondly, some students must return home quickly to look after brothers or sisters when their parents are working. Hiring a babysitter is too expensive for many families, so these students focus on household chores like cooking, cleaning, or laundry, often doing schoolwork alongside. Juggling these responsibilities with academic demands can be very challenging, so forcing them into school-run activities would only add pressure.

Finally, there are students who simply want to follow their interests in sports, art, or clubs unrelated to academics. Whether practicing basketball, painting, or joining an environmental group, these students decide how best to use their time after school. They don’t need schools to dictate their choices.

For these reasons, I believe schools should not control students’ after-school activities. When we acknowledge each person’s individual dreams and difficulties, we will better appreciate how hard people work to find success and happiness.

In various cultures, students are often asked to choose a career path as they enter high school. The main issue is whether it is wise for young people to decide so early on.

One clear advantage of selecting a profession at a young age is that time becomes an ally for those aiming at lengthy training programs. For instance, future doctors, lawyers, educators and similar specialists need many years to complete their studies. Beginning preparation sooner helps them build a strong foundation and contributes positively to society’s growth.

Moreover, early commitment can increase flexibility over time. A student who has already started specialized studies in one field still has the chance to pivot if their interests shift. For example, a young person training to become a teacher might later pursue a different discipline while retaining the study skills they developed.

On the other hand, choosing a career too soon carries risks. Teenagers may become exhausted by prolonged schooling or realize only after several years that their chosen field does not match their true interests. This mismatch can lead to frustration and lost time.

In conclusion, deciding on a career path early can be highly beneficial if students receive the right support and information. Therefore, schools should offer career guidance programs and involve teachers and counselors to help young people explore options and make informed choices.

Should we choose our own path or look to others for direction? I believe that while it’s wise to learn from our parents’ experience, we must ultimately guide our own lives. Parents have already dealt with many difficulties and naturally want us to avoid the mistakes they made. For example, if you’re thinking about buying a car, it makes sense to discuss your budget and options with them—they’ve gone through similar decisions and can highlight things you might miss. Yet when it comes to picking a career or setting personal goals, that responsibility belongs to you. You decide whether you aim for a rewarding job, a spacious home, or a comfortable lifestyle—and then you have to work for it, because no success arrives without effort.

My older brother shows how this balance of advice and independence works. At twenty-one, he moved out with a clear plan: to own his own apartment and a reliable car while taking college courses part-time. I admire how he managed to work, save money, and study all at once. Despite his independence, he didn’t hesitate to ask our parents for guidance when needed, and their support helped him avoid costly errors. He often tells me that taking thoughtful risks is essential for moving forward in life.

In the end, no one can force you to make the right choices—only you hold that power. The decisions you make will shape your character and your future. Life outside of school is a very different world; you will make wrong turns as well as smart moves, and that’s perfectly normal. These mistakes are not failures but chances to learn and build stronger judgment. I’ve seen my parents make errors they regretted and others that proved to be invaluable lessons, guiding them toward happier outcomes.

It is important to have someone or something that inspires you, but you must also trust your own instincts. You can even become a source of motivation for others by showing determination and sharing your experiences. Remember that success is rarely handed out; there will always be obstacles, from financial worries to unexpected setbacks. When you face these challenges, encourage yourself to keep going and stay focused on your objectives. In doing so, you will grow more confident and capable.

In conclusion, although parental advice can offer valuable insight, the ultimate responsibility for your life choices rests with you. Your dreams and ambitions deserve to be pursued with your own judgment and effort. So seize each moment, trust your heart, and take charge of the future you want.

Thomas Jefferson once advised, “Never allow yourself to be idle… You will be amazed at how much can be achieved if you keep busy.” I fully support this view, since whenever I remain inactive, I become unhappy or even gloomy, so I always look for ways to stay engaged.

There are many methods to chase away boredom. Last summer, for instance, I helped my father at his carpentry job. Not everyone can do that, though, so here are three ideas: join a fitness centre, go for regular walks, or find some kind of work.

First, becoming a gym member may seem expensive, but the benefits for both mind and body are huge. Exercising releases feel-good chemicals that boost your mood, and you might notice improvements in your strength and appearance. That’s why I suggest the gym as a way to avoid doing nothing.

Secondly, taking walks is simple and calming. I discovered that wandering around my neighbourhood helps me relax—breathing fresh air and noticing the beauty of nature. You don’t have to go solo: invite a friend, a family member, or even your pet. It’s a pleasant way to enjoy the world we live in.

My final recommendation is to find a job. Working alongside my dad gave me extra income—I was able to buy shoes, clothes, and treat my family to small gifts. More important, though, was the life lesson I gained: real life requires effort and persistence. Watching a building take shape day by day was rewarding; by the end, the unfinished site seemed like a complex puzzle I had helped solve.

For these reasons, I believe boredom and inactivity are unacceptable. Think of all the goals you could reach if you keep busy. That is why I agree so much with Jefferson’s words: “You will be amazed at how much can be achieved if you keep busy.”

While many people believe it’s best to stick with what you already know, others argue that taking on harder tasks can help you surpass your own expectations. Challenging yourself beyond familiar territory not only pushes you further in life but also turns everyday activities—such as work and study—into exciting adventures.

When you aim to achieve more than your original objectives, you open doors to new opportunities. You may discover fresh interests or talents, and your job can feel less like a routine and more like an engaging pursuit. At the same time, tackling tougher subjects or projects helps you expand your knowledge and skills in ways that simply repeating what you already master cannot.

None of this is possible without confidence in your own abilities. If you convince yourself that a goal is out of reach, you won’t put in the effort needed to reach it. Believing in yourself is the first step toward making real progress. For example, a student I know decided to enroll in a challenging chemistry course, even though she doubted her abilities at first. By sticking with it and asking questions, she not only passed the class but also gained a newfound appreciation for science.

Turning everyday tasks into enjoyable challenges can also breathe new life into your work. Start by identifying an aspect of your job that interests you, then set a small goal each week—perhaps improving a process or learning a new technique. Treat these targets like levels in a game. Since most people enjoy games, framing your tasks this way can keep you motivated and eager to succeed.

Education isn’t limited to classrooms; it happens all around us. You can learn by watching how others handle problems, listening to different perspectives, or reflecting on your own experiences. To make the most of these lessons, try to stay mentally, emotionally, and physically prepared for whatever comes your way. Life will surprise you with both challenges and rewards, and each experience teaches something valuable.

As Ralph Waldo Emerson famously wrote, “Do not go where the path may lead; go instead where there is no path and leave a trail.” In other words, push yourself beyond the skills you’ve already mastered. Believe in your capacity to grow, set your sights higher than before, and aim to improve a little more each day. By doing so, you’ll discover that life’s challenges are really opportunities in disguise.

Summer projects can be fun if students choose them. If they pick their own projects based on the subject, they would be more interested, more likely to complete them, and would enjoy them as well.

Teachers spend a whole summer or a school year coming up with a topic for students’ summer work. It turns out that students aren’t giving much thought or effort to the assignment. That can be a waste of the teachers’ time and energy, but if students come up with their own topic and idea, they would complete the project.

If students choose their own projects, they are more likely to do them because they focus on something they want to learn and are curious about. When students are curious, they tend to explore their interests, become more engaged in the subject, and want to learn more. Students can come up with great ideas for their own projects. Choosing a topic that interests them can open students’ minds and lead them to do things they never thought of doing.

The summer project can improve your grades in class. For example, a student who struggles in class because they cannot keep pace can work at their own speed during the summer. If students are not great at working in an environment full of other students, this gives them a chance to do independent study. A summer project can give an opportunity for students to increase their grades. If students choose their own assignments, they can work at a pace that suits them, and they do not have to worry about a due date. They have the whole summer to finish the project, and if they do not finish it with an entire summer ahead, now that’s just being lazy, which can affect their grade.

The subject can have a great impact on students. If a student is given an assignment in a certain subject, there is a chance they will start to procrastinate or not do it at all. Therefore, they would have zero interest in doing the summer assignment. For example, if I had a history project and a science project, and my science teacher gave me a research paper on how genes mutate—which sounds interesting—I would not do it because science does not fascinate me as much as history.

Being able to choose their own project can be fun; it gives students something to look forward to and makes them more fascinated by their work. Students should design their summer projects because it’s less work for the teacher, gives them an opportunity to think outside the box, and allows them to make their teachers proud by doing their work well, so they can look forward to a better school year.

Summer assignments can be enjoyable when students are allowed to select their own topics. If learners choose projects that match their interests in a particular subject, they are far more likely to stay engaged, complete the work, and actually have fun doing it.

Often, teachers spend a great deal of time planning project topics over the school year or during the summer break. However, many students put in little effort or fail to take these assignments seriously. This not only wastes teachers’ time and energy but also misses an opportunity for meaningful learning. If students designed their own projects, they would feel a stronger sense of responsibility and be more committed to finishing the task.

When students pick subjects that genuinely fascinate them, their natural curiosity drives their work. Curious learners tend to explore ideas more deeply, ask questions, and look for answers on their own. Allowing them to choose topics encourages original thinking, and they often come up with creative approaches that teachers might not have imagined. By working on something they care about, students expand their minds and discover new skills.

Summer projects can also help improve academic performance. For example, a student who falls behind during the regular school year might struggle to keep up in class. A self-chosen summer assignment lets that student work at their own pace without feeling rushed. Those who find crowded classrooms overwhelming get a chance to study independently and build confidence. With the freedom to set their own schedule, students can focus on strengthening weak areas and boosting their grades.

The subject matter itself plays a big role in motivation. If a student receives an assignment in a topic they dislike, they are likely to procrastinate or ignore it completely. For instance, I might enjoy history but find science unappealing; no matter how interesting a genetics project might sound, I would probably delay working on it. When students have no say in the topic, they risk losing interest before they even start.

By giving students the option to design their own summer projects, schools make learning more exciting and relevant. It reduces the planning load for teachers and helps students think creatively outside the usual classroom routine. In the end, students take pride in their achievements and return to school feeling more enthusiastic about the year ahead.

Many of us are still working there, and our improved mood has made the workplace a more positive environment.

Every person faces setbacks that can make them give up, but a single supportive voice can encourage them to carry on. My family once faced a serious money problem when my father lost his job. We were four months behind on the rent and feared losing our home. My father became very discouraged as he searched for work without success for nearly three months. My mother, however, stayed calm and said, “Don’t worry, sweetheart. We always find a way out of difficulties together.” Her faith in him brought a smile back to his face. He hugged her, took our car keys, and went out to find a new position. Within days he was offered a job that paid even better than his previous one, and our financial worries vanished.

Believing in yourself isn’t always easy. In tenth grade, I struggled in algebra and so did many classmates. Our teacher constantly told us to trust our abilities, but at first we paid little attention and mostly gave up when we didn’t understand a problem. After the first quarter, many of us had failing grades. Then our teacher held a meeting with us, encouraging each student to try, even when the questions seemed too hard. She made us believe we were capable of learning anything we set our minds to. That attitude shift led us to study harder and ask questions without fear. By the end of the second quarter, our scores rose from around fifty to eighty or ninety. I will always be grateful to her, because her positive support improved both our marks and our self-belief.

Our attitude needs to stay positive even in the worst moments. Some people think optimism is only for celebrations or important events, but I believe they are mistaken. We should keep a hopeful outlook every day. In families, grandparents, parents, and older siblings must lead by example so that children learn to face life’s challenges with confidence and enthusiasm.

When you face a decision, talking to several people for advice can be more helpful than asking just one. I remember reading a quote by LeBron James who said that seeking input from more than one person gives you broader perspectives, because one person’s view might be solid while another’s could be off. So don’t be afraid to consult different people, especially those you respect. Gathering a range of opinions usually leads to better guidance.

However, if you’re someone who prefers not to open up to many people, sticking to a single trusted advisor also works. In that case, choose someone you know well and who consistently makes wise choices. A person you trust can give honest feedback and accurate information, helping you avoid decisions you might regret. The key is to ensure the person you turn to has your best interests at heart, so you don’t end up following misleading counsel.

On the other hand, sharing personal issues with multiple people can risk your privacy. If sensitive details spread, you might feel betrayed or worry about being bullied. That’s why, for deeply personal matters, confiding in just one reliable person is often safer. And if you really can’t find someone you trust among your friends or family, talking to a school counselor or another professional can be a good solution—they are bound by confidentiality and can understand from experience or training.

In the end, whether you choose one source or several, the advice you receive can shape your future. Just be careful not to take guidance from someone who makes poor choices themselves. Good advice has the power to change lives for the better.

In my opinion, schools should offer courses that help students prepare for their future professions. Deciding on a career path early means that as adults they are less likely to end up in dull or poorly paid jobs.

As an eleventh grader, I already know I want to serve in the United States Marine Corps. At my high school, I am enrolled in the Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (JROTC) program. JROTC introduces students to life in the U.S. Armed Forces and develops leadership skills, discipline and teamwork. This class gives me firsthand knowledge of the military and helps me decide if I truly enjoy this path.

I am also taking Economics and Finance, which is required for graduation. Although it is mandatory, I appreciate this subject because it teaches useful money-management skills. Understanding budgets, investments and economic principles will be valuable whether I stay in the Marines or change careers later.

Without starting to prepare for our chosen fields in high school, we risk feeling lost, uncertain and even struggling financially after graduation. In my family, none of my relatives studied subjects they enjoyed in school. My mother once wanted to become an artist but her school did not offer art classes, so she eventually left and raised her children instead of pursuing her dream.

Working is something everyone must do, so it makes sense to begin exploring what we like early on. For me, JROTC and Economics are the first steps toward becoming a United States Marine, and I am confident these courses will support my future goals.

There is a debate about whether we should push ourselves beyond the skills we already possess or simply stop once we feel competent. I believe we must keep exploring new challenges and learning throughout our lives—otherwise, we risk remaining stuck in one place. I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s view on lifelong growth, and here are my reasons why.

First, taking on new tasks gives us valuable experience that cannot be measured only in dollars. Imagine two people applying for the same job: one has only a high school diploma, while the other has that diploma plus vocational training as a plumber. The second candidate clearly has broader expertise and is more likely to be hired. In many situations, being prepared and well-rounded can make all the difference.

Second, learning fresh skills helps us become more mature and resilient. When we step outside our comfort zone, we make mistakes—and learning from those errors teaches us patience and determination. Many people quit after one or two failures, but real personal growth comes from persisting through setbacks and refusing to give up when things get tough.

Finally, trying new things allows us to set and achieve a wider range of goals, which today often translates into greater opportunities. For example, I aim to become a police officer, but I won’t stop there. I plan to pursue promotions and specialized training so that I can grow financially, physically, and mentally. Each new target I reach will also strengthen my skills and confidence.

In conclusion, choosing the easiest path may seem attractive, but it rarely leads to meaningful progress. Every obstacle we face is actually a chance to learn, and the more we try, the more doors open for us. It is never too late to continue learning, because the more we know, the more we grow.
