Do you ever feel it's difficult to remain true to yourself in a world that pushes you to fit in? We grow up surrounded by expectations that often lead us to follow the crowd instead of discovering our own path and finding real happiness. In this essay, I will explore how society tries to reshape us each day, how these influences gradually alter our behavior, and why it seems like our generation encounters more problems every year.

Every day, society presents new ideas about what we should be or how we should live. It’s important to pause and ask ourselves: Where do I want to be in ten years? Do I really aim to blend in and follow others, or do I want to set my own goals and reach them on my own terms? Success, in my view, comes from embracing our unique qualities. The world will not shape us into someone authentic; if we hope to achieve our dreams, we must stand firm in who we are.

In many ways, we absorb society’s preferences—from the way we speak and the hobbies we choose to our style of dressing and even our beliefs. Fashion offers a clear example: if we don’t wear the latest trends or branded items, others may see us as uncool. Sometimes this is simply because we lack the money or opportunity to purchase certain clothes, or perhaps we prefer a different look. Yet, society often views us as outsiders for these choices. This pressure can lead to bullying and feelings of low self-worth. It’s alarming that some young people suffer from anxiety or depression because they cannot meet these standards.

Beyond fashion, society also influences us through the music we hear and the news we see. Some popular songs glorify drug use, violence or sexual content, which can send harmful messages to listeners. On top of that, real-world issues like conflicts between nations and the easy availability of illegal substances only worsen the situation. If we continue to accept these negative influences without question, our generation could face even greater problems. We need to focus on positive role models and healthy activities, so each person can grow without being trapped by harmful societal trends.

Some might blame society entirely for spreading bad influences. However, it is often our own choice if we allow ourselves to get pulled into unhealthy behaviors. Instead of pointing fingers, we should reflect on our decisions and build resilience against harmful pressures. Fortunately, there is still time to change course. I believe Ralph Waldo Emerson was right when he said that real maturity isn’t simply a matter of getting older. Many people finish college, earn a degree, and then still live with their parents. Even if you could find a job, save money, and buy your own home, you might choose to stay under your parents’ roof. In that situation, your family will always see you as their child, no matter how old you become. I think Emerson wanted to point out that age doesn’t change the way others view you—it’s your actions that do.

In the wider world, you prove you’re an adult by building your own life. When you have your own car, house, and family to support, you begin to understand what your parents went through. You’ll protect and work for your loved ones just as they did for you. This cycle of care continues: your children will look up to you as their parent for their whole lives. I saw this clearly when I watched my older sister raise her daughter. That experience made me reflect on my own life.

Although I was only fifteen when I moved out, I quickly realized that growing up isn’t about age but about responsibility. I had to manage my daily needs, handle work, and make decisions on my own. From that point on, I understood Emerson’s message more deeply. True growth happens when you focus on becoming the person you want to be instead of worrying about what others think. In the end, family and close friends are the most important, and they’ll recognize your maturity by how you live your life—not by how many birthdays you’ve had.

The option to take classes online can bring both advantages and disadvantages. While some schools offer virtual programs, others do not, and people have different opinions on their value. Supporters argue that learning online allows students to work at their own speed without waiting for classmates, but critics point out potential problems such as unreliable internet connections, lack of social interaction, and the temptation to skip assignments.

One difficulty of online learning is understanding assignments without immediate help. When you study remotely, you cannot simply raise your hand and ask a teacher for an explanation. Searching the internet might lead you to inaccurate solutions, and there may not be enough tutorial videos on the exact topic you need. As a result, you could spend hours trying to figure out a problem on your own. In a physical classroom, a teacher could guide you through each step, making the lesson clearer and more effective.

Another drawback is the absence of peers in the same situation. In a school environment, you can compare study methods, share notes, or form study groups with classmates of your own age. Online, you are often alone with your computer. Even if you have friends, they might not be enrolled in the same course, so collaborating becomes difficult. This isolation can reduce motivation and limit the chance to develop new friendships.

Time management is also a challenge in virtual schooling. Instructors may assign several tasks at once, all due on the same day, and if you do not fully understand the material, meeting deadlines can become stressful. Some students may procrastinate or look for quick answers online instead of engaging with the lesson, which can lead to poor grades or even failure. Distractions at home—family responsibilities, chores, or social media—can make it harder to focus and complete work promptly.

Despite these issues, online classes offer flexibility that traditional classrooms do not. Students who need more free time for other commitments, such as jobs or family care, can benefit from this arrangement. However, that same flexibility can tempt some students to neglect their studies. When life becomes difficult, and no teacher is present to offer support, online learners must rely on their own discipline and resources. Ultimately, each student must decide which mode of learning best suits their needs.

In conclusion, attending classes online can be a useful alternative to in-person education, but it is not without its challenges. Technical problems, limited interaction with teachers and peers, and the need for strong self-management skills can make virtual learning tough for some. While it works well for those who are organized and self-motivated, others may find that traditional classrooms still provide the structure and support they need.

Working with a team offers greater advantages than working alone. First, in a group, people contribute varied perspectives and suggestions. By discussing and combining these different viewpoints, the team develops more complete and innovative ideas than any individual could achieve alone. Even when some ideas seem challenging, partners can support each other, turning difficult plans into reality.

Second, collaborating helps a team succeed in competitions. Members share responsibilities by taking on specific roles on stage or behind the scenes. For instance, some participants lead the performance, while others handle lighting or sound. Though rehearsals may demand long hours and personal sacrifices, practicing as a unit ensures everyone understands their task, improving overall delivery and chances of winning.

Finally, engaging the audience requires teamwork. Spectators come to be entertained, and a well-coordinated group knows how to capture their interest. With a clear leader guiding the timing and interactions, each performer can play their part effectively, creating an interactive and memorable show.

In conclusion, working in a team not only fosters creativity and success in competitions but also brings joy to the audience and pride to friends, family, and mentors. Overall, collaborating with others is more rewarding and enjoyable than going solo.

Half of people use technology for social media rather than face-to-face conversation. Many online studies suggest that constant device use over time can lead to depression. We should limit technology for fun to improve our quality of life and protect our eyes from strain. For example, one of my closest friends needed glasses at age five because he watched TV too close to the screen.

Technology does offer useful features, such as sending photos to distant relatives, researching homework, or checking the time. It also makes it easy to call family and friends living abroad. Yet these benefits can be expensive, and overall I believe technology often harms us by overstimulating our brains.

Excessive phone use can turn us into lazy thinkers. Students who spend more time online than studying usually get poor quiz and test results. A friend of mine even cheated on a test using his phone, and surprisingly, the teacher was just sitting there playing with his own device. I’ve even seen a favorite teacher scroll through social media during class.

This problem doesn’t stop at the classroom. In gym class, many people simply sit and scroll on their phones instead of playing sports. Personally, I prefer to stay active by playing soccer, basketball, or baseball, which keeps both my body and mind healthy.

We all see these habits every day and everywhere. Am I the only one noticing how technology consumes our attention and weakens our social and mental skills? We should rethink our screen time before it affects us even more.

“Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” This famous line by Winston Churchill resonates with me because real achievement usually demands persistence. Rarely do our first attempts lead us directly to our goals, so we must keep trying until we finally succeed.

Some people insist that you can succeed simply by choosing to win and never actually failing. They believe a determined mindset alone is enough to reach any goal. Although determination is vital, I think that encountering setbacks teaches crucial lessons. Without experiencing mistakes, it is hard to grow and improve.

Keeping enthusiasm alive while working hard is essential. When we rush or become impatient, our energy fades and our interest wanes. Enthusiasm is the deep eagerness and passion that drives us forward, even when progress is slow. Each failure becomes a learning opportunity: we analyse what went wrong, adopt a fresh approach, and continue with renewed motivation.

Research supports this idea. One study found that 78.2 percent of people never meet their aims because they prefer comfort over challenge and lack the motivation to push through obstacles. In contrast, those who embrace the possibility of failure and stay committed are more likely to fulfil their ambitions.

In conclusion, I agree with Churchill that success involves moving from one disappointment to another without losing zeal. By keeping our enthusiasm high, learning from failures, and persevering patiently, we increase our chances of finally achieving our goals.

I believe our school should offer an after-school homework club because many students struggle with assignments and need extra guidance. Although homework might seem unimportant, it actually counts for ten percent of our final grade. While that may not sound like much, completing it correctly can really boost your overall score. The concepts practiced in each task prepare you for quizzes and tests, so missing out on this practice could be the reason you don’t pass an exam.

Middle schoolers often juggle homework for up to seven different subjects, and some teachers give multiple exercises every night. It can quickly become overwhelming. Having a dedicated time and place to work through assignments would help many students finish their homework on time. Instead of guessing at answers, they could ask questions about any part of the lesson they found unclear. A teacher or tutor at the club could explain difficult ideas, ensuring that students learn the material rather than simply copying solutions.

This extra help would likely improve individual grades. A student stuck on one question might decide not to finish homework at all, but in the club, they could figure out that issue immediately and move on confidently. Improving homework completion rates from a B level to an A is entirely possible when students understand the work and have the support they need.

Moreover, the school would benefit if more students handed in their homework on time and performed better on assessments. Higher grades mean a stronger academic reputation for our school. Teachers would also feel more confident that students genuinely understand their lessons instead of relying on shortcuts or guessing answers.

Some students are capable of doing assignments on their own but struggle with organization or time management. The homework club would help these students by providing structure: a consistent period after school focused solely on completing assignments. This would free up their evenings for other activities, reducing stress and giving them more free time.

In conclusion, an after-school homework club would address a major issue for many students: the challenge of understanding and completing assignments. By offering personalized support, improving grades, and easing stress, this club would benefit both students and the school as a whole. With this resource in place, homework would no longer be a source of anxiety but an opportunity to learn and succeed.

“To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment,” wrote Ralph Waldo Emerson. I firmly agree with this idea. Before I explain why, it is useful to understand the meaning of “accomplish.” To accomplish something means to complete or achieve a goal. Living your true life helps you achieve genuine success, whereas pretending to be someone else only leads to failure and shame.

For example, I once heard about a company looking for a new director. They advertised a position that offered thousands of dollars every week to a well-known, wealthy figure. One applicant decided to invent a lavish lifestyle. She borrowed nearly $500,000 from banks to buy two houses and three new cars, hoping to impress everyone. The other candidate was much poorer but had strong experience and true talent. Both waited anxiously for weeks, confident in their chances. When the judges gathered to announce the winner, the company’s spokesperson began by praising each candidate’s qualities. Then he revealed the proof of the first woman’s deception. Because she had lied about her wealth, the board concluded she would only misuse company funds and harm its reputation. They chose the honest candidate, who had remained herself throughout the process and truly deserved the role.

This story shows that living an authentic life leads to real fulfillment, while faking your identity brings public disgrace if you are found out. In a world full of pressure to conform or impress, staying true to yourself remains the greatest achievement you can attain.

One question has been asked during a long time. Is it better to work alone or to work in a group?

Most of the people and analysts have got the conclusion that working in groups could be more beneficial.

A factor the support this idea it is because you get to have different thoughts, ideas and ways to see the life that can help you in bad situations. For example, if you are planning either something as big as a school event, or something as simple as a classroom presentation, there is occasions when you run out of ideas. You can count in the group. They are going to be there giving diverse solutions to the problem, otherwise, by yourself you could be struggling like if you are in road with no exit.

Working in a group sometimes can make you relax, laugh and bring positivism, even in challenging moments or when you are facing stress. Every time you have to work in this way, you do not spend boring moments. There will be always something to talk about. You and your team would be saving memories that in a future would be a moment of laugh.

Another fact about working in group is that you get to finish the work in a faster. More people working in the a series of things in a quickly way than just one, makes a big difference. It will give space to the creativity, where you can practice more, give details to the work or even do new creations.

Because you are working in a team you do not focus only in "I" you open your mind and start thinking in "we". This is going to be useful in the future, when you go out to the real world. Working with other people, you have to deal with different personalities and thoughts. The team working abilities are going to be place in your mind.

When as a team all your tasks are completed you will find a great euphoria in the results. It is going to make everyone proud of themselves and also it is going to be a method to keep pushing them up and never give up.

Sometimes when you get to work in a group it might sound or seem a difficult task. But instead, you learned new experiences and new abilities. It become a helpful tool to develop character and to grow as a person. You have to learn how to speak with the people and how to tell your ideas in a clear manner. That is why many people agreed that working in teams brings more benefits than just working alone.

People have long debated whether working alone or collaborating in a team is the better approach. Many experts and individuals agree that joining forces with others brings greater advantages.

For instance, organizing a school festival or preparing a class presentation can hit a creative wall. In a group, your peers can suggest new solutions and alternative angles, preventing you from feeling stuck and offering clearer direction.

Even under pressure, teammates can share jokes and support one another, turning stressful moments into opportunities for bonding. These shared experiences not only keep boredom at bay but also build memories that you can look back on with a smile.

Another benefit is efficiency. Distributing tasks among several people means that you can complete assignments more quickly than you would on your own. With more hands contributing, there is time to refine details, explore fresh ideas, and enhance the overall quality of the work.

Collaborative projects also encourage you to think beyond your personal goals and embrace a collective mindset. This shift from “I” to “we” is invaluable in real-life situations, where interacting with different personalities and viewpoints is essential. Learning to cooperate effectively lays a strong foundation for future careers.

Finally, finishing a task as a team brings a special thrill. Celebrating success together boosts everyone’s confidence and motivates the group to tackle new challenges. Through teamwork, you also develop communication skills, adapt to various roles, and grow personally. For these reasons, many believe that working in groups offers more benefits than working alone.

I believe first impressions are nearly impossible to alter because they capture a unique moment that cannot be exactly recreated. You only feel something for the first time once. Even if a similar situation happens later, it won’t have the same freshness or surprise. That original feeling stays with you, and often you don’t want to change it because it left a strong, positive mark on you.

Imagine walking through town and seeing someone dressed in a very unusual or eye-catching outfit. Immediately, that person stands out because you haven’t encountered anyone like them before. Some onlookers might start speculating about their background or judging them based on appearance. Others might feel curious, eager to learn more about their culture or lifestyle, or simply hoping to have a fun conversation. In all these cases, the first impression appears instantly and shapes how people react.

We constantly encounter new situations, whether among family, friends, or strangers. Each encounter brings its own impressions because we are always exposed to different people and events. It doesn’t matter where you are; you will have first impressions that influence how you feel and what you think in that moment.

First impressions also affect how we see ourselves. Sometimes, noticing something special in someone else makes us reconsider our own habits or style. You might decide to try a new hobby or change your appearance because a single interaction inspired you. In this way, first impressions can even help us grow and improve.

In summary, first impressions remain unique and are very difficult to change. You might rethink your opinion over time, but you can’t really go back to that initial surprise or excitement. Even if you meet the same person again, the sense of novelty is gone. That one-time reaction helps us understand others and enrich our own lives, regardless of differences in background or identity.

Taking classes from home is a good benefit only if you want to take classes from another school, can’t go to school because of where you live or it takes too long to walk to school, or if you don’t feel comfortable in school. I think allowing students to join classes online from any school in the world would have many advantages. Those who live far from educational institutions or cannot find reliable transportation would benefit greatly. Studying from home also offers a more relaxed atmosphere, where students may feel at ease.

Online learning is especially useful for pupils seeking courses that their local schools do not provide. For example, a young person in France might enroll in classes offered by an American school and experience a different teaching style and curriculum. This flexibility also helps students who move temporarily to another country; they can continue their studies without interruption and later bring that knowledge back to their home country.

Remote education makes schooling accessible to young people who otherwise would have to walk for hours. I once saw a video about a girl who trekked through mountainous terrain for four hours just to attend class. In many cold or remote regions, children are denied regular schooling simply because schools are too distant. During the recent coronavirus outbreak, many schools closed to prevent the virus from spreading, and students shifted to home-based learning to stay safe while continuing their education.

Another advantage is that home study can help those who feel anxious or intimidated in a traditional classroom. At home, students are surrounded by their family and in a familiar setting, which can boost their confidence. Bullying and peer pressure often make school life unbearable for some children. I recall a tragic story about a seven-year-old boy who, tormented by classmates, became so distraught that he asked his mother for a knife. Eventually, he was homeschooled and received therapy, which improved his well-being.

However, not everyone sees online classes as ideal. Some worry that students will lose out on face-to-face interaction and teamwork skills. A friend of mine who was homeschooled has found it hard to make friends at his new high school, and he remains quite reserved. In conclusion, while distance learning suits those seeking special courses, living in isolated areas, or looking for a safer environment, it may not be the best choice for every student due to its social limitations.

Last week I had a math exam first thing in the morning. I had studied hard, but on the test day I overslept and missed my school bus. To avoid being late, I ended up walking all the way to school. By the time I arrived, I was worn out and anxious, and I couldn’t concentrate during the exam. If my school had offered the test online, I could have taken it at home and avoided that stressful journey. In general, online learning can protect students from these kinds of setbacks and make better use of our time.

Critics argue that studying from home can make it harder for pupils to follow lessons or finish assignments. They worry that, without a teacher physically present, learners may struggle to understand new topics or instructions for projects. For example, if a student has to complete a complex homework task, they might not find the guidance they need through a screen and end up confused.

Despite these concerns, the advantages of attending classes online are significant. First, when students are unwell or away from their usual home, they don’t have to miss school entirely. If I catch a cold, for instance, I could stay in bed and still listen to lectures and join discussions. Likewise, if I’m visiting relatives or friends in another town, I could log on to lessons from there. This flexibility ensures that illness or travel won’t interrupt my education.

Another benefit is the time saved by not commuting to campus. High school students often have part-time jobs or extracurricular interests, and online classes free up hours that would otherwise be spent on the road. With that extra time, I could work more shifts during the week and earn money for college. I could also tackle additional online courses that strengthen my resume or devote time to sports, music, or other hobbies I enjoy.

In conclusion, allowing students to take classes online from home brings valuable benefits. It prevents disruptions caused by sickness or travel and recovers lost hours usually spent getting to school. As a result, learners can stay on top of their studies, hold down jobs, and explore extra activities. Online education not only saves time but also offers opportunities to grow outside the traditional classroom.

Students should have their career in mind by the time they enter High School so they can learn more and prepare for college. This will allow them to learn much more and be an inspiration for many other teenagers, encouraging others to think about the importance of having a good education and career.

When young people reach the eighth grade in middle school, they often begin to explore different professions and consider what they might want to do in the future. It is important that students have the freedom to decide their own career path, rather than being pushed into jobs their parents prefer. In many cases, teenagers feel they have no real choice. Today’s adolescents should be encouraged to pick studies that match their interests. During high school, they acquire a variety of skills and knowledge, and this training can help them adapt to many kinds of work or unexpected challenges later on. Guiding young students toward subjects they enjoy allows them to grow more confident. For example, when they research a field or speak with professionals already working in it, they gain clear insights into the career they hope to pursue. By the time they graduate, they are better prepared to choose the right college courses and set goals for themselves.

In some regions around the world—places like Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and parts of Africa—many teenagers cannot continue their education because resources are scarce. Instead of attending school, they often have to take low-paying jobs to support their families. This shortage of opportunities drives many young people to migrate to the United States, where they believe a strong education will secure their future. Arriving with big dreams and determination, these students aim to make their families proud by earning a diploma and finding steady work. Back home, as populations grow and jobs remain limited, even those with degrees can struggle. Parents who discourage schooling by saying it “won’t get you anywhere” can unintentionally force their children into risky or unstable situations. To break this cycle, families need to support their children’s right to learn and discuss the value of planning a career early in life.

Thinking about the future from a young age makes a real difference. While some teenagers worldwide ignore their education, in the U.S. students generally have more chances to attend quality schools, find good jobs, and enjoy a healthy life. When young people enter high school with a clear idea of the career they want, they gain confidence, set realistic goals, and stay motivated. In the end, having a plan helps them succeed after graduation, inspires others, and leads to a more fulfilling professional life.

My greatest strengths are drawing, painting, coloring, and writing. I enjoy creating cartoons, sketching illustrations, and adding vivid hues to my artwork, and I love developing stories and novels. Last year, I devoted myself to art by joining various clubs and enrolling in classes. Although I aspired to become a professional cartoonist, this year I have decided to focus on writing. Good writing can captivate readers, present facts and opinions clearly, and explore feelings through vivid language.

Art, in turn, surrounds us everywhere. Attention to spelling and vocabulary ensures that both the writing and the artwork communicate effectively.

In the future, I plan to keep nurturing my talents and exploring how art and writing enrich my life. Whether I’m drawing comics or composing stories, these skills remain my greatest passions.

Dear Manager,

I am writing to request a visit to your company so I can discover whether a career there would suit me. By observing your daily operations, I aim to learn how tasks are assigned, how different departments work together, and what skills are essential for success.

Your company’s large staff likely speeds up production. It would be helpful to see how managers coordinate teams during a typical seven-hour workday, schedule breaks, and ensure that every step in the process runs smoothly. I would also like to know how the plant is laid out and where to find the tools and materials needed for each stage of production.

I wonder about the maximum size a company can reach and how much land is needed for expansion. Could you explain the costs of building and maintaining a facility? Do factories need remodeling every few years? Is there a benefit to locating in an urban area rather than a rural one? How do you estimate expenses for raw materials and utilities so the company remains profitable without overspending?

Additionally, I am interested in how you handle financial challenges. What steps do you take if you run out of funds or supplies? Do you raise money by selling assets or taking loans? How do you manage electricity bills and other overheads? What happens when a product fails to meet quality standards, and are there legal penalties for producing substandard goods?

I am also curious about intellectual property protection. If one company steals an idea from another, what legal fines or penalties apply? Do companies ever face downtime due to slow orders, and how do you keep employees engaged during quieter periods?

Finally, I would like to learn about working schedules and staff welfare. Do you operate on holidays like Christmas or New Year’s? How do you handle employee vacations and sick leave? If someone falls ill on the job, is a replacement sent immediately? And in emergencies such as fires, does insurance cover the losses?

Visiting your company would give students valuable insight into running a successful business. Observing managers balance budgets, deal with unexpected problems, and maintain production would help me and other students prepare for future careers in management or industry.

Thank you for considering my request.

Sincerely,

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” I fully agree with this idea because life is full of setbacks, and only those who keep their spirits high can reach their goals. When we fail, it is important to continue believing in ourselves and to keep moving forward, because we never know when our next attempt will succeed.

Some people understand success as the ability to face each failure with fresh energy. They refuse to let disappointments discourage them. Imagine someone who hopes to become prime minister but hears critics say it can’t be done. Instead of giving in to doubt, this person studies hard, improves their speeches, and builds a plan for their campaign. Their enthusiasm gives them the strength to carry on, even when others say the dream is out of reach.

Others view success as the result of repeated practice and gradual improvement. They accept failure as part of learning and focus on refining their actions every time. For example, a novelist might receive many rejections before finding a publisher. Rather than stopping, they revise their manuscript, take feedback on board, and send it out again. Through persistence and steady work, their writing grows stronger until it finally earns recognition.

There are those who prefer to avoid risk by steering clear of tasks where they might fail repeatedly. This choice may feel safe, but it also prevents growth. By contrast, people who welcome challenges—whether by preserving their enthusiasm or by mastering skills through repetition—develop resilience and move closer to success.

In the end, Churchill’s message is clear: progressing from one failure to another is part of the journey, but maintaining enthusiasm and staying determined turn setbacks into stepping stones. With a positive attitude and persistent effort, we can turn our failures into victories.

Should students complete high school in three years so they can start college and enter the workforce sooner? I believe this shorter path offers real advantages: graduates finish university earlier, find jobs faster, and gain independence at a younger age.

In El Salvador, high school already lasts three years. My older sister finished at seventeen and began nursing studies right away. By twenty-one, she will hold her nursing degree. Watching her progress convinced me that a three-year cycle speeds up higher education and boosts career prospects. Right now I’m in high school too, and I’ll graduate at nineteen. If high school took four years here, I would enter university a year later and delay my professional goals, especially in a field that demands lengthy study.

At my school, we held a vote among students, parents, and teachers about keeping high school to three years. Seventy percent supported the shorter term. Teachers argued it helps students move ahead more quickly, since many struggle with certain grades and risk repeating years. That happened to my brother—he failed ninth grade and must spend five years instead of four to finish. A three-year program would have prevented this extra delay and kept him on a steadier track.

My mother also benefited from three years of high school. She graduated at seventeen, then earned her medical degree by twenty-five. Later, she attended night classes to specialize in cardiology and completed that training by age thirty. Today she holds two positions in local hospitals and enjoys a comfortable life. She often says getting out of high school early gave her the time to pursue both her studies and her career goals.

Overall, a three-year high school helps young people graduate sooner, enter college without delay, and begin work earlier. Although some districts oppose this change, they overlook the possibility of faster progress and earlier independence. I hope more regions will adopt a three-year model so students can start shaping their futures without unnecessary waiting.

Heard the cheerful laughs of youngsters immersed in video games echoing from living rooms. This pastime has grown into a widespread hobby, with titles like Fortnite, League of Legends, and Roblox appealing to players from childhood through their thirties. Do people in their thirties truly find these games as enjoyable as kids?

What draws individuals toward gaming? First, children are hooked by the fast-paced action, looming dangers, and sense of triumph each time they succeed. Although some levels can become aggravating, others—for instance Tetris or Pokemon—offer a gentle pace that helps relieve stress and clear the mind for both youths and adults.

Moreover, the sheer variety of games ensures there’s something for every taste. Kids often pursue gaming sessions as eagerly as wolves hunting their prey, unaware they’re also giving their minds a workout. While playing, they rely on hearing to detect in-game sounds, touch to operate controllers or keyboards, and sight to track moving images. This mental engagement turns gaming into more than just entertainment; it becomes a sensory exercise that strengthens multiple skills.

Nevertheless, spending too much time in front of screens isn’t without negative effects. Extended gaming can lead to eye strain, blurred vision, and headaches. It may also shorten attention spans and foster social withdrawal, making some players less inclined to interact with people face-to-face. Despite the immediate joy, these risks are often ignored during long play sessions.

In conclusion, children dive into games without worrying about what lies ahead, while adults—though aware of potential pitfalls—continue to play simply for enjoyment. Ultimately, video games remain a popular way for both kids and adults to unwind. Why do you reach for your controller or keyboard when it’s time to relax?

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea that you must go beyond what you already know to truly grow. Challenging yourself with higher goals sparks development. Failing along the way is natural and instructive, and trying different pursuits helps you build a diverse set of skills.

First, repeating tasks you’ve already mastered leads to stagnation. For example, scoring easily in every recreational soccer game might feel rewarding, but it won’t improve your skills. To progress, you’d need to join a more competitive team. Moving from a casual league to a travel squad exposes you to stronger opponents who push you to refine your techniques and tactics.

Second, many avoid setting bigger goals because they fear failure and embarrassment. When I aim to score three goals in a match, I don’t always succeed. Rather than feeling defeated, I view each missed opportunity as a lesson. Recognizing that everyone makes mistakes motivates me to identify weaknesses and prevents me from repeating the same errors in future games.

Third, concentrating on a single achievement can limit your potential. By exploring various goals, you discover new talents and interests. If one passion fades, you still have others to pursue, making you more adaptable and well-rounded.

In conclusion, aiming higher than your current expertise is crucial for personal growth. Although facing new challenges may lead to setbacks, these experiences teach valuable lessons. Additionally, mastering different activities broadens your skillset. For these reasons, I support Emerson’s message about pushing yourself beyond familiar ground.

“Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm,” Winston Churchill famously remarked, and many people trying to reach their dreams would agree. Although falling short may at first seem discouraging, it can actually fuel our drive, guide us toward better methods, and build vital experience. In that sense, failure need not be a setback but rather a stepping stone to success.

First of all, failing can light the fire of motivation that some people lack. When students don’t pass a test, for instance, they often realise they must buckle down and keep working instead of giving up. Suppose someone aims for a challenging goal and encounters an obstacle—this is perfectly normal, since ambitious aims usually involve risk. At the moment of defeat, motivation should kick in: the desire to succeed grows stronger, pushing the person to try again. Imagine a student who studied all night, then receives a disappointing test score. That result hurts, but she’s offered a retake and seizes the chance. Her initial failure teaches her perseverance; it reminds her that one setback does not define her abilities.

Failure also highlights areas for improvement. As the saying goes, “You learn from your mistakes.” When something goes wrong because of a certain approach, we learn not to repeat that process. Each error reveals what needs fixing, helping us adjust our strategy. By analysing what caused the problem, we fine-tune our efforts and move closer to our target. In this way, improvement follows failure naturally.

Finally, failure provides valuable experience that shapes future success. If we never stumbled, we wouldn’t have the stories and lessons that enrich our achievements. Overcoming obstacles gives us insights to share with others who might feel discouraged. By describing the challenges we’ve faced and how we pressed on, we can encourage friends or colleagues who fear they can’t recover from their own defeats.

In summary, failure can be a powerful tool when we use it right. Rather than quitting, we should treat each misstep as motivation, as feedback for improvement, and as experience to draw upon. In doing so, we turn failure into a great ally on our path to success.

Many educators and families wonder if a year-round school calendar is a smart choice. I believe it is. Long summer breaks often mean that students return having forgotten much of what they learned. By spreading shorter breaks throughout the year and keeping classes in session more days, we could reinforce knowledge and prevent that “summer slide.”

With more school days and fewer lengthy vacations, teachers wouldn’t have to spend as much time reviewing last year’s material. Instead, we could move into new topics more quickly in subjects like math, history, and English. Regular practice helps information stick, so the extra days in class would give everyone a better chance to master lessons as they go along.

Continuous instruction also means more opportunities to ask questions and get support before tests or standardized exams. When I have a long break, I tend to forget how to solve certain math problems or recall important facts from other courses. If lessons are more evenly distributed, I’d be less likely to lose track of what I’ve learned, and I’d feel more confident when it’s time to demonstrate my skills.

Another advantage is that schools could experiment with different teaching approaches to keep students engaged. Shorter, more frequent breaks might help us stay focused and give teachers a chance to introduce fresh activities without losing momentum. This variety could make learning more enjoyable and help us build stronger connections to the subjects we study.

Although a shorter summer vacation might seem like a drawback, we would still have holiday breaks throughout the year. Overall, a year-round schedule could make it easier to remember important information, improve performance in the classroom, and reduce the stress of cramming after long breaks. I think it’s worth trying because it could benefit many students, including myself, by making school more consistent and effective.

Deciding on a future profession early can be very helpful because children often absorb information more quickly than adults. From a young age, many parents ask their kids what they dream of becoming—doctor, teacher, engineer, or even police officer. Teachers also encourage this by having students draw pictures of their future jobs. These activities help youngsters start thinking about their passions and goals in a concrete way.

Choosing a career path ahead of time gives students the chance to prepare thoroughly. Every profession demands a solid understanding of different subjects, and sometimes students must retake courses they did not pass the first time. For example, becoming a doctor requires many years of study and significant financial resources. Some aspiring medical students must save money to cover tuition, while others may rely on government scholarships. In any case, building the necessary knowledge and skills takes time and dedication.

Another advantage of starting early is the freedom to explore. Young learners can study several fields before selecting the one they like best. If they discover that their first choice does not suit them, they still have the opportunity to switch to a different area. Moreover, by investigating various careers, students can identify which professions offer better salaries or fit their interests, ensuring they make a well-informed decision.

On the other hand, some people argue that children are too immature to choose a lifelong career. They believe that youngsters might simply follow the path of a family member or an admired figure without truly understanding the job’s demands. Critics say that only older students have the maturity and experience to make such a crucial choice responsibly.

In conclusion, while it is important to be aware of the challenges, selecting a career early can give students extra time to learn, practice, and correct mistakes. Those who begin preparing in advance are more likely to build a strong foundation for their future, leading to a satisfying and successful professional life.

I believe that having a positive mindset plays a vital role in achieving success. When you stay hopeful, you refuse to give up even if you face major setbacks. An optimistic outlook, combined with hard work, will eventually lead you toward your goals. When challenges arise, a positive attitude makes them seem less daunting and gives you the strength to find solutions.

Besides helping you tackle obstacles, a positive mindset also supports your physical and mental health. Good health makes it easier to stay focused and energetic, which in turn increases your chances of success. On the other hand, a negative attitude can drain your energy, limit your progress, and make it harder to reach your objectives.

Moreover, optimism doesn’t only benefit you; it can inspire the people around you as well. When friends or family see your confidence and determination, they often feel encouraged to adopt a similar approach in their own lives. In this way, your positive outlook creates a supportive environment where everyone strives to improve.

We can look at famous figures to see this principle in action. Steve Jobs, for example, was once forced out of Apple, the company he co-founded. Instead of giving up, he stayed optimistic, worked on new projects, and even battled serious health issues with courage. A few years later, he returned to Apple and helped it become one of the most valuable companies in the world. Similarly, Cristiano Ronaldo faced discrimination and tough times early in his career. Yet he kept smiling, trained hard, and remained confident in his abilities. Today, he is widely regarded as one of the greatest soccer players ever.

Unfortunately, in modern society many people lose heart after a small defeat and assume they cannot succeed again. We need to remember that hardships are part of life, and a simple smile or encouraging thought can make those hardships feel lighter. By focusing on solutions instead of problems, we give ourselves the best chance to improve.

In conclusion, everyone—from a young child to an elderly person—experiences difficulties. However, maintaining a calm and positive attitude allows us to face any challenge. Whenever you feel discouraged, take a deep breath, remind yourself of your strengths, and keep moving forward with hope.

Our big break. Summer is a season with very hot weather. Schools take this whole season to give students a big break; summer is almost two months of break. Although some educators feel that the summer break is too long and schools should be year-round—which would mean one month of summer and a longer winter break—I think schools should not be year-round because summer has very harsh weather and students use this time to plan trips with family and friends.

Summer’s high temperatures make it hard even to think about going to school. Some days the temperature reaches 96°C or more, which is too hot for students. This heat causes excessive sweating and severe headaches during class. It also raises stress levels, leading to lower grades or constant irritability. Students who work in hot areas find even simple tasks more difficult than those in milder climates. Hot weather makes it hard to focus on any work.

In summer, students have two months to enjoy trips or other activities. Many families use this time to plan big vacations, and students wait all year for these trips. Because summer is a perfect time to go to the beach with family and friends or to visit another country—and since there is no school—we do not miss any classes. Trips can take a lot of time, so summer is ideal for travel. Students also have enough free time to find summer jobs; without school, they can focus on earning money. Summer is very important for spending time with family or making money.

In conclusion, summer’s weather makes school difficult but makes travel and work possible, so the government should not cut off our summer. This is our time—our big break. It’s when students can relax for a long period without any preoccupation about schoolwork. Summer happens only once each year; students have to enjoy it because they deserve it for all the hard work they put in during the school year.

Summer is traditionally the longest break in the school calendar, lasting nearly two months. While some educators argue that this holiday is excessively long and propose a year-round system with only four weeks off in summer and a longer winter recess, I believe such a plan would be misguided. The scorching temperatures at that time of year make school attendance very challenging, and the extended recess offers students essential time to relax, travel with family, and even work.

The extreme heat experienced during summer can make classroom learning almost unbearable. On certain days, the mercury climbs past 35°C, causing pupils to sweat profusely and suffer headaches and fatigue. Such conditions not only distract learners but can also lead to heat-related illnesses if air conditioning is inadequate. In cities where pavement and rooftops trap heat, it is difficult for anyone, let alone teenagers carrying heavy backpacks, to concentrate on lessons. Even those who hold part-time roles in outdoor settings find themselves struggling with low energy and poor focus. Reducing the summer break would force students to endure these harsh conditions and likely harm their academic performance.

Beyond the weather, the long summer vacation serves as a valuable opportunity for personal growth and family bonding. Many students look forward to organizing trips to the seaside, exploring national parks, or visiting relatives in other regions. Such experiences not only create lasting memories but also expose young people to new cultures and environments. Since there are no classes looming, they can travel without worrying about missing important coursework. Additionally, the break allows some students to take up seasonal jobs—working in shops, restaurants, or local attractions—to earn money and develop work skills. Others use the time to pursue hobbies, volunteer in the community, or study a foreign language. The freedom to plan these activities without academic pressure makes summer an ideal period for self-development.

In summary, while shortening summer vacation might seem to address concerns about knowledge retention, it overlooks the practical and emotional benefits of a longer holiday. The intense heat during summer months makes regular attendance difficult, and nearly eight weeks off are crucial for rest, family time, travel, and valuable work experience. This annual break only comes around once each year and is a well-earned reward for students’ dedication and effort throughout the school term. For these reasons, the government should maintain the current summer schedule and allow pupils to enjoy their most significant break of the year.

Imagination is a uniquely human quality with a vital role. It serves as a core foundation for our understanding and acts as the spark that drives every creation. Without the power of imagining possibilities, people could not gather or develop knowledge.

Every part of our lives depends on imagination. Whether we are at work, at home, or in a classroom, we constantly use it to plan actions and determine which skills and information we need for success. When solving a problem at work or arranging a family event, we picture the sequence of steps ahead, drawing on our ability to dream up solutions. Thanks to imagination, humans have been able to grow, adapt, and face new challenges throughout history.

Imagination also represents the first stage in any creative process. Before engineers design a tool or artists paint a scene, they envision its appearance and purpose in their minds. This mental draft helps us understand what is needed and how an object or project can fulfill a specific goal. All concepts start in the imagination before we develop them using our practical knowledge and skills.

If we lacked imagination, we could not build knowledge. It provides the initial ideas that lead to learning and discovery. Even someone with strong mathematical or scientific abilities needs imagination to pose questions and devise experiments. Without imagining possibilities, skills alone would be unable to give rise to innovation and understanding.

In summary, imagination is a fundamental human ability that underpins daily activities, creativity, and learning. It allows us to think ahead, generate ideas, and apply our expertise to bring those ideas to life. Without it, personal growth and human progress would not be possible.

You don’t even need to be upbeat all the time to leave an impression. In Disney’s The Princess and the Frog, Tiana dreams of opening a restaurant because it was her father’s wish. First, your actions speak louder than your mood. Consistently carrying out helpful deeds influences people more than a single gesture. For instance, donating food once to a local pantry may go unnoticed, but doing so regularly will attract attention. If the media covers your ongoing contributions, others are likely to follow your lead and support their community.

Second, setting clear goals can motivate others by example. People with targets often achieve more than those who lack direction. Imagine you want to buy a video game that costs eighty dollars but have no cash left. You clean your room, wash your parents’ car, and mow lawns. When you still haven’t saved enough, you ask neighbors if they need chores done. Your persistence pays off and you earn just the right sum. By defining objectives and working steadily toward them, you inspire people to plan and persevere.

Third, motivation itself is contagious. When you seem enthusiastic and energetic, you encourage others to adopt the same attitude. High energy shows you value your goal and are ready to put in effort. If people see your commitment, they become more willing to try new things and stay focused.

Some may argue that personal behavior shapes influence by creating a positive atmosphere. However, conduct alone doesn’t reveal a person’s true drive or ambitions. Therefore, demonstrating your actions, goals, and motivation is the most effective way to inspire others.

In my English class today, my classmates argued that first impressions are almost impossible to change. I disagreed and asked around for other opinions. After listening to everyone, I realized that they were overlooking important factors: a person might be going through a difficult time, they may treat people differently based on false assumptions, or they could have a condition that affects their behavior. I’d like to explain why first impressions can be misleading.

First, someone might simply be struggling in their life when you meet them. They could have just moved to a new town, left behind close friends or relatives, or suffered a loss in the family. I have experienced this myself many times. My parents’ jobs force us to relocate frequently—sometimes even every year—and each move left me upset and unwilling to focus on school. I only wanted to have fun and feel settled. Although I haven’t moved recently, my parents are considering a new home an hour away, and I already feel anxious about leaving my school, where teachers support me both inside and outside the classroom, and where I’ve made so many friends. That unsettled feeling can easily shape someone’s first impression of a new acquaintance.

Second, people don’t always treat everyone the same way, often for unfair or mistaken reasons. Once I went to a party hoping to catch up with some friends, but when I arrived they ignored me. I couldn’t understand why until a girl explained that they thought I had done something wrong. It turned out they were confusing me with my twin sister, who is basically my opposite in personality, and nobody knew we were twins. Once I cleared up the misunderstanding, everything was fine, and we enjoyed the rest of the evening together. This shows how a simple mix-up can lead to a false first impression.

Finally, some individuals have special challenges that affect their behavior. A classmate told me about a boy who tried hard to be kind but sometimes lost his temper and said hurtful things. He couldn’t always control his emotions because of his condition, but when teachers explained his situation to others, his classmates became more understanding and patient.

Considering these points, I’m convinced that first impressions aren’t set in stone. Everyone has moments they aren’t proud of or circumstances beyond their control. We all make mistakes, and getting to know someone better can completely change your initial opinion.

People often assume that influencing someone requires becoming a role model, yet I believe that influence can occur in various ways, such as through media, conversations, friends, or even family. Therefore, I disagree with Albert Schweitzer’s statement that example is the only thing needed to influence others.

One reason I reject this view is peer pressure. For instance, imagine attending a gathering where underage guests are drinking alcohol. You don’t need to know them personally to feel the urge to join in simply because watching their actions encourages you to do the same. In situations like this, observing behaviors can motivate people to follow along without a clear role model.

Another source of influence is television advertising. Commercials can persuade viewers to buy products they rarely use, often leading them to shop for items they try once and then forget. This example shows how media messages shape our decisions far beyond personal examples.

On the other hand, some maintain that setting a good example is the sole method of influencing someone. In my life, my mother has always been a positive role model. Even if she makes mistakes, I don’t automatically repeat them. Being an example can be valuable when it shows positive actions, but it doesn’t guarantee that others will copy everything you do.

In conclusion, influence extends beyond merely setting an example. It can come from peers or the media, and we can also choose different ways to influence others.

British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once observed, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” I share his view completely. While the people around us can affect our behavior, ultimately each of us has the power to decide what kind of person we become.

First of all, character defines who we are, and it is shaped by our own decisions. Every day we pick our words, actions, and attitudes, whether we realize it or not. Some might follow the crowd and say or do things they later regret, but even then it remains their choice. In this way, character is a personal creation rather than an unchangeable fate handed down by others.

Secondly, people can use their time and resources in many different ways, and these choices reflect their character traits. For example, someone might volunteer at a charity, visit relatives in need, or offer help to neighbors. On the other hand, a person could decide to break rules, lie, or take what does not belong to them. Both kinds of behavior come from individual decisions. No matter what influences are around us, we alone decide whether to do good deeds or harmful ones.

Finally, it is possible to change your character at any time if you genuinely want to. Someone who has been selfish or quick-tempered can work on being more patient and kind. Likewise, a person who has always tried to help others can learn new skills or become more generous. In each case, the transformation depends on a conscious choice to adopt new habits and attitudes.

In conclusion, I agree with John Lubbock’s idea that we shape our own character. Although friends, family, and role models can guide or inspire us, the final decision always lies with ourselves. By choosing our actions carefully, we create the person we wish to be.

I believe Thomas Jefferson wrote his message to encourage people to take responsibility for their own lives and pursue their dreams. When he composed these words, many Americans were still intimidated by their recent experience of slavery and war. Later, when Abraham Lincoln became president of the United States, these ideas proved even more important. Jefferson’s writing shows three main reasons for urging his fellow citizens to act with determination.

First, Jefferson wanted to see whether people would follow his advice and work toward their own goals. Too often we waste time on unimportant matters or let fear stop us from trying. Some are shy or worried that others will criticize them if they fail. Others never attempt anything challenging because it feels too hard. Jefferson believed that if we overcame those fears and spent our energy on our own projects, we could achieve much more in life.

Second, a careful reading of Jefferson’s words reveals that many lack the commitment needed to improve their future. Students, for example, might go to school only because their parents insist, without seeing the opportunities that education offers. Jefferson’s writing teaches us to study hard, focus on our long-term dreams, and earn good grades. By doing so, we prepare ourselves for success rather than drifting through our days without direction.

Third, we now enjoy more freedom and time to pursue our interests than previous generations did. Yet many choose to spend their hours socializing or partying instead of working toward their ambitions. If we continue to ignore our goals, we will never make progress. Jefferson urged us to use our liberty responsibly and dedicate ourselves to what truly matters.

In conclusion, as young people we have both energy and the support of our families to chase our dreams. Thomas Jefferson’s message reminds us to stay focused, work hard, and never give up. By following his advice, we can turn our ambitions into reality.

I disagree with the idea that first impressions are permanent because people can improve how others see them if they get more time and a second opportunity.

First, everyone deserves a fresh start. When someone makes a bad initial impression—whether at a job interview or on a first date—they should be allowed to show their true character later. You might have tripped over your words or seemed nervous the first time you met, but giving you another chance lets you demonstrate your skills or personality more clearly.

Second, in a professional setting, a single awkward moment shouldn’t define your entire reputation. Imagine you stumble through an important presentation and your colleagues think you’re unprepared. If they invite you to speak again after some feedback, you can correct your mistakes. By the end of the second meeting, they may admire your confidence and expertise instead of remembering only your first slip-up.

Finally, personal relationships also benefit from second chances. Suppose you visit your partner’s parents and accidentally offend them. It would be unfair if they judged you forever based on that one error. Returning later with more care and respect gives you the opportunity to leave a positive impression and build trust.

In conclusion, allowing people to change others’ first impressions leads to fairer judgments and stronger connections. Everyone deserves a chance to prove who they really are.

I am grateful for the opportunity to share my views based on personal experience. Life is short, and we never know what tomorrow brings. While many believe that first impressions are nearly impossible to alter, I disagree. I think initial judgments can change, though not in an instant, and here is why.

First, the importance we assign to someone’s opinion varies. When you meet someone you like, you want to make a positive impression. But as you spend more time together, your feelings and opinions naturally shift. For example, I once admired a boy at first sight, yet after getting to know him better, my initial enthusiasm cooled.

Second, people’s expressions can be misleading. I recall meeting a woman whose stern face made me assume she was angry. However, after a longer conversation, I saw she was simply shy, not upset. This taught me that our opening judgment can be wrong and is often corrected through more interaction.

In the end, time is the most powerful factor. It lets us revise early opinions and understand someone more fully. Although we remember first impressions, they need not define us forever. Given time and effort, we can always reshape our initial judgments.

If I were to explain to my teacher whether I like working alone or in groups, I would definitely choose to work independently. Working by myself gives me the freedom to come up with ideas that might not occur to others. For instance, when you concentrate on your own, you can often achieve higher grades than in group projects. Additionally, group work can sometimes lead to unfinished tasks if people are chatting or lose focus. By working alone, students can manage their time better and meet deadlines, which reduces the risk of failing. This punctuality also helps them avoid penalties for late submission.

Furthermore, some learners are naturally quiet or shy and feel more comfortable working on their own rather than speaking up in a group. They can avoid falling behind because they do everything at their own pace. In contrast, group members often fail to share the workload equally. In many cases, two or three students end up doing most of the project while the others contribute little or nothing. Some students might spend the session talking about unrelated topics, using their phones, or playing games instead of helping with the assignment.

Such situations show that collaborating does not always guarantee success. Parents also worry when their children work in groups. If a teacher calls to say their child is failing, parents might blame the classmates, thinking bad company is to blame. This can create tension between families instead of solving the problem. On the other hand, when students work alone, any mistake or delay falls on them, and they learn to take responsibility for their own success.

In my view, it is better to handle tasks independently. Sometimes we have to rely on our own effort rather than counting on others. Earning our achievements through personal hard work is both more efficient and more rewarding.

I believe arranging a field trip to a McDonald’s restaurant could help students understand the real outcome of ignoring their studies. McDonald’s staff often work long hours at a quick pace while earning relatively low wages. Seeing this environment firsthand might inspire students to value their education more and avoid ending up in similar jobs.

By watching employees juggle orders, clean tables, and serve customers under pressure, students would realise how demanding such work can be. Knowing that many workers receive only minimum pay could discourage them from skipping classes or goofing off. Instead, they might feel motivated to focus on school so they can aim for better-paid careers.

It’s also important to remember that not every family can afford private schooling or extra lessons. Some young people must start working immediately when their parents lack the money to support further education. Meanwhile, students with the privilege to attend school should seize the opportunity to learn. Otherwise, they may waste their parents’ investment and have no choice but to settle for low-paying jobs.

If students take their classes seriously and study hard, they stand a much better chance of finding well-paid employment in the future. But those who ignore their lessons risk getting stuck in roles like those they would see at McDonald’s. To organise this experience, I plan to write a letter to the local McDonald’s manager. By inviting our class for a visit, I hope others will realise how important it is to pay attention in school and work toward a successful career.

Many schools now join forces with local companies, offering students a chance to discover different career paths. This cooperation helps young people gain practical insights into various professions. Since students face many challenges to succeed in life, schools must provide opportunities that support their growth.

By collaborating with businesses, schools can better guide students toward their ambitions. Such alliances allow pupils to refine their abilities while applying classroom knowledge in real-world settings. Additionally, students receive valuable time and resources to develop their critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

One benefit of a partnership is that risks are shared among all members. If the project does not succeed, no single person bears all the responsibility. Facing failure alone can be overwhelming and may even lead to financial hardship. Personally, I prefer sharing risks with partners to protect my future and avoid serious losses. Moreover, I enjoy working with others rather than tackling tasks in isolation.

I also value how partners divide rewards and ideas. Collaborators can combine their creativity to boost profits, pool funds to expand the venture, and share both successes and challenges. This teamwork prevents loneliness and makes work more engaging. By interacting closely, partners build trust and a friendly atmosphere, which I believe are crucial for any joint effort.

Of course, some critics argue that partnerships can break down when people clash. While disagreements may arise, selecting compatible partners and allowing time for relationships to develop helps overcome these issues. The chance to learn from different perspectives is one of the most important benefits of working together.

In conclusion, partnerships between schools and local businesses offer practical experience that enhances students’ skills and supports their life goals. Sharing both risks and rewards creates a safer and more enjoyable environment for learning. Therefore, schools should adopt these collaborations to ensure that students are well-prepared for a successful future.

People often argue whether technology brings more benefits or harms to our lives. Some claim it cuts us off from face-to-face contact, while others believe it creates opportunities we could never have before. In my opinion, technology has a mostly positive impact because it helps us in many areas of daily life.

Today, most of us lead very busy lives with work, school and family commitments. Students, in particular, have a lot of homework to finish after classes, and some even have part-time jobs. Without technology, researching topics for essays or projects would require long trips to libraries and buying materials like pictures and articles. This process would take much more time and money. Thanks to the internet, we can find information quickly online, saving both effort and expense.

It is true that some people feel technology damages our personal relationships. For example, family members may sit at the dinner table but spend the whole time looking at their phones instead of talking. However, the same devices let us keep in touch with friends or relatives who live far away. Video calls and messaging apps allow us to see and hear loved ones in real time, even if they are in another city or country. We can also use tools like Google Maps to find unfamiliar addresses, which makes travelling to new places much easier and less stressful.

I experience these benefits every day. Many of my relatives live overseas and I miss them when I cannot visit. By using video chat apps, we celebrate birthdays together online. On my birthday, my family calls me early in the morning through FaceTime, and I do the same for my grandmother on her special day. These moments always make us happy. In addition, my mother relies on Google Maps to pick up my father from his workplace. Without this app, she might get lost or arrive late.

Technology also plays a vital role in medicine and scientific research. Doctors use advanced machines to diagnose illnesses more accurately and to treat patients with precision. Thanks to these innovations, many diseases that were once incurable can now be managed or even eliminated. New discoveries continue to improve our understanding of the human body and how to keep it healthy.

In conclusion, technology offers a wide range of advantages that improve our productivity, help us stay connected and support our health. While people must use it responsibly to avoid negative effects, the positive outcomes outweigh the drawbacks. How we choose to use technology determines its impact on our lives, and with a thoughtful approach, we can enjoy its benefits every day.

Should students seize the chance to complete high school in three years instead of the usual four? I believe this accelerated program offers a valuable opportunity for motivated learners. The program’s summer courses provide a structured way to earn extra credits, ensuring students meet all graduation requirements on an accelerated track. Critics also worry that cramming material into a shorter period might reduce the depth of learning and the overall high school experience. It’s true that maintaining a healthy balance would be challenging, and not everyone has the discipline or resources to stay on top of accelerated studies.

If I chose this path, I would organize my schedule carefully, complete all summer classes needed for my target colleges, and then apply for scholarships and admission. Soon after, I’d begin working to gain experience and offset costs. 

In conclusion, although opinions differ, students who feel ready for the challenge should consider the three-year graduation plan. It can open doors to college sooner, allow early career exploration, and set the stage for achieving personal goals.

I do not agree with Emerson’s view that we should focus solely on our own individuality. While it is natural to think about ourselves at times, we cannot ignore the people who matter in our lives. We owe attention and care to our family—parents, siblings, grandparents—as well as to friends and colleagues who have supported us. 

Consider being part of a team. Your teammates will ask questions, discuss plans for the coming weeks, and work together on projects. If you refuse to help or remain silent, they may see you as selfish and unreliable. In contrast, by offering assistance and sharing ideas, you push yourself to grow and help the group succeed. Teamwork thrives on cooperation, not on isolating yourself.

The same principle applies in a workplace. Employers and coworkers notice how you interact, solve problems, and handle responsibilities. They ask themselves why they should hire you or entrust you with important tasks. Demonstrating respect for others and willingness to collaborate often leads to better opportunities than focusing only on personal gain. In short, a healthy sense of self must include awareness of—and care for—the people around us.

What would happen if our school cafeteria replaced its usual offerings? Most students would probably be disappointed because they love the tasty items on the current menu, even though these foods are not always good for them.

In the United States, fast food is both widely available and heavily consumed, and this contributes to high rates of cholesterol-related illnesses and other health problems. Today’s technology makes us even more inactive. We drive everywhere instead of walking, send text messages rather than walking across the room to talk, and check the weather on our phones instead of opening a window. If we feel like watching a movie, we no longer need to go to a theater—we can stay on the couch and stream dozens of apps.

All these conveniences are great, but they also encourage sedentary habits that can lead to weight gain and serious conditions such as heart disease and high cholesterol. If we continue along this path without making changes, the situation is only going to get worse.

One way to help students develop healthier habits is to show them a wider range of foods beyond the usual fast-food choices. Many healthy items taste excellent—sometimes even better than greasy options. For example, avocado toast, fresh fruit smoothies, Caesar salad, and baked fish are all delicious and nutritious. By offering these foods at school, we can strike a balance between what our bodies need and what we enjoy eating.

Introducing a healthier menu now will mean that, as students grow up, they won’t automatically reach for burgers, fried chicken, or pizza. Instead, they will know that there are many tasty dishes that support their well-being. If we fail to encourage these habits at school, it will be much harder to adopt them later.

As a member of this school community, I believe that adding more nutritious choices to the cafeteria menu is one of the best steps we can take to prevent future health problems. Let’s give ourselves the benefits of both good taste and good health.
