As a student, I can say that I agree with this “benefit,” but in this case I don’t agree with making school two hours longer than usual. For some students, spending eight hours in school is considered enough, because people get exhausted by spending most of the day sitting in a classroom. For example, in every classroom there is someone who is always sleeping during class due to the a lot of work school leaves us to do, people who have work after school, and even sports. These reasons explain why people get too tired to stay awake during class. Imagine having to spend two additional hours in school just to have a three-day weekend, which might seem good but really doesn’t.

Spending two more hours than usual for four days is just a way to keep using energy, even though people think they are saving it but really are not doing any better. For example, the two extra hours we use from Monday to Thursday still make up for the eight hours we lose on the fifth day of class. The extra two hours from Monday through Thursday add up to eight hours of energy use, which means we aren’t really saving energy.

Example number 1: my friend Generic_Name loves the idea of a four-day school week because this means that he will have an extra day to do homework and to spend time with his girlfriend Generic_Name. For him, this new program works perfectly and is an advantage for him.

Example number 2: My boyfriend, Generic_Name, loves to study but does not agree with this new idea because he has two hours of basketball training after school and then works for four hours to help his mom with his car insurance. This means that he won’t get enough sleep at night, because after he gets home from work he still has to do homework so we won’t turn it in late. Like him, there are many more students in the same situation who make sacrifices to help their parents make payments.

However, teachers’ opinions matter too, and they will be tired of teaching ten straight hours, too. Remember that they aren’t robots who are just set up by the government. This means that they might not even agree with this new idea of making school longer for students and teachers.

My school should not follow this model because it should think of everybody’s benefits, including teachers, students, and the staff of every department in the school’s main office, to make a fair decision for everyone in school. We don’t know if this new adaptation will work in our school system, and we don’t have a guarantee that this idea will work well for us as a community. Considering that this program is working for some businesses that have adopted this new schedule, it might not work for us as a high school, because we have different activities that people in business companies don’t have, which makes us a different environment than those businesses.

Many schools are considering a shift to a four-day week with ten-hour days, claiming it saves energy and offers a longer weekend. Although this plan sounds appealing at first, I believe that extending each school day by two hours creates more problems than it solves.

First of all, spending ten hours in class can be exhausting. Students already struggle to stay focused during eight-hour days, and adding extra time only increases fatigue. It is common to see classmates dozing off or losing concentration because they are overwhelmed by homework, part-time jobs, or sports commitments. Imagine having to sit through classes for two additional hours each day just to gain a single day off. A three-day weekend may seem attractive, but the long weekdays would leave many students too tired to make the most of that extra day.

Supporters say that a four-day week saves the same energy lost by shortening the schedule by one day. However, this is misleading. Those extra two hours from Monday to Thursday add up to eight hours—the same amount we would have spent in class on Friday. In reality, the school’s heating, lighting, and cooling systems would still run for the same total time each week, so no real savings occur.

Some students welcome the change. For example, my friend Alex thinks a longer weekend would give him more time to finish assignments and relax with his girlfriend. He feels this arrangement suits his lifestyle perfectly. On the other hand, my boyfriend, Marcus, disagrees. He practices basketball for two hours after school and then works four hours at his mother’s auto shop. With a ten-hour school day, he would have almost no time to sleep or complete his homework, which could harm his grades and well-being. Many students face similar pressures as they juggle family responsibilities and part-time work.

Teachers also deserve consideration. Instructors would need to teach and manage classes for ten straight hours, and they are not machines. Just like students, they would grow tired and less effective as the day goes on. Their ability to plan lessons and grade assignments could suffer, which would ultimately affect the quality of education.

In conclusion, although a four-day school week with longer days might work in certain businesses, our high school environment is very different. We involve sports, clubs, after-school jobs, and extensive homework. Before making such a major change, school leaders should weigh the needs of students, teachers, and support staff. Without clear evidence that this model improves our community, it would be unfair to adopt it. Our school should focus on solutions that genuinely benefit everyone, rather than following a trend that may not suit our unique circumstances.

Dear Principal,

I am writing to express my support for changing our sports and extracurricular eligibility policy so that students must have at least a B average to participate. Allowing those with a C average often leads them to devote too much time to athletics and risk dropping below a passing grade. By raising the requirement to a B, we would remind students that schoolwork comes first and encourage better time management.

Requiring a B average would motivate students who love sports to balance practice with their studies. When they receive progress reports showing lower scores, they will understand the need to improve academically. This standard gives them a clear goal: maintain solid grades in order to enjoy their activities. It also reduces the chance of anyone failing simply because most of their effort went into sports.

To make this change fair, the school could offer extra support, such as tutoring sessions, weekend study groups, or teacher-led review workshops. If a student genuinely attends these sessions, completes all homework on time, and still falls short of a B, we could review individual cases in consultation with their teachers. This approach rewards persistence and ensures that effort is recognized alongside achievement.

Raising the GPA requirement would also benefit the school’s reputation. Teams known for academic strength reflect positively on our entire community. In the long run, students who meet this higher standard will pass their year successfully and gain confidence in both their studies and their sports. Those who choose not to work for a B will learn the importance of commitment before joining extracurricular programs.

I hope you will consider implementing this policy change next term. By setting a B average as the minimum for participation, we can foster an environment where students strive for excellence in all areas. Thank you for your attention to this proposal.

Sincerely,

Many people believe that team projects offer more advantages, but I firmly think that working solo is better. There are several reasons: being able to set your own pace, avoiding conflicts, and gaining independence.

First, when you handle tasks alone, you decide how fast or slow you go. This freedom helps you learn from mistakes without pressure. If you prefer to break the workload into small daily tasks rather than doing everything in one session, working by yourself suits you well. There is no risk of friends dropping by and playing games instead of focusing on the assignment. You know exactly when the deadline is, and you alone manage each step of the work.

Moreover, solo work develops skills that prepare you for real-life challenges. You must trust your own judgment, so if you choose an idea or a method, you cannot blame others later. This self-reliance builds confidence and problem-solving ability. There is no one to hurry you; you set a schedule that works best for you. By being responsible for the whole project, you learn time management and accountability.

Some argue that group work offers diverse perspectives. However, groups often bring distractions and disagreements. Research shows that people frequently complain about group tasks and prefer to work on their own. Team members may not share your level of commitment or ability, so you end up correcting or completing their part of the assignment. This not only adds extra work but can also lower the overall grade if someone underperforms.

In conclusion, while group projects have supporters, working alone remains more beneficial. You avoid conflicts over ideas, maintain your own rhythm, and become more independent. The simplicity and control you gain make individual work a smarter choice.

People often say that being independent leads to a better life. Today, many value self-reliance and trust their own instincts or creative ideas. Although this approach suits some, I maintain that consulting experts and authorities on major matters can ease challenges and benefit those struggling. To illustrate my view, I will present two stories that show how expert advice can transform situations.

The first story happened to me when I was a teenager in 2010. I joined a basketball camp one summer in Generic City, excited because my private school did not offer sports. During a practice session, a collision with a teammate left me with a badly sprained ankle, forcing me to stay in the hospital. I feared I might never play basketball again. Feeling discouraged, I confided in my father, who reminded me that life has both easy and difficult moments, and it rarely goes as planned. He urged me to grow stronger and take control of my path rather than follow someone else’s. His words changed my perspective: instead of giving up, I committed to working harder during my rehabilitation. As a result, I recovered and returned to the court, proving to myself that guidance from someone more experienced can make all the difference.

The second story comes from my mother. She once told me about a young man living in a modest house who wanted to forge his own hammer to build a new dwelling. He traveled far and wide to find the perfect piece of iron, but every piece seemed flawed. One day, he met an old blacksmith working on a hammer. The young man asked how he chose his metal, and the blacksmith smiled, saying, “Nothing is perfect until you shape it. If you treat every piece with care, you will find it useful.” Hearing this, the young man returned home, treated the iron with respect, and successfully crafted a reliable hammer. This story taught me that expert advice can reveal the potential we might otherwise overlook.

Some people believe they should make every decision alone, but I think we should seek help from those who know more. Experts can offer insights that simplify life and support us when we face difficulties.

You shouldn’t decide what someone is like based only on your first meeting. First impressions can be misleading, and it takes time to understand a person’s true character. Instead of labeling someone as unfriendly or uninteresting right away, it makes more sense to ask questions and listen to their story. For instance, if you notice a classmate yawning and assume they are lazy, you might be missing the fact that they stayed up late studying or had a long day at work.

Believing that people can’t change is also wrong. Everyone has the power to grow and develop new habits. I used to be very shy and rarely spoke up in groups because I felt too nervous. Over time, I decided to push myself out of my comfort zone. I introduced myself to new classmates, joined clubs, and practiced small conversations with strangers. Slowly, I became more confident and enjoyed meeting others.

Now, many of my friends are surprised when they learn I was ever quiet. They often recall our first encounters when I hardly said a word. From their perspective, I seemed distant or uninterested. But today I am outgoing and eager to chat, which shows how much a person can change.

In conclusion, judging someone based on a quick glance or a brief chat is unfair. People deserve the chance to reveal who they really are, and they can transform if they choose. I firmly believe we should avoid making snap judgments and remember that everyone’s true qualities often emerge over time.

Technology plays a central role in our lives today and is likely to become even more influential in the future. People have always sought ways to improve daily life and make tasks easier. While many applaud these advances, others worry that technology can harm our social habits. They point out that face-to-face conversations are dwindling, that people are reluctant to leave their homes, and that some individuals react angrily when asked to reduce their screen time.

Not long ago, we met friends in the street or at neighborhood cafés. Today, with a simple tap on a smartphone, we can call someone and see them on a tiny screen. Although this seems convenient, it has led to fewer real-world meetings. Instead of enjoying a walk in the city or planning a coffee date, some prefer to chat with strangers online. They claim it is no different from talking to new people in public, but online contacts carry risks. Fake profiles and scams are common, and unlike meeting someone in person, you cannot judge their behaviour or intentions by looking at their body language.

Childhood fun has also changed. In the past, children spent hours playing outside—racing down the street, visiting friends’ homes, or running around the local park. Now, video games are their main form of entertainment. All it takes is connecting a console to the TV, and players can spend entire days indoors. As a result, they stay inside instead of playing sports or joining friends at someone’s house. In school, conversations often revolve around gaming, leaving little time for studying or completing homework. When the first game consoles appeared, they were a rare luxury that many children could not afford, so they saved money for treats like ice cream or trips to amusement parks. Nowadays, kids seem unwilling to leave their devices even for a moment.

Another worrying development is how some youngsters behave when technology is taken away. If parents limit screen time, children may become irritable or even aggressive. Experts suggest that kids get so absorbed in their virtual worlds that they resist any interruption. Since electronic devices are everywhere, it is increasingly difficult for families to enforce rules. Teenagers have been known to smash game controllers or other items when they lose a match, showing how deeply they depend on these gadgets.

Although technology has brought many helpful tools into our lives, its overuse can damage social skills, health, and study habits. If we do not set clear boundaries, our society may suffer long-term effects from this growing dependence on screens.

Music, drama, and art are usually offered as optional courses because they are not essential for everyday life. Since these subjects are not mandatory for graduation, students have many other choices to fill their schedules. It makes little sense to force everyone to study these areas when each person has their own interests and career goals.

In contrast to practical skills such as basic mathematics—which we rely on for balancing budgets, paying bills, and filing taxes—creative classes tend to be more like hobbies than necessities. How often will you really need to perform a dramatic monologue or compose a song in your daily routine? Employers generally do not expect job applicants to include pictures of their paintings or scripts they have written. Unless someone plans to become a professional artist, musician, or actor, such talents are unlikely to contribute directly to their future employment.

Electives exist precisely to help students explore different fields and find their passions. If art, music, and drama were required, schools would lose flexibility and students might feel pressured to focus on areas that do not interest them. Far from ushering in a cultural golden age, this requirement could limit young people’s freedom to choose other valuable subjects like science, history, or technology, which may lead to careers in medicine, engineering, or business.

Admission officers at colleges rarely consider creative classes as part of their core requirements. They look at grades in fundamental subjects—math, languages, sciences—and standardized test scores when deciding who to accept. If a student later decides to change direction, for instance from pursuing medicine to studying engineering, many of their prior courses will still count because the disciplines share similar foundations. In contrast, music and art classes do not overlap much with other fields, so time spent on them could be less useful if a student’s goals shift.

Undoubtedly, some people achieve fame and fortune by writing hit songs, acting in films, or displaying their artwork in galleries. However, success in these areas depends largely on individual talent, hard work, and sometimes luck. Only a small number of students will turn their creative interests into sustainable careers. Because these subjects do not guarantee stable employment for most people, they are better suited as electives rather than compulsory courses.

Requiring all students to take music, drama, and art would narrow their choices instead of broadening them. Since these subjects are not essential in most professions, they should remain optional, allowing each student to pursue the classes that best support their future ambitions.

All students should be involved in at least one extracurricular activity. The principal’s decision to require this makes sense because such involvement offers many benefits both now and later.

First, taking part in a sport or other activity promotes physical health. Studies show active people face fewer heart and breathing problems. Regular exercise—whether it’s basketball, track, cheerleading or another sport—helps control weight and strengthens the body. Staying active also raises energy levels and encourages lifelong healthy habits.

Second, extracurricular activities improve emotional well-being by providing a break from daily worries. When students join teams or clubs, they focus on something fun instead of stress. This change of pace lifts moods and reduces anxiety. Options like helping with the yearbook, assisting a counselor or volunteering around school give students a chance to unwind while building confidence.

Another key advantage is how these activities enhance college applications. Admissions officers look for more than good grades; they seek students who demonstrate leadership and teamwork. Involvement in sports, clubs or school projects shows commitment and responsibility. Such qualities can boost scholarship opportunities and help applicants stand out.

Moreover, working with classmates in different settings strengthens social skills and independence. Group tasks teach communication, cooperation and problem-solving. Students learn to manage projects, share ideas and support each other. These experiences prepare them for the teamwork and self-management required in college and future careers.

In conclusion, requiring at least one extracurricular activity offers students physical, emotional, academic and social advantages. Since trying something new can only help, I fully agree with the principal’s policy and encourage every student to get involved.

Have you ever done something you later regretted because your friends encouraged you to join them? Everyone knows people with good habits and those with less positive behaviors, but too often teenagers follow the wrong crowd without thinking about the results. I am convinced that showing good behavior yourself is the most effective way to influence others, since people tend to copy the examples they see around them.

First of all, when you act with intelligence, kindness, and a positive attitude, you naturally become a role model. Others will admire you and may even express a desire to be like you. Sadly, many young people destroy their future by following bad examples. Some argue that we are old enough to make our own choices, yet we rarely pause to consider the possible consequences. Bad influences spread because people set harmful examples, leading their friends to repeat the same mistakes. If we hope for a better world for future generations, each of us must strive to be a good example for young people who are still forming their values.

In my own life, I have seen friends and relatives fall into serious trouble after surrounding themselves with the wrong crowd. It is heartbreaking to watch someone end up in prison or worse, simply because they never heard a warning about what might happen. Just as babies learn to talk and walk by imitating their parents, teenagers and adults alike pick up habits—good or bad—from those they spend time with. Even if we don’t follow every piece of advice we receive, we cannot avoid absorbing attitudes and behaviors from our peers.

Because people are always observing and judging each other, you will earn trust and respect only if you set a positive example. If you influence others in a harmful way, you will eventually find yourself isolated, as those you care about distance themselves. As the saying goes, “You reap what you sow.” To me, this means that demonstrating good behavior not only leads to personal success but also encourages others to do the same. There are many paths to achievement, but guiding others in the right direction will always be one of the most rewarding.

For these reasons, I firmly believe that being a good example is the best way to guide those around you. When people see your positive actions, they are more likely to trust you and learn beneficial habits. You will also feel proud knowing that your influence helps create a better world rather than contributing to its problems.

Many students find that studying from home or online offers clear benefits. First, without the usual classroom distractions, learners can focus more fully on their lessons. When classmates are not chatting or playing, it becomes easier to concentrate on the material. This increased attention often leads to a deeper understanding of each subject, and students who study at home may feel better prepared for exams or unexpected questions.

In a traditional school setting, social interactions can sometimes interfere with learning. While making friends is important and can offer support, too much time spent talking or goofing around may cause students to lose track of the lesson. At home, however, there are no idle conversations during study time, so learners stay on task and use their study hours more effectively. As a result, these students often perform better on quizzes and final tests than their peers who are easily distracted in the classroom environment.

On the other hand, attending classes in person has its own appeal. Being with classmates allows students to make friends, exchange ideas, and work together on projects. This social interaction can boost motivation and help learners feel part of a community. For many, school is not just about academics but also about building relationships and developing teamwork skills that are valuable in the future.

Ultimately, choosing between home-based learning and traditional schooling depends on each person’s goals and learning style. If someone wants to maximize focus and achieve strong exam results, studying online might be the best option. But if making friends and collaborating face to face matters more, attending school regularly could be the right choice. Both methods have advantages, and each student can decide which approach suits them best.

When you finish tasks early, you gain extra free time to relax or pursue hobbies. This principle applies after graduation, too: working hard now leads to rewards later. I believe adding an extra hour to the school day is unnecessary. First, students already spend about eight hours on campus each weekday. That amount of time feels more than sufficient, and staying an hour longer would make our day far too long. Second, extending classes cuts into the hours we need to finish assignments. Since teachers already assign quite a bit of homework, most of us would still be working well past dinner, leaving little chance to rest. Third, longer school days mean we lose free moments we could use to relax, pursue hobbies, or spend time with family. With extra lessons in the afternoon and a full load of homework in the evening, our personal time would shrink considerably. For these reasons—being at school for many hours already, having limited time for homework, and facing scarce free time—I am strongly against the idea of tacking on another hour to our daily schedule.

Whether they face financial pressures, family duties or lack of local resources, remote learning helps them stay in education and complete their studies.

First, purely online courses are very flexible. Students can access lessons, readings and assignments on the internet at any hour that suits them. This is especially useful for those who must work part-time or full-time to support themselves or their families. In a regular schedule, many young people fall behind because they need to earn money after school and have no time left for homework or projects. Falling grades often lead them to drop out entirely. With online classes, they decide when to study and can balance both jobs and schoolwork more easily.

Live video conferences are another valuable option. These sessions allow pupils and teachers to meet in real time via a webcam. Learners can ask questions on the spot, join discussions and practice speaking with the instructor, much like in a physical classroom. This real-time interaction can clear up confusion immediately and keep students engaged. It also helps build a sense of community, since participants see each other and exchange ideas face to face, even if they’re miles apart.

The flexibility of these programs means students don’t have to give up work or other responsibilities. They can organise lessons around their daily routines and continue earning an income or taking care of family members. Importantly, distance learning isn’t only for teenagers. Adults who left school years ago because they felt too old or had other obligations can now comfortably finish their high school education without worrying about age limits or strict schedules.

We know that many teenagers leave school early, sometimes because they lack suitable alternatives and sometimes simply because they lose interest. Offering both online and live video classes provides a real choice. Young people who paused their studies can rejoin school from home, while adults and other non-traditional learners gain access to education that was previously out of reach.

In conclusion, if more schools offered distance learning as a permanent option, a larger number of students would stay in education and improve their life chances. With these programs in place, there are fewer excuses for not completing school. Ultimately, online courses and video conferences give everyone—the busy, the working, the older learners—a fair opportunity to achieve a better future.

However, these professionals often overlook how students feel about time off. For these reasons, schools should not switch to a year-round schedule. Some must even work on big projects during evenings and weekends. As a result, they may lose touch with their families and find it hard to share what is happening in their lives. Time away from school gives them a chance to talk openly and support each other.

Second, students have duties outside the classroom. During summer, spring, and winter breaks, they often help with household chores or part-time jobs and enjoy hobbies without the stress of assignments and tests. Many teenagers feel that not everything they learn in school is directly useful, so they quickly forget what they have studied. These pauses give them freedom to rest and pursue activities they value.

Although some people believe that summer vacation is too lengthy and hurts learning retention, the benefits of family time and personal responsibilities show why schools should keep their current breaks rather than move to year-round education.

Many schools in the United States now offer distance learning so that students can join classes from home. They believe this plan will reduce bullying at middle and high schools, since some pupils feel unsafe in person. Consequently, some teenagers choose to attend lessons online rather than going to a campus. However, studying from home often brings its own challenges. In practice, many students struggle to learn effectively when they are not in a physical classroom.

One major problem is the number of distractions at home. It is easy to get sidetracked by smartphones, social media, or video games. Without classmates around, learners may lose focus more quickly, and a long day at home can feel tedious. Some students even spend lesson time sleeping or doing household chores. Additionally, those who work part-time can feel exhausted and struggle to concentrate fully.

Paying attention in a remote class is tougher than in school because the teacher’s presence is limited. Many students listen to music or chat with friends online instead of following the lesson, while others find the home setting too relaxed. As a result, their participation drops and it becomes harder to keep up with the material.

Furthermore, understanding explanations through a screen is not as simple as it seems. In a classroom, pupils can ask questions immediately and get instant help. Online, responses may be delayed and technical issues can interrupt the lesson. Consequently, many learners feel frustrated when they cannot grasp new topics as easily as they would in person.

On the other hand, learning from home has some benefits. Students can enjoy a more comfortable environment, which can lower stress. They also gain extra time for homework and can rest when needed. Being near family provides a sense of security. Despite this, the presence of others at home may tempt students to chat, play, or attend to non-school activities, pulling their attention away from lessons.

In conclusion, although online classes at home provide comfort and safety, they also create significant distractions. Most students find it difficult to stay focused, participate, and understand lessons without a proper learning environment. Therefore, distance learning is not the best choice for everyone, and it can often lead to decreased motivation and poorer academic performance.

Young people need at least 7–8 hours of sleep because their bodies are still growing. Well-rested teens have more energy. Crashes also happen when teens drink and drive after a late night out. To protect teens from early death, curfews should be adopted. When I myself do not sleep well, I cannot concentrate in class. This often affects my grades. Staying awake late also disconnects me from the real world, since I sleep while everyone else is awake.

This curfew also affects teens’ eating habits. Staying out often means eating unhealthy junk food, which is bad for young people’s health. Besides getting enough sleep, teens need healthy food to stay fresh and active. They have their whole lives ahead of them, and unhealthy habits can lead to early diseases. When teens go out with friends, they may also drink alcohol or beer, which is not good at a young age. Unhealthy food weakens their immune system and can cause disease. It also leads to weight gain that affects them socially, mentally, and physically. If teens stay at home, they eat meals provided by their parents, which are healthier and less oily. A city council is debating whether to introduce a curfew for teenagers: 10 p.m. on weekdays and midnight at weekends. While some people welcome this idea, others—especially young people—are strongly opposed. In my view, setting a limit on how late teens can stay out brings several benefits. It can help them develop healthier sleep patterns, reduce their reliance on junk food and alcohol, and encourage them to spend more time with their families.

First, a curfew can greatly improve the amount and quality of sleep that teenagers get. When they return home at a reasonable hour, they are more likely to go to bed early and achieve the seven to eight hours of rest their growing bodies need. Well-rested teens feel more energetic and focused during the day. In contrast, staying out late often leads to tiredness, lack of motivation, and difficulty concentrating. Insufficient sleep also increases the risk of accidents, particularly when driving. Drowsy driving can make a young person dizzy or inattentive at the wheel, and many crashes involving teenagers happen because they are too tired or have been drinking after a late night out. I notice this myself: on the nights I stay up too late, I struggle to pay attention in class, my grades drop, and I miss what’s happening around me because I’m too exhausted.

Second, being at home by curfew usually means eating healthier meals instead of grabbing fast food or snacks on the street. Teenagers who roam late at night often choose greasy or sugary foods, and they might even try alcohol or beer with friends. Over time, these habits can damage their health, weaken their immune system, and lead to obesity. Carrying extra weight can harm them socially, mentally, and physically. At home, meals are typically cooked by parents and include more nutritious ingredients. I can speak from experience: whenever I eat too much junk food, I feel ill, and people around me seem uncomfortable. A relative of mine gained a lot of weight from a diet of takeaway meals and now struggles to walk quickly, often needs help standing up, and faces teasing because of his size. To avoid these problems, teenagers should eat balanced, home-cooked food.

Third, a curfew encourages teens to spend their evenings with family members. This regular time together can bridge the generation gap and strengthen relationships. Sharing a family dinner offers a chance to discuss new experiences, plans, or worries. For example, when my sister and I moved to a new town, our evening meals became the perfect moment to talk about the friends we had made, keep each other informed about local health concerns, and solve any problems we faced. These conversations help everyone feel supported and connected.

In summary, a curfew for teenagers promotes better sleep, healthier eating, and more family bonding. By adopting this rule, we can help young people grow into fit, alert, and responsible citizens. Rather than seeing a curfew as a restriction, teens should view it as a tool for a more balanced and fulfilling lifestyle. Limiting late-night outings can actually enrich their lives and protect their well-being.

Students living in remote areas or those who struggle with traditional lessons may find it hard to keep up and do not always succeed in their classes. When teachers saw declining grades, they reported this problem to the principal. In response, the school organized a meeting and proposed a homeschooling program, allowing pupils to complete assignments, quizzes, and even tests at home. Many students believe this arrangement is easier than attending classes on campus. They value the freedom to eat lunch whenever they want, watch television during breaks, and still meet deadlines for their work.

On the other hand, some students oppose homeschooling because they often feel bored and lonely. Without the daily social interaction of classmates and the immediate support of a teacher, they worry they will miss important information or struggle with difficult topics. Often, families choose homeschooling only because no local schools are available, and parents want their children to receive a quality education for a successful future.

Given these points, I would advise most students to attend regular school. Being part of a school community offers valuable friendships that can help with homework, continuous guidance from teachers, and better preparation for college entrance. Although homeschooling can improve grades in the short term, it may not equip students with the social and academic skills needed later in life. Therefore, students seeking the best overall chance of success should take regular schooling seriously.

Every town sets a curfew to guide its residents, yet some individuals still ignore this rule. Many people wonder if curfews really protect teenagers or if they unjustly limit young lives. In fact, having a curfew can help adolescents learn to manage their time wisely and steer clear of risky situations.

A curfew is a regulation designed to promote order and well-being within a community. When everyone respects this rule, the town enjoys greater harmony and citizens feel more secure.

By enforcing a curfew, teens develop a sense of responsibility. They become accustomed to returning home at a certain hour and gradually learn to take care of themselves without adult reminders.

Critics argue that curfews unnecessarily restrict youth freedom. However, setting a reasonable evening deadline gives teenagers extra hours during the day to study, work, or pursue hobbies. A 10 P.M. limit, for example, ensures they get enough rest and stay safe from potential dangers.

Overall, curfews benefit both families and young people. Parents worry less about their children wandering at night, and teenagers have time each evening to prepare for school or part-time jobs. This simple rule helps them grow up more quickly and responsibly.

Dear Principal,

I believe students ought to be allowed to bring their cell phones to school. These devices are essential for handling emergencies, staying in touch during free time, and getting help when unexpected problems occur.

In an urgent situation, having a phone can be a lifesaver. For instance, if a student is injured, they can immediately dial 911 or alert school staff. If someone faces bullying, they could contact the office or their parents for support. This quick response helps ensure that any dangerous incident is reported and dealt with right away.

Phones also assist with smaller issues that come up during the day. If a student spills lunch on their uniform or suddenly realizes they need a change of clothes, they can call home and ask a family member to bring what they need. Rather than waiting awkwardly or missing class, the student can sort out the problem swiftly.

Moreover, students often have free periods when a phone can be useful. After school, there are many unpredictable events on the way home—like transport delays or accidents. With a phone, they can reach emergency services or let their parents know about any changes in their plans. Allowing cell phones at school therefore offers safety, convenience, and peace of mind for both students and their families.

I have looked into this matter and believe it would be very beneficial to revise our school cafeteria menu to include healthier meals. Although it may require some effort and planning, the change would bring significant advantages to our students, and I have three main reasons to support this proposal.

Many families worry about the amount of fast food or sugary snacks their kids consume during the day. By offering balanced meals packed with fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins, we could eliminate those concerns. Parents would no longer have to wonder whether their children’s lunches are harming their health.

Second, healthier meals would help students maintain higher energy levels and stay focused in class. Junk food often leads to drowsiness or a lack of motivation, making it harder for pupils to concentrate on lessons. In contrast, a diet rich in vitamins and minerals keeps the body strong and the mind alert. As a result, students would likely participate more actively in discussions and be less inclined to feel tired or sluggish.

Finally, by eating well-balanced meals regularly, students could build stronger immune systems and miss fewer school days due to illness. This would not only improve their academic performance but also reduce medical expenses for families. Teaching students the value of healthy eating habits now can encourage them to make better choices throughout their lives.

For these reasons, I urge you to consider updating our cafeteria offerings. Investing in nutritious food will help our students stay healthy, focused, and ready to learn—benefitting both the school community and their futures.

Many people argue about whether students ought to use their phones during school hours. In my view, allowing mobile devices in class brings clear benefits but also serious drawbacks. On one hand, smartphones offer quick access to facts and can make research easier than relying on classroom computers or library visits. On the other hand, they often tempt pupils to lose focus, text friends or browse social media instead of paying attention to the teacher.

One major concern is that phones can turn lessons into a constant distraction. When learners carry their devices, they may choose to scroll through social media feeds, play games or send messages rather than concentrate on classwork. This habit can lead to laziness and poor study skills, since students might depend on their phones for answers instead of thinking things through themselves. There is also the risk of cheating during tests by looking up solutions online, which undermines the purpose of exams and the student’s own development.

To reduce these problems, many teachers ask pupils to hand in their phones at the start of each lesson and return them when class ends. This simple rule helps create an environment where students are less tempted to use their devices at inappropriate times. With their phones safely away, learners are more likely to engage directly with lectures, take notes by hand and discuss ideas with classmates. In turn, they develop stronger concentration and problem-solving skills that will serve them well beyond the classroom.

Despite these issues, there are good reasons to permit the use of smartphones under controlled conditions. For subjects that require up-to-date data or quick fact‐checking—such as science or history—phones can be faster and more convenient than waiting for a desktop computer. Many students find it easier to type short answers on a phone keyboard, and a simple online search can clarify confusing concepts in seconds. By using approved apps or designated websites, pupils can explore different ways of learning and enrich their classroom experience.

In conclusion, phones at school present both advantages and disadvantages. Their ability to provide instant information can support lessons, but unchecked use often leads to distraction and cheating. A balanced approach—where teachers collect devices during instruction yet allow them for designated activities—helps students benefit from technology while maintaining focus on real learning.

On an individual level, important decisions shape our future, whether it is choosing a career path or handling a personal challenge. Advice from others can make us wiser. For example, President Abraham Lincoln faced severe racial injustice in the 1800s. If he had not received guidance from his advisors and from activists who pointed out the cruelty of slavery, he might not have issued the Emancipation Proclamation. His willingness to listen helped end legal slavery in the United States. Likewise, personal advice—such as parents encouraging you not to give up when tasks become difficult—can influence your character for life. Such counsel strengthens perseverance and teaches you to face challenges with confidence.

Seeking different opinions can be compared to sampling dishes from various chefs. You might dislike one recipe but love another; you never know until you try. Similarly, gathering advice from different people opens up new possibilities and often leads to better decisions.

In conclusion, advice exists to guide us toward smarter choices in life. While not every opinion will suit your needs, considering them all can help you grow, become wiser, and better prepared for future situations.

In that case, even though they would technically improve, students would also develop zero tolerance for any criticism and would probably want all the attention focused on them.

For instance, any artist operates on the idea that everything they make is something they’ll hate, even if there’s true improvement. Applying what we learn from artists to education, it would be a terrible approach to praise students unconditionally, since the purpose of a student is to learn and then use what they’ve learned in the world. In the real world, there are always people who criticize your work, and if you can’t handle that criticism, you’re most likely going to get fired.

In conclusion, I’m not saying that praising too much is a bad thing, nor am I saying you should make students hate what they’re doing. Instead, I’m arguing that with every praise there should be a criticism to balance it out, so that students understand that with every positive comes a negative and that the world isn’t just going to offer praise to anyone.

Should a student’s work be praised no matter how bad it is? This sounds like a good idea in theory, but in the educational field it is really a terrible thing to do. We all want to be praised for our work, and we can only improve by practicing something over and over. We gain even more motivation when we are happy with what we’re practicing, and happiness comes with every praise. But if all we got while learning was praise and nothing to improve on, then what would be the point of continuing to learn if all we hear is “this is amazing” or see an A+ on every assignment? Students would improve, but they would also develop zero tolerance for any criticism and likely demand all the attention be focused on them.

A great example of this would be any artist. Artists operate on the idea that they will hate everything they make, even when there is true improvement. They receive praise, but that praise is not what drives them to do better. Instead, it is their dissatisfaction with their own work that motivates them to improve, and it helps them take criticism with a grain of salt and use it to get better. If we apply this lesson to students, praising too much would be a terrible practice. The purpose of a student is to learn and then use what they have learned in the real world, where people will inevitably criticize their work. If they cannot take that criticism, they are most likely going to lose their job.

In conclusion, I’m not saying that praising too much is a bad thing, and I’m not suggesting that students should hate what they are doing. Rather, I am saying that every piece of praise should be balanced with criticism to show students that with every positive comes a negative and that the world is not going to offer only praise.

Should we celebrate every student’s work, even when it falls short? At first glance, that might sound supportive, but in education it can actually backfire. We all enjoy praise, and it can push us to repeat an activity. Yet if learners only ever hear that their efforts are perfect, they won’t know what to work on next. Constant compliments without guidance offer little chance to develop new skills, and students may grow intolerant of any criticism, expecting applause for every task.

Consider artists as an example. Painters, writers, or musicians often feel disappointed with their own creations, despite positive feedback from others. That frustration drives them to keep improving. They learn to accept suggestions without taking offense and use those comments to refine their work. If students never experience anything but praise, they will miss out on this important learning process.

Moreover, life after school includes both compliments and critiques. Future bosses and coworkers will judge a graduate’s performance, and without practice in handling criticism, young people may struggle in their jobs or even risk losing positions. Praise alone does not teach resilience or how to respond constructively to negative remarks.

In conclusion, I am not saying we should stop encouraging students or force them to dislike their work. Rather, I believe every positive remark should be balanced with thoughtful feedback. This blend shows learners that improvement comes from recognizing both strengths and weaknesses, preparing them for a world where both support and criticism play a part in success.

By reflecting on what we truly enjoy and dislike, we can plan our own steps and make choices that match our inner goals.

I am convinced that students reach their fullest potential when they keep themselves busy with meaningful activities instead of remaining idle. Being active not only helps them learn more but also pushes them ahead in life and encourages personal growth. When young people take initiative, they gain knowledge through experience, move further in their careers, and develop the maturity needed to face adult responsibilities. In my view, staying productive is the key to achieving more than those who do nothing.

First of all, when students are involved in tasks, they learn by doing. For instance, I remember disliking math in fourth grade, but I decided to practice every day after school for the rest of the year. As I worked through problems each evening, my grades steadily climbed. Without this daily effort, I would not have improved. Research also supports this idea: students who spend their free time on constructive activities—such as reading, completing projects, or solving puzzles—tend to perform better than classmates who avoid extracurricular study. In addition, juggling different responsibilities teaches learners how to plan and organise their hours, which is a vital skill both in school and beyond.

Another advantage of staying active is that it paves the way to a brighter future. I look at my aunt, who became a doctor through dedication and hard work. She prepared for countless exams, balanced volunteering and study groups, and often multitasked to keep up with her demanding schedule. Her example shows that overcoming challenges requires continuous effort and a willingness to take on responsibilities. Those who set goals and work toward them steadily will often surpass peers who wait for opportunities to come by themselves.

Finally, taking action helps students become more mature and self-reliant. When teenagers start part-time jobs while attending classes, they learn what it means to manage both work and homework. They might use short breaks at work to revise notes or plan assignments for the weekend. By setting priorities and adapting their routines, they develop discipline and time-management skills that are essential in adult life. Having a positive role model—such as a parent, teacher, or successful family member—also inspires them to make wise choices and build confidence.

In conclusion, students who consistently engage in productive activities not only strengthen their academic abilities but also prepare themselves for future success. They learn valuable life lessons, advance more quickly in their chosen paths, and grow into responsible adults. By taking charge of their own learning and using their time wisely, young people ensure that they accomplish far more than those who choose to remain inactive.

I believe that each person’s character is shaped by the choices they make. Three key influences determine who we become: the friends we keep, the home environment we grow up in, and our own drive to improve. By understanding how these factors work, we can take control of our character and guide ourselves toward positive qualities.

First, the company we keep has a powerful effect on our behavior. People around us can pass on both good and bad habits, so it makes sense to choose friends who encourage us to succeed. For instance, if you spend most of your time with classmates who study hard and support each other, you’re likely to feel motivated to learn and set goals. On the other hand, if you surround yourself with people who prefer to waste time and avoid effort, you might find it easy to give in to laziness. In other words, the attitudes and actions of your peers can become your own if you let them.

Second, the atmosphere at home plays a large role in forming character traits. A household where family members argue or barely communicate can create stress and frustration, leaving children feeling insecure or distracted. This often shows up in poor performance at school or low self-esteem in social activities. By contrast, a supportive home filled with respect and encouragement can help a young person grow up with confidence. When everyone in a family shares positive energy—by praising each other’s successes, listening to worries, and solving problems together—children learn to trust themselves and face life’s challenges with a hopeful attitude.

Finally, personal motivation is the foundation of lasting character development. Motivation gives purpose to our actions and helps us overcome obstacles, even when the past was difficult. For example, someone who has faced financial struggles might channel that experience into a determination to work harder and build a better future. This kind of inner drive often leads to qualities such as resilience, discipline, and optimism. With a clear goal in mind—whether it’s a career ambition, an athletic target, or improving relationships—motivated individuals tend to develop habits that reinforce their strength of character.

In conclusion, your character is not something fixed at birth but a result of the decisions you make every day. By choosing positive friends, fostering a healthy home life, and maintaining strong motivation, you can become the person you want to be. Remember, no situation is completely beyond your control. If a friendship drags you down, seek new companions. If your household atmosphere is negative, find constructive ways to change it. Ultimately, every choice lies in your hands, and each decision brings you one step closer to the character you aspire to build.

Many people are debating whether schools should mirror businesses that have switched to a four-day week by adding two extra hours to each school day. The aim is to save energy and resources, but the idea has sparked disagreement among students, teachers, and parents.

Opponents of the plan point out that working ten hours on each of four days could leave everyone feeling exhausted. Rather than having five shorter days, schools would require longer hours in the classroom, and meeting even more graduation requirements might take extra effort and time. Critics also suggest simpler measures to reduce energy use, such as turning off lights when rooms are empty or opening windows instead of running the air conditioning.

From my perspective, lengthening the school day by two hours would be very challenging. Many students hold part-time or full-time jobs after class, and a longer day at school could conflict with their work schedules. If we managed our existing energy more efficiently—by switching off devices when not in use and using natural light wherever possible—we could make a significant impact without extending school hours. In addition, gathering ideas from people outside the school community could help us find practical solutions we might overlook.

Studying only four days a week with ten-hour days would also affect our ability to learn. Getting up earlier and leaving later could leave students too tired to focus effectively. In fact, the total energy saved might be little different from the current five-day schedule, since longer days might increase lighting and climate control needs.

In conclusion, finding the best way to conserve energy requires open discussion and input from everyone involved. Some students need more time in class to grasp new topics, and a four-day system could make learning harder for them. Thankfully, there are plenty of straightforward ways to save energy without cutting down the number of school days.

Isn't it incredible how technology keeps improving our lives? Over the years, we’ve seen advances in everything from skyscrapers and airplanes to the way we dine and shop. Some worry that machines are replacing human interaction, but I believe the benefits far outweigh that concern. Technology speeds up so many routine tasks—whether it’s constructing buildings, producing cars or ordering food—making daily life more convenient for everyone.

Take the automotive industry as an example. Companies like Ford now rely on robots and automated systems to assemble vehicles at a breathtaking pace—often finishing a car every ten minutes. Customers can even buy a truck online without ever speaking to a sales agent. If you need a replacement part, websites such as FordParts.org deliver it to your door by the next day. In fact, my local Ford dealership has a café where every order is handled through tablets and touchscreens, practically eliminating the usual hustle.

Restaurants have also embraced this shift. Instead of waiting for a server, guests can tap on a tablet to place their meal order directly. This means fewer staff members are needed at each table, but it also removes the guesswork of tipping and cuts down on simple mistakes. Diners get exactly what they requested, and employees can focus on other tasks until their service is required. The result is a smoother experience from start to finish.

Grocery stores and supercenters are following suit with self-checkout lanes. We’ve all had the painful experience of waiting for a slow cashier or discovering the wrong change. Self-service checkouts let shoppers scan, pay and leave in minutes. While these machines occasionally hiccup, they are generally reliable and will soon become standard everywhere, making long lines a thing of the past.

If we still relied entirely on human labor, Ford would have to hire thousands more workers to match its current output, restaurants would need large teams—some of whom might be less attentive—and grocery stores would be swamped with lines. Thanks to modern technology, we enjoy faster service, fewer errors and greater convenience in almost every area of life.

Some companies have already switched to a four-day week to cut costs and let employees recharge. I believe schools could do something similar by adding two extra hours each day and reducing classes to four days a week. First, students would have more time for homework or part-time jobs. Second, limiting school to four days would lower energy use in buildings. Finally, young parents who study and care for their children at the same time would gain an essential day off. Personally, I appreciate my school because it offers support for students who must bring their kids along.

From my perspective, this schedule change would help me and many classmates. Right now, I finish classes around three o’clock, then head straight to work. I need that income to cover rent, food, clothing, and other necessities. If school ended on Thursday instead of Friday, I could spend Friday fully on my job and earn extra money to help my mother pay the bills.

I also admire businesses that close one weekday to save energy and funds. Back home, my family often struggled to pay the electricity bill. Sometimes I would forget to turn off the TV, and my mother would shout, “Switch it off—you’re wasting money!” I remember feeling upset because I wanted to watch my favorite shows, but those lessons taught me how important small savings can be.

Many students juggle several roles at once: we may be workers, learners, and parents simultaneously. A four-day school week would give these busy students a vital break. Looking at my own family, I am inspired by how my mother acted as both father and mother to me and my siblings. She woke up early every morning, worked all day, and still made time for us—no matter how exhausted she felt. Her example shows how tough it is to carry so many responsibilities without enough rest.

In conclusion, extending the school day by two hours and shifting to a four-day schedule would bring many benefits. Students would feel less tired, have extra time for work or family duties, and schools could save energy, food, water, and money. I hope the government considers this idea and makes my dream of a four-day school week come true.

People often claim that first impressions cannot be altered. However, I believe that these initial judgments can be revised, because we rarely know what someone else might be dealing with at the moment.

My initial anxiety faded as I learned more about the new environment.

It is true that in some cases, first impressions seem permanent. For instance, during job interviews, employers often look for candidates who appear confident, hardworking, and responsible. If an applicant makes a weak first impression, they may not receive an offer. Nevertheless, if the interviewer decides to give them another opportunity, it can change how they are perceived.

In conclusion, although first impressions can be strong, they do not have to remain unchanged. With time and understanding, we can revise our initial judgments and see people more fairly.

I disagree with students attending classes from home or using video conferencing. Online lessons have several drawbacks that can make learning less effective. Based on my own experience as a student, I believe these issues can lead to poor performance and even failure.

First, many students simply won’t log in when classes are held online. They might promise themselves they will join next time, but then they lose interest and choose other activities, like playing outside with friends or using their phones and gaming consoles. Parents may have to remind them repeatedly to attend, yet some still refuse or ignore the reminders.

Second, it’s easy for students to fall asleep during virtual classes. The teacher cannot see or wake a dozing student through a screen, but in a physical classroom, the teacher can notice and encourage them to stay awake and pay attention. Being in a real classroom helps maintain focus and makes the teacher’s job much easier.

Third, students might skip doing their own work and get someone else to complete assignments for them. They could ask friends or even pay others to finish tasks, undermining the purpose of learning. Although some argue that online classes are convenient because you simply open a laptop in the morning and join the lesson, many learners need a teacher’s presence nearby to understand the material properly.

For these reasons, I believe that attending school from home is not as beneficial as in-person classes.

It's undeniable that a positive mindset drives achievement. Every activity we undertake—from major projects to the smallest gesture—requires self-belief. Even a simple act like blinking can feel overwhelming if we doubt ourselves, and without confidence, we are set up to falter.

Nevertheless, failure shouldn't be viewed purely as a negative. Experiencing setbacks is a vital element of attaining our goals. Through mistakes, we identify what went wrong and gain insight into the challenges ahead. Armed with this knowledge, we return focused, equipped with a fresh strategy, renewed determination, and a stronger outlook. Failure, often seen as disgraceful, is actually a stepping stone toward growth.

We must be honest: why accept defeat when success is within reach? If we resign ourselves to losing, why exert any effort—better to stay home, recline on the couch, and binge-watch shows. Yet the world is full of ambitious individuals fighting for their dreams, and offering only three-quarters of our capacity is simply insufficient.

This is where a confident attitude makes all the difference. When we recognize our value and commit to giving a full hundred percent, doubts fade away. With a resolute belief in yourself and an optimistic outlook, you will pursue your objectives relentlessly—regardless of opposition, critics, or the sacrifices required. That unwavering confidence and positive approach form the true secret to success. Embracing this mindset empowers us to achieve our highest ambitions.

Students already juggle many activities outside of classes, such as part-time jobs, sports practices, or club meetings. Asking them to stay two extra hours at school would disrupt their daily routines and leave them with little free time. Although a four-day school week sounds attractive, extending each school day by two hours could actually be a drawback. Waking up earlier and spending more time in class might leave students exhausted and upset the balance they have worked hard to maintain.

On the positive side, a four-day week would give learners a three-day weekend throughout the year. That extra day off would allow them to rest, work on assignments, or catch up on projects they fell behind on. Many students struggle to finish homework between classes, clubs, and part-time work. Having a longer weekend could be just what they need to improve their grades and reduce stress.

However, very long school days can lead to fatigue and difficulty concentrating. After several hours of lessons, most students find it hard to stay alert and pay attention. Some might even doze off or lose interest in the late afternoon classes. If I personally had to sit through two more hours every day, I know I would struggle to follow the lessons and probably doze off before class ends.

An additional benefit of a shorter week is that the school year itself could be made shorter, allowing longer breaks in winter or spring. This change would give families more time to travel or enjoy holidays together. Overall, while a four-day week has both upsides and downsides, I believe it is worth trying because it provides a well-needed extra day to relax.

Why should you maintain a positive attitude? First, it can boost your chances of success in many aspects of life. There are two main reasons for this: it helps you build strong relationships, and it opens doors to better careers. In contrast, a negative outlook can hold you back, making it harder to find work, secure deals, or even make a good impression in court. Below are three benefits of having a positive attitude: it earns you friends, it brings respect, and it improves job prospects.

People feel drawn to those who have a friendly and positive demeanor. When you show kindness and understanding, others are more likely to return the favor. This mutual respect can support you in various areas of life. During a job interview, for example, a positive attitude can leave a lasting good impression, increasing the likelihood that you will receive an offer. On the other hand, if you appear unfriendly or disinterested, employers may decide to hire someone else.

Being respectful and considerate also helps you earn respect in return. When you treat others well, they are less inclined to undermine you or wish you ill. Gaining respect is not always easy; it requires consistently polite behavior and willingness to help. By showing genuine interest in others and assisting them when you can, you create a network of people who are ready to support you. As these connections grow stronger, your personal and professional success becomes more attainable.

Finally, having a positive mindset greatly simplifies the process of finding a job or entering a good college. I believe we have the power to change the world, even though many people insist it is impossible. Too often, we allow negative ideas in our minds to stop us from taking action. Changing our environment and our way of looking at it should be our first priority. If each of us makes even a small improvement, it can grow into something much bigger over time.

One of the most urgent issues today is global warming. Our planet’s climate is under threat, and we cannot wait for someone else to solve the problem. We must start by changing simple habits: reducing waste, saving energy, and protecting nature. These actions may seem minor, but if many people join together, they will have a real impact. The key is to begin—once we see results, others will be inspired to follow.

Real change starts with ourselves. Becoming more courteous, responsible, punctual, and considerate of others helps build a better community. For example, if I consistently arrive on time and treat people kindly, those around me may adopt the same behaviour. Working as a team is even more powerful than working alone. By encouraging friends, family, and neighbours to join in, we multiply our efforts and unite for a common goal.

I am passionate about technology and renewable energy because they offer practical ways to improve our daily lives. I dream of designing a personal robot to help with household chores. It might carry items, clean floors, or remind us of tasks, freeing up time for more important activities. Of course, such a machine could run into problems or need software updates, but its benefits would be worth it. I also imagine creating a smartphone that charges using solar power, reducing our reliance on non-renewable energy and lowering electricity bills.

We should not fear mistakes, since they teach us valuable lessons. Every error reveals something we can do differently next time. If we never make mistakes, we miss the chance to learn and grow. In fact, many successful inventions came from trial and error. Accepting failure as part of the process helps us keep moving forward until we reach our goals.

Our dreams may not always become reality immediately, but they can guide our efforts. Sharing ideas through social media—perhaps in a short animated video—could inspire millions of people. If they see one person daring to think differently, they might feel motivated to try new things themselves. Teachers and schools also play a vital role by shaping our habits and showing us how to study and plan for the future.

The most important step is to start. No matter how small our first action is, it sets everything in motion. We must not hesitate because time is passing quickly, and every day counts. If each of us does our part, the combined effect will be enormous. Even when progress seems slow, we should remember that steady effort brings lasting change.

In the end, nothing is truly impossible as long as we refuse to give up. Life is short, and the opportunity to make a difference is now. By changing ourselves, supporting one another, and taking the first steps, we can turn our hopes into reality. The world is waiting for our positive actions—it’s time to make the change we wish to see.

Being invited to teach at an elementary school is a truly rewarding opportunity. You meet a variety of students, chat with parents and family members, and work alongside dedicated teachers and staff. Sharing lessons with young learners brings many benefits for both you and the children.

First of all, teaching elementary students can be fun and nostalgic. When you explain a simple math concept or define a noun, you often remember your own school days. For instance, asking a pupil “What is a noun?” and hearing the correct answer may remind you of how exciting it was to discover grammar as a child.

Working with young kids also sharpens your communication and teaching skills. It may seem difficult at first to keep their attention, but once you find creative ways—like storytelling or interactive games—to explain ideas, lessons flow smoothly. You learn to present information clearly and to adapt activities to different learning styles.

Moreover, getting involved in an elementary school community lets you build valuable relationships. You connect with principals, guidance counselors, and other teachers, and sometimes you even run into siblings or relatives at the same school. Observing their methods can inspire you to try new techniques and improve your own approach.

Interacting with children often involves playing games and organizing group activities. Whether it’s a relay race on the playground or a classroom art project, these experiences help you bond with students. They enjoy learning while playing, and you enjoy seeing their excitement and curiosity.

Finally, teaching at this level lays a strong foundation for the students’ futures. By delivering engaging lessons and encouraging them to complete homework on time, you help them develop good study habits and confidence. Watching them grow and succeed is extremely fulfilling.

In summary, being asked to teach elementary students is both enjoyable and meaningful. It helps you relive childhood memories, enhance your teaching abilities, form lasting friendships, and guide young learners toward a brighter future.

Have you ever thought about how many people feel trapped by pretending to be someone they’re not? Around the world today, millions live their lives according to others’ expectations rather than their own desires. In a society that often treats difference as a fault, standing out can feel like an impossible battle. Yet real fulfillment comes when we embrace our individuality. Accepting who we are—flaws and all—is the first step toward genuine happiness, no matter how much pressure we face to conform.

Many assume that a successful life means wealth, fame or luxury possessions. In truth, none of these external markers guarantee contentment. You might own a fancy car or hold an influential position, but if you’re not true to yourself, those things lose their meaning. Research suggests that a large percentage of people—some studies say over sixty per cent—feel unhappy with their lives. However, this grim statistic can improve if individuals choose honesty over pretense, removing from their lives whatever doesn’t align with their true selves. Refusing to live a lie is essential, because hiding your real identity often leads to emotional distress and even depression. By acknowledging your own personality and interests, you protect your well-being and open the door to lasting joy.

Every day we face countless choices, and it’s crucial that the guiding voice we follow belongs to ourselves. Before making a big decision, take a moment to ask: “What do I really want?” When we prioritize our own opinions over those of family, friends or society, we reclaim control of our destinies. It’s all too easy to adopt someone else’s beliefs or goals, but genuine satisfaction comes only when we pursue what truly matters to us.

Across the globe, people are fighting for the freedom to be who they really are. Embracing diversity—whether it shows up in race, language, traditions or beliefs—enriches every community. Prejudice denies us the chance to learn from one another and erodes the basic respect we owe each human being. Still, many activists and everyday citizens work tirelessly to break down these barriers, hoping to create a world where everyone can exist without fear of judgment. When you feel confident in your own identity, others’ negative opinions lose their power, because you stand firm on the foundation of your own self-acceptance.

Historians and philosophers point out that fear of rejection has long made people hide their true interests and feelings. Often, we worry that if we speak up when something feels wrong, we’ll be ridiculed or excluded. That silence then becomes part of the problem, allowing unfair attitudes to persist. Although we’ve made progress in challenging stereotypes and broadening society’s view of what’s “normal,” many still struggle with internal doubts. Our harshest critic can be ourselves, as we set unrealistically high standards and punish ourselves for perceived failures. Reversing this mindset—accepting that being unique is not just okay but valuable—will help everyone feel more at ease in their own skin.

Admittedly, there’s still much to learn, but the direction is promising. Each person must overcome obstacles on the path to individuality—whether those obstacles are external pressures or inner insecurities. By recognizing where we are now and keeping our goal of authenticity in sight, we can continue moving forward.

Ultimately, being yourself may feel like an uphill fight when society insists on conformity. But discovering and celebrating your true identity is one of the greatest achievements anyone can reach. Living authentically brings a sense of freedom and completeness that no material possession can ever match. Embrace who you are, and you’ll find a richer, more fulfilling life than you ever imagined.

Consistently practicing a task helps me improve and accomplish more. Many people believe that the more we repeat an activity, the more skilled we become. When I work on something again and again, I can see progress and feel more confident. For example, if I keep reading and taking on projects, my grades get better, and I manage to complete additional assignments. The same idea applies when I study for quizzes: by reviewing my material over and over, I perform much better.

In my English class, I must read books for different projects. The more I read, the more ideas I gather for my reports, and the higher my grades are. For instance, when we had to do an “ABC project” on The Lions novel, I found that rereading the text helped me create more detailed pages and earn extra points. Continuous reading also means I can try more creative approaches to each project, which teachers appreciate.

Similarly, in History class, I am often asked to read biographies. Every time I finish a new life story, I understand historical events more deeply and can write stronger essays. The extra effort also gives me chances to submit optional work for bonus marks. By reading several biographies, I build a solid foundation of facts, and my final grade improves.

Studying for quizzes is another part of my routine. In Science, I look over my notes regularly rather than waiting until the last minute. This steady review allows me to answer more questions correctly. I also apply the same habit to preparing for my SOL exams, which are very important for my overall performance. Practicing problems and reviewing key concepts multiple times means I rarely get low scores.

Sometimes doing the same thing repeatedly can feel dull. However, if I stay focused while reading, preparing projects, or studying for quizzes, I achieve better results. In my opinion, constant practice combined with concentration leads to strong performance and good grades. For these reasons, I believe it is always better to keep working on a task than to do nothing.
