Is it wise for students to choose a career path at a young age? I believe it is. Some might argue that committing early limits options, especially when teens must balance school with family chores or part-time jobs. However, picking a field while still in high school brings more advantages than drawbacks.

First, students who focus on their preferred career from the start gain valuable practice and knowledge in that area. By studying what really interests them, they can build skills day by day and avoid confusion later on. When graduation comes, they will feel confident demonstrating what they have learned and will face fewer obstacles when entering the workforce.

Second, many societies expect young people to decide on a specialization in high school. This requirement helps students discover their strengths and decide whether they enjoy science, arts, technology, or another subject. Knowing your future direction early gives a clear goal to work toward. For example, when I was a child, my father encouraged me to take courses in English, computing, guitar, and dance. At the time, I refused because I just wanted to play, but now I understand how those lessons could have opened doors and shown the world what I can achieve.

Another benefit is that schools offering career-focused programs often let students work during the summer or after classes. In my country, most schools do not provide these options, so students graduate without any practical skills and do not feel ready to take a job. Instead, parents usually handle all the work. If more schools offered vocational courses, young people would learn to earn money and gain real-life experience before finishing high school.

In conclusion, deciding on a career path as a teenager is very important for both individuals and society. Early specialization helps students learn more, prepares them for real work, and removes doubts about their future. Rather than just studying theory, they develop a profession they enjoy and perform well in. Taking advantage of these opportunities now can make life easier later and set the stage for a rewarding career.

Working in a group is very beneficial because time seems to pass more quickly and the overall experience is more enjoyable. Collaborating with others lets us support one another, share ideas, and build friendships. In contrast, working alone can become boring and slow; without anyone to discuss with or divide tasks, it often feels like the clock is moving too slowly and progress is limited.

For example, when you handle a project all by yourself, you must research, prepare, and present every detail without any help. If you encounter a problem, there is no one to ask for advice, and the work may take much longer. On the other hand, in a team of four people, we can assign each member a specific part of the project, present their section, and step in if someone forgets a point. This way of dividing tasks not only speeds up completion but also improves the final result because teammates can fill in gaps and offer feedback.

Moreover, group work encourages fresh ideas and new ways of thinking for future projects. For these reasons, I believe that collaborating with others is a more effective and satisfying way to work.

I appreciate this quote because it highlights an issue I’ve seen in many families and communities: people feeling pressured into careers they don’t truly care about. I disagree with Emerson’s idea that society determines our path without question. In my view, each person can choose what truly excites them, rather than simply follow their parents’ or peers’ expectations of becoming a doctor or an engineer. When you love your work—whether it’s writing, teaching, researching, healing, or any other field—you feel alive. Every time you solve a problem or learn something new, you gain energy and confidence to push further. On the other hand, being pushed toward something you don’t enjoy can harm your motivation and well-being.

For example, I studied business for most of my life because I dreamed of working in a company setting. After moving to the United States last year, everyone around me insisted I become a nurse. Although nursing is a respected profession, I simply don’t have the passion for it. Choosing nursing without support has left me feeling anxious and doubtful. If I were doing something I truly loved, I’d welcome the hard work and stay determined, believing in my own success. That kind of encouragement makes all the difference.

In conclusion, I don’t accept Emerson’s claim that our surroundings alone shape who we are. Society only has power over us if we let it. By standing up for our passions and explaining why they matter, we can earn respect and find real fulfillment.

Every day, people look for ways to enjoy life and share happiness with others. When I visited Italy, I experienced this firsthand during the annual town celebration. Everyone gathered in the streets to drink, chat, and eat delicious food. You don’t need a lot of money to join in the fun—just good company and a friendly atmosphere. This taught me that true joy comes from being with people who lift your spirits, not from spending a fortune.

It is also important to follow your own path and trust yourself above all. Sometimes, other people’s jealousy or negative comments can make you doubt your goals. If you let someone else decide your choices, you risk giving up on your dreams. By believing in yourself and doing what you love, you grow stronger and more confident, regardless of what others say.

Another moment that showed me the power of kindness happened at an Italian supermarket. My father and I were picking up groceries when a man at the register realized he was fifty cents short for a sandwich. I quietly bought it for him, and his gratitude was immediate. “Thank you, friend,” he said. “You’ve made my day.” That small gesture cost me almost nothing, but it made him very happy. This proved that you don’t have to spend a lot to brighten someone else’s life.

In conclusion, I believe we achieve more when we reach out to help others and stay true to ourselves. Never give up on your dreams, because the moment you lose faith in yourself is when real defeat begins.

People have different views on whether students should take part in community service, but I believe making it compulsory is an excellent idea. First, community service brings real benefits to local areas. For example, volunteering in parks or cleaning litter helps maintain a pleasant environment for everyone. It also gives students the chance to develop important skills like teamwork and responsibility, which cannot always be learned in the classroom.

Some argue that forcing young people to do this work is a punishment rather than a positive experience and that students should have the right to decide. I agree we should listen to students’ opinions and offer them information about the choice. Some people believe that by the time they reach high school, students ought to choose a future profession. Although it is not strictly required, picking a career early can offer several advantages.

First, deciding on a career while still in high school helps students build a solid foundation of knowledge and skills related to their chosen field. Committing to a goal at a younger age encourages responsibility and focus on long-term objectives. For example, a teenager interested in nursing might take extra biology classes or volunteer at a clinic, which not only boosts their experience but also strengthens their university applications. By graduation, they arrive better prepared for higher education.

Second, choosing a profession during high school gives students ample time to explore different options and, if necessary, change their plans. If a student realises that a particular path is not a good fit, they can reconsider before investing time and money in a degree they dislike. This flexibility minimises wasted effort and ensures they enter university confident in their decision.

In conclusion, while identifying a career in high school is not mandatory, doing so early allows young people to gain relevant experience, set clear goals, and adjust their choices before moving on to higher education.

Some schools have started allowing students to bring their cell phones into class for learning activities. While phones can offer quick access to information, I believe they should remain banned during lessons. Students spend so much time on their devices that they lose focus, they can easily use phones for non-educational activities, and overall these gadgets constantly interrupt the learning process.

First, when pupils use their phones throughout the school day, they often ignore the teacher’s explanations. Even if a smartphone might help answer a quick question, most students prefer browsing social media or messaging friends instead of listening in class. As a result, when exams or quizzes arrive, they struggle to recall important facts because they were glued to their screens rather than taking notes or engaging with the lesson.

Second, cell phones open the door to many distractions. During class, students may send texts, play games, watch videos, or listen to music, all of which pull their attention away from the subject at hand. Some even take photos or record videos of classmates, sometimes to embarrass them or post online. These actions not only disrupt the individual student but can also disturb others and create a hostile environment.

Supporters of classroom phone use argue that smartphones can help with homework, research, or group projects, and it is true that they have useful apps. However, in practice, many students end up scrolling through social media or chatting with friends instead of completing assignments. Once they start checking messages or taking calls, they often forget about the task the teacher assigned. This constant switching between apps and schoolwork can cause grades to drop, as unfinished homework and missed classwork add up over time.

In conclusion, although cell phones might offer some benefits for education, they do more harm than good in the classroom. Students who constantly check their devices fail to concentrate on lessons, use phones for unrelated activities that disrupt learning, and ultimately see their academic performance suffer. Some educators believe that praising a student’s work, even when it is not perfect, helps build self-esteem, and I agree with this view. When learners feel confident about their abilities, they are more willing to take on challenges and develop new skills. Without a sense of self-worth, students may shy away from tasks that seem difficult and miss valuable chances to improve. Encouragement, therefore, plays an essential role in helping them move forward instead of remaining stuck.

If a student doubts what they can achieve, they are unlikely to try harder or explore new opportunities. A lack of belief in oneself often leads to doing the same things repeatedly without any real progress, which can further damage confidence. By contrast, when students receive praise, they begin to understand that their efforts matter. This recognition can inspire them to practice more, push their limits, and discover that they can accomplish more than they first thought. In the long run, the habit of trusting one’s own skills can have a significant impact on what a student does later in life.

To foster a positive mindset, students should learn to set small, realistic goals and track their progress. Writing down these objectives can help them see how far they have come and what steps remain. It also gives them a clear plan: which task to tackle first, which skill to develop next, and how to use support from friends or family. Even if their initial attempt falls short of perfection, constructive feedback and kind words can encourage them to try again. Understanding that failure is part of learning makes it easier for students to keep going rather than give up.

In summary, offering praise for a student’s work—even when it is not yet their best—creates a foundation of self-esteem. This positive reinforcement helps learners believe in themselves, set meaningful goals, and persist through challenges. By celebrating every effort along the way, educators and parents can help students grow steadily and prepare them for future success.

Attending classes at school offers many advantages compared to learning online from home. In a classroom, students have access to different resources and can choose from a wider range of subjects. If we don’t understand something, we can ask the teacher in person, and they can explain until we feel confident. Learning in school also gives us energy and a clear schedule, which helps us keep moving towards our goals without losing focus. Of course, studying from home is sometimes necessary, for instance when you are ill or have family responsibilities. In these cases, online classes allow you to stay up to date and continue learning without falling behind.

Remote learning has its own benefits too. At home, you can decide when to join a lesson, which might make you feel more positive and concentrated. Recorded lectures can be watched again, offering extra listening practice. You also have the freedom to organize your time and combine study with other tasks or hobbies, making your learning more flexible.

Many schools now frequently provide home-based lessons, and this flexibility is useful. However, going to school remains very important. In-person attendance gives you more chances to take different classes and graduate alongside your classmates. While video conferencing lets you see and hear the teacher, it does not allow the same immediate help when you have questions.

In conclusion, although distance learning can be helpful in certain situations, face-to-face education is generally more effective. I believe that attending school is essential because it offers greater opportunities and keeps students motivated to achieve their academic goals.

People who value self-reliance believe it is important to trust their own instincts and make decisions without leaning too much on others. In my view, those individuals should depend on themselves rather than constantly seek experts’ opinions. When people work for what they want, they learn responsibility and develop a genuine respect for their belongings.

Take the example of someone who saves up to buy a $100 pair of shoes. If those shoes get dirty or scuffed, it feels upsetting because they know exactly how hard they worked to afford them. In contrast, a cheap pair would not cause as much worry if it became ruined. This reaction comes from the effort spent earning the money and choosing to invest it in higher-quality footwear. By paying their own way, they naturally treat their possessions more carefully.

Teenagers especially benefit from part-time jobs or small chores to earn spending money. When young people constantly ask their parents for expensive sneakers—say $200 or more—they may not grasp the true value of those items. But if they save up themselves, they learn to budget, decide what matters most to them, and take pride in the things they finally purchase. They also discover that it makes more sense to buy a less costly pair of shoes for hard work or outdoor chores, leaving their nicer shoes for special occasions.

I have experienced this myself. I worked extra hours to buy a pair of wireless earbuds for me and another set as a Christmas gift for my close friend. Because I earned every dollar, I felt a strong sense of achievement when I handed him his gift. He was delighted and told me how much he valued our friendship. That moment showed me two things: earning something builds appreciation, and self-reliance can strengthen personal relationships.

In conclusion, people who prize self-reliance should trust their own judgment and rely on personal effort rather than expert advice. By working and saving for the things they want, they gain responsibility, learn to make wiser choices, and develop a deeper appreciation for their achievements.

Some students believe that a long summer holiday is ideal because it gives them plenty of free time. They enjoy having several weeks away from school to relax, catch up with friends, or pursue hobbies. For those whose parents live in another country, a lengthy break also offers the perfect chance to visit family abroad and strengthen those relationships.

However, I support the idea of a year-round school calendar. Under this plan, students would still have significant time off—a three- to four-week holiday in summer, an extended winter vacation, and one-week breaks in both spring and autumn. This approach breaks the year into manageable segments and keeps the routine fresh.

With shorter, more frequent breaks, learners are less likely to become bored or overwhelmed by constant studying. Instead of facing one long interruption that can lead to stress when school restarts, pupils can enjoy brief pauses that let them rest their minds and return to classes with renewed energy. They also avoid the problem of losing motivation, which often happens after a long holiday when it is hard to get back into a learning mindset.

In conclusion, a year-round schedule with varied break lengths provides a healthy balance. It prevents fatigue and boredom, keeps students more engaged, and makes it easier for them to maintain a steady academic rhythm.

Some students choose to study at home because they live too far from school or lack transportation. They might follow video lessons or join online courses, but I believe attending school in person has greater advantages. For example, teachers at school can encourage students directly, explain difficult topics face to face, and assign homework that deepens understanding. Even if a student lives at a distance, they often find a way—by bus, train or other means—because they know this effort will help them in the future.

Online classes are not always helpful for everyone. At home, students may struggle to concentrate, face constant distractions, or miss the chance to ask questions immediately. Teachers teaching online may also find it hard to keep everyone engaged. In contrast, in a classroom setting, students are less likely to be distracted and more likely to focus, while teachers can monitor progress and motivate learners on the spot.

That said, online learning does serve an important purpose for those who cannot attend school. Some people work full time and need flexible hours; others live in remote areas without a nearby school. For instance, many Hispanic immigrants work long hours to pay rent and bills but still want to improve their English. By paying for online courses, they can study at convenient times and aim for better job opportunities. These learners show that, despite challenges, online classes can open doors when in-person schooling isn’t possible.

Overall, school plays a vital role in education, and students who wish to build a strong future benefit most from attending regular classes. However, we must recognize that not everyone has the same chances. Whether online or in person, what truly matters is having clear goals and a dream. With determination, any student can find a way to learn and succeed.

Many people set goals. Some aim high, while others choose easier targets. High ambitions are challenging to achieve, but we should never swap them for simpler ones just because they seem more attainable. Even if you complete a hundred small goals, they cannot compare to the impact of one big, meaningful objective. A lofty aim can lead you to true success, whereas many minor tasks seldom make a lasting difference.

First, having a high goal is essential for personal greatness. For example, actor Keanu Reeves demonstrates that success isn’t only about wealth. His commitment to his work and kindness toward others reveal that meaningful achievements often go beyond financial gain. Sometimes, an ambitious goal involves self-improvement or helping the community rather than earning more money.

Second, aiming high helps you distinguish yourself in any endeavor. Consider Kobe Bryant, one of the NBA’s greatest players. His relentless drive to become the best fueled countless hours of practice and improvement. His story shows that with passion and hard work, anyone can rise to the top of their field.

Finally, settling for low goals prevents real growth. If you only pursue easy tasks, you miss out on opportunities to learn from difficulties and expand your abilities. To achieve true success, pick goals that spark your passion and push you outside your comfort zone.

Ambitious targets may feel overwhelming or even impossible, but you mustn’t give up. By telling yourself “I can do this,” you take the first step on the path to genuine success.

First impressions shape the way we see people and things, and they are often very hard to change. I agree with this idea. For instance, if a dish looks unappealing, you might not taste it even if it is delicious. Similarly, if someone gives you a bad first impression, you may avoid talking to them. Finally, when shopping, poor reviews can deter you from entering a store, no matter how attractive its window display is.

Imagine walking into a restaurant at lunchtime. You are excited to try something tasty, but after waiting fifteen minutes, the dish arrives looking unappetizing. You immediately feel disappointed and assume the food must taste terrible, so you refuse to eat it. On the other hand, a well-plated meal in bright colors would make you eager to take a bite before judging anything else. This shows how the initial appearance of food can determine our enjoyment of it.

Another example comes from meeting a new person. Suppose your parents introduce you to someone who talks without stopping. If you prefer quiet company, you will feel irritated and find it hard to see any positive qualities in this person. Because your first meeting was unpleasant, you might choose not to spend more time with them. That early reaction creates an emotional barrier that keeps you from forming a better opinion later.

When you’re in a strange city with a friend and need to find a shop, you probably check online reviews. You spot a store with nice products in the window, but most of its ratings are one or two stars. Even though the items look good, you decide to go elsewhere, worried that the quality must be poor. Those negative comments leave a strong impression that you cannot easily ignore.

In each of these cases, our first impression settles in our mind almost instantly. Even if we want to rethink our initial judgment, it often resurfaces and affects our behavior. This demonstrates how powerful and lasting first impressions can be.

I strongly support Winston Churchill’s famous idea that success is moving from one failure to another without losing enthusiasm. This well-known phrase emphasizes that passion and optimism are as important as skill in facing difficulties. Although the world has changed since Churchill’s time, the principle still applies. In today’s fast-paced environment—whether in business, religious bodies, or government—making mistakes often leads to criticism instead of encouragement. Despite this, setbacks are a crucial part of our journey toward achievement.

For example, imagine starting your first day at a new company. You may feel overwhelmed by unfamiliar procedures and unclear instructions. If your coworkers notice you hesitating or asking basic questions, they might mock your errors rather than offer guidance. They wait until you make a clear mistake before stepping in, which only increases your frustration. Though these interactions can be painful, they help you understand the company culture and expectations more deeply. Instead of waiting silently, you can also take the initiative to ask for advice before problems arise. Yet facing these difficulties early on pushes you to learn faster. Each correction highlights exactly where you must improve, turning embarrassment into a lesson that draws you closer to competence and confidence.

Many people think life should be easy, but it can be harsh and unforgiving. What truly counts is not how many challenges strike us, but how steadfast we are in overcoming them. It is similar to any sport: you will be knocked down, but the victory goes to those who rise again. When you know your worth, no criticism can stop you from pursuing your goals. Blaming others for every stumble only gives obstacles more power.

In conclusion, the setbacks and negative comments we face can actually give us the momentum we need to advance. Keeping our enthusiasm alive allows us to turn failures into stepping stones. By welcoming criticism as useful feedback and remaining determined after each fall, we eventually reach our objectives and discover real success.

This quotation by Ralph Waldo Emerson—“To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment”—sounds inspiring, but it doesn’t match most people’s experiences. In reality, many of us follow the expectations of others, lose sight of our own ambitions, and end up far from our true selves.

First, achieving personal goals becomes difficult when everyone around you has an opinion on what you ought to do. Parents, teachers, friends and even strangers often pressure us toward certain careers, hobbies or lifestyles. Although their advice may be well meaning, it can lead us to adopt aims that aren’t really ours. As a result, we chase targets that feel forced, and because we never truly owned them, we fail to reach them.

Second, there is a strong temptation to become someone else simply to fit in. In school, at work or on social media, society sets standards for appearance, behavior and success. Under that pressure, people often take on new styles, beliefs or habits that aren’t genuine. They hope to belong, but this disguise rarely brings happiness. By hiding their real identity, they lose touch with what makes them unique and end up feeling empty.

Finally, many people never fully discover who they are. Figuring out your own values, strengths and passions takes time and self‐reflection—luxuries that busy lifestyles rarely allow. Without that self‐knowledge, it is tempting to follow trends and meet other people’s expectations instead. You may achieve status or approval, but inwardly you will wonder if you’re living your own life or someone else’s.

For these reasons, Emerson’s claim seems overly idealistic. Becoming yourself may be a noble goal, but far too often people abandon their own dreams, adopt a different persona, and hide their true nature. Until we learn to identify our real priorities and resist outside pressures, “being yourself” will remain more of a wish than an accomplishment.

The school board is considering lengthening each school day by an extra hour and a half. I disagree with this proposal because it would increase student stress, disrupt after-school activities, and raise operating costs significantly.

First, adding more time in the classroom would put undue pressure on students. Many already feel overwhelmed by their current workload; extending the day further could lead to exhaustion or even depression. With longer hours at school, pupils would have less energy and motivation to complete assignments at home, since they might arrive too tired or with little time left. Consequently, their engagement and interest in learning could decline.

Second, an extended schedule would push back all after-school programs. Clubs, sports teams, and tutoring sessions would start later, making it difficult for students to take part. This is especially challenging for those who depend on school transport. For students living in rural areas, the school bus may already require an early departure; staying later could mean getting home late in the evening. If they only arrive back at six or seven, they have even less time to study or rest, which defeats the purpose of a longer day.

Finally, the cost of electricity and other utilities would rise substantially. School districts already spend millions each year on power to light and heat buildings. An extra ninety minutes per day for every classroom would increase that bill considerably. With tighter budgets, schools might need to cut funding for resources or maintenance elsewhere to cover these new expenses.

For these reasons—heightened student stress, delayed extracurricular activities and transportation issues, and higher operating costs—the school board should not extend the school day by an additional hour and a half.

I prefer working in a group rather than tackling tasks alone. Collaborating with others brings together a variety of ideas and keeps everyone focused on the project. When students join forces, they share suggestions about what to include, how to structure their work, and which topics will interest the class. In addition, group members remind one another of the teacher’s instructions so that each step of the assignment meets the requirements.

Collaboration also offers a chance to improve everyone’s grades. Some students may start with lower marks, but by working alongside classmates who understand the material, they can learn and revise their work. Team members encourage each other to contribute ideas and ask questions when something is unclear. This supportive atmosphere helps weaker students catch up and gives more confident students an opportunity to lead or explain difficult concepts.

Another advantage of group work is how responsibilities are divided. It can be tricky for one person to manage everything alone—from choosing a topic and deciding on a title to preparing the presentation. In a group, one student might research background information, another could write the introduction, and someone else might design visuals or lead the oral presentation. This division of labour not only makes the task easier but also ensures that each part of the project receives enough attention. When the team makes decisions together, they often agree on the best ideas and improve their final output.

Of course, some students feel more comfortable working by themselves and may hesitate to speak up in a group. However, the benefits usually outweigh these concerns. Group members can remind each other to stay on task and avoid distractions like smartphones or side conversations. They can also discuss what the teacher expects and double-check that everyone understands the assignment before moving on.

Overall, I believe that working with a group leads to better results than working alone. Sharing ideas, dividing tasks, and supporting each other help students create more thorough projects and earn higher grades. By collaborating, we not only learn from one another but also build valuable teamwork skills that will be useful beyond the classroom.

Many students could gain from the chance to study at home instead of going to a traditional classroom. Allowing learners to attend lessons online offers them the freedom to manage other responsibilities, such as part-time jobs or caring for family members. For instance, someone who helps out at home or works to support their household would benefit greatly from a more flexible study schedule that fits around their day-to-day tasks.

In some communities, pupils face long journeys to reach school, and not everyone owns reliable transport. When travel costs are too high or public transit is scarce, attendance suffers. By offering online classes, schools can ensure students do not miss important lessons simply because they cannot afford to travel. In fact, teachers could even arrange occasional home visits or virtual meetings to help struggling learners, making education available to everyone.

Responsibility also plays a key role in academic success. If students know they can attend classes online at times that suit them, they often feel more in control of their own learning. This encourages them to stay committed, complete assignments on time, and ultimately earn the grades needed for scholarships or further study. With online options, motivated individuals have a clearer path to graduation and beyond.

Older learners and those who work full-time stand to gain as well. Night classes or recorded lessons mean they can study after work or during evenings when they are free. This flexibility prevents them from choosing between a job and their education. As fewer in-person sessions are required, students no longer risk losing income or skipping classes because of work commitments.

Overall, I believe finishing high school online is an excellent choice for many people. It allows students to balance family duties, jobs, and personal challenges while still gaining a solid education. By taking advantage of remote learning, learners demonstrate responsibility and open doors to better opportunities for themselves and their families.

In many schools, both public and private, students often find the cafeteria food unappealing, which leads some of them to skip lunch or bring meals from home. This is unfortunate, since a balanced meal at school helps students maintain high energy levels and stay focused during lessons. To tackle this issue, schools could introduce an online platform where students can choose their preferred menu options and share feedback. By updating the lunch offerings each year based on these results, schools would ensure that more students enjoy their meals and reap the benefits of proper nutrition.

First, creating a dedicated website for student input is simple and effective. At the start of every school year, the cafeteria team could upload a range of proposed meal plans—taking into account dietary restrictions and allergies. Students would then vote for their favorites or suggest new dishes. After collecting and analyzing the responses, the school would adjust the menu accordingly. This process makes students feel involved and guarantees that the most popular options appear on the final list.

When students eat foods they like, their concentration and energy improve significantly. A varied menu helps prevent boredom and keeps mealtimes exciting. For example, breakfasts might include fresh fruit and whole-grain pastries, while lunch could feature different choices such as tacos, grilled chicken wraps, or vegetarian bowls. Offering a rotation of cuisines—from classic sandwiches to international dishes—ensures that students look forward to each meal. Schools could also provide natural beverages like fruit-infused water, which are both healthy and refreshing.

Changing the menu annually based on student preferences brings another advantage: it reduces food waste. When the same dishes are served day after day, many students simply throw them away or avoid the cafeteria line altogether. By contrast, a menu shaped by votes is more likely to match students’ tastes, so more of the food is eaten. This not only saves money but also keeps the cafeteria line moving faster, reducing long waits and making lunchtime more efficient.

Teachers and staff benefit as well. When students are well-nourished and happy with their meals, classroom behavior tends to improve. Children arrive at afternoon classes with enough energy to participate actively, and they are less likely to feel drowsy or distracted. In addition, a positive dining experience can boost the overall atmosphere in the school, since both students and teachers share meals they enjoy.

In conclusion, schools should adopt a user-friendly website where students can vote on proposed menus each year. By considering allergy information, offering diverse meal options, and rotating dishes based on student feedback, schools can make cafeterias more appealing and nutritious. This approach encourages better eating habits, reduces waste, and helps students stay energized and focused throughout the day.

I am writing to express my support for the proposal to serve healthier meals in our school cafeteria. Swapping out junk food for more nutritious options will improve our overall wellbeing. By choosing balanced lunches, we can avoid gaining excess weight and reduce the risk of obesity, while also feeling more energetic and alert throughout the day.

First of all, nutritious food helps us stay fit and perform better in sports. When we eat heavy, processed meals, our stomachs feel sluggish and it becomes hard to run, jump, or concentrate on physical activities. In contrast, meals rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins give our bodies clean fuel. Professional athletes follow this principle: they maintain a strong, agile physique because they carefully select what they eat. If students adopt the same approach, they will find it easier to take part in gym class or after-school teams.

Secondly, healthier eating can protect us from emotional struggles like depression. Consuming too much fast food often leads to rapid weight gain, and many young people feel unhappy or insecure about their changing bodies. This frustration can spiral into low self-esteem and, in severe cases, depression. By offering balanced meals, the school can help students keep a stable weight and feel more confident in their appearance, which in turn promotes a more positive mood.

In addition, nutritious lunch choices make us more active during lessons and break times. Having clear goals gives us the motivation to keep going, even when we are tired or doubt ourselves. A strong purpose acts like a guiding light: whenever we feel unable to continue, an inner voice reminds us that we can reach our dreams for ourselves and our families. In contrast, if a person has no direction, they may feel lost and need encouragement from relatives and friends. Their support and advice can reignite our determination.

After I finish at 5 p.m., I go straight to evening classes. Although this routine often leaves me exhausted, I think of my family and the example I want to set for my daughter.

Their faith in me and my own desire for a better future keep me focused. Knowing why I work so hard not only motivates me but also makes every effort worthwhile. I believe that determination combined with support from loved ones creates the energy we need to reach our objectives.

Meeting new people can happen in many ways, both online and face to face. You could strike up a conversation in a shop or library, join a sports game at a park, or simply say hello to someone you don’t know. Everyone has their own style of making friends. Some find it easy to talk to strangers, while others feel shy. If you want to meet someone new, start by smiling, being polite, and finding a shared interest to discuss.

I enjoy making friends whenever I can. To build a good friendship, it helps to be kind, open-minded, and helpful. Working on a group project in class or volunteering with others are great opportunities to connect with people. Family gatherings also offer a chance to meet someone new, even if you don’t speak much at first.

Some individuals prefer to keep to themselves and rarely talk to others. That is okay, but taking small steps—like offering a friendly greeting—can make a difference. A positive attitude usually attracts people, whereas someone who avoids social contact might consider getting a pet for companionship.

For example, when I walk my dog around town, I sometimes chat with neighbors. In stores, I ask workers about products, and at school I make friends in lessons or during breaks. While not everyone is welcoming—some people get upset easily—many more are friendly and happy to talk.

Some people say first impressions cannot be changed, but I disagree. First, someone may seem uninterested or distant at first, but as you get to know them better, your opinion shifts. For instance, a quiet person might begin to open up once they feel at ease. At first glance they may appear uncaring, yet when you spend time together, you discover their true personality and understand their behaviour more clearly.

Second, I experienced this in a past relationship. I believed I had met the perfect partner: someone kind and genuine. However, as our friendship grew, I saw a darker side. She often criticised me, harboured anger, and blamed me for trivial matters just to control the situation. I believe that technology has brought many benefits to our daily lives. One major advantage is online shopping. For instance, if you need groceries but can’t visit the store, you can simply order them on a website and have them delivered to your door. My sister often uses this service when she’s unwell or pressed for time. Similarly, many people can now work from home by connecting to their office through a laptop or other devices, making their routines more flexible.

Another useful innovation is ride-hailing apps like Uber. If you don’t own a car or need a quick lift, you can book a driver from your smartphone and reach your destination easily. Shopping for clothes has also become more convenient; instead of going to a mall, you can browse online catalogs and arrange delivery. Even reading has moved into the digital realm, as e-books and online libraries let you access a wide range of titles without visiting a bookstore. You can also pay bills, buy tickets, and manage many other tasks on the internet.

Technology has improved how we stay in touch, too. My grandmother lives in another city, and thanks to video-calling apps, we can speak with her face to face even when we’re abroad. When traveling, my older sister checks us in online for our flights, avoiding long airport lines and allowing us to choose our seats in advance. If you ever forget your wallet at home, you can still make purchases using mobile payment systems like Apple Pay.

Of course, there are downsides. Relying on deliveries means people might get less exercise and become more sedentary. Also, many individuals prefer texting or calling instead of talking in person, which can weaken personal connections. For example, when I visit my cousins during holidays, they often sit quietly on their phones rather than chatting together.

Overall, despite a few drawbacks, I think technology has been overwhelmingly positive. It makes everyday tasks simpler, keeps us connected, and offers new ways to work and travel.

I agree that true growth comes only when we push ourselves beyond what we already know. Some people argue that we can develop naturally over time without taking on new challenges. However, Emerson’s words remind us that we must look past our own beliefs and limitations. By daring to go further, we open the door to new achievements—and as we reach them, we grow even more.

To grow, we have to give our best effort in whatever we attempt. From my own experience, I’ve found that striving hard and encouraging classmates to do the same creates a positive cycle. When students challenge themselves, they not only feel proud but also inspire others around them. Without an open mind and a willingness to try, we risk staying stuck, no matter what happens in life.

Organization and self-reliance also play a big role in personal development. By keeping our tasks and goals in order, we build confidence and avoid unnecessary stress. It’s essential to remain true to ourselves, rather than letting others dictate our choices. In the end, every decision we make is ours alone, and that responsibility helps us grow stronger.

There are moments when we must choose between moving forward or remaining where we are. At those times, believing in ourselves becomes crucial. If we opt for growth, new chances will appear—not only for us but also for people we care about. Standing still might feel safe, but stepping up brings fresh opportunities and a broader impact.

Growth offers many rewards. We become more capable, more sociable, and better accepted in different circles. By striving beyond our comfort zone, we learn to handle varied tasks and connect with new people. The effort we invest today shapes the person we become tomorrow.

Emerson was right: attempting something beyond our current limits is the key to success. If we have the courage to try, we can achieve more than we ever imagined.

Staying active every day is essential because it keeps our bodies moving and helps us avoid illness. People who maintain a regular level of activity often feel more energetic and are less likely to fall sick.

Having daily objectives, whether at work, at home, or during leisure time, encourages constant motion. Some individuals enjoy staying busy from morning until night, and this habit trains their muscles to handle effort more easily. After a full day of activity, what the body really needs is a period of rest and recovery.

An active lifestyle not only strengthens muscles but also supports overall health. Those who are used to being on the move often find it harder to cope when they become ill, so keeping fit is vital. Interestingly, many older adults who remain active tend to maintain good health well into their later years.

In addition to movement, proper nutrition plays a key role. Your body requires vitamins and minerals to function at its best, so a balanced diet is crucial. If you push yourself without fueling your muscles and organs, you risk fatigue or injury. It’s wise to approach exercise and tasks with care, always listening to your body’s signals.

Being busy isn’t just good for the body—it also benefits the mind. Engaging in different activities can clear your thoughts, boost creativity, and improve your mood. Even a short walk or a quick stretch during a long day of sitting can make you feel more alert and refreshed.

Ultimately, it is wonderful to pursue the things you love, but it’s equally important to recognize your limits. Pushing too hard can lead to harm, so balance activity with proper rest. By combining movement, nutrition, and common sense, you can enjoy a healthy, energetic lifestyle.

In my opinion, working as part of a group offers many benefits. One key advantage is that team members can share ideas and information, making it easier to find solutions quickly. When someone faces a difficulty, others can step in to help, for example, taking over tasks if a colleague is unwell. Even when disagreements arise, professionals in a team discuss issues and reach a resolution, so projects move forward smoothly.

Another benefit is financial and productivity gains. Groups often complete tasks more efficiently than individuals because they combine their skills and work extra hours when needed. This higher productivity can lead companies to pay better wages and earn more profit. Moreover, a strong team can help a company win new contracts or collaborate with other businesses, even in foreign markets.

Working collaboratively also means continuous support. Team members motivate each other, divide tasks according to their strengths, and use resources more effectively. This approach not only boosts job performance but also helps employees develop new skills and grow professionally.

In conclusion, I believe that teamwork is more beneficial than working alone. It promotes faster thinking and problem-solving, provides mutual support when challenges arise, and increases earnings and opportunities for both companies and workers.

Some people argue that saving energy and resources at school is beneficial because it reduces consumption and costs. However, when students rely on school computers and internet access to complete their homework, shutting down these services can cause real difficulties. If there is no power for two hours each day, imagine how hard it becomes to finish assignments over a four-day week.

First, students who cannot work at home miss deadlines and lose marks. This can lead to stress, disagreements with parents, and a feeling of helplessness. While some families can afford computers and reliable internet at home, many cannot. Single parents, larger families, or low-income households often lack these resources, so their children depend on school facilities to study.

It is true that energy conservation lowers utility bills and may free up funds for other school resources or outdoor activities. Yet restricting energy too much creates practical problems. In a crowded computer lab, students cannot all use the same machine at once, especially when they have different assignments. This means some spend far more time trying to log on or find the right software.

Critics also say that some pupils abuse internet access by visiting social media or playing games. But banning or limiting access penalizes everyone, including those who use it responsibly for research, reading digital books, and completing projects.

Another issue is comfort and safety. Without electricity, air conditioning or heating systems stop working, which can make classrooms uncomfortably hot or dangerously cold. In emergencies, students and staff would be unable to charge phones or call for help. For these reasons, reliable energy is vital for communication and safety.

In conclusion, although partial energy savings can reduce costs and encourage outdoor lessons, cutting power for several days in a school week creates unfair obstacles for many students. Unlike businesses, schools need continuous energy to support learning and well-being.

I firmly agree with Emerson’s idea that being yourself in a world that constantly pressures you to become someone else is a significant achievement. When you stay true to who you are, every day becomes an opportunity to learn about your own abilities and to enjoy life on your own terms. You make decisions that fit your values, and you gain a sense of freedom that no one else can take from you.

By remaining authentic, you open yourself to new experiences. Trying things you’ve never done can surprise you—it shows you what you’re capable of and builds your confidence. Spontaneity adds excitement to life, and each success encourages you to explore further. As you grow, you’re also better positioned to support others. When you meet someone who has been hurt by bullying or harsh words, your own journey of self-belief can inspire them. Speaking to people with kindness and respect helps heal wounds of resentment, and love is one of the strongest tools we have for positive change.

Unfortunately, some people suffer because of cruelty, racism or contempt, and many lose hope under such pressure. We don’t have to let these problems continue. By showing empathy and standing up against bullying and discrimination, we can help others feel valued and understood. Every act of support, no matter how small, can prevent someone from giving up on themselves.

Caring for yourself is just as important as caring for others. It’s time to listen to your heart and pursue your dreams for your own happiness, not for approval or praise. Surround yourself with people who celebrate your achievements rather than envy them. Share your goals only with those who truly support you so that negativity won’t block your path. When you focus on what you want and refuse to be swayed by criticism, you become more confident, joyful, and resilient.

Working alone can also strengthen your sense of self. Individual projects let you use your own ideas, strategies, and solutions without having to compromise them in a group discussion. You learn to rely on your own creativity and find satisfaction in what you accomplish by yourself.

Choosing to be different and genuine every day is indeed one of life’s greatest accomplishments. It encourages you to keep growing, to find fresh ways of seeing the world, and to share that perspective with others. Your true self shows the values you hold and the kind of person you want to be. It also helps you recognize who your real friends are—those who wish you well in both good times and bad, and who celebrate your successes as if they were their own.

Feeling comfortable in your own skin brings emotional happiness you can share with family, friends, and the people you care about. Confidence in yourself brightens every moment, turning ordinary hours into times of possibility. For me, the greatest support comes from my faith. I believe that God loves me unconditionally and that this love gives me strength to remain true to myself.

In the end, staying authentic amid external pressures is a gift you give yourself—and it’s a gift you can offer to others by encouraging them to believe in themselves, too.

Last year my friend and I took IB Math together, and it was very challenging for both of us. One afternoon she told me, “You’re not going to pass this class. Your grades are too low. You should switch classes or you’ll have to take it again next year.” Her words made me anxious for about an hour, but then I admitted to myself that she might be right. I hadn’t studied for the exam, and I simply didn’t feel like preparing.

On the day of the test, I decided not to worry. I even asked my friend if she had studied, and she said she hadn’t either. We both felt relieved that it was finally Friday. After the exam, we discovered we had failed. When I got home, my father asked me about my grade. I told him I didn’t pass because it was too hard. He became upset and reminded me that my biggest mistake was not trying at all. He said nothing is impossible if you do your best. His disappointment made me feel terrible.

I rang my friend, expecting her to share my regret, but she was almost cheerful and showed no concern. That moment helped me decide that I would strive to be an A+ student not only in Math but in all my classes. I committed to working hard no matter what.

I spent the entire weekend studying for a retake. On Monday I asked my teacher if I could try the exam again. Because I had prepared thoroughly, the test seemed easy this time. My friend, who didn’t study, failed again and now must take the class next year. If she had felt the weight of her failure, she might have performed better.

In conclusion, failure should have a negative impact on us. If it doesn’t, people are likely to ignore their mistakes and fail again. Feeling bad about our errors motivates us to improve and succeed.

When people choose to adopt a positive attitude, their lives tend to improve. Although some individuals focus on negative thoughts and believe nothing will go right, those who stay optimistic look at situations differently. For example, when you hear upsetting news but respond with “Everything will be okay,” you reduce stress and feel more in control. This hopeful view also helps students face challenges at school.

If people maintain optimism in all areas of life and avoid excessive worrying, they can become much happier. Imagine you have a difficult exam at school and doubt you can pass. Yet if you keep a positive mindset and trust your ability to learn, you will study more confidently. A friend or teacher might encourage you by saying you will succeed, and when you do pass that tough test, you feel proud. That achievement shows how believing in yourself can help you keep going instead of giving up.

Another example comes when someone is diagnosed with an illness. It is natural to worry and picture the worst outcome, but if you decide to treat the condition as a small obstacle rather than a life-ending crisis, you stay calmer. You follow the doctor’s advice, make any needed changes in your daily routine, and remind yourself that life can still be enjoyable. This constructive approach makes the situation less frightening and helps you focus on recovery.

Viewing life through an optimistic lens means believing that even big problems can be managed. Instead of fixating on every difficulty, you look for solutions and try to stay cheerful. Even in the most stressful moments, expecting the best outcome and remaining calm can guide you through. In this way, a positive outlook turns obstacles into smaller challenges and helps you live a happier, more fulfilling life.

Modern technology offers numerous benefits that clearly enhance our lives. It accelerates everyday tasks, simplifies communication, and reduces our reliance on paper, saving time and supporting environmental sustainability. Thanks to digital tools, people can complete their work more quickly and focus on what really matters.

One of the most useful advantages is email, which allows us to send important documents to colleagues or clients in an instant without leaving our desks. This removes the need for physical meetings or trips to an office, cutting down on travel time and paper usage. By choosing digital files over printed copies, we not only work faster but also help protect trees and reduce waste.

Technology also makes communication easier for those who feel uncomfortable speaking face to face. Many individuals experience anxiety when they must discuss key tasks or sensitive topics in person. By sending a well-structured email or message, they can express their thoughts clearly and calmly without the stress of direct contact. This approach improves cooperation and ensures that everyone can share information in a way that feels safe.

In addition, technology provides reliable methods for storing and organising data. Important projects, reports, and presentations can be backed up on flash drives or saved in cloud services like Office 365. Students, for example, often use these platforms to keep assignments, slideshows, and essays secure, so they do not worry about losing files or facing last-minute technical problems.

Some people claim that technology has negative effects on daily life, but this view ignores how it boosts our productivity and flexibility. We can create engaging PowerPoint presentations, research topics online in seconds, shop for items from home, and avoid trips to crowded stores. Entrepreneurs can launch new ventures, advertise vacancies, and hire staff through websites and social media. Overall, the benefits of modern technology clearly outweigh any drawbacks, helping us work smarter, communicate better, and handle information securely.

When older students collaborate with younger ones, they not only build friendships but also support each other’s learning.

First, working together encourages both groups to communicate and listen closely. As they share ideas and experiences, they discover common interests and learn about each other’s preferences. This interaction creates a friendly environment where trust grows, helping younger students feel more comfortable in class.

Second, younger children benefit because they can ask questions freely and receive immediate explanations. Often in a crowded classroom, they must wait their turn to speak with the teacher. With an older partner, they have someone who understands their struggles and can rephrase difficult concepts using simpler language. Since the age gap is not too wide, it feels less intimidating for the younger student to express doubts and share opinions.

Finally, older students gain valuable skills too. Explaining ideas in clear, basic terms forces them to slow down, stay patient, and choose words carefully. This process reinforces their own understanding of the subject, as teaching someone else is one of the best ways to remember information. Moreover, guiding a younger peer can reduce stress and build confidence in the older student’s ability to lead.

In conclusion, pairing older and younger students creates a supportive learning partnership. It fosters friendship, helps younger learners grasp lessons more easily, and allows older students to improve their communication and review academic material. For these reasons, I believe it is important to encourage mixed-age teamwork in schools.

I believe that personal experience can be a powerful teacher, but I do not think we should rely on it alone. On the one hand, facing challenges and trying new things gives us confidence and helps us grow. Each time we tackle a difficult task, we learn useful lessons and gain the courage to take on even greater responsibilities. With more practice, we often find it easier to solve problems and spot new opportunities in our lives.

On the other hand, experience by itself can be incomplete. If we simply repeat the same methods without learning from books, teachers, or mentors, we may make avoidable mistakes or miss better solutions. For example, someone who practices a skill without understanding its theory can struggle when unexpected situations arise. Asking questions, reading reliable sources, and seeking advice help us prepare for challenges that our past experiences did not cover.

In conclusion, I disagree with the idea that we should base everything solely on our own experience. Experience is important, but it must be combined with study and guidance to be truly effective.

Technology can bring both benefits and risks into our lives. On the positive side, it allows us to stay connected with friends and family who live far away through video calls, messages, or social apps. It also acts as a convenient tool for finding books or shopping online instead of going to the mall. In the job market, people can search for and apply to positions from home, saving time and effort. Students can gather information or request materials from colleges without making a special trip. When stress builds up, digital games or relaxation apps help clear the mind. Even home repairs or daily tasks become easier thanks to online tutorials and professional services just a click away.

On the other hand, technology can be used against us. Some websites look harmless but are created by unknown individuals with harmful intentions. Extremist groups sometimes exploit social media to recruit young people, especially those without close family oversight. Online shopping can also turn into a scam, with fraudsters selling counterfeit goods and vanishing with customers’ payments. Moreover, spending excessive hours on platforms like Facebook can trap us in endless scrolling, wasting valuable time. In these ways, technology can become a weapon rather than a tool if we’re not cautious.

Ultimately, technology shows two faces, and its impact depends on how we choose to use it.

I agree with the idea that certain health conditions cannot be changed. Some people struggle with mental or physical problems that are hard to improve. For instance, someone with a mental disorder may lose control and become angry, which could lead to fights. In such cases, they often need to see a doctor and take medicine, which might help them feel calmer. However, if their condition remains untreated, they might shout or run into the street, frightening others.

Families usually try to keep their loved one at home to protect both the person and the public. If it is too dangerous, they may place them in a psychiatric hospital, since living alone is not safe. If the person leaves the house and behaves aggressively, bystanders might call the police, and that could lead to an arrest. To prevent these problems, parents often feel they must accompany their family member whenever they go outside.

This constant supervision can cause a lot of stress and frustration for the caretaker, who loses much of their own freedom. The person with the condition also loses independence and cannot go out alone. Even a simple visit to a park can be risky; when many children are playing, any sudden outburst could harm someone and create a serious incident. Overall, these kinds of mental and physical disorders are very serious and difficult to change. Families must offer ongoing care and careful support to keep everyone safe.

Some people claim that you cannot develop unless you push yourself beyond what you already know. I disagree. Even if you make mistakes, you always have another opportunity to learn and improve.

First, consider a group project at school. When students work together, they usually have different ideas. One person often leads, but the entire team must discuss and agree on the final plan. Imagine they finish their presentation only to realize it is not good enough. The leader then tells everyone that the work is incomplete, so they return to the drawing board. Although the group members may feel frustrated, they do not give up. Instead, they talk through the problems again, make changes, and present a stronger project. They never think, “I can’t do this,” because they know they can try again. This experience shows that we grow by learning from our errors and seizing the chance to redo our work.

Second, making a mistake does not mean you’re stuck with it forever. Everyone deserves a second—sometimes even a third—chance to get things right. For example, a person who has committed a crime and is in prison can still study and develop new skills. In my view, denying that person the opportunity to learn is unfair. Education and support can help them become responsible citizens. Some people may argue that criminals don’t deserve another chance, but I believe that offering them a path to improvement benefits everyone. It is through these opportunities that individuals can rebuild their lives and contribute positively to society.

In conclusion, growth does not depend solely on attempting tasks beyond our current abilities. It also comes from correcting our mistakes and taking advantage of new chances. Whether we are students revising a project or people seeking to rebuild after a crime, we all benefit when we are allowed to try again. By supporting second chances, we help ourselves and others become better prepared for the future.

In recent years, many students have gained the option to join classes from home, and I believe this choice offers clear advantages. Firstly, studying remotely eliminates the need for early alarms and long bus rides, giving pupils extra rest and more time to spend with their families. Secondly, home-based learning can be safer and healthier, especially during global threats such as the coronavirus pandemic, since students avoid crowded spaces and reduce the risk of infection. In addition, parents can easily supervise their children’s attendance and progress, knowing they are physically present at home rather than skipping school. Of course, some learners prefer in-person lessons because they find computers challenging or enjoy the school environment. Nevertheless, online classes remain a valuable option for many, helping them balance family life, maintain their well-being, and simplify daily routines. For these reasons, I support allowing students to attend lessons from home whenever possible.

I do not think our school should switch to a four-day week like some companies have done. Although a ten-hour day could cover the same material, it would bring several serious drawbacks. Students would lose precious family time, struggle under a heavier homework load, create challenges for parents and young learners, and suffer fatigue and health risks from such long days.

First, longer school days would leave very little time for family life. If classes run from early morning until late afternoon, students will return home too tired to talk or play with parents and siblings. Having only three full days off each week might sound appealing, but on those four school days children would barely see their families. Weekends would become even more crowded with activities and responsibilities, rather than chances to relax and connect at home.

Second, extending each school day would not reduce overall work—it would likely increase it. Teachers would need to fill ten hours of instruction, so they might assign more homework to reinforce lessons. Students would rush home, still carrying piles of tasks to finish in the evening. With so much work left after class, they would have almost no free moments to eat properly, talk with friends, or simply unwind before bedtime.

Third, a four-day schedule causes real difficulties for parents and for students under eighteen. Many younger children rely on parents to drive them to and from school. With such long days, parents would have to adjust work schedules or arrange costly childcare when they cannot pick up their children until late in the afternoon. Meanwhile, some older students hold part-time jobs to earn money and gain experience. They might prefer shorter weeks at work, but if their school day extends to ten hours, they will face even tougher decisions about balancing pay and education. In either case, the rigid timing would make life harder for families and students alike.

Fourth, spending ten hours each day in a classroom would be exhausting and could harm students’ wellbeing. Sitting still for so long leads to tiredness and lack of focus, making it harder to learn. Many children use computers and phones at school, and these devices, though helpful, can cause eye strain and mental fatigue when used excessively. If students are stuck in classes or doing online work for such lengthy periods, they may feel uncomfortable, suffer headaches, or lose interest in learning altogether.

In conclusion, a four-day school week with ten-hour days may work for some businesses, but it would not suit most students or families. It would cut into time at home, pile on homework, cause logistical headaches for parents, and increase physical and mental strain. For these reasons, our school should keep its current schedule rather than adopt this model.

I disagree with the idea that first impressions can never be changed. Although they often shape our opinions of people, things or animals, it is still possible to revise these initial judgments. Many people hold on to their first thoughts because they believe they are certain, but it is wiser to stop and collect more evidence before deciding if that initial reaction is valid. I will explain this with my own experience.

One afternoon, I was at home working out when I suddenly became convinced that my girlfriend was secretly meeting my best friend. This thought upset me so much that I felt angry and betrayed, even though I had no real proof. In moments like these, you must control your emotions and avoid acting on a hasty suspicion. I chose to call her and talk things over, but it was hard to explain why I felt that way. I found myself torn between trusting my gut and risking damage to our relationship.

During our long conversation, I discovered there was no truth to my worries. I realised my mind had played tricks on me, filling in gaps with fear rather than facts. At that moment, I let go of my first impression and accepted that it had been wrong. This taught me that not all first impressions are reliable; sometimes they come from insecurity or a lack of information.

Since then, I prefer to keep my initial feelings to myself until I have gathered enough proof. Allowing time to reflect and confirm what really happened helps me decide whether to keep or change that first impression. In this way, I form fairer judgments and avoid unnecessary conflicts.

I believe that completing high school in three years by attending summer classes is a smart option because it lets students enter the workforce or pursue other goals sooner. For instance, after graduating, you could find a good job, earn money to support your family, or buy things you need, such as a car or clothes.

This approach is especially helpful for students who start high school later. Many Hispanic students arrive in ninth grade at age 15 or 16. If they finish in three years, they will be around 18 when they graduate, which is an ideal age to begin working while still improving their English skills. In contrast, many American students who speak English fluently face fewer language challenges and can also benefit from finishing early.

Although entering the job market one year ahead of peers can be demanding, it offers real advantages for many young people aged 18 to 20. By graduating early, they can gain work experience and start earning money without waiting an extra year.

For students whose main language is not English, staying the full four years might help them improve language skills before they work. However, for many native English speakers, an accelerated program is straightforward. Given the choice, I would definitely opt to finish high school in three years because it fits my age and career goals better.

I believe students should choose elective courses because they enrich learning and help you graduate on time. Electives let you explore new subjects, gain extra credits, and build a stronger academic record—all of which are important if you want to finish your degree in four years.

If you skip elective classes, you miss chances to learn and may become lazy. By taking extra courses, you show discipline and give your family reason to celebrate your achievements. A good diploma also opens more doors in the job market. Many people struggle to find work because they stopped studying too soon.

Electives also allow you to prove yourself to others. When people doubt your abilities, completing challenging courses demonstrates your determination and makes loved ones proud of you.

On the other hand, summer electives may not be as useful. Because the term lasts only two or three months, you cannot cover as much material as during a full semester. For this reason, I think regular electives are more beneficial than summer ones.

Working together in a group brings many advantages compared to working on your own. First of all, collaborating with classmates often means projects are completed more quickly. When several people contribute their efforts, each person can handle a portion of the work, making large tasks more manageable. In contrast, someone working alone faces the entire workload by themselves and may struggle to meet deadlines.

Another benefit of group work is the chance to build friendships and improve social skills. By cooperating with others, you learn to respect different viewpoints and listen carefully to what each team member has to say. This not only creates a friendlier atmosphere but also teaches you to be considerate and supportive. These interpersonal skills are essential both in school and later in professional life.

Moreover, teammates can offer advice and help when you encounter difficulties. If one person is struggling with a particular part of the project, others can step in and share their knowledge or suggest new ideas. This kind of mutual support often leads to a higher-quality result and better grades than working alone.

Some people argue that group assignments are unfair because not everyone contributes equally. However, when tasks are divided fairly and each member takes responsibility for their share, everyone benefits. You learn to be accountable for your work and dependable to your peers.

Overall, group work not only speeds up the completion of projects but also teaches valuable lessons in cooperation, respect, and responsibility. For these reasons, I believe studying in teams is more beneficial than studying alone.

The minister Winston Churchill says that in life or in any other endeavor, there will be failure. He advises not to lose enthusiasm because of small setbacks or a single failure in your attempt.

I agree with minister Churchill because success is a way to improve your skills and become better at what you do. When you try, you may make mistakes, but success can include failure if you learn from it. By learning to resolve your problems and trying again and again, you gain more experience and reduce mistakes over time.

I think success teaches you a lot of experience in your life because failure shows you what to learn. If you leave failures unaddressed, you are not trying or exploring yourself. By exploring yourself, you can see how far you can go to resolve your problems or mistakes.

So if you push yourself by trying more and more, you may resolve the problem or discover how far you can go to find a solution. Often, if you keep trying your best at something you do not fully understand, you can still find a solution and fix it.

Failure does not mean you will never resolve it. If you are doing your best but keep failing, it may be because there is a problem you are not seeing. Failure is not because it is not working; success is finding the solution to your problem.

In conclusion, success requires passing through many problems and mistakes to find solutions. In your life, if you do not explore yourself, you won’t know what the problem is; if you explore yourself, you can find the solution and learn from it. By trying hard most of the time, you can find a solution for everything, and this is how you can also help others with their problems, as the saying goes: two heads are better than one.

Winston Churchill once pointed out that in any pursuit—whether personal or professional—failure is bound to happen, and it is important not to let these setbacks dampen your enthusiasm. Rather than seeing a single misstep as the end of the road, he urged people to view it as part of the journey toward success.

I agree with Churchill’s perspective because failing offers a valuable chance to sharpen our skills. When we make mistakes, we learn exactly where we need to improve. Each attempt teaches us something new, and by applying these lessons, we gradually reduce our errors. In this way, failure is not a sign of defeat but a tool for growth that helps us become more capable and confident in what we do.

When you face the same obstacle again and again, you begin to understand the problem more deeply. You can experiment with different strategies, analyze where you went wrong, and adjust your approach. This repeated effort builds experience and reveals solutions that might have remained hidden if you had given up after the first try. Persistence turns each failure into a teaching moment.

It is also important to realize that failure often highlights aspects of the problem you couldn’t see before. If you keep working at it, you eventually uncover the real issue and find a way to fix it. In this sense, failure does not mean that success is impossible—it simply means you haven’t yet identified the key to solving the problem.

In conclusion, achieving success means encountering and overcoming many challenges. By embracing failure as a learning opportunity, maintaining your enthusiasm, and persevering through difficulties, you not only find solutions for yourself but also gain the experience to help others. After all, as the saying goes, two heads are better than one, and collaboration can often guide us past our toughest obstacles.
